import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; import SourceBox from '@components/SourceBox.astro'; Before adjusting your carburetor needle, it is important to confirm that the needle is actually the cause of your problem. The carburetor has three main circuits — the **idle circuit** (0–25% throttle), the **needle circuit** (25%–75% throttle), and the **main jet circuit** (75%–100% throttle). Symptoms in different throttle ranges point to different circuits. This guide walks you through a systematic checklist to determine whether your mid-throttle symptoms are needle-related, and whether the needle is running too rich or too lean. 🎬 How to Diagnose a Carbureted Scooter — Rich vs Lean "Rich vs Lean — How to Diagnose Your Carburetor" by MC Garage — [↗ Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pTKZrV5MHHA) ## Step 1 — Confirm the Problem is in the Mid-Throttle Range The carburetor needle only has a meaningful effect between approximately **25% and 75% throttle**. To check whether your problem falls in this range, do the following test on a safe, quiet road: 1. Start the engine and let it warm up fully (at least 5 minutes of riding). 2. Hold the throttle at roughly **1/4 open** (just off idle). Note whether the engine feels smooth or whether it hesitates, surges, or pops. 3. Open to roughly **1/2 throttle** — a gentle cruising speed. This is the range most affected by needle position. Note any flat spots, stumbles, black smoke, or surging. 4. Open to **3/4 and full throttle**. Note whether top-end power feels strong or if performance drops off. � **Throttle range test rule of thumb:** If the symptom only happens at idle or just off idle → **idle circuit**. If it happens mainly in the cruise/mid range → **needle**. If it mainly affects wide-open power → **main jet**. Many problems span more than one range, so look for where the symptom is _worst_. IDLE CIRCUIT 0–25% throttle NEEDLE CIRCUIT ◀ this guide 25–75% throttle MAIN JET 75–100% throttle Closed Full open If your problem is clearly in the mid-throttle range, continue to Step 2 to determine whether it is rich or lean. ## Step 2 — Rule Out Other Common Causes First Before blaming the needle, work through this quick exclusion checklist. Each of these issues can mimic a needle problem and should be checked first because they are easier to inspect. - 1 **Air filter — clean or replace** A clogged air filter restricts airflow and makes the mixture artificially rich at all throttle positions. Remove and inspect the filter. If it is grey or black with dirt, clean or replace it before making any fuel adjustments. - 2 **Air leaks — check intake manifold and carb gaskets** A vacuum leak between the carburetor and the engine introduces unmetered air, which leans the mixture. Spray a small amount of carb cleaner around the intake manifold joints while the engine idles — if the idle changes, you have found a leak. Fix this before adjusting the needle. - 3 **Fuel delivery — verify the float level is correct** A float set too high causes a persistently rich mixture across all throttle positions. If fuel is dripping from the overflow tube, the float is too high and should be adjusted before touching the needle. - 4 **Needle jet — check for wear or blockage** The needle jet is the small brass tube the needle slides through. If it is partially blocked with varnish or gum, it will restrict fuel delivery. If it is worn oval (common on high-mileage engines), the mixture will be permanently rich. Remove, inspect, and clean the jet with carb cleaner and a fine wire. - 5 **Choke — confirm it is fully open when warm** A choke that is stuck partially closed will make the engine run rich at all throttle openings. Confirm the choke plate or enrichment circuit is fully disengaged once the engine is warm. - 6 **Spark plug — read it for mixture confirmation** Remove the spark plug after a ride and read its colour (see Step 3 below). This is the most direct evidence of whether the mixture is rich or lean, and confirms the needle diagnosis before you make a physical change. ️ **Don't skip the exclusion checklist:** Adjusting the needle on top of an air leak or a partially blocked jet will not solve the problem and may make it harder to diagnose. Take 10 minutes to run through each check before opening the carburetor. ## Step 3 — Read the Spark Plug Colour The spark plug is a direct window into what is happening in the combustion chamber. Removing it after a warm ride tells you immediately whether the mixture is rich, lean, or correct. This is the most reliable single diagnostic step. � **How to get a clean reading:** Do a warm ride at mid-throttle (not idle, not wide open) for 5–10 minutes, then pull over and stop the engine _without idling it down_. Remove the spark plug immediately. The colour you see now reflects your mid-throttle mixture. ##### Light tan / grey ✅ Correct mixture. Needle is set well. ##### Black / sooty 🔵 Running **rich**. Move clip up (lean out). ##### White / chalk 🔴 Running **lean**. Move clip down (richen). ##### Dark brown / oily ⚠️ Possible oil burning — check engine compression and valve seals. ## Step 4 — Identify Your Symptoms: Rich or Lean? Use the symptom cards below to match what your scooter is doing to a rich or lean needle condition. It is common to have several symptoms from the same column — they reinforce each other. #### 🔵 Needle Too High — RICH mid-throttle - Sluggish acceleration from 25%–75% throttle - Black or dark grey smoke from the exhaust, especially under load - Strong smell of unburnt petrol from the exhaust - Engine "blubbering" or four-stroking at cruise speed (burbling, irregular note) - Black sooty deposit on spark plug after a ride - Poor fuel economy - Engine feels flat and lazy in the mid-range but idles fine - Throttle response improves briefly with choke partially open (unusual) #### 🔴 Needle Too Low — LEAN mid-throttle - Hesitation or stumble when opening the throttle to mid-range - Surging or hunting at a steady cruise speed - Engine pinging or pinking under load (lean knock) - Overheating — engine runs hotter than usual - White or chalky spark plug after a ride - Acceleration feels jerky rather than smooth - Top speed reached but mid-range feels strained - Symptoms worsen in hot weather or at lower altitudes ## Step 5 — Diagnostic Flowchart Work through the flowchart below from top to bottom. It combines your throttle range test, spark plug reading, and symptoms to give you a clear action. START: Scooter runs poorly Is the problem mainly at 25%–75% throttle (cruising)? YES NO Check idle circuit or main jet Have you checked air filter, air leaks, choke & fuel delivery? NO Complete Step 2 exclusion checklist YES Read spark plug colour after a mid-throttle ride Black/sooty RICH mixture Move circlip UP (lower groove #) White/chalk LEAN mixture Move circlip DOWN (higher groove #) Tan/grey Mixture is CORRECT Problem is elsewhere → Follow the Repair Guide to adjust ## Step 6 — Confirm the Diagnosis After Adjustment After moving the clip one groove and reassembling the carburetor, carry out another road test and another plug reading. This is how you confirm the diagnosis and know whether further adjustment is needed.
Result After AdjustmentWhat It MeansNext Action
Symptoms clearly improved, plug now tanNeedle was the problem; adjustment correctDone — no further change needed
Symptoms partially improvedMoving in the right directionMove clip one more groove in the same direction; test again

� **Always return to baseline first:** If you are unsure which direction you came from, or if you have made several changes in a row without clear improvement, reset the circlip to the middle groove (groove 3 on a 5-groove needle, groove 2 on a 3-groove needle) and start the diagnosis fresh with a clean spark plug reading. 🎬 Spark Plug Reading — Rich vs Lean Diagnosis "How to Read Spark Plugs — Rich or Lean?" by Delicious Moto — [↗ Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8bLiErHiXEw) ## When to Suspect Something Other Than the Needle Not every mid-throttle problem is a needle problem. The following conditions can produce very similar symptoms but require different fixes: - **Partially blocked needle jet:** Causes lean running at mid-throttle that does not fully respond to moving the clip down. Solution — remove, clean, and inspect the needle jet. - **Worn needle or needle jet:** An oval or scored needle jet causes an inconsistently rich condition regardless of clip position. Solution — replace both the needle and jet as a matched pair. - **Intake manifold crack or loose clamp:** Causes lean running that is difficult to tune out, because the unmetered air is outside the carburetor's control. Solution — replace the manifold or tighten clamps; seal cracks with intake manifold gasket sealant. - **Incorrect main jet size:** A jet that is far too small will make the scooter feel lean from about 50% throttle upward — overlapping with the needle range. Solution — check jet size against spec and replace if incorrect. - **Dirty pilot/idle jet:** A blocked idle jet causes problems at low throttle that can "feel" like a mid-range issue because the transition from idle to mid is rough. Solution — remove and clean the pilot jet. ## Related Videos & Resources #### Carburetor Needle Adjustment — Step-by-Step Repair Once you've confirmed the needle is the issue, follow our full repair guide to make the adjustment safely. [Read the Repair Guide →](/repair-guides/carburetor-needle-height-adjustment.html) #### Carburetor Idle Screw Adjustment If your problem is at very low throttle (idle or just off idle), the idle mixture screw is the correct adjustment. [Search on YouTube →](https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=scooter+carburetor+idle+mixture+screw+adjustment) #### Main Jet Size Selection If the problem is mainly at wide-open throttle, the main jet size is the variable to check. [Search on YouTube →](https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=gy6+main+jet+size+selection) ## Frequently Asked Questions My scooter has both idle problems and mid-range problems. Where do I start? Fix the idle circuit first. Idle problems often persist into the mid-range because the transition from idle to needle circuit is not clean. Set the idle mixture screw correctly, confirm idle is smooth, then re-test the mid-range before touching the needle. Can I use the choke to test whether the mixture is rich or lean? Yes, with care. Engaging the choke enriches the mixture. If your symptoms _improve_ slightly with the choke on (when warm — not at startup), the engine was running lean. If symptoms _worsen_, it was already running rich. This is a quick rough test, not a substitute for a spark plug reading. How do altitude and temperature affect needle position? At higher altitude, air is thinner. This means the mixture becomes richer for the same throttle position. If you move from sea level to high altitude (above ~1000 m), you may need to move the clip one groove up to lean the mixture. Similarly, cold dense air can make the mixture slightly lean — moving the clip one groove down can help in very cold climates. The plug is tan but the scooter still runs poorly. What next? A tan plug confirms the mixture at mid-throttle is correct. Look for mechanical causes: worn piston rings (causing low compression), a slipping CVT belt or variator, blocked exhaust, or valve timing issues. A compression test is a good next step.

HUD ECU Hacker is a Windows-based OBD2 diagnostic application that connects to your scooter's ECU via a K-line or CAN-bus USB adapter and streams real-time sensor data directly to your laptop. Unlike generic OBD2 scanners that only show fault codes, HUD Hacker's **Data Grid** tab exposes every parameter the ECU broadcasts — engine load, fuel trims, ignition timing, coolant temperature, throttle position, and more — updated several times per second while the engine runs. This guide explains what every field means, what values are normal at idle and under load, and which readings immediately indicate a problem. Use it alongside the [Diagnosis Wizard](/diagnostics/wizard.html) to pinpoint faults quickly without removing any components. Safety first: Always connect the OBD2 adapter and launch HUD Hacker before starting the engine. Keep the laptop away from hot engine parts and moving CVT components. Never ride while monitoring the laptop — use a helper to ride or place the scooter on a centre stand for stationary tests. ## What You Need - **HUD ECU Hacker v5.8+** — free download, runs on Windows 7/10/11 - **OBD2 USB adapter** — K-line / ELM327-compatible (blue or black cable type); avoid cheap Bluetooth ELM327 clones as they drop data at high refresh rates - **OBD2 diagnostic connector** — usually a 4- or 6-pin proprietary plug under the seat or near the battery; you may need a scooter-specific adapter harness (see connector photos below) - **Windows laptop** — the software does not run on macOS or Linux natively Connector tip: Many GY6 EFI scooters use a 4-pin Sumitomo connector rather than the standard 16-pin OBD2 socket. A short adapter cable with the correct pin-out is available cheaply online — search for "GY6 EFI OBD2 diagnostic cable". Piaggio models from 2007+ often have a dedicated 3-pin EOBD connector under the seat cowl. ## Connector & Setup Photos

## Connecting and Opening Live Data 1. Plug the OBD2 adapter into the scooter's diagnostic socket and into the laptop's USB port. 2. Turn the scooter's ignition key to **ON** (do not start the engine yet). 3. Open HUD ECU Hacker. On the **Control** tab, select *Autodetect (All OBD2 compliant ECUs)* from the protocol dropdown. 4. Click **Connect**. The status bar at the bottom should show "Scanning" followed by "Connected". If it fails, try toggling the COM port or checking the adapter driver. 5. Start the engine. 6. ## Live Data Fields Explained — Normal Values The table below covers every field visible in the HUD Hacker Data Grid for a typical GY6 / Piaggio EFI ECU. Values are given for **warm idle** (engine at operating temperature, no throttle) and **light cruise** (~30–40 km/h, light throttle). A cold engine will read differently — always allow 3–5 minutes for the coolant temperature to stabilise before drawing conclusions. ### Engine Parameters
Field (UID) Unit Normal — Warm Idle Normal — Light Cruise What it means & what to check
Engine Speed (RPM) rpm 1,000–1,400 3,500–6,000 Current crankshaft speed. Idle below 800 rpm indicates a lean mixture, air leak, or low idle screw setting. High idle (above 1,800 rpm) suggests a stuck throttle body, air leak, or incorrect TPS zero-point.
Calculated Engine Load (LOA) % 0–15 % 20–60 % How hard the engine is working, derived from airflow and RPM. Unusually high load at idle (above 25 %) can point to an air leak letting unmetered air past the MAP sensor, or a blocked exhaust.
Spark Advance (SPA) °CA BTDC 4–10 ° 20–32 ° How many degrees before top dead centre the ECU fires the spark plug. Very low advance at cruise (below 15 °) suggests the ECU is retarding timing due to knock or a coolant/MAP sensor fault. Very high advance (above 38 °) risks detonation.
Air/Fuel Ratio λ or A/F ratio ~14.7:1 (λ=1.00) 13.5–15.5:1 Stoichiometric target for a catalytic converter is 14.7:1. Rich mixture (below 13.0) wastes fuel and can foul the plug. Lean mixture (above 16.0) causes overheating and potential damage. If the ECU cannot reach stoich, check the injector, fuel pressure, and O2 sensor.
Air Status text Upstream O2 control Upstream O2 control Describes the current air management mode. Should always show O2 sensor-based closed-loop control once the engine is warm. "Open Loop" means the ECU is ignoring the O2 sensor — a cold start state or a sensor fault.
### Fuel System & Closed Loop
Field (UID) Unit Normal — Warm Idle Normal — Light Cruise What it means & what to check
Closed Loop #1 / #2 (FUE) enum Closed Loop Closed Loop Indicates whether the fuel system is in closed-loop (actively corrected by the O2 sensor) or open-loop (fixed fuel map, no O2 correction). "Unavailable" or "Open Loop" on a warm engine almost always means a failed or unplugged O2 sensor.
Short Term Fuel Trim Bank 1 (STF) % −5 % to +5 % −8 % to +8 % The ECU's real-time fuel correction applied on top of the base fuel map. Consistently positive (e.g. +15 %) means the engine is running lean and the ECU is adding fuel to compensate — look for an air leak, weak injector, or low fuel pressure. Consistently negative means running rich — check for a leaking injector or stuck choke/cold-start enrichment.
Long Term Fuel Trim Bank 1 (LTF) % −10 % to +10 % −10 % to +10 % A learned correction built up over many drive cycles. LTFT drifting beyond ±15 % is a red flag. Unlike STFT (which reacts second-by-second), LTFT reveals a persistent underlying problem. Reset LTFT by clearing adaptive memory (via the DTC clear function) after fixing the root cause.
Short Term Fuel Trim Bank 3 / Bank 4 % N/A on single-cylinder N/A on single-cylinder On single-cylinder GY6 and Piaggio engines, Banks 3 and 4 will show N/A or 0. Non-zero values indicate a multi-bank ECU protocol mismatch.
Long Term Fuel Trim Bank 2 (LTF) % −2.3 % (typical) Within ±10 % Same interpretation as Bank 1 LTFT. On the test scooter, −2.3 % at idle is normal — a slight learned lean correction.

Below 60 °C after 10 min of riding indicates a stuck-open thermostat or faulty sensor. Above 120 °C at idle means overheating — check coolant level, fan, and water pump (liquid-cooled) or check for lean mixture / ignition timing (air-cooled). ## Common Patterns & What They Tell You ### Pattern 1 — Lean mixture with high idle STFT strongly positive (+15 % or more), RPM above 1,600 at idle, MAP pressure high (above 60 kPa at idle). This combination almost always means an **air leak** between the throttle body and the engine — a cracked intake boot, loose injector O-ring, or split vacuum hose. Spray carb cleaner briefly around joints while watching RPM; the engine will stumble and RPM will change over the leak point. ### Pattern 2 — Rich mixture with black smoke STFT strongly negative (−15 % or more), O2 voltage stuck high (0.8–0.9 V), possible fuel smell. Causes: leaking injector (drips fuel when not commanded), incorrect TPS zero-point causing the ECU to think the throttle is open at idle, or a failed O2 sensor that reads rich when the mixture is actually stoichiometric. ### Pattern 3 — Open loop on a warm engine Closed Loop status shows "Open Loop" or "Unavailable" after the engine has been running for 5+ minutes. The O2 sensor either is not heating up (check the heater circuit — usually 2 wires plus the signal wire) or is completely failed. The ECU will run on a fixed fuelling map, typically making the engine slightly rich. Fuel trim values will show 0 % because no corrections are being made. ### Pattern 4 — Erratic RPM / hunting idle RPM oscillates between 800 and 1,800 in a slow wave, STFT swings between +20 % and −20 % rapidly. This is characteristic of a **lazy or slow O2 sensor** causing the closed-loop system to over-correct. Replace the O2 sensor if it is more than 20,000 km old or shows no brisk switching in the live data. ### Pattern 5 — High coolant temperature with normal fuelling COO above 115 °C, fuel trims and MAP normal. On an air-cooled engine, check for a blocked cylinder fin area (mud or debris), a lean ignition condition caused by advanced timing, or a faulty temperature sensor giving a false reading. On liquid-cooled engines, check the coolant level, radiator fan operation, and thermostat. ## Related Videos & Resources

## Frequently Asked Questions
My HUD Hacker shows "Scanning" indefinitely and never connects. What should I check?

First confirm the correct COM port is selected — open Device Manager in Windows and look for the USB serial adapter under "Ports (COM & LPT)". Also check that the ignition is ON before connecting (the ECU must be powered). Some cheap ELM327 adapters require you to select "ISO 9141-2" or "KWP2000 fast" protocol manually rather than Autodetect. Try toggling the protocol selector on the Control tab.

The software connects but most fields show "N/A" or 0. Is that normal?

Partially — many advanced fields (multi-bank fuel trims, wide-range O2 sensors, torque parameters) are not supported by budget scooter ECUs and will always show N/A. The important fields — RPM, coolant temp, MAP, IAT, TPS, fuel trims, and closed loop status — should all have live values once the engine is running. If core fields are also blank, try a different OBD2 protocol setting or check the adapter cable connection.

Should I clear fault codes after reading them?

Only after you have fixed the underlying problem. Clearing codes without repairing the fault will temporarily turn off the MIL lamp, but the code will return within one drive cycle once the ECU re-detects the fault. Also note: clearing codes resets the Long Term Fuel Trim, the freeze frame data, and the MIL-distance/time counters — so take a screenshot or note down everything before clearing.

My LTFT is at +18 % but there are no fault codes. Should I be worried?

Yes — a Long Term Fuel Trim beyond ±15 % is a significant lean (positive) or rich (negative) condition. The ECU is compensating for a real problem without yet setting a code because the fault may be intermittent or just below the code-setting threshold. Investigate intake air leaks, fuel pressure, and injector condition. If left unaddressed, the LTFT will continue to climb until a P0171 (System Too Lean) or similar code appears.

What is the difference between the Data Grid and Dashboard views?

The Data Grid shows every single PID as a scrollable table with raw values, scaled values, min/max columns, and a bar graph gauge. It is the most complete view and best for systematic diagnosis. The Dashboard groups parameters into logical panels (Engine, Sensors, Throttle, Fuel, Closed Loop, O2 Sensors) with a cleaner layout — useful for a quick overview or for showing a customer what the readings mean.

import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; ## Video Guide ## What Is an Air Leak? An **air leak** (also called a **vacuum leak** or **false air**) is an unintended gap or crack somewhere in the intake path — between the air filter and the combustion chamber — through which unmetered air enters the engine. Because a carburetor or EFI injector measures only the air passing through its own throat, any air that bypasses this measurement causes the engine to run lean. On a carbureted engine, the effect is particularly pronounced because the carburetor relies on intake vacuum to draw fuel. Extra air reduces vacuum signal, weakens fuel delivery, and upsets the carefully calibrated air-fuel mixture. ## Symptoms of an Air Leak
SymptomAir Leak Likelihood
Idle is erratic, hunting, or surging (revs rise and fall repeatedly)Very high
Idle that is much higher than normal and cannot be lowered with idle screwVery high
Engine starts fine but dies at idle; recovers when throttle is cracked openHigh
Hard cold start; starts easily on choke but won't idle without itHigh
Lean backfire or popping on decelerationMedium–High
Loss of power at low rpm; normal power at higher rpmMedium
Spark plug reads white/light grey (lean mixture)Medium
EFI CEL Code 21 (O₂ sensor lean) — see CEL flash codes guideHigh (EFI)
## Common Air Leak Locations on GY6 Engines - **Intake manifold gasket (most common)** The rubber or paper gasket between the intake manifold and cylinder head. It hardens and cracks with age. Inspect where the manifold bolts to the head. - **Carburetor-to-manifold clamp and boot** The rubber inlet boot (also called the intake sock) that connects the carburetor inlet to the manifold. The jubilee clamp can loosen, and the rubber develops cracks after several years. Check both ends. - **Air filter-to-carburetor connection** The joint between the air filter box and the carburetor inlet. Foam or rubber seal degrades. Also check that the air filter lid is properly seated. - **Vacuum port hoses (carburetor)** Small vacuum ports on the carburetor body connected to petcock, EGR (if fitted), or emissions hoses. Cracked, loose, or plugged hoses create significant leaks. These are often capped with small rubber plugs that can fall off. - **Choke plunger seal (carb)** The rubber O-ring on the enrichment circuit plunger (tickler or butterfly choke). Worn O-rings allow air entry around the plunger body. - **Throttle shaft bushings (carb)** The throttle slide shaft passes through the carb body. Worn bushings allow air to enter around the shaft — common on high-mileage carburetors. - **MAP sensor vacuum hose (EFI only)** A cracked or disconnected vacuum hose between the throttle body and MAP sensor causes the ECU to misread manifold pressure and run the engine lean. - **Cylinder head gasket (less common)** A minor head gasket leak between intake port and the combustion chamber is rare but possible. Usually accompanied by other symptoms (overheating, white smoke, coolant loss on LC engines). ## Photo Reference ![Cracked and worn GY6 intake manifold rubber boot — a common air leak source](/images/diagnostics/gy6-air-leak-diagnosis-1.png) Cracked GY6 intake manifold rubber boot. Note the split around the port opening — this is a classic source of vacuum leaks causing erratic idle. ## Diagnostic Methods ### Method 1 — Carb Cleaner Spray Test (Most Effective) This is the fastest and most reliable method for locating an air leak without dismantling anything. **🔥 Fire hazard:** Carb cleaner is highly flammable. Work in a well-ventilated area, away from ignition sources and hot exhaust. Never spray near a running engine's exhaust pipe. Keep a fire extinguisher nearby. Do not smoke. 1. Start the engine and allow it to reach normal idle (even if the idle is erratic). 2. With a short burst, spray a small amount of carb cleaner around the **intake manifold gasket** — where the manifold meets the cylinder head. 3. Listen carefully. If the idle speed changes (smooths out, increases, or the engine bogs for a moment), you have found a leak at that joint. 4. Move systematically: spray around the **carb-to-manifold boot**, then the **air filter joint**, then any **vacuum hose connections**. 5. FOUND: Idle changes when you spray a specific area — that is your leak location. Mark it and stop spraying. 6. NOT FOUND: No idle change at any location — air leak is unlikely; investigate other causes of erratic idle (carb jetting, pilot jet blockage). **Alternative:** WD-40 can be used instead of carb cleaner and is less flammable, though it is less reliable on very small leaks. Avoid starting fluid (ether) — it is too flammable for this test. ### Method 2 — Visual Inspection 1. With the engine **off and cold**, remove the air filter and inspect the intake boot/sock for cracks, tears, or deformation. Squeeze and twist the rubber — cracks hidden inside folds will open under flex. 2. Check that the jubilee clamp at the carburetor inlet and manifold end are tight (requires a flathead screwdriver — tighten until snug, do not overtighten on rubber). 3. Inspect the intake manifold mounting bolts. Hand-tighten if loose, but do not overtorque — the manifold is aluminium and the studs strip easily. 4. Trace all vacuum hoses from the carburetor. Look for cracks, kinks, or missing end caps. Gently tug each hose — a loose-fitting hose will pull free easily. ### Method 3 — Smoke Test (Workshop Method) A smoke machine forces low-pressure smoke into the intake system with the engine off. Smoke escaping from any point reveals the exact leak location. This is the professional workshop method and is unambiguous, but requires a smoke machine. Many independent scooter shops offer this test for a small fee if you do not own the equipment. 1. Remove the air filter and connect the smoke machine to the intake. 2. Block all known openings (throttle, choke plunger port) to pressurise the system. 3. Introduce smoke at low pressure (~0.5 psi). 4. Watch for smoke escaping around gaskets, hose joints, or manifold faces. ## Fixing the Air Leak
LocationFixParts Needed
Intake manifold gasketReplace gasket. Clean mating faces. Torque bolts evenly to ~10 Nm.GY6 intake manifold gasket (≈€1–3)
Intake boot / rubber sockReplace the rubber intake boot. Do not attempt to repair cracks with sealant — they will return.GY6 intake rubber boot + jubilee clamps (≈€3–8)
Loose jubilee clampTighten or replace the clamp. Use worm-drive type for secure seating on rubber.Jubilee clamp (≈€0.50)
Vacuum port hose cracked/missingReplace hose or fit a vacuum cap (short rubber nipple cap). Use fuel-rated rubber hose.Vacuum hose per metre / vacuum cap plugs
Choke plunger O-ringRemove plunger, measure O-ring OD and cross-section, replace with fuel-rated Viton O-ring.O-ring (≈€0.20–0.50)
Throttle shaft worn bushingsCarburetor body replacement is generally required; shaft bushings are not sold separately for most GY6 carbs. A complete PWK or VM22 carb is often more practical.Replacement carb (≈€15–40)
MAP sensor vacuum hose (EFI)Replace hose. Confirm sensor is fully seated and hose is pushed firmly onto nipple.Vacuum hose
**Do not use RTV sealant or exhaust paste as a permanent fix** on the intake manifold gasket. These sealants can be sucked into the engine if they fail, causing serious damage. Always use a proper replacement gasket. ## After Repair — Verifying the Fix 1. Reassemble all components and start the engine. 2. Allow the engine to warm for 3–4 minutes at idle. 3. Observe the idle: it should be stable and consistent, without hunting or surging. 4. Repeat the carb cleaner spray test to confirm no remaining leaks. 5. If the idle is now stable but set too high, adjust the idle speed screw (clockwise to lower) until the engine idles at approximately 1,500–1,800 rpm. 6. On EFI scooters, clear any stored fault codes (see [CEL flash codes guide](gy6-efi-cel-flash-codes.html)) and confirm the CEL does not return after a short ride. ## Related Guides - [GY6 Won't Start — Troubleshooting Checklist](gy6-no-start-troubleshooting.html) - [Carburetor Pilot & Idle Jet Diagnosis](gy6-carburetor-pilot-idle-jet.html) - [GY6 EFI CEL Flash Codes Reference](gy6-efi-cel-flash-codes.html) - [GY6 Carburetor Cleaning Guide](/repair-guides/gy6-carburetor-cleaning-guide.html) Sources: GY6 service documentation; scootdawg.com community diagnostics; modernvespa.com forum threads on vacuum leaks. import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; ## The Pilot Jet — What It Does and Why It Blocks The **pilot jet** (also called the **slow jet**) is a small brass jet with a tiny metering hole — typically 0.35–0.42 mm in diameter on a stock GY6 carburetor. It supplies fuel to the engine at idle and at throttle openings below approximately 1/4. At these low throttle positions, the main jet plays almost no role — the entire idle and low-speed fuel circuit depends entirely on the pilot jet being clean and clear. Because the pilot jet hole is so small, even a microscopic deposit of varnish — formed when old fuel evaporates inside the carburetor — can partially or fully block it. This is extremely common on scooters that have been stored for a season, or that run on fuel with ethanol content (E10 or higher), which degrades faster and leaves more varnish residue. ## Symptoms of a Blocked Pilot Jet
SymptomPilot Jet Blocked?
Engine starts and runs at high rpm but will not idle — dies when throttle is releasedVery likely — classic pilot jet blockage
Engine only runs with choke on; dies when choke is turned offVery likely — choke enriches mixture to compensate for lean pilot circuit
Idle is erratic, surging, or hunting — not a steady rpmLikely — combined with possible air leak (check both)
Engine starts fine when warm but not from coldLikely — partial blockage that only affects cold idle circuit
Scooter runs well at half to full throttle but poorly at small throttle openingsHighly likely — pilot circuit is responsible for 0–1/4 throttle fuelling
Engine won't idle even with idle screw fully in (clockwise)Likely pilot blockage or air/fuel mixture screw issue
## Reference Videos ### Idle Circuit — Diagnosis and Pilot Jet Identification Identifying pilot jet blockage and the idle fuel circuit on GY6 carburetor. Step-by-step pilot/idle jet cleaning procedure. Idle screw and pilot jet adjustment after cleaning. Poor idling caused by dirty pilot circuit — complete diagnosis and fix. ## GY6 Carburetor Idle Circuit — How It Works Understanding the circuit helps you know where to look and what to clean: - **Pilot jet:** A small brass jet screwed into the carb body, typically accessible from the bowl side. Meters fuel into the idle circuit. - **Pilot fuel passage:** A small drilled channel inside the carb body that carries fuel from the pilot jet to the idle mixture screw and then up to the pilot outlet hole in the carb throat. - **Air/fuel mixture screw (pilot air screw):** A tapered brass screw sealed with an O-ring, usually covered by a tamper-proof plug from the factory. It meters air (on some GY6 carbs) or fuel (on others) into the idle circuit. Standard setting is 1.5–2.5 turns out from lightly seated. - **Idle speed screw:** A separate, larger screw (not the mixture screw) that controls how far the throttle slide sits off its seat at idle, setting engine speed. This does not affect mixture, only rpm. - **Pilot outlet port:** A small hole in the carburetor throat (below the slide), through which the idle mixture enters the engine air stream. Can become blocked with varnish. A blockage at any point in this circuit causes idle failure. The most common blockage is in the pilot jet itself and in the small drillings within the carb body. ## Step-by-Step Pilot Jet Cleaning ### Step 1 — Preparation **⚠ Fire safety:** Work in a well-ventilated area away from ignition sources. Carburetor cleaner is highly flammable. Have a fire extinguisher nearby. Protect your eyes — carb cleaner is caustic. 1. Allow the engine to cool completely — at least 30 minutes after last running. 2. Turn the fuel petcock to **OFF** or close the fuel valve. 3. Place a small container under the float bowl drain screw (if fitted) or under the bowl itself. You will be draining residual fuel. ### Step 2 — Remove the Float Bowl 1. Locate the float bowl drain screw at the bottom of the carburetor bowl (if present) and loosen it to drain residual fuel. 2. Remove the single retaining screw (or two screws, depending on carb type) from the bottom of the float bowl. 3. Lower the float bowl carefully — it may still contain fuel. Note the condition of the fuel: if it is dark brown, thick, or smells of varnish, the entire carb needs a full clean. 4. Inspect the float bowl gasket — replace if it shows cracks, compression set, or deformation. ### Step 3 — Remove and Inspect the Pilot Jet 1. With the bowl removed, identify the **pilot jet**: it is the **smaller** of the two jets. On GY6 carbs it is typically the jet closest to the engine side (rear), while the main jet is larger and sits towards the centre or front. 2. Use a flat-head screwdriver that fits the slot precisely — a poor-fitting screwdriver will damage the soft brass jet head. A proper jet screwdriver with a wide, thin blade is ideal. 3. Unscrew the pilot jet anti-clockwise. It should come free with moderate effort. Do not use excessive force — the jet is soft brass and strips easily. 4. Hold the jet up to a light source and look through it. Clear hole: Jet is unobstructed. Move to cleaning the passages. Blocked or no light visible: Jet is blocked. ### Step 4 — Clean the Pilot Jet 1. Soak the pilot jet in **carb cleaner** for 10–15 minutes. Fresh cleaner dissolves varnish deposits effectively. 2. After soaking, spray carb cleaner through the jet from both ends using the tube nozzle on the carb cleaner can. 3. Hold the jet up to light — you should see a clean, round hole. If not, soak again for 30 minutes and repeat. 4. **Do not use wire, drill bits, or anything solid** to push through the jet hole. The hole size is precisely calibrated — enlarging it even slightly will permanently alter the fuel mixture. The only acceptable mechanical cleaning is with a **jet cleaning wire** (a soft bristle from a brass wire brush, or a strand from a brass wire). Even this should be used with great care. 5. Blow the jet out with compressed air. Confirm the hole is clear visually. ### Step 5 — Clean the Carburetor Body Passages 1. With the pilot jet removed and the bowl off, spray carb cleaner into the **pilot jet port** (the threaded hole where the jet sits). Watch for cleaner to emerge from the small pilot outlet port in the carb throat — if it does, the main passage is clear. 2. Spray cleaner into all small holes and drillings visible in the carb body. Each small hole should show cleaner emerging from somewhere else in the carb — if it does not, the passage is blocked. 3. Use compressed air to blow through all passages after spraying with cleaner. 4. If the pilot outlet port in the carb throat (the small hole below the slide) is blocked with varnish, carefully clear it with a thin strand of wire or a strand of straw bristle. It is critical that this port is clear. ### Step 6 — Check and Clean the Air/Fuel Mixture Screw 1. Locate the mixture screw — a tapered brass screw on the engine side of the carb body, often covered with a small aluminium plug from the factory (emissions tamper-proof cap). 2. If a plug is present, remove it with a small pick or drill (use a 4 mm drill bit carefully — just enough to create a grip point for the pick). 3. Carefully unscrew the mixture screw fully. Note exactly how many turns it takes to remove it from lightly seated — this is your baseline. It should be approximately 1.5–2.5 turns out. 4. The mixture screw will have a small O-ring and a small spring — do not lose these. 5. Soak the screw in carb cleaner. Spray carb cleaner through the mixture screw port and the adjacent air bleed passages. 6. Inspect the O-ring — replace if hardened, cracked, or deformed (use a fuel-grade O-ring matching the original diameter). 7. Reinstall the mixture screw to its original number of turns. Do not tighten past lightly seated — the tapered tip seats on a soft aluminium seat and is easily damaged. ### Step 7 — Reassemble and Test 1. Reinstall the pilot jet. Tighten firmly but not with excessive force — snug is enough. 2. Reinstall the main jet (if removed). 3. Fit a new float bowl gasket if the old one is compromised. Reinstall the float bowl and tighten the screw. 4. Open the fuel petcock to ON. Check for fuel leaks around the bowl. 5. Start the engine. Allow it to warm for 2–3 minutes. 6. With the engine warm, set the idle speed to approximately **1,500–1,800 rpm** using the idle speed screw. 7. Fine-tune the mixture screw: turn it out (anti-clockwise) in 1/4-turn increments and listen. The idle should rise slightly as mixture richens. Find the position that gives the highest, smoothest idle, then turn the idle speed screw back down to your desired idle rpm. ## Pilot Jet Size Reference (GY6 Stock)
EngineCarburetorStandard Pilot JetStandard Main Jet
GY6 50cc (139QMB)PZ19 or PZ18#38–#42#78–#82
GY6 125cc (152QMI)PZ20 or CV22#38–#42#95–#100
GY6 150cc (157QMJ)PZ22 or CV24#42–#45#105–#110
**When to replace rather than clean:** If the pilot jet is clear but the engine still idles poorly, and all passages are unobstructed, the jet itself may have enlarged from wear or improper cleaning. Replace with an exact OEM-spec jet — they cost less than €1 each. Always carry a spare pilot jet on older carbureted GY6 scooters. ## After a Full Clean — Setting Idle Correctly After cleaning, the carburetor requires proper idle adjustment. There are two separate adjustments — do not confuse them: - **Idle speed screw (large, spring-loaded, on the side of the carb body):** Controls engine rpm at idle. Turn clockwise to raise idle, anti-clockwise to lower. Target: 1,500–1,800 rpm when fully warm. - **Air/fuel mixture screw (small, tapered, usually under a plug):** Controls the richness of the idle mixture. Turn out (anti-clockwise) to richen, in (clockwise) to lean. Adjust for highest smooth idle, then set idle speed with the idle speed screw. ## Related Guides - [GY6 Carburetor Full Cleaning Guide](/repair-guides/gy6-carburetor-cleaning-guide.html) - [GY6 Carburetor Adjustment Guide](/repair-guides/gy6-carburetor-adjustment-guide.html) - [GY6 Carburetor Jetting Guide](/repair-guides/gy6-carburetor-jetting-guide.html) - [Air Leak Diagnosis (can mimic pilot jet symptoms)](gy6-air-leak-diagnosis.html) - [GY6 Won't Start — Full Troubleshooting Checklist](gy6-no-start-troubleshooting.html)

import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; ## Understanding the Sound A metallic rattling, knocking, or scraping noise from the front-left side of the engine (CVT cover side) on a GY6 scooter is a classic symptom of **worn or broken CVT variator rollers**. When rollers wear unevenly, crack, or flatten on one side, they no longer roll smoothly in the variator ramps — instead they slide, bounce, and strike the variator housing walls. The noise typically: - Is most pronounced at **low to mid throttle** (when the variator is mid-travel) - Increases or changes pitch with acceleration - **Disappears or decreases at full throttle** (rollers pressed hard against the outer ramp) - May be accompanied by **poor acceleration, flat spots, or the scooter reaching top speed more slowly** ## Reference Video Demonstration of the metallic CVT roller noise and how to identify it on a GY6 scooter. ## Quick Symptom Table
Noise DescriptionMost Likely CauseAction
Metallic rattle, worst at 20–50 km/h under gentle throttleWorn/flat CVT rollersInspect rollers — this guide
Clunking when pulling away from standstillBroken roller fragment loose inside variatorInspect immediately — broken piece can damage variator
Continuous scraping at all speedsCVT belt contacting side of casing, or large debris insideOpen CVT cover, inspect belt and casing walls
High-pitched squeal under loadWorn/glazed CVT beltInspect belt width and condition — see belt replacement guide
Clicking from rear — worse under brakingNot CVT — check rear brake disc, caliper, or wheel bearingInspect rear end separately
## What Are CVT Rollers? CVT rollers (also called **variator weights**) are cylindrical weights that sit inside the drive face of the variator (front pulley). Under centrifugal force as engine rpm rises, the rollers move outward along angled ramps, pushing the movable drive face inward, which increases the effective pulley diameter and changes the drive ratio — this is how the CVT automatically varies its ratio without a conventional gearbox. GY6 engines typically use **6 rollers**. Standard weights are 10–18 grams depending on engine size and application. Over time, the plastic or rubber outer skin of the roller wears flat on one side, the roller deforms under heat, or the outer casing cracks — all of which cause noise and loss of performance. ## Step-by-Step Diagnosis ### Step 1 — Confirm the Noise Source 1. Start the engine and hold the scooter on the centre stand with the rear wheel clear of the ground. 2. Slowly open the throttle from idle to about half throttle. Listen carefully for the metallic rattle. 3. Place your hand lightly on the **CVT cover (left side panel)** — you should be able to feel a vibration corresponding to the noise if rollers are the cause. 4. Have an assistant press on the rear of the scooter to load the rear wheel while you hold the throttle steady at ~3,000–4,000 rpm. A loaded CVT accentuates roller noise. 5. CONFIRMED: Noise is clearly from the CVT cover area, varies with throttle position. Proceed to Step 2. 6. NOT CVT: Noise comes from the engine cases, exhaust, or head area — check valve clearance, cam chain, or exhaust gasket instead. ### Step 2 — Open the CVT Cover **⚠ Safety:** Engine must be fully off and cool before opening the CVT cover. The CVT belt and variator spin at high speed and can cause serious injury. 1. Remove the left side panel (two to four screws, depending on model). 2. Remove the CVT cover — typically 5–7 bolts around the perimeter. On GY6 engines these are M6 bolts. 3. Carefully remove the cover. Note if there is any debris, rubber dust, or fragments inside the casing — this indicates a broken roller or belt. ### Step 3 — Inspect the Variator and Rollers 1. Grip the front variator assembly and rotate it by hand to feel for roughness. 2. Using a variator holder tool (or improvised wedge), lock the variator against rotation. 3. Remove the variator nut (typically M20, left-hand thread on GY6 — turn **clockwise** to loosen). Use a breaker bar. 4. Slide off the front variator face. The rollers will be visible in the ramp channels of the rear variator half (the slotted disc). 5. Remove each roller by hand and inspect:
Roller ConditionDiagnosisAction
Smooth, round, uniform surfaceGood — roller is serviceableClean and reinstall
Flat spot on one side (D-shaped cross section)Worn — causing rattle and performance lossReplace full set of 6
Cracked, chipped, or broken outer skinFailed — urgent replacementReplace full set of 6 immediately
Oval or bulging shapeHeat-deformed — common with wrong weight rollersReplace full set with correct weight
Metal core visible through worn plasticSeverely wornReplace full set; inspect ramp channels for gouging
### Step 4 — Inspect Ramp Channels While the rollers are removed, inspect the angled ramp channels in the variator disc (the rear variator half). Run your fingernail across each ramp surface. - Surface should be smooth and slightly shiny. - Grooves, gouges, or rough patches indicate the rollers were running in worn condition for a long time. - Light surface marks are acceptable. Deep grooves mean the variator itself should be replaced. ## Replacement: Roller Specifications
EngineStandard Roller WeightQuantityRoller Dimensions (typical)
GY6 50cc (139QMB)7.5–8.5 g6Ø16 × 13 mm
GY6 125cc (152QMI)12–13 g6Ø18 × 14 mm
GY6 150cc (157QMJ)15–16 g6Ø18 × 14 mm
Piaggio Vespa Primavera 12511 g6Ø23 × 18 mm (Piaggio-specific)
Piaggio Zip 4T 50cc3.5–6 g6Ø19 × 15.5 mm
**Performance tip:** Heavier rollers cause the variator to shift up (higher ratio) at lower rpm — more top speed, slower acceleration. Lighter rollers cause earlier upshift — quicker acceleration, lower top speed. For daily commuting, stick to OEM specification weight. ## Reassembly Notes - Install all 6 new rollers in the ramp channels. Ensure each roller sits in its slot fully before reassembling the front variator face. - Apply a very light smear of clean grease (high-melting-point grease, not lithium) to the ramp channels — but do **not** grease the roller outer surface or the belt pulley faces. - Torque the variator nut to the specification for your engine: typically **35–45 Nm** for GY6, **50 Nm** for Piaggio. The nut is left-hand thread on GY6 — tighten counter-clockwise. - Reinstall the CVT cover and test-ride at varying throttle positions to confirm the rattle has gone. **Always replace all 6 rollers at once.** Mixing old and new rollers results in uneven loading on the variator ramps, which causes noise, uneven wear, and poor shifting — exactly the problem you were trying to fix. ## Related Guides - [CVT Variator and Belt Replacement](/repair-guides/gy6-cvt-variator-belt-replacement.html) - [CVT Clutch and Variator Complete Guide](/repair-guides/scooter-cvt-clutch-variator-guide.html) Sources: GY6 CVT service documentation; community-verified diagnostic information from scootdawg.com. import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; ## How Handlebar Buttons Can Prevent Starting The handlebar switch cluster on the right side contains the **kill switch** (engine stop switch) and the **electric starter button**. The kill switch is normally closed — meaning it completes the ignition circuit when in the "RUN" position. When it fails due to corrosion or debris, it can open the circuit even in the RUN position, cutting ignition exactly as if you had pressed "STOP." The starter button on the left cluster (or right, depending on model) can also develop resistance buildup on its contacts that prevents it from passing enough current to energise the starter relay. The engine appears to do nothing when you press the starter — no click, no crank. ## Symptoms of Dirty or Faulty Handlebar Buttons
SymptomMost Likely Button Fault
Engine cranks but will not fire (no spark)Kill switch in open/fault state — engine thinks it is switched off
Starter button does nothing — no click, no crankStarter button contacts dirty/oxidised or circuit open
Starter engages intermittently — sometimes works, sometimes does notDirty or worn starter button contacts
Engine runs fine once started but stalls randomlyKill switch momentarily opening due to vibration or dirt
Engine will start by bridging the starter relay directly but not from the buttonStarter button or its circuit confirmed faulty
## Reference Videos Part 1 — Identifying dirty buttons as the cause of a no-start condition. Part 2 — Opening the switch cluster and cleaning the contacts. ## Quick Test — Kill Switch 1. Set the kill switch to **RUN**. 2. Attempt to start the engine — no spark or no start. 3. Wiggle the kill switch rapidly between RUN and STOP positions 10–15 times. This can temporarily clean the contact through mechanical action. 4. Return to RUN and try starting again. 5. Starts: Kill switch contact is dirty. Clean or replace the switch cluster. 6. Still no start: Check for spark directly — if spark is present at the plug with the kill switch bypassed (Step 2 below), the kill switch is confirmed faulty. ### Bypass Test — Kill Switch This test definitively confirms whether the kill switch circuit is preventing ignition. 1. Locate the wiring connector for the right-hand switch cluster. On GY6 scooters this is typically a multi-pin connector near the headstock, or individual bullet connectors under the fairings. 2. Find the two wires for the kill switch (usually **black/white and black**, or just two black wires). On a working kill switch these two wires are connected together in RUN and disconnected in STOP. 3. Disconnect the kill switch connector from the main harness. 4. Attempt to start the engine (on many GY6 scooters the engine will run without the kill switch connected — the circuit defaults to "run" when open). 5. Starts: Kill switch is confirmed faulty. Clean or replace. 6. Still no start: Kill switch is not the cause. Reconnect and investigate other no-start causes. **Note:** On some wiring configurations the kill switch grounds the CDI — in that case the engine will not start with the circuit open. Consult your wiring diagram to confirm which configuration your scooter uses before concluding from this test. ## Opening and Cleaning the Switch Cluster ### Right-Hand Cluster (Kill Switch + Starter Button) 1. Turn the ignition **off**. 2. Remove the two small screws (typically Phillips #1 or #2) from the back of the right-hand switch cluster housing. The housing is in two halves clamped around the handlebar. 3. Carefully separate the two halves. Do not pull on the wires. 4. Inside you will find: - The kill switch rocker or slider mechanism with two copper contacts. - The starter button with a spring-loaded plunger and two copper contacts. 5. Inspect the contacts under good lighting: - **Black oxidation** on copper contacts — clean with contact cleaner and a cotton swab. - **Green verdigris** — heavy oxidation, clean with contact cleaner and a fine abrasive (500-grit wet/dry sandpaper folded in half, use very gentle strokes). - **Melted or pitted contacts** — replace the switch cluster. 6. Spray a small burst of **electrical contact cleaner** into the switch mechanism. Operate each button or switch 20–30 times to work the cleaner through. 7. Allow to dry fully (5–10 minutes). 8. Apply a tiny amount of **dielectric grease** or conductive electrical grease to the contacts before reassembly to resist future corrosion. 9. Reassemble the housing halves and tighten the screws. Do not overtighten — the housing is thin plastic. ### Left-Hand Cluster (Horn + Light Switches) The same process applies. If the horn button is not working or the headlight switch is intermittent, the entire left cluster can be cleaned using the same method. While it is open, check all the wire connections for corrosion at the crimp terminals inside the housing. ## Replacing the Switch Cluster If cleaning does not restore reliable operation, replacement clusters are widely available and inexpensive for GY6 scooters. When ordering: - Specify left or right cluster (they are different). - Check the number of wires — some clusters include a choke switch or hazard function that yours may not have. - GY6 replacement clusters use the same colour-coded bullet connectors — match colour to colour when reconnecting to the main harness. - Piaggio/Vespa switch clusters are model-specific — use OEM part numbers. **Prevention:** When washing the scooter, avoid directing pressurised water into the handlebar switch clusters. After washing, spray the button slots with a water-displacing lubricant (WD-40 or equivalent). Apply a thin film of dielectric grease inside the cluster housings annually on scooters used in wet climates. ## Related Guides - [GY6 Scooter Won't Start — Full Troubleshooting Checklist](gy6-no-start-troubleshooting.html) - [Side Stand Kill Switch Diagnosis](gy6-side-stand-kill-switch.html) Sources: GY6 wiring documentation; community repair threads from scootdawg.com; video references: YouTube Shorts. import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; ## What Is the CEL / MIL? The **Check Engine Light (CEL)**, also called the **Malfunction Indicator Lamp (MIL)**, is the dashboard warning light — typically an engine outline icon or the words "CHECK" or "INJECTION." When the ECU detects a sensor reading outside its acceptable range, it stores a fault code and illuminates this light. Most GY6 EFI ECUs support a built-in **manual diagnostic mode** that flashes stored fault codes as a sequence of light pulses — no OBD scanner required. This guide explains how to enter that mode and how to read the resulting flash patterns. **⚠ Note on ECU variants:** Chinese GY6 EFI scooters may use any of several ECU types (KEIHIN PGM-FI clones, Delphi MT05 variants, proprietary clones). Flash code sequences and activation procedures are largely standardised across these, but minor differences exist. If in doubt, cross-reference your scooter's service manual. **ℹ️ Wrong page?** This guide covers **CEL blink/flash codes** — the older diagnostic method used by KEIHIN PGM-FI clone ECUs that flash patterns without any scanner. **If your scooter has a Rongmao, Delphi, or Motion EFI system** (typically Euro 4 / Euro 5 models from approx. 2017+), it uses standard OBD-2 P-codes and does not support blink codes. See the [GY6 EFI OBD-2 DTC Fault Codes guide](gy6-efi-obd2-dtc-fault-codes.html) instead. ## How to Enter Manual Diagnostic Mode ### Standard Activation Procedure (most GY6 EFI and Chinese EFI scooters) 1. Park the scooter on its centre stand on level ground. Engine must be **off**. 2. Turn the ignition key to **ON** — do not start the engine. 3. Watch the CEL: it will illuminate for ~2 seconds (self-check), then go out. This is normal. 4. If no fault is stored, the CEL stays off and you are done — no codes present. 5. If one or more fault codes are stored, the CEL will begin **flashing sequences automatically** after the self-check (no further input needed on most units). On some ECUs (particularly older Piaggio D-Tronik / Wave ECU), the manual mode requires a specific sequence — see below. ### Piaggio / Vespa Activation Procedure (D-Tronik ECU, pre-2015) 1. Turn ignition key to **OFF**. 2. Turn ignition key to **ON** (do not start). 3. Immediately turn back to **OFF**. 4. Turn to **ON** again within 5 seconds. 5. The CEL will flash stored codes. If the CEL flashes once then holds steady for 3 seconds, no codes are stored. ### Activation with Diagnostic Toggle Wire (some Chinese ECUs) Some Chinese EFI scooters have a **diagnostic wire** — a short pigtail under the seat or near the ECU, usually **white or green**, with a connector plug or bare terminal. To enter diagnostic mode: 1. Turn ignition to **OFF**. 2. Connect the diagnostic wire to **ground** (any clean chassis bolt). 3. Turn ignition to **ON**. 4. The CEL will flash the stored codes. 5. Disconnect the wire from ground when done. ## How to Read the Flash Codes GY6 EFI ECUs use one of two flash code patterns depending on the ECU generation. Identify which pattern your scooter uses before trying to decode any codes. --- ### Pattern 1 — Long + Short Flashes (KEIHIN PGM-FI clones, older Chinese ECUs) Codes are expressed as **two groups of pulses** separated by a brief pause. The **first group uses longer flashes** to encode the tens digit; the **second group uses shorter flashes** for the units digit. A longer pause separates one code from the next, and the ECU loops through all stored codes continuously. **Reading tip:** Count the long flashes first, then the short flashes after the pause. Write the pair as a two-digit number — for example, 1 long + 2 short = Code **12**.
What you see (CEL)How to read itCode

--- ### Pattern 2 — All Short Flashes, Tens as 10 Pulses (some Chinese / Taiwanese EFI ECUs) Some ECU variants use **only short flashes of equal length** — there are no long flashes at all. The tens digit is encoded by counting out exactly **10 individual short pulses**, followed by a **short pause (~1 s)**. The units digit then follows as additional short pulses, then a **longer pause (~2 s)** before the next code. If multiple codes are stored, they play back-to-back; when the full sequence ends, the ECU waits with a **triple-length pause (~4–5 s)** before looping. **Examples:** - Code **13** → 10 short flashes · short pause (~1 s) · 3 short flashes · longer pause (~2 s) · loop - Code **08** → 8 short flashes · longer pause (~2 s) · loop *(single-digit codes: no tens group, just the units count)* - Codes **13 + 08** in sequence → 10 flashes · short pause · 3 flashes · longer pause · 8 flashes · triple-long pause (~4 s) · repeat **Reading tip:** Count every flash group carefully. If a group has exactly 10 pulses followed by a short gap, those 10 are the tens digit — wait for the units group after the pause. If a group has fewer than 10 pulses and is followed by a longer pause, that group is the entire code (a single-digit code, e.g. 8 flashes = Code 08).

**Which pattern does my scooter use?** Watch the first flash group carefully. If you see two clearly different flash lengths (some obviously longer than others), you have Pattern 1. If every flash looks identical in length and only the gaps between groups differ, you have Pattern 2. When counting Pattern 2, a group of exactly 10 identical flashes is always the tens digit — stop counting and wait for the short pause, then count the next group for the units digit. ## GY6 EFI Flash Code Reference Table The following codes are used by GY6-compatible EFI ECUs (KEIHIN PGM-FI clones, MT05-type, and Piaggio D-Tronik variants). ## Clearing Stored Fault Codes ### Method 1 — Battery Disconnect (Universal) 1. Ensure the ignition is **OFF**. 2. Disconnect the **negative (–) terminal** from the battery. 3. Wait at least **10 minutes** for ECU capacitors to discharge fully. 4. Reconnect the battery. Start the engine and confirm the CEL is extinguished. **Important:** Clearing codes does not fix the underlying fault. If the root cause is not repaired, the code will return within a few minutes of running. ### Method 2 — Ignition Cycle Reset (some ECUs) Perform five full ignition ON → OFF cycles in quick succession. On some ECU types this triggers an adaptive memory reset. Codes may persist on other types — use Method 1 if codes return immediately. ## Sensor Location Reference

## Diagnostic Flow — CEL Is On 1. **Enter manual diagnostic mode** using the procedure above for your ECU type. 2. **Record all flash codes** — multiple codes may be stored. Write every code down before starting repairs. 3. **Cross-reference the code table** above to identify the affected component. 4. **Inspect wiring and connectors first** — the majority of faults on Chinese EFI scooters are due to corroded connectors or chafed wiring, not failed sensors. 5. **Test the sensor** with a multimeter (resistance, voltage, or signal as appropriate for the sensor type). 6. **Repair or replace** as required. 7. **Clear the code** (battery disconnect method) and retest. 8. If the same code returns immediately, recheck your repair. If a different code appears, continue through the code table. **Pro tip:** Always repair the highest-severity code first. A battery voltage fault (Code 56/57) can cause multiple secondary sensor codes to appear because sensor supply voltages are affected. Fixing the root voltage issue may clear several codes at once. ## Related Guides - [GY6 EFI Fuel Injection Full Troubleshooting Guide](gy6-efi-fuel-injection-troubleshooting.html) - [GY6 Scooter Won't Start — Troubleshooting Checklist](gy6-no-start-troubleshooting.html) - [Diagnosing Air Leaks and Vacuum Sucking](gy6-air-leak-diagnosis.html) - [Ignition Coil Replacement Guide](/repair-guides/gy6-ignition-coil-guide.html) Sources: GY6 EFI service manuals (KEIHIN PGM-FI, Delphi MT05); Piaggio D-Tronik ECU documentation; community-verified flash code data from scootdawg.com and modernvespa.com forums. import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; import SourceBox from '@components/SourceBox.astro'; Added: 2026-05-08  |  Sources: [rollingwrenchdenver.com](https://www.rollingwrenchdenver.com/blogs/news/i-am-having-trouble-with-my-gy6-efi-system), [kemsoracing.com](https://www.kemsoracing.com/blogs/news/the-ultimate-guide-to-gy6-fuel-pump-maintenance-troubleshooting-replacement), [49ccscoot.proboards.com](https://49ccscoot.proboards.com/thread/32665/gy6-fuel-injection-build) GY6 Fuel Injection EFI Diagnostics While the majority of GY6-engined scooters sold in Europe and the UK use a carburetor, a growing number of models — and all Euro 5-compliant variants — use electronic fuel injection (EFI). Some owners also retrofit aftermarket EFI systems (such as the Ecotrons or Rolling Wrench ProBld kit) to carbureted GY6 engines. This guide covers the most common EFI fault symptoms and how to diagnose them systematically. ## GY6 EFI System Overview A typical GY6 EFI system consists of the following components working together: - **ECU (Engine Control Unit):** The electronic brain; maps fuel injection quantity and ignition timing based on sensor inputs. - **Electric fuel pump:** Mounted in or near the fuel tank; delivers fuel at 15–25 PSI (1.0–1.7 bar) to the injector. - **Fuel injector:** A solenoid valve that sprays a metered amount of fuel into the intake port. - **Throttle position sensor (TPS):** Reports throttle angle to the ECU. - **Manifold absolute pressure sensor (MAP) or intake air temperature sensor (IAT):** Measures intake conditions for fuel map corrections. - **Coolant temperature sensor (CTS):** Enables cold-start enrichment. - **Crankshaft/camshaft position sensor:** Triggers injection timing. ## First Steps: Before Any Diagnosis 1. Check the battery voltage with a multimeter. EFI systems need a minimum of approximately 11.5 V to operate correctly. A weak battery is a very common cause of erratic EFI behaviour. 2. Check the main fuse and any EFI-specific inline fuses in the wiring harness. 3. Inspect all EFI connector plugs for corrosion, pushed-back terminals, or water ingress. Clean with electrical contact cleaner and reseat firmly. 4. Verify the ground connections: the EFI system requires a clean, low-resistance earth. A dedicated earth wire from battery negative to a bare metal chassis point is essential. A poor earth is responsible for a significant proportion of EFI faults. ️ **EFI vs carburetor:** Do not apply aerosol starting fluid (ether) to a fuel-injected GY6 engine — it can damage the injector seal and the catalytic converter if fitted. Use the correct cold-start procedure instead. ## Symptom-Based Diagnostic Table
SymptomMost Likely CauseDiagnostic Action
Engine cranks but will not fireNo fuel pressure; dead fuel pump; ECU not poweredListen for pump prime (2-sec buzz on key-on); test fuel pressure at injector inlet (target: 15–25 PSI)
Hard cold start onlyCTS fault; cold-start enrichment not workingCheck CTS resistance (typically 2–3 kΩ at 20°C); inspect CTS wiring connector
Rough idle, intermittent stallTPS out of range; air leak; dirty injectorCheck TPS voltage (typically 0.4–0.8 V at idle); spray intake manifold joints with carb cleaner while running to detect air leaks
Black smoke, rich runningTPS stuck or miscalibrated; injector stuck open; MAP sensor faultCheck TPS signal sweep from idle to WOT (should read 0.4 V to ~4.5 V); test injector resistance (typically 11–16 Ω)
White smoke, lean runningFuel pump weak; injector clogged; fuel filter blockedTest fuel pressure under load; replace fuel filter; clean injector with ultrasonic cleaner or injector-cleaning kit
Loss of power above half throttleFuel pump not maintaining pressure at high demand; clogged fuel filterTest pump pressure at full throttle simulation (should not drop below 15 PSI); replace filter
Engine misfires, popping on decelerationIgnition coil; crankshaft position sensor; air leakCheck spark output; test crank position sensor resistance per manufacturer spec
Check-engine / fault lamp illuminatedStored fault code(s)Read fault codes (see below)
## Reading EFI Fault Codes on GY6 Factory EFI GY6 scooters and aftermarket EFI kits typically signal fault codes either through a malfunction indicator lamp (MIL) blink pattern or via a diagnostic connector that accepts a generic OBD-II style reader or the manufacturer's proprietary tool. ## Blink-Code Method (No Scanner) 1. Switch the ignition on (do not start the engine). 2. Observe the warning lamp: it will flash a series of long and short pulses to indicate a fault code. The pattern is typically: long flashes = tens digit, short flashes = units digit. For example, two long flashes followed by three short flashes = fault code 23. 3. Count all flash sequences carefully and write them down. 4. Cross-reference against your ECU's fault code table (supplied with aftermarket kits; available in the manufacturer service manual for factory EFI models). ## Common Ecotrons / ProBld EFI Fault Codes
CodeDescriptionTypical Cause
11Crankshaft position sensor signal absentSensor gap too large; wiring break; sensor failure
13MAP/vacuum sensor out of rangeDisconnected vacuum line; sensor failure
14Intake air temperature sensor faultConnector corrosion; sensor open circuit
21Coolant temperature sensor faultOpen or short in CTS circuit; sensor failure
22Throttle position sensor faultTPS connector loose; incorrect idle voltage; sensor failure
44O₂ / lambda sensor (lean)Air leak; lean fuel map; O₂ sensor aging
45O₂ / lambda sensor (rich)Stuck injector; rich fuel map; O₂ sensor failure
� **Tip:** For aftermarket EFI kits (Ecotrons SE-EFI, Rolling Wrench ProBld), the installation manual PDF contains full fault code tables and sensor resistance charts. Download it from the manufacturer's website and keep a copy with the scooter's documents. ## Fuel Pump Testing The electric fuel pump on an EFI GY6 typically operates at 15–25 PSI. Testing procedure: 1. Connect a fuel pressure gauge (T-fitting or Schrader port if available) between the fuel pump outlet and the injector inlet. 2. Switch the ignition on — the pump should run for approximately 2 seconds to prime, then stop. Pressure should rise to the operating range and hold. 3. If pressure does not rise, test voltage at the pump connector (should be battery voltage when the ECU activates the pump relay). 4. If voltage is present but pressure is absent or low, the pump is failing and should be replaced. Kemso Racing and VMC Chinese Parts both supply direct-replacement GY6 EFI pumps at affordable prices. � **Related guides:** [GY6 Won't Start — Troubleshooting Checklist](gy6-no-start-troubleshooting.html) | [GY6 carburetor Deep-Cleaning Guide](/repair-guides/gy6-carburetor-cleaning-guide.html)

The connector is usually left unconnected when no diagnostic tool is attached — this is normal. ![Under-seat area of a GY6 scooter showing the 6-pin diagnostic connector near the battery](/diagnostics/images/ecu-hacker/6connector.jpg) Under-seat area — the 6-pin connector is the white plug near the battery ![Hand holding the GY6 scooter 6-pin diagnostic plug showing orange internal contacts](/diagnostics/images/ecu-hacker/7connector.jpg) The 6-pin diagnostic plug — orange/yellow contacts, white housing **ℹ️ Can't find it?** On the Delphi EFI system the connector is almost always near the battery. On some models it may be taped to the wiring harness or tucked behind a side panel near the ECU box. Consult the wiring diagram for your specific model if needed. 4 ### Connect the Adapter Chain 1. Plug the **6-pin end** of the adapter cable into the scooter's diagnostic connector. It fits in one orientation only — do not force it. 2. Connect the **OBD2 end** of the adapter to the OBD2 socket of the KKL cable. 3. Plug the **USB end** of the KKL cable into your laptop. 4. Turn the scooter ignition to **ON** (do not start the engine — key-on is sufficient). **⚠️ Ignition must be ON:** The ECU only powers its K-line interface when the ignition is on. Connecting with the ignition off will result in a "Timeout waiting for response" error in HUD ECU Hacker. ![VAG KKL cable connected to a Lenovo laptop, ready to connect to scooter](/diagnostics/images/ecu-hacker/5cables_laptop.jpg) Cable connected to the laptop — USB end in, ready to plug into the scooter ![Full diagnostic setup: scooter open under seat, KKL cable running to laptop on the ground](/diagnostics/images/ecu-hacker/8setupconnected.jpg) Full setup in the field — laptop next to the scooter, cable connected to the 6-pin port 5 ### Configure HUD ECU Hacker and Connect 1. Open HUD ECU Hacker. In the **Control** tab, click **ECU Model** and select the correct ECU for your scooter: - **Delphi MT05 / MT05.2** — most GY6 EFI scooters sold in Europe (BTC Riva, La Souris, Santini, etc.) - **Rongmao MT05** — some Chinese-market and grey-import models - **Motion SE08** — certain Euro 5 models (2021+), though compatibility varies — see Caveats belowNot sure which ECU your scooter has? Check the label on the ECU box under the seat. 2. From the **COM port** dropdown, select the port you noted in Step 1 (e.g. `COM3`). If you see multiple ports, try each one until the connection succeeds. 3. Click **Echo Test**, then click **Connect**. You will see a stream of raw data in the Trace tab. If no red "Timeout" errors appear, the Echo Test passed. 4. Click **Echo Test** again to toggle it off, then click **Connect** to establish a live session with the ECU. 5. The status bar should now show **Connected** and a session timer. ![HUD ECU Hacker software main screen showing the Control tab with ECU model and COM port selection](/diagnostics/images/ecu-hacker/9appview.jpg) HUD ECU Hacker v5.8.8 — Control tab showing ECU model selector and Connect button **⚠️ "Timeout waiting for response" — this is normal.** K-line timing is highly sensitive. The connection may fail on the first 5–10 attempts. Simply go back to the Control tab and click Connect again. If it consistently fails after many attempts, try reducing the baud rate in the software's Troubleshooting settings (see the HUD ECU Hacker documentation on netcult.ch under "Trouble Shooting"). 6 ### Read Live Data and Fault Codes Once connected you have access to all ECU data in real time. Key tabs: - **Dashboard** — graphical overview of all sensor groups: engine, throttle, fuel, O2 sensors, temperatures. - **Data Grid** — tabular view of every raw parameter: RPM, coolant temp, MAP pressure, IAT, throttle position, short/long term fuel trims, spark advance, vehicle speed, and more. - **DTC (Fault Codes)** — read and clear stored Diagnostic Trouble Codes. On Euro 4 and later models, codes must be cleared with this tool — they do not auto-reset after the fault disappears. - **Graph** — plot any parameter over time for intermittent fault diagnosis. - **Tuning** — advanced: read/write ECU maps (only for experienced users). ![HUD ECU Hacker Data Grid showing live sensor readings: coolant temp, MAP, throttle, fuel trims](/diagnostics/images/ecu-hacker/10livedata.jpg) Data Grid — all live sensor values including coolant temp, MAP pressure and fuel trims ![HUD ECU Hacker Dashboard view showing comprehensive sensor panels across the full screen](/diagnostics/images/ecu-hacker/12livedata.jpg) Dashboard view — all sensor groups visible simultaneously when connected ![HUD ECU Hacker Data Grid alternative view showing emission count DTC and O2 sensor data](/diagnostics/images/ecu-hacker/11livedata.jpg) Data Grid with emission DTC count visible — O2 sensor status and closed-loop operation **💡 Clearing fault codes:** Navigate to the DTC tab, confirm the codes, resolve the underlying fault, then click _Clear DTCs_. On Euro 4 scooters the MIL (engine warning light) will only go off after the ECU confirms the fault is no longer present — clearing the code alone does not guarantee the light stays off if the problem persists. ## Additional Reference Video **Video:** "Testing HUD ECU Hacker — Lexmoto Titan" (2024) — real-world walkthrough on a Chinese EFI scooter with Delphi ECU. [↗ Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BI4WgTFN8mM) ## Important Caveats Based on community experience and forum reports, be aware of the following before you start: - 🚫 **Generic OBD2 readers will not work.** Many users with standard Bluetooth ELM327 scanners or generic car-OBD apps receive a _"Vehicle not connected"_ error. This is because the GY6 ECU uses the K-line (ISO 9141-2 / KWP2000) protocol — not the CAN bus found in modern cars. Standard ELM327 dongles often lack K-line support or have incompatible timing. The OBD2 KKL cable with FTDI chip and HUD ECU Hacker together form a K-line-aware combination that actually works. Source: [ScooterForum.net](https://scooterforum.net/tags/la-souris/) - ⚠️ **Euro 4 fault codes do not self-clear.** From Euro 4 onwards, stored DTCs remain in the ECU memory even after the underlying fault is repaired. The engine warning light will stay on until you actively clear the codes with a diagnostic tool like HUD ECU Hacker. Simply fixing the problem is not enough — you must connect and erase the codes. Source: [Gentlemen Riders](https://www.gentlemen-riders.com/lecteur-obdii-pour-code-defaut/9519-lecteur-obdii-pour-moto-euro4.html) - 🔴 **Motion EFI (Euro 5, some 2021+ models) may not connect.** Some newer scooters — particularly those with a **Motion SE08** ECU introduced for Euro 5 compliance — use a proprietary protocol that HUD ECU Hacker cannot fully support. If your scooter was registered after 2021 and HUD ECU Hacker consistently fails to connect despite correct hardware and settings, check the ECU label. If it reads "Motion" or "SE08 E5", you likely need a dedicated Motion diagnostic scanner instead. - ⏳ **Connection attempts may take multiple tries.** K-line timing is extremely sensitive. It is normal for the first 5–15 connection attempts to time out. Simply return to the Control tab and click Connect again. If it never connects after 20+ attempts with the ignition on, try a different COM port or reduce the baud rate via the software's Troubleshooting settings. - 💾 **Never use the Tuning / Flash functions unless you know what you are doing.** HUD ECU Hacker can read and write ECU flash memory and fuel maps. Incorrect values can make the scooter unrideable or damage the ECU. The diagnostic and DTC functions covered in this guide are safe; the Tuning tab is for experienced users only. ## Troubleshooting

## Frequently Asked Questions Does this work on macOS or Linux? HUD ECU Hacker is Windows-only. It does not run natively on macOS or Linux. You can use a Windows virtual machine (VMware, Parallels, VirtualBox) and pass through the USB adapter — most users report this works well. Alternatively, keep an old cheap Windows laptop (like the Lenovo ThinkPad shown in the photos) dedicated to scooter diagnostics. Can I use this on a Piaggio Vespa (Primavera, Zip, Sprint)? No — Piaggio uses its own proprietary diagnostic interface (Piaggio Diagnostic Tool / PDT), not the Delphi K-line protocol used by GY6 clones. HUD ECU Hacker is specifically for Chinese GY6 EFI systems with Delphi or Rongmao ECUs. Is HUD ECU Hacker really free? Yes, HUD ECU Hacker is free for diagnostics (reading data, reading and clearing fault codes, monitoring sensors). Advanced features such as ECU flash and map editing are unlocked with a small paid licence. For the purposes of this guide — setting up, connecting, and reading/clearing codes — everything is free. What fault codes are available on the GY6 Delphi ECU? The Delphi MT05 reports standard OBD2 DTC codes plus some manufacturer-specific codes covering: oxygen sensor faults, coolant temperature sensor, throttle position sensor (TPS), MAP sensor, IAT sensor, injector circuit, IACV (idle air control), and ignition coil. Refer to our [GY6 EFI CEL Flash Codes guide](gy6-efi-cel-flash-codes.html) for a full list of codes and their meanings. The 6-pin connector on my scooter looks different — could it still work? There are a few variants of the GY6 diagnostic connector. The most common is the 6-pin white rectangular connector shown in this guide. Some models use a 4-pin connector or a different housing. If your connector doesn't match, check the ECU label to confirm it is a Delphi MT05 — if it is, the wiring pinout is the same and an adapter may still exist. Post on a GY6-specific forum with photos for community guidance. ## Related Guides - [GY6 EFI CEL Flash Codes — Manual Diagnostic Mode](gy6-efi-cel-flash-codes.html) — decode check-engine blink patterns without any tools - [GY6 EFI Fuel Injection Troubleshooting](gy6-efi-fuel-injection-troubleshooting.html) — systematic guide to injection faults - [All Repair Guides](/repair-guides/index.html) {/* SOURCE_BOX_PLACEHOLDER */} **Last Updated:** 2026-05-12  |  **License:** CC BY-SA 4.0  |  _Have corrections or improvements?
