Complete OBD-2 DTC fault code reference for GY6 EFI scooters with Rongmao, Delphi, and Motion injection systems. Includes step-by-step diagnostic procedures…

import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; import SourceBox from '@components/SourceBox.astro'; **ℹ️ This page vs the flash code page:** Older GY6 EFI ECUs (KEIHIN PGM-FI clones) communicate faults as _blink sequences_ — no scanner needed. Modern Rongmao, Delphi, and Motion ECUs speak standard **OBD-2 DTCs** (P0xxx codes) and require an OBD-2 reader. This page covers the OBD-2 / DTC system only. ## What You Need To read and clear fault codes on a Rongmao / Delphi / Motion EFI system you need an OBD-2 reader. The ECU communicates over the K-line (ISO 9141-2) or CAN bus depending on the variant. The following tools are confirmed to work: - **Car Scanner** (Android / iOS) — free app, works with a generic ELM327 Bluetooth or Wi-Fi adapter - **HUD ECU Hacker** (Windows PC) — purpose-built for Rongmao/Delphi GY6 ECUs; allows reading, clearing, and remapping - Any generic OBD-2 scanner that supports ISO 9141-2 / KWP2000 **⚠️ Before reading codes:** Check the MIL (malfunction indicator lamp) is working correctly by verifying it illuminates on key-on. Clear any history codes first, then repeat the fault condition and re-read. A code that appears only in history but not as a current fault may have been a one-off transient event. ## Reading Codes with Car Scanner Connect a generic **ELM327 Bluetooth or Wi-Fi adapter** to the 6-pin OBD-2 diagnostic port (usually under the seat or near the battery). Open **Car Scanner** (Android / iOS), select the ELM327 adapter, and choose *Read fault codes*. The app will list any active P-codes — cross-reference them in the DTC table below. Use *Clear fault codes* after completing your repair to reset the MIL. ## Precautions (from Rongmao EFI Owner Manual) - Ensure battery positive and negative terminals are reliable and cannot be interchanged. When the engine is running, the battery cannot be disassembled. - If the fuel gauge alarm sounds, refuel as soon as possible — the fuel pump cannot operate in air or media other than fuel. - Do not arbitrarily disassemble vehicle parts, especially the fuel system (pipeline pressure approx. 250 kPa). Disassembly must be carried out by professional maintenance personnel to prevent fire risk. - Do not arbitrarily adjust the throttle valve door plate limit screw. Idle speed on EFI scooters is controlled automatically by the ECU via the IACV. - Vehicles may only use the same type of parts specified by the manufacturer. Turn off the ignition switch before disassembly or replacement of any electrical parts. - Never pierce the wiring harness to measure signals — use back-probing tools or proper breakout connectors. - Ensure the ECU temperature remains below 80 °C. ## DTC Reference Table — All Codes The following OBD-2 P-codes apply to GY6 EFI scooters using Rongmao, Delphi, and Motion injection systems. ## Symptom-Based Diagnostic Flows If you cannot read a fault code, or want to verify the code is the root cause, use these symptom-driven checklists directly from the Rongmao EFI Owner Manual. 🚫 Engine Cannot Start 1. Check battery voltage — should be 8–12 V 2. Crank engine; check cranking voltage remains above 8 V 3. Check starter motor operation 4. In winter: check oil and gearbox oil viscosity 5. Check engine rotation resistance is not excessive ⚡ Hard / Difficult to Start 1. Check fuel pump pressure — approx. 250 kPa at idle 2. Remove spark plug; check spark is normal 3. Check engine temperature sensor connector and signal 4. With slightly more throttle, check if engine starts — clean throttle body and bypass channel if yes 5. Pull injector; crank engine — check injector spray pattern 6. Check if spark plug is wet (flooding) — dry plug and combustion chamber 7. Check cylinder compression pressure 〰️ Unstable Idle 1. Check air filter and intake pipe for leaks or blockage 2. Check throttle body for carbon deposits in bypass channel 3. Check IACV operation 4. Check fuel pressure — approx. 250 kPa 5. Check injector for blockage 6. Verify correct spark plug type and condition 7. Check cylinder compression pressure 8. Check engine temperature sensor signal 9. Check TPS signal with throttle at idle ⬆️ High Idle 1. Check throttle cable for sticking or incorrect adjustment 2. Check idle pintle adjustment of throttle body 3. Check intake pipe for air leaks 4. Check IACV operation 5. Remove engine temperature sensor; check if engine runs well — change sensor if yes 📉 Poor Acceleration 1. Check air filter and intake pipe for blockage or leaks 2. Check fuel pressure — approx. 250 kPa 3. Remove spark plug — check if wet or dry 4. Check T-MAP sensor, TPS, and all connectors 5. Check injector for blockage 6. Check spark plug type and electrode gap 7. Check cylinder compression pressure 8. Check exhaust pipe for blockage 💥 Backfire 1. Remove spark plug; check spark is normal 2. Check ignition timing is correct 3. Check valve clearance for leakage 4. Check injector for blockage or leaking 5. Check oxygen sensor operation ## Before Starting Fault Analysis — Checklist From the Rongmao EFI Owner Manual — complete this checklist before beginning any fault code diagnosis: 1. Confirm the MIL lamp works correctly (illuminates on key-on self-check). 2. Clear history fault codes, then repeat the fault condition and re-read. 3. When a new fault code appears, note the exact conditions (hot/cold, idle/acceleration, etc.). 4. Visually inspect: check for fuel pipe leakage; check for blockage or damage to the intake pipe; check ground connections are secure; check all connectors are properly seated. 5. If any visual defect is found, repair it first before proceeding with fault code diagnosis. 6. If no cause is found after completing all steps: do not ignore maintenance items (cylinder pressure, mechanical timing, fuel quality). As a last resort, swap the ECU to test — if the fault disappears, the ECU was the root cause. ## Clearing DTCs On Rongmao / Delphi / Motion systems, codes must be cleared with an OBD-2 scanner — the battery-disconnect method is not guaranteed to clear stored codes on these ECUs (it will reset live data but not always non-volatile fault memory). Use Car Scanner or HUD ECU Hacker to send the "Clear fault codes" command after completing your repair. **⚠️ Always repair the root cause first.** Clearing a code without fixing the underlying fault will cause it to return within minutes of running the engine. ## Related Guides & Resources - [GY6 EFI CEL Flash Codes — older KEIHIN/clone ECUs without OBD-2](/diagnostics/gy6-efi-cel-flash-codes.html) - [GY6 EFI Fuel Injection Full Troubleshooting Guide](/diagnostics/gy6-efi-fuel-injection-troubleshooting.html) - [HUD ECU Hacker Setup Guide](/diagnostics/gy6-efi-hud-ecu-hacker-setup.html) - [Diagnosing Air Leaks and Vacuum Leaks](/diagnostics/gy6-air-leak-diagnosis.html) - [Ignition Coil Replacement Guide](/repair-guides/gy6-ignition-coil-guide.html)

import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; import SourceBox from '@components/SourceBox.astro'; Your EFI scooter runs fine at speed but dies the moment you come to a stop at a red light — unless you blip the throttle to keep it alive. This is one of the most common and easily fixed EFI idle faults on GY6 50cc and 150cc scooters. The root cause is almost always a Throttle Position Sensor (TPS) that is not fully registering "closed throttle," which prevents the ECU from activating the Idle Air Control (IAC) valve — the component responsible for maintaining idle speed. ## Applies To - GY6 139QMB Euro 4/5 EFI (50cc) — BTC Riva, La Souris Sourini/City, Santini Capri, AGM VX50 - GY6 157QMJ EFI (150cc) variants with Delphi MT05 or Motion ECU --- ⚠️ **Safety first:** Work on a cold or fully cooled engine only. Keep naked flames and smoking materials away from the fuel system at all times. Do not run the engine in an enclosed space. ## Video Guide --- ## Background: Why the ECU Needs to Know Throttle Is Fully Closed On a carbureted scooter, idle is maintained mechanically by the pilot jet and the idle air/fuel screw. On an EFI scooter, that job belongs to the **Idle Air Control (IAC) valve** — a motorised valve that the ECU opens slightly to let in extra air and keep the engine running at a stable idle speed when the throttle is fully closed. The ECU decides to engage the IAC based on the signal from the **Throttle Position Sensor (TPS)**. When the TPS output voltage drops to its fully-closed threshold (typically around 0.50–0.55 V on Delphi MT05 systems), the ECU recognises idle condition and activates IAC control. The problem arises when the **throttle cable has too much tension** — or the TPS is slightly rotated out of its optimal position — so that even with the throttle grip fully released, the throttle butterfly inside the body is not 100% closed. The TPS voltage stays slightly above the closed-throttle threshold. The ECU interprets this as "partial throttle open" and therefore: 1. Does **not** activate the IAC valve 2. Does **not** apply idle enrichment 3. Applies a slightly **lean** fuelling map (as if you are gently rolling on) The result: at a stop, with the butterfly valve essentially closed but the ECU unaware of it, air supply collapses and the mixture goes rich — the engine stumbles and stalls. Giving it a small blip of throttle temporarily restores airflow and keeps it running, which is the tell-tale symptom. --- ## Symptoms - Engine stalls when coming to a complete stop (traffic lights, junctions) - Keeping a small amount of throttle prevents the stall - Idle is unstable or hunts (surges up and down) when warm - No fault codes stored — the TPS voltage is in range, just slightly off the closed-throttle threshold - Scooter runs normally at all other throttle positions 💡 **No CEL?** This fault usually does not trigger a Check Engine Light because the TPS voltage is technically within the valid operating range — it is just not low enough to signal "fully closed." That is why it is easy to overlook. --- ## Fix 1 — Relax the Throttle Cable The quickest fix is to reduce cable tension so the throttle butterfly can fully close. ### Step 1 — Locate the throttle cable adjuster 1. At the handlebar, pull back the rubber boot on the throttle housing to expose the cable adjuster (a barrel nut threaded into the housing). 2. Loosen the lock nut (turn anti-clockwise) if present. ### Step 2 — Add cable slack 1. Turn the barrel adjuster **clockwise** (thread it inward) to add slack to the cable — typically 1–2 full turns. 2. Check that the throttle grip returns fully and snaps back freely when released. There should be 2–3 mm of free play at the grip before the throttle begins to open. 3. Re-tighten the lock nut. ⚠️ **Do not add excessive slack.** The throttle must still open fully at wide open throttle (WOT). Check that the grip twists all the way to its stop and that the throttle snaps back crisply. A sluggish return is a safety risk. ### Step 3 — Test ride Start the engine, warm it up for 2–3 minutes, then test at idle with the scooter stationary. If the stall is gone, you are done. If the idle is still unstable, proceed to Fix 2. --- ## Fix 2 — Rotate the TPS Body If relaxing the cable alone does not resolve the stall, the TPS itself may be sitting slightly off its optimal closed-throttle position. Rotating it a small amount lowers the closed-throttle voltage to the point where the ECU correctly engages the IAC. 💡 This procedure does not require any special tools. You are physically rotating the TPS housing — the same adjustment described in the TPS replacement guide — without removing the sensor. ### Step 1 — Locate the TPS on the throttle body The TPS is the small sensor clipped onto the side of the throttle body, connected by a 3-wire plug. It sits on the end of the throttle shaft — the same shaft the butterfly valve and the throttle cable drum are connected to. ### Step 2 — Loosen the TPS mounting screws 1. Using a Phillips screwdriver, loosen (do not remove) the two screws that hold the TPS body to the throttle body. Turn each screw anti-clockwise by about half a turn — just enough to allow the TPS to rotate. ### Step 3 — Rotate the TPS and test 1. With the ignition ON and the engine off (or running at idle), grasp the TPS body and rotate it slowly toward the **closed throttle direction** — this is usually a small rotation in the direction that lowers the signal voltage. 2. Rotate by the smallest amount you can feel — typically 1–2 mm of arc at the outer edge of the sensor housing. 3. Restart the engine and check whether idle is stable and the stall at stop is gone. 4. If not, rotate a fraction further and retest. Do this iteratively in small steps. ⚠️ **Do not over-rotate.** If you rotate too far, the ECU will think the throttle is permanently in a sub-idle state and idle quality will worsen. The target is the smallest rotation that eliminates the stall. ### Step 4 — Lock the TPS in position Once the idle is stable and the scooter no longer stalls at a stop: 1. Hold the TPS in position and tighten both mounting screws firmly — but do not over-torque them; the TPS housing is plastic. 2. Perform a final check: open the throttle to wide open and release it. Confirm the engine returns to a stable idle immediately. --- ## Setting the TPS With a Multimeter (No Scanner Needed) A basic multimeter set to DC voltage is all you need to adjust the TPS precisely — no OBD2 scanner or laptop required. This gives you a definitive target to hit instead of adjusting by feel. ### Step 1 — Identify the three TPS pins The TPS connector has three wires. On virtually all GY6 EFI throttle bodies (Delphi MT05 and Motion ECU systems) the pin functions are:
Wire colourFunctionWhat to connect your meter to
Green or white5 V reference from ECUDo not probe this for the adjustment
BlackGround (0 V)Negative (COM) probe — black lead
Yellow, orange, or blueSignal output to ECUPositive probe — red lead
💡 **Not sure which wire is which?** With the ignition ON, probe between any wire and a known chassis ground. The wire that reads a steady 4.8–5.2 V is the reference; the wire that reads 0 V is ground; the remaining wire is the signal. ### Step 2 — Back-probe the connector Do **not** unplug the TPS connector — the ECU must be powered and the circuit must be complete for the reading to be valid. Instead, insert the multimeter probes from the **rear** of the connector alongside the existing wires (back-probing). A sewing pin or thin paperclip pushed gently into the back of the connector socket works if your probes are too thick to reach the terminals directly. 1. Set your multimeter to **DC Voltage**, range **0–20 V** (or auto-range). 2. Connect the black (COM) lead to the **black ground wire** terminal. 3. Connect the red lead to the **signal wire** terminal (yellow/orange/blue). 4. Turn the ignition ON. The meter should display a reading immediately. ### Step 3 — Read the closed-throttle voltage With the throttle grip fully released (no tension at all on the cable): - **Target:** 0.48–0.55 V - If you read **above 0.55 V**: the TPS is registering slightly open — this is the cause of your stall. Proceed to Step 4. - If you already read 0.48–0.55 V but the scooter still stalls, the issue may be the IAC valve rather than TPS calibration — see the FAQ below. ### Step 4 — Adjust while watching the meter With the TPS mounting screws loosened half a turn (as described in Fix 2 above): 1. With the ignition ON and the multimeter connected, watch the live voltage reading on the display. 2. **Slowly rotate the TPS body** in small increments — the direction that causes the displayed voltage to drop toward the target range. 3. Stop when the reading stabilises between **0.50 and 0.55 V** with the throttle fully released. 4. Hold the TPS firmly in position and tighten the mounting screws without letting it move. ### Step 5 — Verify the full sweep Once locked in position, perform the full sweep check: 1. Throttle fully closed → reading should be **0.50–0.55 V** 2. Slowly open to half throttle → voltage should rise smoothly and continuously to approximately **2.0–2.5 V** 3. Wide open throttle (WOT) → reading should reach approximately **4.3–4.8 V** 4. Release → voltage should return cleanly to **0.50–0.55 V** with no hesitation or jump ⚠️ **Any flat spot, sudden jump, or drop-out during the sweep** (where the voltage sticks at one value then skips) indicates a worn TPS sliding contact. In that case the sensor needs replacement — see the [GY6 EFI TPS Sensor Diagnosis guide](/diagnostics/gy6-efi-tps-sensor-diagnosis.html). A smooth sweep from 0.5 V to 4.5 V and back is your confirmation that the TPS is both correctly set and in good health. --- ## Troubleshooting
Symptom after fixLikely causeAction
Still stalls at stopTPS not rotated far enough, or IAC valve faultyRotate TPS a fraction further; if still no improvement, check IAC valve operation and wiring
Idle too high after fixTPS rotated too far or cable over-slackenedReturn TPS to previous position; re-adjust cable to restore correct free play
Throttle stiff or slow to returnCable slack excessive or cable kinkedReduce slack at adjuster; inspect cable routing for tight bends
CEL lit after adjustmentTPS voltage outside valid range (too low)Rotate TPS back slightly; target 0.50–0.55 V at closed throttle
--- ## Frequently Asked Questions
Could this be an IAC valve fault rather than a TPS issue? ＋
It is possible, but TPS calibration is the far more common cause and should always be checked first because it costs nothing to fix. A failed IAC valve usually causes a much more severe idle problem — the engine will barely idle at all, even when warm and in motion. If relaxing the cable and rotating the TPS does not help, test the IAC valve resistance (typically 20–30 Ω across its terminals) and confirm it is receiving a PWM signal from the ECU.
Will this fault ever throw a fault code? ＋
Rarely. Because the TPS voltage is within its valid operating range (just slightly above the closed-throttle threshold rather than completely out of range), most ECUs will not store a DTC. If a P0121 or similar code is present, follow the GY6 EFI TPS Sensor Diagnosis guide to rule out a defective sensor first.
Does this apply to carbureted GY6 models? ＋
No. Carbureted engines do not have a TPS or IAC valve. If a carbureted scooter stalls at idle, the cause is almost always a blocked pilot jet or incorrect idle mixture screw setting — see the GY6 Carburetor Pilot Jet guide.
My scooter has been fine for years — why has this only started happening? ＋
Throttle cables stretch slightly over time, and the plastic TPS housing can shift very gradually from vibration. A small amount of cable stretch alone is often enough to push the closed-throttle TPS voltage just above the IAC activation threshold after many thousands of kilometres.
Do I need an expensive multimeter for the voltage check? ＋
No. Any basic digital multimeter with a DC Voltage setting will work — even a €10 unit from a hardware store. You are measuring a stable DC signal between 0.5 V and 4.5 V, which is well within the range of the cheapest meters. An auto-ranging meter is slightly more convenient but not required.
What if I cannot reach 0.5 V no matter how far I rotate the TPS? ＋
If you have already relaxed the throttle cable fully and rotated the TPS to its mechanical limit in the correct direction but the voltage still reads above 0.55 V at closed throttle, the throttle body butterfly is likely not seating fully closed due to carbon build-up on the butterfly valve edges or a stuck/binding throttle shaft. Clean the throttle body bore and butterfly plate with throttle body cleaner, then repeat the adjustment.

## Introduction

If your GY6 EFI scooter won't start, idles roughly, or stalls, work through this checklist in order before replacing parts. Most EFI faults on GY6 scooters come down to a handful of root causes: poor grounding, insufficient fuel pressure, air leaks, or a TPS that needs resetting. This guide applies to BTC Riva, La Souris Sourini, Santini Capri, and other GY6-platform scooters fitted with Rongmao, Delphi, or Rolling Wrench ProBld EFI systems.

<Callout type="warn">
  Always confirm ignition is off and the fuel system is depressurised before disconnecting fuel lines. Fuel sprayed onto a hot engine is a fire hazard.
</Callout>

## Tools & Parts Needed

- Multimeter (DC voltage and resistance)
- Fuel pressure gauge rated to at least 70 PSI (5 bar)
- OBD2 / KKL 6-pin diagnostic cable (for fault code reading)
- Carburetor cleaner spray (air leak detection — do NOT use near flame)
- 8-gauge ground wire and ring terminals

---

## Step-by-Step Diagnostic Checklist

### Step 1 — Verify Ground Connection

A weak ground is the single most common cause of EFI faults on GY6 scooters.

1. Locate the EFI system's ground wire (usually black, from the ECU harness).
2. Run a dedicated 8-gauge wire from the **negative battery terminal directly to the starter motor mounting bolt**.
3. Connect the EFI system's ground wire to that same bolt, sharing the earthing point.
4. Check with a multimeter: resistance between battery negative and ECU ground should be < 0.2 Ω.

<Callout type="tip">
  Do not rely on chassis grounds through frame bolts painted or corroded with oxidation — always use a direct battery-to-starter dedicated ground.
</Callout>

### Step 2 — Check Fuel Supply to Tank

An air bubble at the inlet can prevent the pump from priming.

1. Confirm the fuel tank is at least one-quarter full.
2. Trace the fuel inlet line from the pump to the tank. **No part of the inlet line should run above the bottom of the fuel tank** — any high loop creates an air bubble the pump cannot overcome.
3. Disconnect the inlet line at the pump and allow fuel to flow briefly onto a rag to purge any air pocket, then reconnect.

### Step 3 — Measure Fuel Pressure at Injector

1. Connect a fuel pressure gauge between the fuel pump outlet and the injector supply line using a T-fitting.
2. Key on (engine not started) — the pump should prime and hold pressure within 5 seconds.
3. **Target pressure: 42 PSI (2.9 bar).** Low pressure indicates a failing pump or clogged filter; high pressure indicates a faulty regulator.

| Pressure | Likely Cause |
|----------|--------------|
| < 35 PSI | Weak pump, clogged inline filter, or air in inlet |
| 42 PSI ± 3 | Normal |
| > 50 PSI | Faulty fuel pressure regulator |

### Step 4 — Check for Air Leaks at Intake

Air leaks cause the ECU to run lean, leading to rough idle, hesitation, or stalling.

<Callout type="warn">
  Use carburetor cleaner for leak detection only with the engine cold or idling at low RPM. Keep a fire extinguisher nearby and do not use near ignition sources.
</Callout>

1. Confirm the plastic intake manifold spacer is **removed** — EFI systems tuned for a specific throttle body bore do not use this spacer.
2. Start the engine and allow it to idle.
3. Spray short bursts of carburetor cleaner around the intake manifold joint, throttle body clocking flange, and any vacuum ports.
4. If engine RPM changes (rises then drops) when sprayed, that location is sucking air — reseal with fresh clamps or RTV sealant and re-test.

### Step 5 — Read Fault Codes (OBD2)

1. With the ignition off, plug the KKL OBD2 cable into the 6-pin diagnostic connector (typically under the seat or near the battery).
2. Open HUD ECU Hacker or a compatible OBD2 app and key on.
3. Navigate to **Fault Codes / DTC** — note all stored codes.
4. Clear codes and re-test after completing other steps. Codes that reappear after clearing indicate active faults.

Common codes and their meanings are documented in the [GY6 EFI OBD-2 DTC Fault Codes guide](/diagnostics/gy6-efi-obd2-dtc-fault-codes.html).

### Step 6 — Reset the Throttle Position Sensor (TPS)

A TPS out of calibration causes idle instability, stalling on deceleration, and hesitation off idle.

1. Key on, engine off.
2. Follow the TPS reset procedure for your ECU variant — typically: key on → slowly open throttle from fully closed to fully open 3 times → key off → wait 10 seconds → key on.
3. Alternatively, connect the OBD2 cable and use the ECU software's **TPS Reset / Throttle Adaptation** function.
4. After reset, start the engine and verify idle stabilises within 30 seconds of warm-up.

For a detailed TPS diagnosis and replacement guide, see [GY6 EFI TPS Sensor Diagnosis & Replacement](/diagnostics/gy6-efi-tps-sensor-diagnosis.html).

### Step 7 — Adjust the Idle Air/Fuel Screw

The finger screw (mixture screw) on the throttle body is a manual trim for the idle zone (below approximately 2,800 RPM). The ECU does not auto-tune at idle.

1. With the engine warm and at idle, turn the screw in (clockwise) by ¼-turn increments and wait 10 seconds after each.
2. Turn back out if idle drops or engine hunts.
3. Find the position where idle RPM is **highest and most stable** — this is the correct setting.
4. If the engine stalls when coming to a stop from road speed, this screw is the adjustment to make.

### Step 8 — Verify Woodruff Key and Magneto Timing

If none of the above resolves a no-start:

1. Remove the left engine cover and inspect the magneto rotor.
2. Confirm the **woodruff key slot on the magneto rotor is fully seated over the woodruff key on the crankshaft**. A displaced woodruff key throws ignition timing off completely and causes no-start with no spark fault code.
3. Remove the rotor with a flywheel puller if needed, inspect the key and slot for damage, and reinstall with the key seated.

<Callout type="danger">
  Never attempt to hammer the rotor onto the crankshaft — this damages the key slot and crankshaft taper. Always use a flywheel puller for removal and hand-tighten plus torque spec for installation (typically 35–40 Nm).
</Callout>

### Step 9 — Confirm Correct EFI Kit for Engine Size

If the scooter was recently converted to EFI or the ECU was replaced:

- A **150cc kit (157QMJ)** uses different injector sizing, fuel maps, and throttle body bore than a **125cc kit (152QMI)**.
- Using the wrong kit results in chronic rich or lean running that no amount of adjustment will correct — the ECU must match the engine displacement.

### Step 10 — Check the Fuel Pump Regulator

A failing pressure regulator allows pressure to bleed off after the pump stops, causing hard hot-start and lean surging.

1. Run the pump until pressure is at 42 PSI.
2. Key off — note pressure on the gauge.
3. If pressure drops below 30 PSI within 2 minutes, the check valve in the pump or the pressure regulator is leaking.
4. Replace the integrated pump/regulator assembly.

---

## Specifications Summary

| Parameter | Specification |
|-----------|--------------|
| Fuel pressure (static) | 42 PSI (2.9 bar) |
| Ground resistance (battery neg to ECU) | < 0.2 Ω |
| Idle RPM (warm, GY6 150cc EFI) | 1,400–1,800 RPM |
| TPS voltage at idle (closed throttle) | ~0.5 V |
| TPS voltage at WOT (wide open throttle) | ~4.5 V |

---

## Next Steps if Fault Persists

If all 10 steps pass but the fault remains:

1. Verify the fuel injector is spraying — disconnect the return line and observe injector spray pattern.
2. Swap the ECU for a known-good unit to rule out ECU failure.
3. Contact the EFI manufacturer for an ECU re-flash with updated fuel maps.

import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; import SourceBox from '@components/SourceBox.astro'; The Throttle Position Sensor (TPS) is a variable resistor mounted on the throttle body of GY6 EFI scooters. As you open the throttle, a sliding contact inside the TPS changes resistance, sending a voltage signal to the ECU that represents throttle opening angle. The ECU uses this data — alongside the MAP sensor and O2 sensor — to calculate the correct fuel injection duration and ignition timing. On Euro 4 and Euro 5 GY6 50cc scooters (2017 onwards), the TPS is part of the throttle body assembly used by the Delphi MT05 or Motion EFI systems. A faulty TPS causes erratic fuelling, stuttering, poor idle, or a complete no-start with a CEL (Check Engine Light) flashing. ## Fault Codes for TPS Faults Most GY6 EFI systems flash a code sequence via the CEL/MIL light. On Delphi MT05-based systems:
DTC CodeMeaningCEL Blink Pattern
P0121TPS signal out of range — intermittent1 long, 2 short
P0122TPS circuit low (below 0.2 V)1 long, 2 short (variant)
P0123TPS circuit high (above 4.8 V)1 long, 2 short (variant)
—TPS not connected or contact problemCEL permanent on
For GY6 EFI scooters sold in Belgium and the Netherlands (BTC Riva, La Souris Sourini/City, AGM VX50), the fault code list published by motorroller.de covers the 4T50E4 ECU blink code protocol used on many Chinese Euro 4 50cc scooters. See the [GY6 EFI OBD-2 DTC Fault Codes guide](/diagnostics/gy6-efi-obd2-dtc-fault-codes.html) for the complete list. ## Symptoms of a Failing TPS - Engine stutters or hesitates when opening throttle from idle - Erratic idle speed — surging up and down - Poor fuel economy or black exhaust smoke (ECU over-fuelling due to incorrect TPS signal) - CEL/MIL illuminated — flashing P0121, P0122, or P0123 - Engine runs fine at idle but cuts out under load - Hard starting (ECU applies incorrect starting enrichment) ## Step 1 — Visual Inspection Before testing with a multimeter, inspect the TPS physically: 1. Locate the throttle body on the intake side of the engine. The TPS is a small sensor plugged into the side of the throttle body with a 3-wire connector. 2. Unplug the connector and inspect both the sensor pins and the harness connector for: - Corrosion (green or white residue on the pins) - Bent or pushed-back pins - Cracked or chafed wiring near the connector 3. Reconnect and wiggle the connector while the engine idles. If this changes idle behaviour, the connection is intermittent — clean and re-pin before replacing the sensor. ## Step 2 — Voltage Test (Live Signal) This test checks whether the TPS is producing a correct, smooth voltage output as the throttle is opened. **Setup:** 1. With the ignition ON and engine off (or running), back-probe the TPS connector with a multimeter set to DC Voltage. 2. Identify the three wires: - **5 V reference (Vref)** — from ECU, typically green or white wire - **Ground** — black wire - **Signal output** — yellow, orange, or blue wire (goes back to ECU) 3. Measure between the Signal wire and Ground wire. **Expected readings:**
Throttle PositionExpected Voltage
Fully closed (idle)0.4–0.7 V
Half throttle (~45°)~2.0–2.5 V
Wide open throttle (WOT)4.0–4.8 V
**Key test:** Slowly open and close the throttle while watching the multimeter. The voltage must change **smoothly and continuously** — no sudden jumps, flat spots, or drop-outs. Any discontinuity in the sweep means the sliding contact inside the TPS is worn or damaged and the sensor must be replaced. If the voltage is stuck at 0 V or 5 V regardless of throttle position, check the 5 V reference supply and ground first. If those are correct, the TPS itself is faulty. ## Step 3 — Reference Voltage Check 1. Unplug the TPS connector. 2. With ignition ON, measure between the Vref pin in the harness connector and the Ground pin. 3. Expected: **4.8–5.2 V DC**. 4. If you read 0 V or battery voltage: the ECU or wiring harness has a fault — not the TPS. ## Step 4 — Replacing the TPS On most GY6 EFI throttle bodies, the TPS is a bolt-on sensor on the throttle body: 1. Unplug the 3-wire TPS connector. 2. Remove the 2 Phillips screws securing the TPS to the throttle body. 3. Slide the old TPS off the throttle shaft. 4. Fit the new TPS — align the slot on the sensor's drive with the throttle shaft flat. 5. Reinstall and tighten the screws finger-tight. **Do not fully tighten yet** — the TPS may need adjustment. **TPS Adjustment (Closed Throttle Voltage):** 1. With the ignition ON, measure the TPS signal voltage with the throttle fully closed. 2. Rotate the TPS body slightly while watching the voltage until it reads **0.50–0.55 V** (fully closed position per Delphi MT05 spec). 3. Once set, tighten the mounting screws firmly. 4. Recheck: open the throttle to WOT and confirm voltage reaches approximately 4.5 V, then returns to 0.5 V when released. **Clear fault codes after replacement.** If you have an OBD2 KKL cable and HUD ECU Hacker, clear any stored P0121–P0123 codes after fitting the new sensor. Without a scanner, disconnect the battery for 5 minutes to reset the ECU — the CEL will extinguish if the fault is resolved. ## Replacement TPS Part Notes Euro 4/5 GY6 50cc scooters (BTC Riva, La Souris, AGM etc.) use a TPS integrated into the throttle body for the Delphi MT05 or Motion EFI system. The TPS and MAP sensor are often combined into a single unit on these platforms. When ordering a replacement, specify: - **ECU type:** Delphi MT05 or Motion (check the ECU label under the seat panel) - **Engine code:** 139QMB (50cc) or 157QMJ (150cc) - **Euro standard:** Euro 4 or Euro 5

Work through this checklist in order — most no-start problems can be diagnosed and fixed in under an hour using only basic hand tools. ## Quick Symptom Guide (Start Here)

Starts with choke but dies without itPilot jet blocked, mixture too leanSection 2B
Starts cold but not hot (or hot but not cold)Auto-choke malfunctionSection 2C
Kick-start works but electric starter doesn'tBattery, starter motor, or relay faultSection 4
## Section 1 — Spark ### 1A — Basic Spark Test 1. Remove the spark plug lead from the spark plug. 2. Remove the spark plug using a spark plug socket (usually 16 mm or 18 mm). 3. Reconnect the spark plug lead to the plug and rest the threaded body of the plug against a bare metal part of the engine (ground contact is essential). 4. Have an assistant crank the engine while you observe the electrode gap. 5. PASS: A fat blue-white spark jumps across the gap — spark system is good, proceed to Section 2. 6. FAIL: No spark, weak orange spark, or intermittent spark — proceed to 1B. ### 1B — Spark Plug Condition Inspect the removed spark plug tip:
Plug AppearanceDiagnosis
Light tan/grey — dryNormal. Plug is probably fine. Check ignition system.
Black, sooty, dryRunning rich or plug too cold. Clean or replace plug.
Black, oilyOil getting past rings — compression issue, possible engine wear.
White/light grey, eroded electrodeRunning lean or plug too hot. Check fuel system.
Wet with fuelEngine is flooded. Remove plug, crank 5× with throttle fully open to clear.
Replace the spark plug if in doubt — they cost very little and eliminate the plug as a variable. Standard NGK plug for all GY6 50cc–150cc (139QMB, 152QMI, 157QMJ): **`CR7HSA`** (resistor type, recommended for EFI and CDI scooters). Non-resistor equivalent: `C7HSA`. Iridium upgrade: `CR7HIX`. Thread: 10 mm, reach: 12.7 mm, gap: 0.6–0.7 mm. The older Chinese-market codes `A7TC` / `A7RTC` cross-reference to `C7HSA` / `CR7HSA` respectively — use the NGK part number when sourcing. ### 1C — Ignition System Check If a new plug still shows no spark: 1. **Check the kill switch** — flip it to the RUN position. Test with it disconnected entirely (short the wires). 2. **Check the main fuse** — usually a 10A or 15A blade fuse in the wiring loom near the battery or under the seat. A blown fuse means no power to the CDI unit. 3. **Inspect the CDI unit** — the small black box connected to several wires, typically under the seat or behind the panels. Check the connector for corrosion or pushed-out pins. A faulty CDI is a common cause of total no-spark on GY6 engines. 4. **Check the ignition coil** — disconnect and test resistance: primary winding should read **0.4–0.6 Ω**; secondary (to plug cap) should read **4–6 kΩ**. 5. **Check the stator pick-up coil** (pulse generator coil) — resistance typically **80–120 Ω**. Located inside the left engine cover behind the flywheel. ## Section 2 — Fuel ### 2A — Basic Fuel Flow Check 1. Ensure there is fuel in the tank (check visually — fuel gauges on Chinese scooters are notoriously inaccurate). 2. Locate the fuel petcock (tap) on the underside of the tank. Ensure it is in the **ON** or **RES** position. 3. Disconnect the fuel line from the carburetor inlet. Place a container below and briefly open the petcock — fuel should flow freely. If it trickles or doesn't flow, the petcock filter is blocked. Remove and clean the petcock screen. ### 2B — Carburetor Check 1. Remove the float bowl (one screw at the bottom of the carburetor). Check for fuel presence — if empty, fuel is not reaching the carb (check petcock and fuel line). If full, fuel delivery is OK. 2. Inspect the main jet and pilot jet for blockage. Even a partially blocked pilot jet causes lean stumble and no-start when cold. Clean with carburetor cleaner and compressed air — never use wire through the jet orifice. 3. Check the float needle valve: a stuck or worn needle valve floods the engine. If the plug was found wet, this is likely the cause. 4. Check the emulsion tube passages are clear (the brass tube with holes inside the carburetor body). ### 2C — Auto-Choke (Thermostatic Enricher) Check Most GY6 50cc scooters use an automatic choke (enricher valve) instead of a manual choke lever. It is a wax-element or bimetal device that opens when cold (rich mixture) and closes when warm. 1. Locate the auto-choke on the side of the carburetor — a small cylindrical device with a wire or hose attached. 2. **Cold test:** Disconnect the choke from the carburetor. When cold, the choke plunger should be extended (pushed out). If it is retracted when cold, the choke is stuck open — the engine will run lean and refuse to start cold. 3. **Warm test:** After warming the choke with a heat gun or hot water for 1 minute, the plunger should retract. If it stays extended, it is stuck — the engine will run rich when warm and flood after warm-up. 4. If the auto-choke is malfunctioning, replace it (inexpensive and widely available for GY6) or temporarily disconnect and use a manually operated enrichment procedure (crack throttle open slightly when starting cold). ## Section 3 — Compression ### 3A — Basic Compression Check 1. Remove the spark plug. 2. Cover the spark plug hole with your thumb and crank the engine (kick or electric). 3. PASS: Your thumb is pushed off firmly — there is compression. Proceed to Sections 1 and 2 for the no-start cause. 4. FAIL: Little or no resistance felt — low or zero compression. Proceed to 3B. ### 3B — Compression Test (with gauge) A proper compression gauge gives a reading. Specifications for GY6:
EngineMinimum AcceptableHealthy Range
GY6 50cc (139QMB)70 PSI (4.8 bar)90–120 PSI (6.2–8.3 bar)
GY6 150cc (157QMJ)80 PSI (5.5 bar)100–130 PSI (6.9–9.0 bar)
Low compression causes: worn or stuck piston rings, burned valves, blown head gasket, worn cylinder bore, or valves with zero clearance (not seating properly). Check valve clearance first (see the [valve adjustment guide](/repair-guides/gy6-valve-adjustment-guide.html)) before condemning rings or bore. ## Section 4 — Starter System & Battery ### 4A — Battery Check 1. Check battery voltage with a multimeter: **12.6 V or above** = fully charged; **below 12.0 V** = discharged or failing. 2. If the starter sounds slow or clicks but doesn't crank, the battery is likely the cause. Charge for 4 hours and retest. 3. GY6 scooter batteries (typically YTX5L-BS or YTX7A-BS) have a short lifespan — 2–3 years is typical. If the battery is over 2 years old, replacement is the most reliable fix. ### 4B — Starter Relay (Solenoid) 1. When pressing the electric starter, you should hear a click from the starter relay (located near the battery). No click = relay or wiring fault. 2. Bypass test: use a jumper wire directly between the starter motor terminal and the battery positive. If the engine cranks, the starter relay or its wiring is faulty. 3. The relay can be tested with a multimeter or simply replaced — they cost very little and are standard across all GY6 scooters. ## Checklist Summary
#CheckTool Needed
1Spark plug — condition and spark testPlug socket, assistant
2Kill switch and fuseVisual / multimeter
3CDI unit connector — clean contactsContact spray
4Fuel in tank — visually confirmNone
5Fuel petcock — open and flowing freelyContainer
6Float bowl — fuel present and jets clearFlat-head screwdriver
7Auto-choke — functioning correctlyVisual / heat source
8Compression — thumb test or gaugeCompression gauge
9Valve clearance — set to specFeeler gauge
10Battery voltage ≥ 12.6 VMultimeter
11Starter relay — clicking when operatedMultimeter / jumper wire
� **Pro tip:** When a GY6 starts with easy starting fluid or carb cleaner sprayed into the intake but won't start on its own, you have confirmed spark and compression are good — the problem is always in the fuel system (petcock, jet, auto-choke, or fuel line).

import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; ## What Is the Side Stand Kill Switch? The **side stand kill switch** (also called a side stand inhibitor or kickstand switch) is a safety device that prevents the engine from running while the side stand is deployed. The switch is mounted at the base of the side stand pivot. When the stand is down, the switch opens the ignition circuit, cutting power to the CDI unit or ECU and stopping the engine (or preventing it from starting). This is an important safety feature — but the switch is exposed to road dirt, water, and corrosion, and it is one of the **most common electrical causes of a no-start condition** on older scooters. The switch can fail in the open position, which makes the ECU or CDI think the side stand is always down, even when it is fully retracted. ## How to Quickly Check (First Test) ### The Stand-Up Test 1. Ensure the side stand is **fully retracted (up)** and you are sitting on the scooter. 2. Attempt to start the engine normally. 3. If it does not start, try **pushing the side stand down and back up again** several times. Sometimes the switch contact is dirty and this mechanical cycling cleans the contact momentarily. 4. Now try starting again with the stand fully up. 5. Starts: The switch contact was dirty or sticking. Clean or replace the switch. 6. Still won't start: Proceed to the multimeter test below. ## Reference Video Complete walkthrough of diagnosing and testing the side stand kill switch on a GY6 scooter. ## Locating the Side Stand Switch The switch is a small black plastic or metal unit mounted on the frame near the base of the side stand pivot. It has either two or three wires connected to it. Trace the wires from the side stand hinge point upward — they typically route along the frame and connect to a 2-pin or 3-pin inline connector under the bodywork or under the seat. ## Full Diagnostic Procedure ### Step 1 — Visual Inspection 1. Locate the side stand switch and its wiring connector. 2. Check the connector for **corrosion, green/white oxidation, or moisture** inside the connector housing. 3. Check the wires close to the switch for chafing against the frame, cracked insulation, or bare wire touching metal. 4. Check the switch body itself — the plunger or lever that the stand actuates should move freely when you operate the stand by hand. ### Step 2 — Bypass Test (Temporary) This test confirms whether the side stand switch circuit is the cause of the no-start, without needing a multimeter. **⚠ Safety:** Bypassing the side stand switch removes the safety interlock. Only do this as a temporary diagnostic test with the scooter on its centre stand. Do not ride the scooter with the switch bypassed permanently. 1. Locate the **2-pin or 3-pin connector** in the side stand switch wiring loom (typically under the bodywork near the left footboard area). 2. Disconnect the connector. 3. Using a short length of wire or a paperclip, **bridge the two terminals** on the loom side of the connector (the side that goes into the harness, not the side that goes to the switch). 4. Attempt to start the engine. 5. Engine starts: The side stand switch is confirmed faulty. The switch needs to be cleaned or replaced. 6. Engine still won't start: The side stand switch is not the cause. Remove your bridge wire, reconnect the connector, and continue to the full no-start troubleshooting guide. **Note on 3-wire switches:** Some scooters use a 3-wire inhibitor switch that interacts with the gear/neutral switch. If the bypass test does not work, try bridging a different pair of terminals. Consult your model's wiring diagram. ### Step 3 — Multimeter Test This confirms the switch is operating correctly (or not) before you purchase a replacement. 1. Disconnect the switch connector. 2. Set your multimeter to **continuity / resistance (Ω)** mode. 3. Probe the two terminals on the **switch side** of the connector. 4. With the side stand **up (retracted)**: the circuit should be **closed (continuity / near 0 Ω)**. 5. With the side stand **down (deployed)**: the circuit should be **open (no continuity / infinite Ω)**. 6. PASS: Switch behaves as described — switch is working correctly. Look for a wiring fault between switch and CDI/ECU. 7. FAIL: Switch shows open circuit with stand up, or closed circuit with stand down — switch has failed. Replace it. ## Cleaning a Dirty Switch 1. Disconnect the switch connector. 2. Spray a small amount of **electrical contact cleaner** into the switch body through any available opening. 3. Operate the side stand up and down 10–15 times to work the cleaner through the contact mechanism. 4. Allow to dry for 5 minutes. 5. Reconnect the switch and retest. 6. Also clean the connector terminals: use contact cleaner on a small brush, or use a connector cleaning tool. Apply dielectric grease to the connector pins before reassembly to prevent future corrosion. ## Replacing the Side Stand Switch
StepDetail
1. Source replacement switchGY6 side stand switches are largely standardised. Search for "GY6 side stand switch" or "kickstand inhibitor switch 2-pin." Piaggio/Vespa units are manufacturer-specific — use OEM part number.
2. Remove old switchTypically one or two M6 bolts. Disconnect wiring connector.
3. Install new switchPosition switch so the actuator lever contacts the side stand arm correctly when the stand is deployed. Test stand movement before fully tightening.
4. Route wiringEnsure wires are routed away from moving parts (stand pivot, exhaust). Secure with a cable tie if needed.
5. TestConfirm engine starts with stand up and cuts out (or does not start) with stand down.
**Permanent bypass (not recommended, but documented):** Some riders permanently bridge the side stand switch to eliminate the circuit entirely. This means the engine will run with the stand down — a genuine safety hazard on a scooter, as the stand can dig into the road surface when cornering. Replace the switch instead of bypassing it permanently. ## Related Guides - [GY6 Scooter Won't Start — Full Troubleshooting Checklist](gy6-no-start-troubleshooting.html) - [Dirty Handlebar Buttons Causing No-Start](gy6-dirty-buttons-no-start.html) Sources: GY6 and Piaggio wiring diagrams; community diagnostic data from scootdawg.com; video reference: YouTube. import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; import SourceBox from '@components/SourceBox.astro'; This guide covers systematic ignition fault-finding for all 50cc Piaggio and Gilera 2-stroke scooters (plus some geared 50cc engines such as Derbi which share the same ignition architecture). You will need a multimeter. The Piaggio/Gilera ignition system is completely independent from the rest of the bike's electrics — it is unaffected by battery condition, charging system faults, or other electrical problems — which makes it straightforward to test methodically. ️ **Important — spark strength matters:** Seeing a spark out of the engine is not enough. A weak spark may jump a 1 mm gap in open air but fail to fire the compressed mixture in the cylinder. The spark must be able to jump **at least 7 mm in open air**, which corresponds to over 15,000 V. Use a dedicated spark tester with an adjustable gap, or improvise with two screws in a wooden block set 7–10 mm apart. ## Component Overview The Piaggio 2-stroke ignition circuit has four main parts:
ComponentWire colourFunction
Pickup coilRed → CDIGenerates a voltage pulse each time a lobe on the flywheel passes, triggering the CDI to fire
CDI earthWhite → CDIMust be solidly earthed (0 Ω) at all times
Stator power coilGreen → CDIGenerates ~80 V AC to power the CDI; independent of the charging coils
CDI unitAll wiresProcesses the pickup signal and controls the HT coil to produce spark
## Step 1 — Verify the Spark Quality Remove the spark plug and connect a known-good plug (or a new one) to the HT lead. Rest the threaded portion against a clean engine-earth point, or secure it with a jump lead. Turn the engine over on the starter or kick it with the ignition on. If using a spark tester, increase the gap until the spark stops jumping; **7 mm minimum** is required for reliable ignition. If spark is absent or weak, proceed to Step 2. ## Step 2 — Test the Pickup Coil (Red Wire) Disconnect the CDI multi-connector (so a faulty CDI cannot skew readings). 1. Set your multimeter to resistance (Ω). 2. Measure between the **red wire** at the CDI connector and a good engine earth point. 3. Expected reading: **80–140 Ω** (Piaggio spec is 80–90 Ω, but healthy units typically read 120–130 Ω). 4. Also check the air gap between the pickup and flywheel lobe: it should be approximately **0.8 mm**. Anything over 1 mm, loosen the two mounting screws and reposition the pickup. If the reading is outside range, disconnect the flywheel block connector and retest the red wire from there. If it reads correctly there but not at the CDI connector, the fault is in the wiring between the flywheel connector and the CDI (often a corroded or damaged block connector). If the reading is still out of spec from the flywheel connector, the pickup/stator assembly needs replacement. ## Step 3 — Test the CDI Earth (White Wire) With the flywheel block connector reconnected and the CDI block connector still disconnected: 1. Measure resistance between the **white wire** at the CDI connector and battery negative (or a solid earth point). 2. Expected reading: **0 Ω** — the white wire must be a direct earth. If not 0 Ω, disconnect the flywheel connector and retest. A good reading there confirms a broken or corroded earth between the flywheel connector and the CDI. Rectify the wiring before proceeding. ## Step 4 — Test the Stator Power Coil (Green Wire) The green wire carries approximately 80 V AC from the stator to the CDI when the engine is cranked. The ignition key must be in the **ON** position. ### Quick voltage test With both block connectors reconnected, measure AC voltage between the **green wire** at the CDI connector and earth while cranking. If you read **50 V AC or more**, the stator coil output is sufficient — skip to Step 5. ### Resistance test (static) 1. Disconnect the CDI block connector (leave flywheel block connected). 2. Set multimeter to Ω, measure between green wire and earth. 3. Expected: **600–1,000 Ω**. Open circuit (∞) or short (0 Ω) indicates a definite fault. ### Ignition switch test With both block connectors disconnected, measure resistance between the green wire at the CDI connector and earth:
Key positionExpected reading
OFF0 Ω (switch grounds the coil to kill ignition)
ON>20 MΩ (open circuit — coil is free to generate voltage)
Any intermediate value indicates a faulty ignition switch or tacho wiring. ### Load test Reconnect both block connectors and measure green-wire AC voltage again while cranking. It should still be **≥50 V AC** under load. If it drops below this, the stator fails under load and the stator/pickup assembly must be replaced. ## Step 5 — If All Tests Pass: Replace the CDI If Steps 2–4 all return correct readings, every component except the CDI has been verified. The CDI unit itself is faulty and should be replaced. The standard Piaggio/Gilera CDI is restricted to approximately **10,500–11,000 rpm**. If higher revs are needed (e.g., after fitting a 70cc cylinder kit), consider an unrestricted aftermarket CDI such as an Athena de-restricted unit. ## Quick-Reference Fault Table
SymptomLikely cause
No spark at allFaulty CDI, broken pickup, open-circuit stator coil, or wiring fault
Weak spark (fails 7 mm gap test)Failing HT coil or CDI nearing end of life
Pickup resistance out of rangeFaulty pickup coil or damaged flywheel-block connector
Stator reads 0 Ω or ∞ Ω (green wire)Stator coil shorted or open-circuited — replace stator/pickup assembly
White wire not 0 ΩBroken or corroded earth connection — check flywheel block connector
Green wire reads mid-range in OFF positionFaulty ignition switch or tacho short-circuit

import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; import SourceBox from '@components/SourceBox.astro'; This guide covers step-by-step electrical fault-finding for the starter motor circuit on all Piaggio and Gilera 50cc 2-stroke scooters. The approach can largely be adapted to other 50cc mopeds, though note that the **low-current relay trigger circuit differs by manufacturer**: Piaggio/Gilera switch the positive supply to the relay; Yamaha switches both the negative (starter button) and the positive (brake light switches). ️ **Safety first:** The high-current circuit is _not fused_ and carries approximately 50 A when the starter operates. Join the thick red wires deliberately and firmly. Do not allow them to contact the scooter frame. Read through this entire guide before starting. ## How the Starter Circuit Works The starter motor circuit splits into two separate sub-circuits: ### 1 — High-current circuit Thick wires run directly from the battery to the starter motor. A **relay** (the electrically operated switch) joins the two heavy red wires when 12 V is applied to it. The relay is necessary because the starter motor draws approximately 50 A — too much to route through a handlebar switch. The high-current path is kept as short as possible for efficiency and safety. ### 2 — Low-current circuit This circuit decides whether 12 V is sent to the relay. On Piaggio/Gilera 2-strokes, the relay only fires when **all three** of the following are satisfied simultaneously: - Ignition key is ON - At least one brake lever is pulled (brake light on) - Starter button is pressed � **Tip:** Before starting fault-finding, confirm the brake light illuminates when you pull a brake lever. If the brake lights do not work, the starter circuit will never activate — fix the brakes first. ## Section 1 — High-Current Circuit Testing Complete this section fully before moving to Section 2. 1. **Locate the starter relay.** Trace the thick red wire from the battery — it leads directly to the relay. On a Gilera Stalker it is behind the left-hand rear panel; location varies by model. 2. **Bypass the relay.** Unplug the two thick red wires from the relay and bridge them together with spade connectors or a short length of thick wire. Do not let them contact the frame. If the starter motor turns over normally, the high-current circuit is fine — skip straight to Section 2. If not, continue. 3. **Test or replace the battery.** Ideally substitute a known-good fully charged battery. Alternatively jump-start from a car battery (connect +ve to +ve, −ve to −ve; do _not_ run the car engine — elevated voltage from a running alternator can damage the moped's voltage regulator). Retest step 2. If the starter now works, replace the battery. 4. **Test the battery earth cable.** Connect a jump lead directly from the battery negative terminal to the starter motor body. Retest step 2. If it now works, the thick black earth cable from battery negative to engine casing is the fault — clean, tighten, or replace it. 5. **Test the starter motor directly.** Remove the starter motor from the engine. Connect battery negative to the motor body and battery positive to the motor's spade terminal using jump leads. Secure the motor in a vice — it will try to jump when it fires. If it still does not operate, the starter motor is faulty and must be replaced (they are not economically repairable). If it fires, refit the motor and return to step 2. ## Section 2 — Low-Current Circuit Testing Only proceed here once the starter motor turns over correctly when the relay is bypassed (step 2 above). 6. **Confirm brake lights function** with ignition on and a brake lever pulled. If not, fix the brake light circuit first. 7. **Check for a relay click.** If the starter motor clicks but does not turn when you press the button — and the motor works when bypassed — the relay internal contacts are burned. Replace the starter relay. 8. **Test the relay earth (thin black wire).** Disconnect the thin black wire from the relay. Connect one side of a test bulb to it and the other to battery positive. The bulb must light regardless of key position. If it does not, the black wire is not earthed — run a new wire directly to earth or the bare frame. 9. **Test the relay trigger wire (green/black wire).** With the black wire still connected, disconnect the thin green/black wire from the relay and connect the other bulb terminal to it. Switch ignition on, pull a brake lever, and press the starter button. If the bulb glows, the low-current circuit is working and the relay is faulty — replace it. If the bulb does not glow, continue. 10. **Confirm the circuit works when powered directly.** Reconnect the black wire to the relay. Run a wire from battery positive directly to the relay's green/black terminal. The starter motor should now operate. This confirms the fault is in the green/black signal wire, not the motor or high-current circuit. 11. **Trace the starter button.** Remove the handlebar cover to expose the starter button. Test the white/black wire (the +12 V feed from the brake light switches) with a bulb to battery negative — it should light every time the brake light operates. Then test across the starter button itself: with a brake lever pulled and the button pressed, voltage should pass through the button and continue along the green/black wire to the relay. If the button does not pass voltage when pressed, replace the starter button. If it does, there is a break in the green/black wire between the handlebar and the relay — inspect the loom for damage. ## Quick Fault Diagnosis Table
SymptomMost likely cause
Nothing happens when button pressedDead battery, blown fuse, or broken wiring
Relay clicks but motor does not crankBurned relay contacts — replace relay
Starter works when relay bypassed, not normallyLow-current circuit fault (brake switch, starter button, relay)
Starter slow or weak, gets hotLow battery voltage or failing starter motor brushes
Starter works without brake leverBrake light switch stuck closed or wiring fault
Starter works from cold, not when warmFailing starter motor (thermal breakdown of brushes/commutator)

import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; Added: 2026-05-10  |  Updated: 2026-05-10  |  Sources: Official Piaggio MSS ZIP 100 4T Service Station Manual, [ManualsLib — Piaggio ZIP](https://www.manualslib.com/brand/piaggio/zip/)  |  Piaggio ZIP 50 ZIP 100 Carburetor Diagnostics This guide covers the official fault diagnosis and remedy procedures for the Piaggio ZIP 50/100 4T as published in the Piaggio service station manual. Work systematically through each possible cause in order. If a problem persists after addressing all listed causes, the vehicle should be referred to an authorised Piaggio Service Centre. ️ **Safety first:** Always work on a cold engine unless the fault can only be detected at operating temperature (e.g., oil leaks under pressure, idle hunting). Use wheel chocks. Petrol is highly flammable — keep away from open flames and ensure adequate ventilation. ## Engine Will Not Start / Difficult to Start ### 🔌 1. Check the Spark Plug First
Possible CauseDiagnosis & Remedy
Defective spark plug or incorrect electrode gapRemove the spark plug and inspect. Replace if the insulator is chipped, cracked, or heavily fouled. Check the electrode gap with a feeler gauge — correct gap is 0.7–0.8 mm. If worn, bend the outer electrode carefully to restore gap. Torque to 10–15 Nm on reinstallation.

Correct spark plug: NGK CR9EB (100 cc) or NGK CR8EB (50 cc).
Incorrect valve sealing or valve adjustmentLow compression prevents starting. Check compression with a gauge (should be consistent with 10.5–11.5:1 compression ratio). If low, remove the head and grind valve seats, descale valve heads, replace faulty parts as needed. Verify valve clearance: intake 0.10 mm, exhaust 0.15 mm (cold engine). Lock nuts torque: 7–9 Nm.
Wrong ignition advanceCheck flywheel keying on the crankshaft. If the woodruff key is sheared or displaced, ignition timing will be off. Replace CDI control unit if advance values cannot be corrected mechanically.
### ⛽ 2. Check Fuel Supply
Possible CauseDiagnosis & Remedy
Vacuum-operated fuel cock failureThe fuel tap on the ZIP is vacuum-operated. Check that fuel flows adequately through the pipe by applying a vacuum on the suction pipe. If fuel does not flow freely when vacuum is applied, replace the fuel tap.
Carburettor jets clogged or dirtyDisassemble the carburettor (KEIHIN CVK 20). Clean all passages with solvent and dry with compressed air. Verify main jet (75) and pilot jet (35) are clear and properly seated. Replace all gaskets on reassembly.
Altered or degraded fuelIf the scooter has been stored for extended periods, the petrol in the tank and carburettor bowl may have degraded. Drain all fuel from tank and carburettor. Refill with fresh unleaded petrol (minimum 95 RON).
Engine floodedIf the engine has been repeatedly cranked without starting, it may be flooded (excess fuel in cylinder). To clear: hold the throttle fully open and crank the engine for approximately 5 seconds, then stop for 5 seconds. Repeat 3–4 times. If still flooded: remove the spark plug, crank with the throttle open (keep the HT cap touching the plug body, earthed away from the hole), refit a dry spark plug and attempt to start.
### 🌡️ 3. Check the Automatic Cold-Start Device (Choke)
Possible CauseDiagnosis & Remedy
Automatic starter (choke) not functioningThe ZIP uses an automatic thermostatic cold-start device on the carburettor. Check the electrical wiring and mechanical movement. If the starter device fails open (remains on when engine is warm), the engine will run very rich. Replace the starter device if defective. Starter piston protrusion should be 11 mm at 24°C.
### 🔋 4. Check the Battery & Starter Motor
Possible CauseDiagnosis & Remedy
Battery discharged or sulphatedCheck the battery state. If sluggish cranking, charge the battery. If the battery shows signs of sulphation (white crust on plates, will not hold charge), replace it. Charge a new battery for 8 hours at 1/10 of its capacity (e.g., 0.4 A for a 4 Ah battery) before first use.
Starter motor failure / start-up rpm too lowIf the battery tests good but cranking is slow or the starter does not engage, check starter motor brushes, the starter relay, and wiring connections. A weak crank that can't overcome compression indicates a failing starter motor or corroded wiring.
## Poor Engine Performance / Loss of Power ### 📉 Low Compression
Possible CauseDiagnosis & Remedy
Wrong valve adjustmentAdjust valve clearance with a cold engine: intake 0.10 mm, exhaust 0.15 mm. Lock nuts torque: 7–9 Nm.
Incorrect valve sealingRemove the head and valves. Grind valve seats, descale valve heads. Replace any cracked or bent valve. Check valve stem clearance.
Valve seat distortedReplace the complete head assembly — seat distortion cannot be corrected by grinding alone.
Worn or broken piston ringsMeasure cylinder bore and piston clearance. Standard piston-cylinder clearance: 0.038–0.052 mm. If bore is worn beyond first oversize (+0.2 mm), replace the piston and cylinder assembly. Piston rings are available in standard, 1st oversize (+0.2 mm), 2nd oversize (+0.4 mm), and 3rd oversize (+0.6 mm).
### 🐌 General Power Loss (Compression OK)
Possible CauseDiagnosis & Remedy
Carburettor dirty / vacuum cock failureDisassemble the KEIHIN CVK 20. Wash all parts with solvent, dry passages with compressed air. Inspect the vacuum diaphragm (throttle slide) for cracks or holes — a perforated diaphragm causes very poor throttle response. Replace if damaged; a cracked diaphragm cannot be repaired.
Excess carbon deposits in combustion chamberDecarbonise the cylinder, piston crown, head, and valves. Stubborn deposits on valves require removal and cleaning with a wire brush or valve seat tool.
Incorrect timing or worn timing chainRe-check camshaft timing mark alignment. A stretched timing chain can cause mild retard. Inspect chain and tensioner; replace if worn.
Exhaust muffler obstructedA blocked catalytic converter or baffles cause severe back-pressure and power loss. If blowing through the exhaust confirms obstruction, replace the silencer.
Overheated or burnt valvesCaused by incorrect clearance (too tight) or poor seating. Remove the head, grind or replace the valves and seats.
Drive belt wornA worn, cracked, or glazed drive belt slips under load. Inspect the belt surface — replace as a complete set including the variator rollers if the belt has been slipping.
Inefficient automatic transmission (CVT)Inspect the variator rollers for flat spots and oval wear. Check the pulley faces for wear grooves. Replace damaged parts as a set. Lubricate the movable driven pulley guide with Montblanc Molybdenum Grease (never use any other grease here — incorrect lubricant causes belt slippage).
Clutch slippingCheck the clutch friction masses for oil contamination or abnormal wear. Verify the clutch bell is not scored. The clutch mass contact with the bell should be predominantly in the middle and equal across all three masses. Replace clutch masses and/or bell if worn.
Oil level exceeds maximumExcess engine oil causes crankcase foaming, which can enter the combustion chamber. Check for cause (failed gasket, overfilling). Drain to correct level (MAX mark on dipstick).
Air filter blockedA saturated air filter restricts airflow, making the mixture very rich. Engine runs flat and smokes. Clean the filter sponge (water, shampoo, then 50/50 oil/petrol soak).
## Excessive Fuel Consumption
Possible CauseDiagnosis & Remedy
Air filter obstructed or dirtyA blocked filter forces the engine to draw in less air, running excessively rich. Clean the sponge: wash with water and shampoo, soak in 50% Selenia Air Filter Oil + 50% petrol, wring gently by hand without twisting, allow to drip-dry, then refit.
Automatic cold-start (choke) remains onVerify the automatic starter device de-activates correctly as the engine warms up. Check electrical wiring to the thermostatic starter and mechanical movement. Replace if stuck in the open (enriched) position.
Loose or incorrect jetsCheck that the main jet (75) and pilot jet (35) are correctly fitted and tightened. A loose jet allows fuel to flow unmetered.
Incorrect float levelRemove the float bowl. The float must be parallel to the upper cover contact plane (the throttle valve membrane cover) when held upside down. Adjust the tab on the float arm if the level is incorrect. An incorrect float level causes the carburettor to flood or run lean.
## Rear Wheel Spins at Idle
Possible CauseDiagnosis & Remedy
Idle rpm set too highAdjust the idle speed screw on the carburettor. Correct idle: 1,500 ± 150 rpm (CO: 3.2% ± 0.5). Also verify the C.O. (carbon monoxide) level if an exhaust gas analyser is available.
Clutch faultCheck the clutch springs for fatigue and the friction masses for wear or oil contamination. If the masses are glazed or oil-contaminated, clean with brake cleaner (or replace) and inspect for the source of oil ingress. Check the clutch bell for scoring.
Air filter housing not sealedIf the air box lid or intake boot is not fully sealed, unmetered air enters the engine, causing a lean condition and erratic high idle. Refit the housing correctly; replace any damaged seals or the housing itself.
Carburettor–air filter connection damagedInspect the rubber boot between the carburettor and air filter box. Cracks or splits allow air leaks that lean out the mixture at idle and cause hunting. Replace the connection boot if damaged.
## Clutch Faults
Symptom / CauseDiagnosis & Remedy
Clutch slips (engine revs but vehicle does not accelerate)Inspect the clutch friction masses — verify no grease or oil is present on the contact surfaces. The contact pattern with the clutch bell should be mainly in the middle, uniform across all three masses. Verify the clutch bell is not scored or worn abnormally. Replace worn or contaminated components.
Clutch drag (vehicle creeps at idle)First check idle speed is at 1,500 ± 150 rpm. If idle is correct, inspect clutch spring tension and mass pivot pins. Replace springs if fatigued (set, not elastic). Check for deformed clutch bell.
## Quick-Reference Diagnostic Table
SymptomStart HereIf No Improvement
Engine cranks but won't fireCheck spark plug (gap 0.7–0.8 mm, NGK CR9EB). Check fuel supply via vacuum cock.Check compression; inspect carburettor for blocked jets; check CDI/ignition advance.
Hard to start when coldCheck automatic cold-start device wiring and mechanical movement.Inspect choke piston protrusion (11 mm @ 24°C); replace if stuck.
Hard to start when hot (flooded)Crank with throttle wide open to clear flood. Check float level.Inspect needle valve — replace if worn (float level drifts).
Weak acceleration, low top speedInspect drive belt surface for glazing/cracks. Check CVT roller condition.Check clutch masses for oil; inspect variator pulley faces; check air filter.
Engine revs but no driveClutch masses worn, oil-contaminated, or spring-fatigued. Inspect and replace.Check drive belt for breakage.
Rear wheel turns at idleReduce idle to 1,500 rpm with idle screw. Check for air leaks at intake boot.Inspect clutch spring tension; replace fatigued springs.
Excessive fuel consumptionClean or replace air filter. Check cold-start device is not stuck open.Check float level; verify jets (main 75, pilot 35) are correct and tight.
Engine runs rough at idle onlyPilot (idle) jet (35) blocked — disassemble carburettor and clean with compressed air.Air leak at carburettor boot or air box; intake manifold screws loose (7–9 Nm).
Engine smokes (blue)Oil level above MAX — drain to correct level. Check valve stem seals.Measure cylinder/piston clearance; replace rings if worn.
� **Systematic approach:** Always work through the simplest, most accessible checks first (spark plug, fuel supply, air filter, idle speed) before dismantling the carburettor or engine internals. More than 70% of no-start and poor-performance faults on carbureted scooters are resolved at the spark plug, fuel, or air filter level. ## Valve Clearance — Quick Reference Incorrect valve clearance is a common cause of hard starting and poor performance. Check only on a **cold engine** (ambient temperature, not run for at least 2 hours).

## Known Issues & Common Repairs ### Cold-Start Problems The most frequently reported issue on Dutch scooter forums is difficulty starting in cold or damp weather. The root causes are typically the **auto-choke thermostatic element** becoming sluggish in temperatures below 5°C, a partially blocked pilot jet, or a slightly low float level. See the [GY6 Carburetor Adjustment Guide](/repair-guides/gy6-carburetor-adjustment-guide.html) and [GY6 No-Start Troubleshooting](/diagnostics/gy6-no-start-troubleshooting.html) for systematic diagnosis. ### Carburetor Type La Souris Sourini and City S carbureted models typically use a **Rongmao** or **Keihin PD18J clone** carburetor. Pilot jet size is typically `35`–`38` and main jet is typically `72`–`78` for the restricted 25 km/h snorfiets version. ## Lighting All La Souris City models have conventional halogen bulbs accessible through an access flap behind the headlamp — no special tools required for bulb replacement. City S models from 2019 onwards may have LED daytime running lights combined with halogen low beam. ## Parts Interchangeability The La Souris Sourini and City S share the GY6 platform with several other European-market Chinese scooters. The following models are mechanically similar and share most engine and drivetrain parts: - **BTC Riva** (same engine, same CVT belt, same GY6 carburetor) - **AGM VX50** - **Senzo Rivalux** - **GTS Toscana** - Generic Chinese 50cc scooters marketed under many brand names Body panels, headlamp units, mirrors, and instruments are **not** interchangeable between these brands — each has its own styling. Engine internals (pistons, camshafts, valves, bearings, seals), CVT components (rollers, belt, variator), and electrical components (CDI, rectifier, ignition coil) are largely interchangeable as they all derive from the same GY6 platform. � **Parts sourcing tip:** In the Netherlands and Belgium, [chinascooteronderdelen.nl](https://en.chinascooteronderdelen.nl/product-category/scooter-parts/parts-btc-agm-iva-senzo-la-souris/) specifically stocks parts for La Souris, BTC Riva, AGM, and Senzo models. For generic GY6 engine parts, any supplier stocking `139QMB` parts will work. ## Maintenance Schedule

## Engine Oil — Checking & Changing The ZIP uses a dipstick on the right crankcase cover (no drain-plug sight glass). To check the level correctly: 1. Park the scooter on level ground on the centre stand. 2. Remove the dipstick, wipe it clean, reinsert it fully (screw in tightly), then remove it again to read the level. 3. The oil level must be between the MIN and MAX marks. Do not overfill — excess oil causes foaming and oil consumption. 4. To drain, unscrew the drain plug at the bottom of the crankcase. Torque to **25–28 Nm** on refitting. 5. Fill with approximately **850 cm³** of SELENIA HI SCOOTER 4Tech or equivalent SAE 5W-40 synthetic meeting JASO MA. ## Rear Hub Oil — Checking & Changing 1. Park on the centre stand on level ground. 2. Unscrew the dipstick (cap A), wipe dry, reinsert fully, then remove and check level is between the 2nd and 3rd notches from the bottom (MIN to MAX). 3. To change: remove the oil fill cap/dipstick and unscrew the drain cap (B). Drain fully. 4. Refit drain cap and fill with approximately **80 cm³** of AGIP ROTRA 80W-90 (SAE 80W/90, API GL3). 5. Hub oil must be changed at every 1,000 km or 4 months (whichever comes first) during the initial break-in period. ## Air Filter — Cleaning Procedure 1. Undo the 6 fixing screws and remove the air cleaner cover. 2. Extract the foam sponge filter element. 3. Wash with water and shampoo (household washing-up liquid is acceptable). 4. Rinse thoroughly, then dry with a clean cloth — do not wring or compress the sponge. 5. Soak the sponge in a 50/50 mixture of Selenia Air Filter Oil and unleaded petrol. 6. Allow to drip dry on a clean cloth, then gently squeeze by hand to remove excess oil without distorting the sponge. 7. Refit. Clean more frequently than the service schedule when riding on dusty roads. ️ **Never run without air filter:** Operating the engine with a missing or damaged air filter allows unfiltered air and dust to enter the cylinder, causing accelerated bore and piston ring wear. ## Common Issues & Known Faults - **Excessive fuel consumption:** Most commonly caused by a blocked air filter restricting airflow (engine runs rich), a stuck automatic cold-start (choke) device, loose main or pilot jets, or an incorrect float level in the KEIHIN carburettor. Clean the air filter and check the starter device mechanically before disassembling the carburettor. - **Drive belt slipping or glazing:** In urban stop-start use the drive belt can glaze before reaching its measured wear limit. If acceleration feels weak but the engine revs freely, inspect the belt surface for glazing and the clutch shoes for oil contamination. - **CVT roller flat-spotting:** The variator rollers develop flat spots over distance, causing a harsh, stepped sensation during acceleration and a top-speed reduction. Inspect at every 6,000 km service; replace as a complete set — never mix old and new rollers. - **Rear wheel spinning at idle:** Indicates idle speed set too high, or a faulty clutch with grease-contaminated friction masses. Verify idle is at 1,500 ± 150 rpm and inspect clutch masses for contamination. - **Front brake spongy feel:** Air in the hydraulic circuit. Bleed the front brake circuit using DOT 4 fluid; bleed valve torque is 8–12 Nm. - **Oil weeping from crankcase joint:** Crankcase half union screws (8–10 Nm) may need checking for torque and gasket condition if oil weeps from the centre joint. ## Service Manual & Documentation Resources - [ManualsLib — Piaggio ZIP manuals (PDF)](https://www.manualslib.com/brand/piaggio/zip/) - [Carl Salter — Free Piaggio/Vespa Workshop Manuals](https://www.carlsalter.com/piaggio-vespa-service-manuals.asp) - [Modern Vespa Forum — Workshop Manuals Wiki](https://www.modernvespa.com/forum/wiki-workshop-manuals) - [Piaggio official website](https://www.piaggio.com) — contact authorised dealer for current service documentation � **50cc maintenance:** Engine oil, rear hub oil, brake fluid, air filter, and scheduled service intervals are identical for both variants. The carburettor on the 50cc (KEIHIN CVK Ø 18 mm) uses the same cleaning and float-adjustment procedure as described for the 100cc unit, but jets and needle are not interchangeable between variants. All 50cc-specific specifications are in the _Engine Specifications — 50cc_ and _50cc vs 100cc — Key Differences at a Glance_ sections above.

## Carburetor — Dell'Orto PHBN 12 HS The Piaggio ZIP 50 4T uses a **Dell'Orto PHBN 12 HS** slide carburetor. The 12 refers to the bore diameter in mm. This is a simple, reliable unit that rarely requires adjustment in normal use. Key settings:
SettingSpecification
Main jet56 (standard, sea level)
Idle jet (pilot jet)35
Needle position3rd clip from top (middle position, standard)

### Idle Speed Adjustment Procedure 1. Warm the engine to full operating temperature — at least 10 minutes of riding or idling. 2. Locate the idle speed screw on the carburettor body — a flat-head screw with a spring, accessible from the right side of the engine. 3. With the rear wheel off the ground, turn the screw clockwise to increase idle speed, anti-clockwise to decrease. 4. Set idle to 1,800–2,000 RPM. The rear wheel must not spin at idle — if it does, decrease idle speed. 5. Check that idle drops cleanly after releasing the throttle from cruising speed. A stumble or stall indicates a lean idle mixture — turn the mixture screw anti-clockwise by ¼ turns until idle is smooth. ### Air/Fuel Mixture Screw The mixture screw is located on the engine-side of the carburettor body, often covered by a pressed-in cap to prevent tampering. Factory setting is typically 1.5–2.0 turns out from lightly seated. To adjust: turn in (clockwise) to lean the idle mixture; turn out (anti-clockwise) to richen. Make ¼-turn increments and re-check idle quality after each adjustment. ## Common Problems & Solutions
