Excessive fuel consumptionFloat stuck open (carb flooding); rich mixtureInspect and clean float valve; adjust mixture screw
Engine overheatingLow oil level; blocked cooling fins; lean mixtureCheck and top up oil; clean cylinder fin area; check jetting
Blue-white exhaust smokeOil consumption — worn piston rings or valve stem sealsCompression test; consider top end inspection
No electric startWeak battery; blown fuse; failed starter relayCharge/replace battery; check 15A main fuse; test starter relay
## Identification & Model History The Piaggio ZIP 50 4T has gone through several generations. Key identifiers: - **ZIP 50 4T (2001–2008):** ZAPC25 frame code. Rounded body style. Dell'Orto PHBN carburettor. Single front disc or drum depending on market. Covered by the Haynes manual (publication 4837). - **ZIP 50 4T (2008–2013, Euro 2):** ZAPC2510 frame code. Updated front fairing, same powertrain. Carburettor. - **ZIP 50 4T (2013–2017, Euro 3):** Updated suspension, catalytic converter, retained carburettor on some markets. - **ZIP 50 4T (2018–present, Euro 4/5):** Fuel injection replaces carburettor. Electronic throttle. Different ECU-based diagnostics. Refer to EFI fault code guide for diagnostics. The Vehicle Identification Number (VIN/VIN plate) is located on the steering head (headset) and also stamped into the frame under the seat. The VIN encodes the model year, assembly plant, and engine variant. ## Parts Sourcing OEM parts are available from authorised Piaggio dealers and online from [EasyParts](https://www.easyparts.com/models/Piaggio-m420), [CMS NL](https://www.cmsnl.com/), and [SIP Scootershop](https://www.sip-scootershop.com/). Aftermarket parts (drive belts, rollers, filters, spark plugs) are widely available and often interchangeable with other Piaggio 50cc 4T platforms including the Vespa ET2 4T, Piaggio Liberty 50 4T, and Gilera Runner 50 4T, which share the same engine family.

import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; import SourceBox from '@components/SourceBox.astro'; The GY6 engine family is the most widely used small-displacement four-stroke engine platform in the world, powering hundreds of scooter models from manufacturers across China, Taiwan, and Europe. Understanding GY6 engine codes is essential for identifying the correct replacement parts, as the codes encode displacement, bore size, and cylinder head type directly into the engine designation. ## How to Read a GY6 Engine Code The engine code is stamped or cast on the lower side of the engine, near the CVT cover — just beside the oil drain bolt. It follows a consistent pattern across all variants. Taking the code `157QMJ` as an example:
PositionCharactersMeaning
1st digit1Number of cylinders (all GY6 engines are single-cylinder, so always "1")
2nd–3rd digits57Bore diameter in millimetres — 57 mm in this case (determines displacement)
4th characterQCooling type: "Q" = forced air-cooled (not liquid-cooled)
5th characterMEngine type: "M" = motorcycle/scooter/ATV application
6th characterJCrankcase variant: "J" = horizontal case (scooter layout), "I" = inclined
**⚠️ "P" Series Engines:** Some engines have a prefix "1P" instead of just "1" — for example, `1P57QMJ`. The "P" indicates a performance variant with a taller cylinder head and a different cam seating depth. The crankcase is the same dimensions, but the cylinder and cylinder head must be matched (both P or both non-P). Do not mix P and non-P top-end components without converting both together. ## Common GY6 Engine Codes
Engine CodeDisplacementBore × StrokeStud SpacingCommon Applications
139QMB50 cc39 mm × 41.4 mm44 mm (B-Block)BTC Riva 50, La Souris Sourini, Santini Capri, generic Chinese 50cc scooters
152QMI125 cc54 mm × 54 mm54 mm (A-Block)Generic 125cc Chinese scooters, some GY6 125 variants
157QMJ150 cc57 mm × 57.8 mm54 mm (A-Block)Most common 150cc GY6 scooters and ATVs worldwide
1P39QMB50 cc39 mm × 41.4 mm44 mm (B-Block)Performance 50cc variant — taller head than standard 139QMB
1P57QMJ150 cc57 mm × 57.8 mm54 mm (A-Block)Performance 150cc variant — taller cylinder head
## Crankcase Block Types: A-Block vs B-Block Parts compatibility is primarily determined by the crankcase "block type", which controls cylinder stud spacing and overall engine dimensions.
Block TypeStud SpacingEngine CodesNotes
A-Block54 mm152QMI, 157QMJ, 1P57QMJ125cc and 150cc GY6 — largest installed base, most aftermarket parts
B-Block44 mm139QMB, 1P39QMB50cc GY6 — different cylinder, head, and variator sizes; NOT interchangeable with A-Block
**⚠️ Critical Compatibility Rule:** A-Block and B-Block parts are NOT interchangeable. A 157QMJ (150cc) cylinder cannot be fitted to a 139QMB (50cc) crankcase and vice versa. Always confirm your block type before ordering. ## Parts Interchangeability Reference ### GY6 50cc (139QMB / B-Block)

## How to Locate Your Engine Code 1. Place the scooter on its centre stand or lean it against a wall. 2. Look at the lower-left side of the engine block, just above the oil drain bolt and beside the CVT cover. 3. The code is stamped directly into the casting. It may be partially obscured by grime — clean with a cloth and solvent if needed. 4. Photograph the code before ordering parts to avoid errors. ## Big Bore Upgrade Compatibility Big bore kits increase displacement by fitting a larger-bore cylinder and matching piston. Compatibility rules: - **150cc → 171cc (61 mm bore):** Fits without crankcase modification on most A-Block engines. This is the recommended first step for performance upgrades. - **150cc → 180cc (63 mm bore):** Requires crankcase boring/machining. Not a beginner job. - **50cc → 70cc (47 mm bore):** Common upgrade for B-Block engines. Drop-in on most 139QMB crankcases. When fitting a big bore kit, always re-jet the carburetor (or remap the EFI) to match the increased displacement. A larger bore burns more fuel at the same air/fuel ratio — running lean will damage the engine. ## Key Torque Specifications (GY6 Reference)

import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; import SourceBox from '@components/SourceBox.astro'; The carburetor needle controls how much fuel mixes with air during the **mid-throttle range** (roughly 25%–75% open). When it is set too high, the mixture becomes too rich and the engine runs sluggishly, smokes black, and smells of unburnt fuel. When it is set too low, the mixture becomes too lean and the engine hesitates, surges, or overheats. Adjusting the needle is free, takes under an hour, and requires no special tools — making it one of the most rewarding first tuning jobs for any beginner. ️ **Fire safety — read before you start:** Petrol is highly flammable. Work in a well-ventilated space away from open flames, sparks, and hot surfaces. Keep a dry-powder fire extinguisher nearby. Do not smoke. Allow the engine to cool for at least 30 minutes before starting work — the exhaust pipe and engine cases hold heat long after the engine stops. 🎬 Needle Clip Position Explained "Carburetor Needle Clip Position" by Bikes and Beards — [↗ YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qP7omWBEgUg) 🎬 Needle Height on a Real Scooter Carb Practical scooter carburetor needle walkthrough — [↗ YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KXxxJrA5hNY) ## How the Needle and Circlip Work A slide carburetor uses a cylindrical **throttle slide** that rises and falls as you twist the throttle. A tapered metal **needle** hangs down through the centre of the slide and sits inside the **needle jet** — a small brass tube in the carburetor body. As the slide rises, the needle also rises, and its taper progressively opens the gap between the needle and the jet, allowing more fuel to flow. The needle has a series of **grooves** machined into it near the top — usually 3, 4, or 5 grooves. A small spring clip (the **circlip**) sits in one of these grooves and rests on the top of the slide, holding the needle at a fixed height. Moving the circlip changes which groove it sits in, which raises or lowers the needle inside the jet: Throttle Slide ◀ Circlip (groove 3 — default) Groove 1 → lean Groove 2 Groove 3 (std) Groove 4 Groove 5 → rich Needle Jet CLIP UP (lower groove #) \= Needle LOWERS \= LEANER mix CLIP DOWN (higher groove #) \= Needle RISES \= RICHER mix Schematic — clip up = needle down = leaner; clip down = needle up = richer [![Real carburetor needle and circlip on a scooter — YouTube video thumbnail](https://img.youtube.com/vi/KXxxJrA5hNY/hqdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KXxxJrA5hNY) Real-world view: needle, grooves, and circlip on an actual scooter carburetor. [↗ Watch the full walkthrough on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KXxxJrA5hNY) � **Counterintuitive but important:** Moving the circlip _up_ on the needle makes the mixture _leaner_, and moving it _down_ makes it _richer_. This is because moving the clip up pushes the needle body downward inside the jet, reducing fuel flow. Take a moment to picture this before you start. ## Clip Position Quick Reference
Clip PositionNeedle PositionMixture EffectWhen to Use
Groove 1 (top)Needle lowestLeanestHigh altitude (>1500 m) or persistent rich fouling
Groove 2Needle lowSlightly leanMild rich symptoms, warm climate
Groove 3 (middle)Needle centredStandard / stockDefault — start here
Groove 4Needle highSlightly richMild lean symptoms, cold climate
Groove 5 (bottom)Needle highestRichestCold start problems or oversized air filter
## Tools Required - **Phillips screwdriver (No. 2)** — for the carburetor top cap screws on most GY6 units - **Flat-head screwdriver** — useful for the top cap on some Piaggio/Dellorto carbs, and for gently prying parts - **Needle-nose pliers** — to grip and remove the small circlip without losing it - **Small pick, dental pick, or circlip tool** — to lever the circlip out of its groove without scratching the needle - **Clean cloth or paper towels** — to catch any petrol drips and keep parts clean during reassembly ️ **Don't lose the circlip:** The circlip is tiny — around 2–3 mm in diameter — and will immediately disappear into the floor if dropped. Work over a clean tray or cloth. Some mechanics place a magnet nearby to catch it. Always have a spare circlip on hand; they cost pennies. ## Parts & Materials

## Step-by-Step Instructions ### Step 1 — Safety Preparation Before touching anything, make sure the engine is safe to work on. 1. Turn the fuel tap (petcock) to the **OFF** position. On GY6 scooters this is typically under the seat or near the frame rail. On Piaggio models it is usually below the left panel. 2. Allow the engine to cool for at least **30 minutes** — touch the cylinder head; it should feel no warmer than room temperature. 3. Place the scooter on its centre stand on firm, level ground. 4. Lay a clean cloth or tray under the carburetor to catch any petrol residue. � **Note your starting position:** Before making any change, note which groove the circlip is in. If the adjustment makes things worse, you can always return to where you started. ### Step 2 — Access the Carburetor The carburetor is usually accessed by removing a side panel or the seat. The exact location varies by model. 1. **GY6 scooters:** Remove the left or right body panel (usually 2–4 Phillips screws). The carburetor sits on the right side of the engine, between the air filter box and the engine intake manifold. 2. **Piaggio Zip / Vespa models:** Open the underseat storage. The carburetor and air filter assembly are accessible from the right side of the frame after removing the plastic side cowl (3–5 screws). 3. Once the carburetor is visible, identify the **top cap** — the round or rectangular cover on top of the carb body. This is where the throttle cable enters. � **Take a photo first:** Before disassembling anything, photograph the carburetor, the throttle cable routing, and the throttle slide orientation. Referring to your own photos during reassembly is much easier than trying to remember. ### Step 3 — Remove the Carburetor Top Cap The top cap holds the throttle slide inside the carburetor body. Removing it gives you access to the slide and needle. 1. Locate the two to four screws around the top cap perimeter and remove them. On GY6 carbs (PD-type, CVK-type) these are Phillips screws. On Dellorto PHBG (Piaggio Zip 2T) there is a single large cap screw or a lock-ring. 2. Gently lift the top cap upward. The throttle cable and slide will come with it — **do not pull hard**. If the slide feels stuck, wiggle it gently; it may be a vacuum-type slide (CV carburetor) seated by engine vacuum. 3. Lift the slide out of the carburetor bore and let it hang from the throttle cable. Do not disconnect the cable unless necessary. 🎬 Removing the Slide & Needle — GY6 CV Carburetor "GY6 Carburetor Teardown and Needle Clip Adjustment" by ScooterDynasty — [↗ Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DcSSMw9hGLI) ### Step 4 — Remove the Needle from the Slide The needle passes through a hole in the centre of the throttle slide and is held in place by the circlip sitting in a groove. 1. Hold the slide in one hand over your tray. Look through the centre hole — you will see the top of the needle protruding slightly, with the circlip sitting in one of the grooves. 2. Using your pick or a small flat-head screwdriver, carefully lever the circlip out of its groove. Work slowly — the clip is under slight spring tension and can ping away. 3. Once the circlip is free, slide the needle downward and out through the bottom of the slide. Set the needle and circlip aside on your cloth — do not place them near an edge. 4. Count the grooves on the needle and note which groove the circlip was sitting in (1 = top groove, highest number = bottom groove). ️ **Inspect the needle while you have it out:** Run your fingernail along the needle's surface. It should be smooth with no scoring, flat spots, or visible taper wear. A worn needle will cause an inconsistent mixture no matter what groove the clip is in — replace it if in doubt (cost: €3–8). ### Step 5 — Reposition the Circlip This is the actual adjustment. Move the circlip by one groove at a time and test before moving further. 1. Decide which direction to move the clip based on your symptoms. Refer to the [Carburetor Needle Height Diagnostics guide](/diagnostics/carburetor-needle-height-diagnostics.html) if you are unsure of your symptoms. 2. **Rich mixture (black smoke, poor top speed, strong fuel smell):** Move the clip one groove _up_ toward the top of the needle (lower groove number). This lowers the needle and leans the mixture. 3. **Lean mixture (hesitation, surging, overheating):** Move the clip one groove _down_ toward the bottom of the needle (higher groove number). This raises the needle and richens the mixture. 4. To move the clip: use needle-nose pliers to grip the clip, then compress it slightly and push it into the new groove. The clip should snap in with a small click and feel secure — it should not spin freely. � **One groove at a time:** The difference between one groove and the next is significant. Always make a single-groove change, reassemble, road-test, and then decide if a further adjustment is needed. Jumping two grooves at once makes it harder to identify the correct setting. ### Step 6 — Reinstall the Needle and Slide 1. Insert the needle back up through the centre hole of the slide, pointed (tapered) end first, so the circlip end protrudes from the top. 2. The needle may have a small key or flat side that must align with a corresponding slot in the slide — check your photo from Step 2. Rotate the needle until it drops fully into position. 3. Confirm the circlip is fully seated in its groove and the needle cannot move up or down by hand. 4. Slide the throttle slide back into the carburetor body. Make sure the slide's anti-rotation pin (a small peg on the slide's side) lines up with the corresponding slot in the carburetor bore — the slide will not fit if rotated incorrectly. 5. Refit the top cap and tighten the screws evenly — do not over-tighten. ### Step 7 — Road Test and Fine-Tune 1. Turn the fuel tap back to the **ON** position. 2. Start the engine and let it warm up for 2–3 minutes without riding. 3. Take the scooter for a test ride on a quiet road. Focus on how it pulls from 25%–75% throttle — this is the mid-range where the needle has the most effect. 4. If the symptom has improved but is not fully resolved, repeat the adjustment (Steps 3–6) moving the clip by one more groove in the same direction. 5. Once mid-range feels crisp and responsive, the needle is correctly set. If idle or full-throttle behaviour is still off, those are adjusted separately with the idle screw and main jet respectively — see the related guides below. ## Troubleshooting
Problem After AdjustmentLikely CauseFix
No improvement at allSymptoms are not needle-related; may be idle circuit, main jet, or air leakCheck idle mixture screw and main jet size; inspect intake manifold for air leaks
Slide sticks or throttle feels heavyNeedle not fully seated in slide; anti-rotation pin misalignedRemove slide and re-seat needle; ensure pin is in groove before refitting cap
Fuel smell from carburetor area after reassemblyTop-cap O-ring damaged or not seated; float bowl disturbedInspect O-ring and replace if cracked; check float bowl bolt is tight

[Search on YouTube →](https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=how+to+read+spark+plug+color+scooter) ## Frequently Asked Questions How do I know if my problem is the needle and not the main jet or idle screw? The needle primarily affects the **mid-throttle range (25%–75%)**. If the problem appears or disappears only when you are at very low throttle (idle circuit) or wide-open throttle (main jet), the needle is probably not the issue. See the [Diagnostics Guide](/diagnostics/carburetor-needle-height-diagnostics.html) for a full symptom flowchart. My carburetor only has 3 grooves. Which is the standard position? On a 3-groove needle, the standard (stock) position is **groove 2** — the middle groove. On a 5-groove needle it is groove 3. If you are unsure, start in the middle groove and adjust from there. Can I adjust the needle without removing the carburetor from the scooter? Yes — on most scooters the top cap is accessible without fully removing the carburetor. You only need to remove the carburetor body if the top cap is obstructed by frame members or bodywork. Many GY6 scooters allow full access with just the side panel removed. After moving the clip, the engine is now worse. What should I do? Return the circlip to the groove it was in before your adjustment. If you noted your starting position in Step 1, this is straightforward. Then re-read the symptoms carefully and consider whether the issue might be in a different circuit — idle, choke, main jet — or whether there is a vacuum leak or blocked jet. Does this apply to injected (EFI) scooters? No. Fuel-injected scooters do not have a carburetor needle. The fuel delivery on EFI models is controlled by the ECU and cannot be adjusted with hand tools. This guide applies only to **carbureted** scooters.

import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; import SourceBox from '@components/SourceBox.astro'; The fuel valve (petcock) on carburettor-equipped scooters is **vacuum-operated** — it stays closed when the engine is off, and opens automatically when the engine runs. It has exactly two barbed hose fittings. Getting them mixed up means the engine gets no fuel, or creates a fuel leak. This guide explains how it works, how to identify which hose is which in under two minutes, and how to connect everything correctly. --- ## How the Vacuum Petcock Works Inside the fuel valve is a rubber diaphragm. Atmospheric pressure holds it closed when there is no vacuum. As soon as the engine cranks, the piston creates a **negative pressure (vacuum)** on the intake stroke. This vacuum is piped from the intake manifold to the diaphragm, pulling it open and allowing fuel to flow. The result: fuel only flows when the engine is running (or cranking). If a fuel line cracks and falls off while the scooter is parked, the tank does not drain — a useful safety feature. **Two ports on the valve body:** | Port | Connects to | Position (typical) | Hose size | |------|-------------|-------------------|-----------| | **FUEL OUT** | Carburettor fuel inlet (bottom of float bowl / side nipple) | Upper barb (or marked with arrow) | ~6 mm ID | | **VACUUM** | Intake manifold vacuum nipple | Lower barb | ~4–5 mm ID | On most GY6 valves the two barbs are **different diameters** — the fuel barb is slightly larger (~6 mm) and the vacuum barb is slightly smaller (~4 mm). If you have two different-sized hoses, that alone tells you which goes where before you do any test. On Piaggio Zip 50/100 4T the petcock is mounted on the left side of the tank and the ports are usually labelled with moulded arrows or the letters **F** (fuel) and **VAC** (vacuum). Check for markings before reaching for the hose. --- ## Before You Start — Safety Work in a well-ventilated area away from open flames or sparks. Fuel vapour is heavier than air and pools at floor level. Keep a rag handy to mop up any spills immediately. If you are reconnecting hoses after removing the tank, make sure the fuel tap is in the **OFF** position (if your valve has a manual override lever) before disconnecting anything. --- ## Step 1 — Identify the Two Ports Without Any Tools Look at the fuel valve where it is mounted on the tank. **a. Check for markings first.** Many valves have moulded or stamped text: `FUEL`, `OUT`, `VAC`, `PRI`, or small arrows. If markings are present, you are done — skip to Step 3. **b. Check hose diameters.** If you have the original hoses still attached (or removed but labelled), compare their inner diameter. The fuel hose is typically 6 mm ID (slightly thicker wall). The vacuum hose is 4–5 mm ID (thinner). Different diameters → the valve body barbs are also different diameters, which makes it physically much harder to swap them accidentally. **c. Check port position.** As a general rule on GY6 and Piaggio: - **Top or rear barb** → fuel outlet - **Bottom or front barb** → vacuum inlet This is a guideline, not a guarantee — always confirm with the suck-test below if you are unsure. --- ## Step 2 — The "Suck Test" (Positive Identification in 60 Seconds) Use this test any time you are unsure which port is which, or when fitting a replacement valve with no markings. **What you need:** a short (~20 cm) scrap of hose that fits over each barb, a small container, and someone to hold the scooter (or a centre-stand). 1. Make sure the tank has **a small amount of fuel** — at least 100–200 ml. Tilt the scooter slightly so fuel sits near the valve. 2. Place your container on the floor under the valve. 3. Fit the scrap hose over **one barb** (no fuel should flow by itself — the valve is closed with no vacuum). 4. **Suck firmly on the scrap hose** with your mouth for 1–2 seconds, then release. **Interpret the result:** | What happens | What it means | |---|---| | Fuel flows out of the **other** barb (into your container) | The barb you sucked on is the **VACUUM port** — connect it to the intake manifold. The other barb is **FUEL OUT** — connect it to the carburettor. | | Nothing happens from the other barb | You sucked on the **FUEL OUT** port — swap your scrap hose to the other barb and repeat. | | Fuel comes into your mouth | You accidentally sucked on the FUEL OUT port with a non-vacuum-operated valve or a faulty diaphragm. Spit, rinse, check the valve. | You are applying a small suction to mimic what the engine intake does. The valve diaphragm opens and fuel flows out the other port. As soon as you release suction, flow stops. If the flow does **not** stop when you release, the diaphragm is torn — replace the valve before riding. --- ## Step 3 — Connect the Hoses ### Fuel hose (FUEL OUT → carburettor) 1. Route the **fuel hose** from the FUEL OUT barb on the valve down to the **carburettor fuel inlet** — the small barbed nipple on the side of the float bowl or on the bottom of the carb body. On GY6 carbs (PD18/PZ19/PD24/CVK) it is typically on the **left side** of the carb body, pointing downward at a slight angle. 2. Push the hose firmly over the barb until it bottoms out — you should feel a definite stop. 3. Fit a hose clamp (spring-type or screw-type) at least 5 mm back from the end of the barb. On GY6 50cc engines the fuel hose is often a push-fit without a clamp from the factory, but a small spring clamp is good practice, especially if the hose is old. ### Vacuum hose (VACUUM → intake manifold) 1. Route the **vacuum hose** from the VACUUM barb on the valve to the **small nipple on the intake manifold** (the rubber or aluminium tube between the carburettor and the cylinder head). On GY6 engines this nipple is usually on the **underside** of the manifold, pointing downward — it is smaller in diameter than the main carb inlet and sometimes has a blanking cap if it has never been used. 2. On **Piaggio Zip / Vespa** engines the vacuum nipple is on the intake manifold near the carburettor flange, also on the underside. 3. Push the hose fully onto the nipple. No clamp is needed on the vacuum side (low pressure), but a cable tie is fine if the hose feels loose. Do **not** leave the intake manifold vacuum nipple open (uncapped) even temporarily — a vacuum leak here causes the engine to idle very fast or not idle at all, and can lean out the mixture enough to cause engine damage at speed. --- ## Step 4 — Verify the Connections Before starting the engine, do a quick visual and function check: 1. **Visually trace both hoses** — no kinks, no sharp bends, no contact with hot surfaces (exhaust pipe), no contact with moving parts (drive belt cover, variator). 2. **Check hose ends are fully seated** on both barbs — you should not be able to pull them off with light finger pressure. 3. **Start the engine.** Within a few seconds of cranking, fuel should be flowing through the system and the engine should start and idle normally. 4. **After starting, inspect both hose connections** for drips or seeping fuel. Any wet spot at a hose join means the hose is not fully seated or the clamp is too loose. If the engine cranks but does not start, turn the fuel tap to **PRI** (prime) if fitted — this bypasses the vacuum diaphragm and opens the valve mechanically. If fuel then flows and the engine starts, the diaphragm is intact but there may be an air leak in the vacuum hose circuit preventing the valve from opening on its own. --- ## Common Mistakes **Swapping the two hoses** — the most common error. The vacuum barb connected to the carburettor will deliver no fuel (the carb fuel inlet expects liquid, not vacuum). The engine will crank but not start, or start briefly on residual fuel then die. Run the suck-test in Step 2 to confirm which is which. **Using a fuel hose for the vacuum line** — thick-walled fuel hose will fit the vacuum barb but collapses slightly under suction, restricting or blocking the vacuum signal. Always use a vacuum-rated hose (thinner wall, slightly stiffer) on the vacuum side. **Leaving the vacuum nipple on the intake manifold uncapped** — if you remove the vacuum hose for any reason and do not immediately reconnect it, cap the manifold nipple with a short bolt, a golf tee, or a purpose-made vacuum cap. Even a minute of running with an open vacuum port will cause a severe lean condition. **Hose routing too close to the exhaust** — fuel hose routed near the exhaust header will soften, crack, and eventually leak. Route hoses on the cold side of the engine and secure them with a cable tie to prevent vibration wear. --- ## GY6 — Specific Routing Reference ``` [Fuel Tank] | [Fuel Valve / Petcock] | \ FUEL OUT VACUUM | \ [Carb fuel inlet] [Intake manifold vacuum nipple] (side of carb body) (underside of manifold, near carb flange) ``` On the GY6 139QMB (50cc), the intake manifold vacuum nipple points **straight down** and is approximately 4 mm OD. The carburettor fuel inlet is a 6 mm OD barb on the left side of the PD18J/PD22J body. --- ## Piaggio Zip / Vespa — Specific Routing Reference ``` [Fuel Tank — left side of scooter] | [Fuel Valve — mounted on tank underside or left frame rail] | \ FUEL OUT (upper) VACUUM (lower) | \ [Carb fuel inlet] [Intake manifold vacuum nipple] (left side of PHVA carb) (underside of manifold stub) ``` On the Piaggio Zip 50 4T and Vespa Primavera 50, the carburettor is a **Dellorto PHVA 12** or **PHVA 17.5**. The fuel inlet is a single 6 mm barb on the left of the body. The vacuum nipple on the manifold is 4 mm and points downward — it may have a factory cap if the bike came without vacuum-operated accessories. --- ## Related Guides - [GY6 Carburetor Cleaning Guide](/repair-guides/gy6-carburetor-cleaning-guide) - [GY6 Hard Start / Intake Flooding](/repair-guides/gy6-hard-start-intake-flooding) - [GY6 Carburetor Adjustment Guide](/repair-guides/gy6-carburetor-adjustment-guide)

These engines are robust and reliable when properly maintained, but neglect — particularly of oil and air filtration — leads to accelerated wear. This schedule applies to GY6 50cc, 125cc, and 150cc four-stroke engines in both carbureted and fuel-injected variants. Intervals are given in kilometres. Where a time-based interval is listed, use whichever limit comes first — kilometres or months. ## Complete Maintenance Schedule

Every rideTyre pressuresCheckFront: 1.5–1.75 bar (22–25 psi); Rear: 2.0–2.25 bar (29–33 psi) — verify with your model's label

## Seasonal Storage Checklist If the scooter will be stored for more than 4 weeks (over winter or during extended non-use), take these steps to avoid fuel system and battery problems: 1. Run the engine until warm, then drain the carburetor float bowl (turn the fuel tap to OFF, then run until the engine dies from fuel starvation). This prevents varnish build-up. 2. Change the engine oil before storage — used oil contains acidic combustion by-products that attack internal surfaces over months of non-use. 3. Remove the battery and store it indoors on a trickle charger (battery tender) — cold temperatures combined with self-discharge kill sealed lead-acid batteries. 4. Inflate tyres to the maximum rated pressure to resist flat-spotting. 5. Cover the scooter or store it away from UV exposure and moisture. **💡 Keep a Maintenance Log:** Record the date, odometer reading, and work performed for each service. A simple notebook or spreadsheet suffices. This is invaluable when diagnosing intermittent faults and essential if you sell the scooter. ## Symptoms of Overdue Maintenance If you are unsure when the scooter was last serviced, watch for these warning signs: - **Hard starting, rough idle:** Likely overdue spark plug, dirty carburetor, or out-of-spec valve clearances - **Excessive oil consumption:** Possible worn piston rings — often related to overdue oil changes that allowed breakdown of lubricating film - **Sluggish acceleration / vibration under throttle:** Likely worn variator rollers or failing drive belt - **Long braking distance or spongy lever:** Worn pads, contaminated fluid, or air in hydraulic lines - **Noisy engine at idle:** Often valve clearances out of range — particularly if the tapping noise increases when warm

The filter prevents dust, grit, and insects from entering the engine — a single unfiltered ride on a dusty road can cause more cylinder bore wear than 10,000 km of normal use. ## Air Filter Types by Model

� **Never run a GY6 scooter without an air filter fitted**, even briefly for testing. Without filtration, abrasive particles enter the cylinder and cause rapid bore wear within minutes of running. If the filter is being washed and is still drying, wait — do not start the engine. ## Symptoms of a Clogged Air Filter - **Loss of power and acceleration** — engine is starved of air, mixture is too rich - **Increased fuel consumption** — rich mixture burns more fuel for the same output - **Black, sooty spark plug** — carbon deposits from incomplete combustion - **Difficulty starting**, especially when warm - **Black smoke from the exhaust** - **Rough idle** that cannot be cured by carburetor adjustment alone ## Tools & Materials Required - Phillips screwdriver or 8 mm socket (airbox cover screws) - Mild dish soap and warm water (foam filters) - Clean dry cloth or paper towels - Foam filter oil (available at motorcycle shops — do not substitute with engine oil) - Replacement filter element (foam or paper, model-specific) 🎬 Video Guide — GY6 Air Filter Maintenance: Clean or Replace **Video:** "GY6 Air Filter Maintenance — Clean or Replace" | YouTube   [↗ Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dklHU1KW2bQ) ## Procedure — GY6 Foam Filter (Most Common) 1. **Locate the airbox.** On GY6 scooters it is on the right side of the scooter under a body panel, connected to the carburetor inlet via a rubber intake boot. On most models two screws or a single wing nut secure the airbox cover. 2. **Remove the airbox cover** and lift out the foam element. Note the orientation — some elements are directional. 3. **Inspect the element.** If it is torn, deformed, or the foam has begun to crumble, replace it — cleaning a damaged filter is pointless. Also inspect the inside of the airbox housing for water, dirt, or insects and wipe it clean. 4. **Wash the foam element** in a basin of warm water with a few drops of dish soap. Squeeze gently (do not wring or twist) and work the soap through the foam until the rinse water runs completely clear. 5. **Rinse thoroughly** with clean water until all soap is gone. Soap residue left in the filter reduces airflow. 6. **Dry completely.** Squeeze out excess water gently. Pat dry with a clean cloth and leave to air-dry for at least 30–60 minutes. _The filter must be fully dry before re-oiling or reinstalling._ 7. **Apply foam filter oil.** Drizzle a small amount of filter oil onto the foam and work it in evenly with your fingers. The element should be lightly, evenly coated — not dripping wet. Excess oil gets drawn into the engine and fouls the spark plug. 8. **Reinstall the element** in the correct orientation. Refit the airbox cover and tighten the screws or wing nut firmly — air leaks around the filter housing bypass the filter entirely. 9. **Check the intake boot** (the rubber tube connecting the airbox to the carburetor) for cracks or loose clamps. A cracked boot allows unfiltered air to bypass the filter. � **No filter oil?** In an emergency, a very thin smear of clean engine oil can be used on the foam, but proper foam filter oil has a tackier consistency that traps fine dust particles more effectively. Buy dedicated filter oil for the next service. ## Procedure — Vespa / Paper Filter 1. **Access the airbox** — on Vespa Primavera and Sprint models the airbox is under the left body panel. Remove the 2–3 screws securing the panel, then open the airbox cover. 2. **Remove the paper element** and hold it up to a light source. If you cannot see light clearly through the filter paper, it must be replaced — paper filters cannot be washed back to full effectiveness. 3. **Tap the element gently** against your palm to dislodge loose dust, if the element is only lightly soiled. Do not use compressed air — high pressure damages the paper fibres. 4. **Wipe out the airbox housing** with a dry cloth. 5. **Fit the new or cleaned element** and reclose the airbox. Ensure the cover seal is seated correctly — even a small gap allows unfiltered air in. ## Service Intervals
ConditionActionInterval

Dusty roads, gravel, construction areasClean foam elementEvery 1,500 km / 3 months
Any filter — replaceNew elementEvery 8,000–12,000 km or when damaged
Paper filter — replaceNew element (do not wash)Every 6,000–8,000 km

The stock main jet is calibrated for the stock airbox restriction. A free-flowing pod filter leans the mixture and can cause overheating and piston damage if the carb is not rejetted to compensate. ## Applicable Models Foam filter procedure applies to all GY6-engined scooters: **BTC Riva 50/125**, **La Souris Sourini / City**, **Santini Capri**, and all Chinese `139QMB` / `157QMJ` clones. import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; import SourceBox from '@components/SourceBox.astro'; A big bore kit is the most impactful single upgrade you can make to a GY6 engine. By fitting a larger cylinder and matched piston, displacement increases — bringing noticeably improved acceleration and higher top speed without requiring exotic parts. This guide covers what big bore kits are, how to choose the right one, and how to install it correctly. ## What Is a Big Bore Kit? A big bore kit replaces the stock cylinder, piston, piston rings, and sometimes the cylinder head with larger-bore equivalents. The crankcase, crankshaft, and valve train typically remain stock. The displacement increase comes entirely from the wider bore — stroke length stays the same. On a standard GY6 150cc engine (`157QMJ`, 57 mm bore), a 171cc upgrade uses a 61 mm bore cylinder. This 4 mm bore increase raises displacement from 150 cc to approximately 171 cc — a gain of about 14 percent. ## Available Upgrades for GY6 Engines
EngineStock BoreBig Bore OptionNew DisplacementMachining Required?
GY6 50cc (139QMB)39 mm47 mm kit (70cc)~70 ccNo — drop-in on most B-Block cases
GY6 150cc (157QMJ)57 mm61 mm kit (171cc)~171 ccNo — fits stock A-Block cases
GY6 150cc (157QMJ)57 mm63 mm kit (180cc)~180 ccYes — case boring required
**⚠️ Beware of "No Machining Required" 63 mm Kits:** Some vendors sell 63 mm kits claiming no case machining is needed. Experienced builders strongly advise against these — the cylinder wall is too thin for long-term reliability at that bore size without proper case preparation. If you want 180cc, have the cases professionally bored. ## What to Buy — Kit Components A reputable big bore kit should include: a new cylinder (barrel), piston with circlips, piston rings, a base gasket, and a head gasket. Some kits include a matching cylinder head; others require you to reuse or source a head separately. Quality varies enormously. Key markers of a good kit: - Cylinder bore is honed (cross-hatch pattern visible inside) — not just drilled - Piston rings fit the ring grooves precisely — no side-play when pushed down - Ring end-gaps are within specification — check with feeler gauges (see below) - Base gasket is the correct thickness for your head gasket combination ## Tools Required - Socket set and combination spanners (8, 10, 12, 14, 17 mm) - Torque wrench (capable of 10–50 Nm) - Feeler gauges - Piston ring compressor (or careful hands) - Gasket scraper / razor blade - Engine oil and assembly lube - Thread-locking compound (Loctite 243 or equivalent) - Camera or phone — photograph everything before disassembly ## Installation Procedure ### Step 1: Prepare the Engine 1. Allow the engine to cool completely. Drain the engine oil. 2. Remove the seat, bodywork panels, and air filter assembly to gain access to the engine. 3. Disconnect the spark plug cap. Remove the spark plug. 4. For easier access, consider removing the engine from the frame (disconnect the carburetor, exhaust, wiring loom, rear shock mount, and engine hanger bolt). ### Step 2: Remove the Cylinder Head and Cylinder 1. Remove the valve cover (cam cap). Photograph the cam chain routing before disassembly. 2. Rotate the engine to Top Dead Centre (TDC) on the compression stroke — both valves closed, timing mark aligned. 3. Remove the cam chain tensioner bolt and slide the tensioner out. 4. Undo the camshaft bearing cap (two bolts). Lift out the camshaft carefully, keeping the cam chain loop over the sprocket — secure it with a zip tie through the chain to prevent it dropping into the case. 5. Undo the four cylinder head nuts in a cross pattern. Lift the head off — it may need gentle tapping with a rubber mallet. Do not use a metal hammer directly on the head. 6. Lift the cylinder off the studs. The piston will be exposed. Place a clean rag over the crankcase mouth immediately to prevent debris entering. ### Step 3: Remove the Old Piston 1. Note which way the piston arrow or notch faces (it must point toward the exhaust side on reassembly). 2. Use a small screwdriver or circlip pliers to remove the piston pin circlips from both sides of the piston. Keep these — they are reusable if undamaged. 3. Push the piston pin out by hand or with a dowel. The piston will slide off the connecting rod. ### Step 4: Check and Prepare the New Components 1. Inspect the new cylinder bore — it should be smooth with a visible cross-hatch honing pattern. 2. Check piston ring end-gaps by placing each ring individually inside the new cylinder bore and measuring the gap with feeler gauges. Standard acceptable range: 0.15–0.40 mm. Replace rings if gaps are outside this range. 3. Lubricate the cylinder bore, piston, and piston pin with fresh engine oil. 4. Install the piston rings onto the new piston — top ring, second ring, then oil scraper ring. Stagger the ring gaps 120° apart around the piston to minimise blow-by. ### Step 5: Install the New Piston and Cylinder 1. Fit the new piston onto the connecting rod with the arrow or "EX" marking facing the exhaust port. Insert the piston pin and reinstall the circlips — ensure both circlips are fully seated in their grooves. 2. Clean the crankcase mating surface and cylinder base — remove all old gasket material. 3. Place the new base gasket on the crankcase studs (dry — no sealant). 4. Oil the cylinder bore again. Compress the piston rings using a ring compressor or your thumbs. Carefully lower the new cylinder over the piston, keeping the cam chain guided through the chain tunnel. 5. Seat the cylinder fully on the base gasket. ### Step 6: Reassemble the Top End 1. Install the new head gasket. Lower the cylinder head into place over the studs. 2. Fit the head nuts finger-tight, then torque in a cross pattern: 10–12 Nm for M6 studs. Do not overtighten — the aluminium will strip. 3. Reinstall the camshaft, aligning the timing marks on the cam sprocket with the marks on the cylinder head. 4. Reinstall the cam chain tensioner. Reinstall the valve cover. 5. Reinstall the spark plug: 10–14 Nm. ### Step 7: Re-jet the Carburetor A larger engine displaces more air per intake stroke. The stock main jet (typically 95–105 for a 150cc GY6) will run lean with a 171cc cylinder. Fit a larger main jet — start 5–10 sizes up from stock (e.g., jet #108 for a 61 mm / 171cc build). Test and adjust until the spark plug reads a light tan colour after a full-throttle run. **💡 Re-torque After First Heat Cycle:** After the engine has warmed up to operating temperature for the first time and cooled back down, re-torque the cylinder head nuts. Aluminium expands and contracts significantly with temperature, which can cause head gasket settling. This step prevents head gasket failure in the first few hundred kilometres. ## Common Mistakes - **Forgetting to re-jet:** Running lean after a displacement increase will burn the piston. Always re-jet. - **Installing rings with gaps aligned:** Piston rings must have staggered gaps. Aligned gaps cause excessive blow-by and oil consumption. - **Overtorquing the head:** The aluminium head strips very easily. Use a torque wrench — don't rely on feel. - **Dropping the cam chain:** Secure it with a zip tie before removing the camshaft. Retrieving a dropped cam chain can mean splitting the cases. - **Skipping the break-in period:** For the first 200–300 km after a big bore install, avoid full throttle. Vary engine speed to allow the rings to bed in properly. ## Expected Performance Gains A 150cc → 171cc big bore conversion on a GY6 scooter typically delivers: 10–15% more torque at low-to-mid RPM, noticeably stronger acceleration from a standstill, and a modest top speed increase (2–5 km/h in most cases). The biggest benefit is felt in the mid-range — the scooter pulls harder up hills and when two-up riding. For further gains, the big bore upgrade pairs well with a performance exhaust, upgraded variator rollers matched to the new power delivery, and — if running carburetion — a matching performance air filter and jet kit.

import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; DOT brake fluid is hygroscopic — it absorbs moisture from the atmosphere through the reservoir vent and brake line walls. As water content builds up over time, the fluid's boiling point drops. Under hard or prolonged braking the fluid can boil, creating vapour bubbles in the line. Vapour compresses (liquid does not), so the lever becomes spongy and braking force is lost — this is called _vapour lock_. Fresh fluid prevents this and also reduces internal corrosion in the master cylinder and caliper pistons. � **Hazard:** Brake fluid strips paint and damages plastic within seconds. Protect all painted and plastic surfaces with rags before starting. Wear nitrile gloves. If skin contact occurs, wash immediately with soap and water. Dispose of old brake fluid at a recycling centre — never pour it down the drain. ## Fluid Specification
ModelFluid typeNotes
GY6 125/150 (most clones)DOT 4Check reservoir cap — it is stamped with the correct grade
Vespa Primavera / SprintDOT 4Piaggio recommends DOT 4 for all modern hydraulic systems
Vespa GTS 250/300DOT 4Both front and rear circuits
� **Never mix fluid grades or brands.** DOT 3, 4, and 5.1 are glycol-based and miscible with each other — but mixing grades lowers the effective boiling point of the blend. DOT 5 (silicone-based) is **completely incompatible** with DOT 3/4/5.1 systems and must never be used unless the entire system has been flushed and rebuilt. ## Tools & Materials Required - 8 mm ring spanner (bleed nipple) - Phillips screwdriver (master cylinder reservoir cap screws) - Fresh, sealed DOT 4 brake fluid (100–200 ml is sufficient for one circuit) - Clear vinyl bleed tube (~30 cm, 4–5 mm inner diameter) - Small glass jar or container for old fluid - Syringe or turkey baster (for reservoir management) - Rags and newspaper to protect painted surfaces - Nitrile gloves 🎬 Video Guide — Bleeding the Front Brake on a 150cc GY6 Scooter **Video:** "Bleeding the Front Brake on a 150cc GY6 Scooter" | YouTube   [↗ Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nhfPUISx-FU) ## Step-by-Step Brake Bleed Procedure ### Preparation 1. **Protect surrounding surfaces** — lay rags over the scooter's painted panels, plastics, and the fuel tank around the handlebar area. Brake fluid contact causes immediate paint damage. 2. **Locate the brake caliper bleed nipple** — a small valve on the caliper body with a rubber dust cap. Remove the dust cap. 3. **Attach the bleed tube** over the nipple. Place the other end into the collection jar. Loop the tube upward above the caliper height — this prevents air from being drawn back into the system between pumps. ### Draining & Filling 4. **Open the master cylinder reservoir** on the handlebar — remove the two Phillips screws, lift off the cap, and remove the rubber diaphragm. Keep the reservoir level at all times to prevent air entry. 5. **Note the fluid color** — fresh DOT 4 is clear/pale yellow. Old fluid is amber to dark brown. Heavily contaminated fluid may be almost black. 6. **Top up the reservoir** with fresh fluid to the MAX line before opening the bleed nipple. This prevents the reservoir from running dry and drawing air into the system. ### Bleeding (Two-Person or One-Person Method) 7. **Open the bleed nipple** ½ turn counter-clockwise. Old fluid will begin to flow by gravity. 8. **Pump-bleed cycle** — squeeze the brake lever _slowly_ to the handlebar. With the lever held in, open the nipple ½ turn and allow fluid to flow out. Close the nipple before releasing the lever. Repeat this cycle 8–10 times. This pushes old fluid out faster and purges air bubbles. 9. **Watch the reservoir constantly** — top up with fresh fluid every 3–4 pump cycles. If the reservoir runs empty, air enters the system and you must start over. 10. **Continue until** the fluid flowing out of the bleed tube is clear and pale yellow (matching the fresh fluid in the bottle), with no air bubbles visible in the tube. 11. **Final close:** with the brake lever squeezed to the handlebar, close the bleed nipple firmly (5–8 Nm — snug, not over-tight). Release the lever. ### Finishing 12. **Top up the reservoir** to the MAX line with fresh fluid. Refit the rubber diaphragm (ensure it seats without folds) and reinstall the cap and screws. 13. **Pump the lever** several times — it should feel firm throughout its travel with no sponginess. If still spongy, air remains in the system and the bleed procedure must be repeated. 14. **Refit the bleed nipple dust cap.** 15. **Wipe down all surfaces** that may have been contaminated with fluid. Check carefully around the reservoir cap and bleed nipple. 16. **Test ride carefully** at low speed before normal use. � **One-person bleeding tip:** A cheap vacuum bleeder kit (syringe + tube with one-way valve, ~€10 online) makes solo bleeding much easier and faster. You can also use the gravity-bleed method — open the nipple ½ turn and let fluid drip out by gravity while keeping the reservoir topped up, no lever pumping needed. Gravity bleed is slower but foolproof for removing old fluid. ## Service Intervals
SituationAction
Every 2 years (regardless of km)Full fluid change — drain and refill both circuits
Spongy lever feel at any timeCheck for leaks, then bleed to remove air
After any brake line or caliper workFull bleed required to remove introduced air
After new brake pads fittedTop up reservoir, pump lever to re-seat pistons

import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; Brakes are the single most safety-critical system on your scooter. On most GY6 clones the front uses a hydraulic disc brake with pads, and the rear uses a mechanical drum brake with shoes. Vespa Primavera and Sprint models use disc brakes on both wheels. This guide covers both types. � **Safety:** Never ride with brakes worn to the metal backing plate. Stopping distance increases dramatically and rotor or drum damage will occur. Wear nitrile gloves when handling brake components — brake dust may contain asbestos fibres in older pads. ## When to Replace - **Squealing or grinding noise** when braking — wear indicators contacting the rotor - **Increased lever/pedal travel** — lever reaching the handlebar before full braking force - **Pulsing or vibration** through the lever — warped rotor or uneven pad wear - **Friction material ≤ 2 mm** on visual inspection through the caliper inspection slot - **One pad much more worn than the other** — indicates a seized caliper piston or slide pin ## Tools & Materials Required - 10 mm socket (caliper mounting bolts on most GY6) - Flat-head screwdriver or piston retraction tool - 12 mm open-end spanner (rear drum adjuster nut) - Brake cleaner spray - Copper grease / anti-seize (for pad backs and slide pins — _not_ friction surfaces) - New front brake pads (GY6 generic disc pads) - New rear drum brake shoes (GY6 generic drum shoe set) - Nitrile gloves 🎬 Video Guide — Replace Scooter Front Brakes & Adjust Rear Drum [ ![Replace Scooter Front Brakes and Adjust Rear Drum thumbnail](https://img.youtube.com/vi/nat0lVKkuSk/hqdefault.jpg) ▶ ](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nat0lVKkuSk "Watch on YouTube") **Video:** "Replace Scooter Front Brakes & Adjust Rear Drum" | YouTube   [↗ Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nat0lVKkuSk) ## Part A — Front Disc Brake Pad Replacement ️ When pushing the caliper piston back in, brake fluid is displaced upward into the master cylinder reservoir. Check the reservoir level before you start and remove a small amount with a syringe if it is at MAX — otherwise it will overflow when the piston is retracted. 1. **Support the scooter** on its centre stand on a flat, stable surface. 2. **Remove the two caliper mounting bolts** (usually 10 mm) and slide the caliper off the rotor. Support the caliper with a wire or bungee cord — do not let it hang by the brake line. 3. **Remove the pad retaining pin** (a bolt or cotter pin depending on caliper type) and slide the old pads out of the caliper. 4. **Inspect the brake rotor** for deep grooves, scoring, or cracks. Minimum thickness is typically stamped on the rotor. A heavily grooved rotor reduces new pad effectiveness and should be replaced. 5. **Retract the caliper piston:** place the old pad against the piston face and press it back into the caliper body using a large flat-head screwdriver or C-clamp. Push slowly and evenly. The piston must be fully retracted to accommodate the thickness of new pads. 6. **Clean the caliper carrier** with brake cleaner — remove all dust, rust, and debris from the pad slide channels. 7. **Apply a thin film of copper grease** to the back face of each new pad and to the caliper slide pins. Do not get any grease on the friction surface or the rotor. 8. **Insert the new pads** into the caliper and refit the retaining pin. Reinstall the caliper and torque the mounting bolts to **25–30 Nm**. 9. **Pump the brake lever** 10–15 times until the lever feels firm — this pushes the pistons out to contact the new pads. Check the brake fluid reservoir level and top up to MAX if needed. 10. **Bed in the pads:** perform 5–6 firm stops from 30 km/h before normal riding. This transfers a thin even layer of pad material onto the rotor surface for optimal friction. ## Part B — Rear Drum Brake Shoe Replacement (GY6) 1. **Remove the rear wheel:** loosen the axle nut, disconnect the rear brake cable or rod, and slide the wheel off. Place the scooter on a paddock stand or support it securely. 2. **Expose the brake shoes:** the drum is integral to the wheel hub. The shoes are mounted on a brake plate (backing plate) attached to the swingarm. With the wheel removed, the shoes are visible. 3. **Photograph the spring arrangement** before removing anything — reassembly requires knowing exactly where each return spring attaches. 4. **Remove the return springs** using brake spring pliers or needle-nose pliers. Slide the old shoes off the pivot pins and cam. 5. **Inspect the drum surface** (inside the wheel hub) for scoring. Light scores are normal; deep grooves require drum skimming or replacement. 6. **Clean the backing plate** with brake cleaner. Apply a small amount of high-temperature grease to the shoe contact points on the backing plate — the raised pads where the shoe metal slides. Do not apply any grease near the friction surface. 7. **Fit the new shoes** onto the pivot pins and cam. Reattach the return springs — the springs should pull the shoes back toward each other (away from the drum). 8. **Reinstall the wheel** and tighten the axle nut to the specified torque (typically 50–60 Nm). 9. **Adjust the brake cable or rod** so the rear brake has approximately 10–15 mm of free play at the lever/pedal tip before resistance begins. Too little free play causes the brake to drag; too much increases stopping distance. 10. **Test** by walking the scooter and applying the rear brake firmly several times before riding. ## GY6 Brake Pad & Shoe Reference
ComponentTypeMinimum thicknessNotes
Front disc pads (GY6 125/150)Sintered or organic2 mm (friction material)Generic GY6 pads fit most clones
Rear drum shoes (GY6)Bonded lining1 mm above rivet headsReplace both shoes together
Vespa front/rear disc padsOEM sintered2 mmUse Piaggio OEM or equivalent quality
� **Tip:** If one front pad is significantly more worn than the other, the caliper slide pins are likely seized with corrosion. Remove, clean, and lubricate them with silicone grease. Failing to do this will cause the new pads to wear unevenly again within 1,000 km. ## Applicable Models Front disc procedure applies to all GY6 125/150cc scooters with hydraulic front disc brakes including **BTC Riva 125**, **La Souris Sourini**, **Santini Capri**, and most Chinese 125cc clones. Rear drum procedure applies to GY6 models with drum rear brakes. Proper adjustment is critical: a mis-tuned carburetor causes hard starting, poor idle, bogging at mid-throttle, and poor fuel economy. GY6 Engines Piaggio ZIP Piaggio Primavera Vespa ## GY6 Carburetor Adjustment The GY6 carburetor is a simple slide-type or CV (constant velocity) carburetor — most 50cc models use a **Keihin PD18J**\-type clone, while 150cc models typically use a **PZ30** or similar. 🎬 Video Guide — Full Walkthrough **Video:** "GY6 Carburetor Inspection, Problems, Removal, & Adjustment" | YouTube   [↗ Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D9UnD1ibIIw) ### Tools Required - Flat-head screwdriver (small) - Phillips screwdriver - Tachometer (even a cheap clip-on type works) - Clean carburetor spray cleaner - Compressed air or a bulb blower ### GY6 Specifications by Displacement

### Understanding the Adjusters Two screws control most of the tune: - **Idle speed screw (throttle stop screw):** Controls minimum throttle position — turning it clockwise raises idle RPM, counter-clockwise lowers it. - **Air/fuel mixture screw (pilot screw):** Controls the fuel richness at idle and low throttle. Located under a small brass plug on the carburetor body (sometimes covered by an anti-tamper cap). Turning counter-clockwise (out) richens the mixture; clockwise (in) leans it out. ### Step-by-Step Procedure 1 Initial Mixture Screw Setting 1. Gently turn the mixture screw clockwise until it seats lightly. **Do not force it** — the needle tip is fragile. 2. Back it out the following number of turns as a starting baseline:
EngineStarting Position

GY6 125cc (152QMI)2.0–2.5 turns out
GY6 150cc (157QMJ)2.5–2.75 turns out
2 Set Idle Speed 1. Start the engine and allow it to reach full operating temperature (10 minutes minimum). 2. Using the idle speed screw, adjust RPM to the target range (see specifications table above). 3. If you do not have a tachometer, set idle to the lowest stable speed at which the engine will not stall. 3 Fine-Tune the Air/Fuel Mixture 1. With the engine at full operating temperature and idle set, slowly turn the mixture screw counter-clockwise (richer) in ¼-turn increments. Pause 10–15 seconds after each adjustment. 2. Listen: RPM should rise as you approach the ideal mixture. Note the position where RPM peaks. 3. From the peak-RPM position, turn the screw clockwise (leaner) by ¼ turn. This is your optimal idle mixture setting. 4. Re-adjust the idle speed screw to bring the RPM back to the target range. 5. Snap the throttle open quickly and release — the engine should rev cleanly without hesitation or stumble. If it stumbles, richen the mixture slightly (counter-clockwise ¼ turn). 4 Float Level Adjustment An incorrectly set float is one of the most common causes of GY6 carburetor problems: too high causes rich running, fuel overflow, and stalling at idle; too low causes lean surge and bog. 🎬 Float Adjustment Technique **Video:** "How to Adjust a Float on a Carburetor | Simple Trick!" — Demonstrates the proper technique for bending the float tab without damaging it. 1. Remove the float bowl (bottom of carburetor, held by one screw). Drain any fuel into a rag. 2. Hold the carburetor body with the float upright (as if gravity were pulling it closed). 3. The bottom of the float should be parallel to the carburetor body gasket surface. Typical specification: **14–16 mm** from the gasket surface to the bottom of the float. 4. To adjust, gently bend the small metal tab that contacts the needle valve until the float sits at the correct height. 5. Reinstall float bowl with a new gasket if available. Tighten the bowl screw snugly — do not overtighten (it is often plastic-threaded). � **Tip:** If the float bowl gasket leaks, a thin smear of petrol-resistant RTV sealant works as a temporary fix, but a proper replacement O-ring or gasket is always better. 5 Pilot Jet & Main Jet (Cleaning) Before adjusting, confirm the jets are clean. A partially blocked pilot jet causes lean stumble at idle; a blocked main jet causes flat top-speed. 1. Remove the pilot jet (see specifications table for sizes) and main jet. 2. Spray carburetor cleaner through the jet holes and blow clear with compressed air. **Never use wire** — it enlarges the orifice. 3. Hold the jet up to light — you should see a clean round hole straight through. 4. Reinstall jets snug but do not overtighten (they strip easily). ### Symptom Diagnosis Quick Reference
SymptomLikely CauseAction
Black smoke, sooty plug, fuel overflowRunning too richTurn mixture screw IN (clockwise), lower float level
White/grey plug, lean surge, overheatingRunning too leanTurn mixture screw OUT (counter-clockwise), raise float level
Stumble/bog off idleBlocked pilot jet or lean mixtureClean pilot jet, richen mixture screw ¼ turn
Poor top-end performanceBlocked main jet or small main jet sizeClean or upsize main jet by 2–5 sizes
Fuel dripping from overflow tubeFloat level too high or needle valve stuckLower float, clean/replace needle valve
Hard start when coldAuto-choke not functioningTest auto-choke thermostatic element (see choke guide)
### Applicable Models This guide applies directly to GY6-engined scooters commonly sold in the Benelux market and Europe, including: **BTC Riva** (50cc, Euro 2/4), **La Souris Sourini** and **La Souris City S** (50cc, carbureted variants), **Santini Capri** (50cc GY6), and any other scooter using the `139QMB`, `152QMI`, or `157QMJ` engine codes. ## Piaggio ZIP Carburetor Adjustment The Piaggio ZIP (50cc and 125cc) uses a **Dellorto SHA** or **Astra** carburetor, both of which are slide-type designs. These carburetors are slightly more refined than GY6 clones and have excellent adjustment range for fine-tuning performance. ### ZIP Specifications by Displacement
Year / VersionDisplacementCarb TypePilot JetMain JetTarget Idle
ZIP Classic / SP (1992–2000)50ccDellorto SHA 13/1340–5085–981,400–1,600 RPM

ZIP 125 / 125 Liberty125ccDellorto PHBG 18–2050–65105–1251,200–1,400 RPM
### Carburetor Overview - **Slide type:** Dellorto designs use a needle position system similar to GY6 but with more granular control. - **Mixture screw:** Located on the lower side of the carburetor body. Turning **out (counter-clockwise)** richens; **in (clockwise)** leans out. - **Idle speed:** Adjusted via a throttle stop screw on the side of the carburetor. Accessible without removing the carb. ### Adjustment Steps for Piaggio ZIP 1 Initial Setup 1. Locate the mixture screw on the left side of the carburetor, below the float bowl. 2. Gently turn clockwise until the screw seats (do not force). This is the fully lean position. 3. Back off the screw: - **ZIP 50cc:** 2.0–2.5 turns out - **ZIP 125:** 2.5–3.0 turns out 2 Warm the Engine & Set Idle 1. Start the engine and let it warm for 10–15 minutes (Dellortos respond well to warmth). 2. Using the idle speed screw (throttle stop), adjust to the target idle RPM range (see specifications table). 3. Dellortos typically idle very clean — aim for the **lower end** of the range for best stability. 3 Fine-Tune Mixture on Dellorto 1. With the engine at full temperature, turn the mixture screw slowly counter-clockwise in **⅛-turn increments** (Dellortos are more sensitive than GY6). 2. Wait 8–10 seconds between adjustments. 3. Listen for the RPM to rise slightly, then peak. 4. Once you find the peak, turn **¼ turn leaner (clockwise)** — this is the sweet spot for Dellorto carburetors. 5. Snap the throttle: the engine should accelerate smoothly without hesitation or burble. 4 Float Level (Dellorto) 1. Remove the float bowl. 2. Hold the carburetor upright; the float should sit at **13–15 mm** from the gasket surface (slightly lower than GY6). 3. Bend the float tab gently if adjustment is needed. 4. Dellorto float bowls often have a small inspection window — use this to verify fuel level without removing the bowl. ### Piaggio ZIP Diagnostics

Excellent idle but poor top-endMain jet too small or cloggedClean main jet, upsize by 5–10 numbers

The throttle diaphragm (vacuum slide) must move freely — any crack in the diaphragm causes severe throttle response issues and requires carburettor replacement. See the [Piaggio ZIP 100 Technical Overview](/models/piaggio-zip-100-technical-overview.html) for full specifications. ## Piaggio Primavera Carburetor Adjustment The Piaggio Primavera (50cc, 125cc, 150cc) is known for conservative tuning from the factory. Most use **Dellorto PHBG** or **SHA** carburetors. Modern Primavera models (2013+) are fuel-injected, but classic and 2000s-era models use carburetors that respond extremely well to proper tuning. ### Primavera Specifications
Model Year / CCCarb TypePilot JetMain JetNeedleTarget Idle
Primavera 50cc (Pre-2013)Dellorto SHA 13/1445–5588–100C1,500–1,700 RPM
Primavera 125cc (Carb)Dellorto PHBG 18/2055–70110–130E / F1,200–1,400 RPM
Primavera 150cc (Carb)Dellorto PHBG 2060–75130–150F / G1,000–1,200 RPM
### Understanding Primavera Carburetors - **Needle position:** Primavera uses **C-clip needle selection** (different from GY6). The clip position affects middle-range response significantly. - **Jetting:** Factory conservative. Many owners upsize main jet by 10–15 numbers for better mid-range and top-end. - **Mixture screw:** Standard Dellorto type, counter-clockwise = rich, clockwise = lean. ### Adjustment Steps 1 Baseline Setting 1. Set mixture screw to factory baseline: - **50cc Primavera:** 2.25 turns out - **125cc Primavera:** 2.5 turns out - **150cc Primavera:** 2.75 turns out 2. Verify the needle clip is in the **middle groove** (usually groove 2 or 3 from top). 2 Warm & Idle 1. Warm the engine thoroughly — Primavera tends to run rich when cold. 2. Set idle to target RPM using the throttle stop screw. 3. The Primavera idle should feel **smooth and consistent**, rarely needing choke at normal temps. 3 Mixture Refinement 1. Turn mixture screw counter-clockwise in ⅛-turn steps, waiting 10 seconds between each. 2. Find the RPM peak and note the position. 3. Lean back ¼ turn (clockwise) from peak — this is optimal Primavera tuning. 4. **Optional:** If the engine hesitates during acceleration, move the needle clip UP one groove and test again. This enriches the mid-range. 4 Needle Position (Mid-Range Tuning) 1. The C-clip on the needle has typically 5–6 positions (1=leanest, 5–6=richest). 2. **Factory position:** Usually groove 3 (middle). 3. **For better mid-range response:** Move clip UP one position (richer mid-range). 4. **For leaner/fuel-efficient cruise:** Move clip DOWN one position. 5. Warm the engine and test throttle response 2,000–6,000 RPM after any clip change. ### Primavera Float Level - **Dellorto PHBG (125/150):** Float should sit **12–14 mm** from gasket surface. - **SHA (50cc):** Float should sit **13–15 mm** from gasket surface. - Primavera floats are more robust than ZIP — they rarely need bending. ### Primavera Diagnostics

### Models Covered Piaggio Primavera 50cc, 125cc, 150cc (pre-2013 carbureted models; 2013+ are EFI and not covered here). ## Vespa Carburetor Adjustment Vespa scooters use a range of carburetors depending on model year and displacement. Classic Vespas (PX, PK) typically use **Dellorto SHA**, while modern Vespa Primavera and Sprint (2013+) use fuel injection. This section covers **Carbureted Vespas**. ### Vespa Specifications
Model / YearDisplacementCarb TypePilot JetMain JetTarget Idle

� **Classic Vespa Tip:** Vespa carburetors from the 1970s–1990s are extremely durable. If your Vespa idles rough, fuel leaks, or surges, the issue is almost always **jet blockage**, not adjustment. Always clean the jets before attempting to tune. ### Tools for Vespa Carburetor Work - Small flat-head screwdriver (mixture screw) - Tachometer (strongly recommended for Vespa — factory specs are tight) - Carburetor cleaner spray - Compressed air (for jets) - Allen keys (some float bowl screws are socket-head) ### Vespa Carburetor Layout **Key differences from Piaggio:** - Mixture screw is typically on the **left side** of the carburetor, below the float bowl. - Idle speed is set via a **throttle stop screw** on the right side of the carb body. - Many classic Vespa models have a **remote choke cable** — ensure the choke lever returns fully to prevent rich running. ### Adjustment Steps for Vespa 1 Pre-Adjustment Inspection 1. Check that the choke cable operates freely and returns fully to the open position. 2. Verify the throttle cable does not bind — snap the throttle hard; the carburetor slide should snap back immediately. 3. Look for fuel leaks around the float bowl gasket. If leaking, replace the gasket before tuning. 2 Initial Mixture & Idle 1. Set mixture screw to factory baseline: - **Vespa PX 50cc:** 2.0–2.25 turns out - **Vespa PX 125cc / 150cc:** 2.25–2.5 turns out 2. Start the engine (use choke if cold). 3. Once warmed, close the choke fully and allow 3–5 minutes to idle. 4. Adjust the idle speed screw until the engine settles at the target RPM (see table). 3 Fine-Tune Mixture 1. With the engine warm and at idle speed, turn the mixture screw counter-clockwise in **⅛-turn increments**. Wait 10 seconds between turns. 2. Watch the tachometer (or listen for RPM change). The idle RPM should rise slightly, then peak, then start to drop (as mixture becomes too rich). 3. Note the position where RPM peaks. 4. From peak, turn the screw clockwise (leaner) by **¼ turn**. This is the optimal idle setting. 5. Snap the throttle open to 3,000 RPM and release — the engine should respond cleanly. 4 Verify Float Level 1. Remove the float bowl (usually 1 screw on the bottom). 2. Hold the carburetor upright. The bottom of the float should be **15–17 mm** from the carburetor gasket surface (slightly higher than other models). 3. Gently bend the float tab if adjustment is needed. **Do not force the tab** — Vespa floats are vintage brass and can crack. 4. Reinstall with a new gasket or petrol-resistant sealant. � **Vespa Float Gasket Tip:** Many classic Vespa owners use a thin RTV sealant instead of gaskets — this works well but makes future disassembly harder. For longevity, source an original cork gasket from a Vespa parts supplier. ### Vespa Diagnostics

Good idle but weak accelerationBlocked main jet or throttle cable bindingClean main jet; verify throttle snap-back
Fuel drips from overflow; runs richFloat level too high or needle valve stuckLower float by 1–2 mm; clean needle/seat
Backfire on deceleration (common symptom)Mixture too lean (common factory setting)Richen mixture ⅜–½ turn; upsize main jet by 5 numbers

import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; import SourceBox from '@components/SourceBox.astro'; A dirty or partially blocked carburetor is the most common cause of poor GY6 engine performance: rough idle, hard starting, hesitation on throttle, and stalling. This guide covers a thorough disassembly-and-clean — going further than a quick spray of carb cleaner — for the standard slide-type carburetors (PD18J / PD22J / PD24J / CVK) fitted to GY6 139QMB (50cc) and 157QMJ (125cc / 150cc) engines. ## Video Walkthrough ## Tools & Materials - JIS cross-head screwdrivers (sizes #1 and #2) — not standard Phillips - Flat-blade screwdriver, 3 mm and 5 mm - Aerosol carburetor cleaner (non-residue formula) - Compressed air with fine nozzle - Small wire brush (soft brass bristles) - Clean rag or lint-free cloth - Parts tray or egg carton (to sort jets and screws) - New float-bowl gasket (O-ring or flat, depending on carb model) - Nitrile gloves and eye protection Fire hazard: Work in a well-ventilated area away from ignition sources. Petrol and carburetor cleaner are highly flammable. Disconnect the fuel tap (petcock) before removing the float bowl. ## Step-by-Step Procedure ### 1 — Preparation 1. Allow the engine to cool completely. A warm carburetor is easier to smell fumes from, but a hot engine is a burn hazard. 2. Turn the fuel tap to the **OFF** or **PRI** (prime) position so no fuel flows to the carburetor. 3. Remove the side panel or access cover on your scooter to expose the carburetor body. 4. Place a rag or drain pan under the float bowl to catch residual fuel. ### 2 — Remove the Carburetor 1. Loosen the intake manifold clamp screw (the band clamp connecting carburetor to engine inlet). Do not remove — just loosen until the carburetor can twist free. 2. Loosen the air-box clamp in the same way on the air-filter side. 3. Disconnect the throttle cable: compress the cable end and unhook it from the slide. Note the cable routing. 4. Detach the fuel line from the carburetor inlet nipple. Plug or clamp the line to prevent dripping. 5. Disconnect the choke cable (or automatic choke wiring connector if fitted). 6. Twist and pull the carburetor free from both clamps. Set it on your work surface. ### 3 — Disassemble the Float Bowl 1. Unscrew the float-bowl drain screw (bottom of bowl, if present) and drain remaining fuel into a container. 2. Remove the float-bowl retaining screw(s) — usually one or two at the bottom or side. Lift the bowl away. 3. Inspect the bowl for sediment, rust particles, or a dark varnish residue. These indicate stale fuel contamination. 4. Remove the float by pushing out its hinge pin sideways. The float and needle will come away as one unit. 5. Unscrew the main jet (brass screw in the centre of the carb body) using a flat-blade screwdriver. Note its size — it is stamped on the side (e.g., `#75`, `#85`, `#98`). 6. Unscrew the pilot jet (smaller brass screw nearby, sometimes recessed). Note its size as well. | Engine | Typical Main Jet | Pilot Jet | Carburetor | |---|---|---|---| | GY6 50cc (139QMB) | #75–#78 | #35–#38 | PD18J | | GY6 125cc (152QMI) | #95–#98 | #38–#42 | PD22J / CVK22 | | GY6 150cc (157QMJ) | #98–#105 | #38–#42 | PD24J / CVK24 | ### 4 — Clean All Components 1. **Float bowl:** Spray interior with carburetor cleaner, scrub with a soft brush, rinse, dry with compressed air. 2. **Main jet:** Hold up to light and check that the hole is clear and round. Spray cleaner through it. If blocked, use a bristle from the wire brush — never a drill bit or wire, which will enlarge the calibrated orifice. 3. **Pilot jet:** Same process. The pilot jet feeds fuel at idle and low throttle; a partially blocked pilot jet causes rough idle and stumbling below ¼ throttle. 4. **Carburetor body passages:** Spray cleaner into every port and passage you can see, including the emulsion tube holes (the small holes in the main bore). Follow with compressed air from the opposite side to clear debris outward. 5. **Needle and slide:** Remove the top cap of the carburetor to extract the slide. Inspect the needle for wear (grooves, bends). Clean the slide bore with a cloth dampened in cleaner. 6. **Air/fuel mixture screw:** Count and record how many turns out it is currently set before removing. Remove it carefully (it may have a small O-ring, washer, and spring). Clean the passage with cleaner and air. Reinstall to the recorded position. Tip: If the carburetor body shows brown or black varnish inside the float bowl or emulsion passages, soak it for 30 minutes in a commercial carburetor dip (or a solution of acetone and water). This dissolves hardened gum deposits that aerosol cleaner cannot shift. ### 5 — Inspect the Float & Needle Valve 1. Shake the float gently next to your ear — if you hear liquid sloshing inside, the float has a pinhole and must be replaced. A sinking float will cause fuel to flood the engine. 2. Inspect the tip of the needle valve (the rubber or brass cone that seats against the float seat). If it shows wear or has a groove, replace it — a worn needle valve will cause fuel overflow and a rich condition. 3. Set float height: with the float bowl mating face horizontal, the float arms should be roughly parallel to that face. Bend the small tab that contacts the needle valve to adjust if needed. Refer to your engine's service manual for the exact specification (typically 14–16 mm on GY6 157QMJ). ### 6 — Reassembly 1. Install jets finger-tight, then snug (do not overtighten — they are brass in an aluminium body). 2. Refit the float and hinge pin. 3. Install a new float-bowl O-ring or gasket if the old one is compressed or cracked. 4. Refit the float bowl and tighten evenly. 5. Reinstall the slide and needle (ensure the needle clip is seated in the correct groove — middle groove for standard tune). 6. Refit the carburetor to the scooter, reversing the removal steps. Ensure both clamps are properly tightened to prevent air leaks. 7. Reconnect fuel line, throttle cable, and choke cable. 8. Turn the fuel tap on and check for leaks before starting. ### 7 — First-Start Tuning 1. Start the engine and allow it to reach operating temperature (approximately 5 minutes of running). 2. Adjust the idle speed screw (the large thumb or flat-blade screw on the side of the carb body) until idle is stable at approximately 1,500–1,800 rpm. 3. Adjust the air/fuel mixture screw (the small recessed screw) ½ turn at a time, waiting 30 seconds between adjustments, until idle is smooth and highest. Typical range is 1½ to 2½ turns out from gently seated. 4. Snap the throttle open and release it — the engine should rev cleanly without hesitation or hanging. import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; import SourceBox from '@components/SourceBox.astro'; Added: 2026-05-08  |  Sources: [scooterworks.com](https://www.scooterworks.com/blogs/news/carburetor-jetting-101), [rollingwrenchdenver.com](https://www.rollingwrenchdenver.com/blogs/news/carburetor-help-jetting-and-tuning-help), [jetsrus.com](https://www.jetsrus.com/FAQs/FAQ_rejetting_101_how_to_rejet.htm)  |  GY6 Carburetor 139QMB 157QMJ Jetting refers to selecting the correct size of the brass main jet and pilot jet inside the carburetor to achieve the right air-to-fuel ratio for your engine's conditions. A stock GY6 scooter is jetted conservatively from the factory — usually slightly lean — which can cause hesitation, flat spots, or overheating. If you have added an aftermarket exhaust, performance air filter, or high-compression piston, rejetting is essential. ## Understanding the Throttle Zones The GY6 slide-type carburetor (PD-series or CVK) controls the mixture across the throttle range via different circuits. Knowing which circuit governs each zone tells you which component to adjust: - **0–¼ throttle (idle and off-idle):** Governed by the pilot jet and the air/fuel mixture screw. Symptoms of a lean pilot: stumbling, stalling at idle, engine hunts. - **¼–¾ throttle (mid-range):** Governed by the needle position and its clip groove. A needle that is too lean causes hesitation when rolling on from partial throttle. - **¾–full throttle (wide-open):** Governed by the main jet size. A lean main jet causes flat top-end power and possible overheating at sustained full throttle. ## Diagnosing Rich vs Lean
SymptomLikely CauseCorrection
Black sooty spark plug, dark smokeRich mixture (too large a jet)Go down 2–5 jet sizes
White/grey spark plug, overheatingLean mixture (too small a jet)Go up 2–5 jet sizes
Stumbling at idle, stalls when warmLean pilot circuitRichen mixture screw or upsize pilot jet
Hesitation at ¼–½ throttle roll-onLean needle positionRaise needle clip (lower the clip groove number)
Bog at full throttleLean main jet or clogged main jetUpsize main jet by 3–5 sizes; clean jet first
Rich surge, black plug at full throttleRich main jetDownsize main jet by 3–5 sizes

139QMB50cc (49cc)PD18J#75#353rd groove (middle)
