157QMJ150ccPD24J / CVK24#98–#102#403rd groove
## Jetting for Modifications ## Performance Air Filter A high-flow air filter (K&N style pod filter or similar) allows more air through the carburetor. This leans the mixture and requires a main jet increase. A typical starting point is to increase the main jet by **5–8 sizes** (e.g., from #98 to #105 on a 150cc engine) and adjust from there using the spark plug color method. ## Performance Exhaust An aftermarket exhaust that reduces back-pressure also leans the mixture, especially in the mid-to-high throttle range. Increase the main jet by **3–5 sizes** as a starting point, and raise the needle one clip position (move the clip from the 3rd to the 2nd groove from the top). ## Altitude Correction At higher altitudes, air is thinner, so the stock jetting becomes progressively richer as altitude increases. A rough rule of thumb is to decrease the main jet by **3 sizes per 1,000 m** of altitude above sea level.
AltitudeApprox. Main Jet Correction (GY6 150cc baseline #98)
0–500 mStock (#98–#102)

## How to Change a Main Jet 1. Ensure the engine is cold. Turn the fuel tap off. 2. Remove the float bowl (see the [Deep-Cleaning Guide](gy6-carburetor-cleaning-guide.html) for step-by-step bowl removal). 3. Unscrew the main jet with a flat-blade screwdriver. Note the existing size stamped on the jet body. 4. Thread in the new jet finger-tight, then snug with the screwdriver. Do not overtighten. 5. Refit the float bowl, turn the fuel on, and start the engine. 6. After a warm-up run, remove the spark plug and read its color. A correct mixture gives a tan to light brown plug tip. Black = too rich; white/grey = too lean. 7. Adjust one jet size at a time until the plug color is correct. ️ Always clean the carburetor thoroughly before rejetting. A partially blocked jet will give false lean symptoms regardless of jet size. See the [Deep-Cleaning Guide](gy6-carburetor-cleaning-guide.html) first. � **Tip:** Jets are typically sized in increments of 2–3 (e.g., #95, #98, #100, #102, #105). Buy a jet kit covering a range of ±15 from your stock size so you can tune without repeated ordering. ## Where to Buy GY6 Jets Replacement GY6 jets (both main and pilot) are widely available from vendors including [VMC Chinese Parts](https://www.vmcchineseparts.com/), [Rolling Wrench Denver](https://www.rollingwrenchdenver.com/), and [Scooterworks USA](https://www.scooterworks.com/collections/gy6). When ordering, confirm the carburetor model (PD18J, PD22J, PD24J, or CVK) to ensure thread pitch compatibility.

import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; import SourceBox from '@components/SourceBox.astro'; Added: 2026-05-11  |  Sources: [buggydepot.com](https://www.buggydepot.com/tech-center/gy6-150cc-ignition-troubleshooting-guide-no-spark/), [moowiring.com](https://moowiring.com/2025/05/24/gy6-dc-cdi-wiring-diagram/) GY6 Ignition CDI Carburettor Fuel Injection A GY6-engine scooter that cranks normally but produces no spark is one of the most common breakdown scenarios. The ignition system has three main electrical components that work together to fire the spark plug: the **stator / pick-up coil**, the **CDI unit** (Capacitor Discharge Ignition), and the **ignition coil**. This guide walks through a logical, test-before-replace diagnostic sequence so you replace only the component that has actually failed. **Applies to:** All GY6 50 cc (139QMB) and 125/150 cc (157QMJ / QMI152) engines — both carburetor and fuel-injected variants. The AC-CDI ignition circuit is identical across carburetted and EFI models. ⚠️ **Safety:** Work with the ignition off and the kill switch in the OFF position except when explicitly told to crank the engine during a test step. Keep hands and tools clear of the flywheel and cooling fan during cranking. ## Understanding the GY6 Ignition Circuit On all standard GY6 engines the CDI is an AC-CDI: the stator generates its own alternating current to power the CDI capacitor — the main battery is not involved in spark production. Current flow is: stator charging coil → CDI capacitor → CDI trigger from pick-up coil → ignition coil primary winding → secondary winding → HT lead → spark plug. The most commonly sold replacement CDIs for GY6 scooters are the 5-pin AC-CDI (most 50 cc models) and the 6-pin AC-CDI (most 125/150 cc models). DC-CDI units (powered from the battery) are found on some fuel-injected variants and EFI conversion kits. ## Tools Required - Digital multimeter (AC and DC voltage, resistance) - Inline spark tester or spare known-good spark plug - Screwdrivers (Phillips and flat) - Side cutters and electrical tape or crimp connectors for any wiring repairs ## Step 1 — Confirm the Symptom Is No Spark 1. Remove the spark plug and reconnect the HT lead to it. 2. Lay the plug body against the engine casing (good earth contact is essential). 3. Ask a helper to crank the engine for 3–4 seconds while you watch the plug gap. 4. A healthy spark is bright blue-white and consistent. A weak orange/yellow spark or no spark at all requires investigation. ## Step 2 — Inspect the Basics Before Testing Components Before reaching for the multimeter, visually inspect these quick-fail points — they account for roughly 40 % of no-spark faults: - **Spark plug condition:** A fouled, cracked, or incorrectly gapped plug will not spark. Replace it with a new `NGK C7HSA` (50 cc) or `NGK CR7HSA` (125/150 cc) and retest. - **Kill switch:** Disconnect the kill-switch wire from the CDI. Many kill switches fail internally and earth the CDI permanently. Retest with it disconnected. - **Side-stand switch:** Some models have a side-stand interlock that grounds the CDI when the stand is down. Raise the stand and retest, or disconnect the switch wire. - **Earth/ground wires:** Inspect every earth strap on the engine, frame, and battery. A corroded or broken ground is a very common cause of no-spark. - **HT lead and cap:** A cracked lead or a loose cap will break the secondary circuit. Replace if the rubber insulation is hard or cracked. ## Step 3 — Test the Pick-Up Coil (Trigger Coil) The pick-up coil sits inside the left-hand engine cover behind the flywheel and generates the timing pulse that tells the CDI when to fire. 1. Locate the pick-up coil connector — typically a 2-pin or 3-pin connector coming out of the stator cover. On a 5-pin CDI the trigger wires are usually `white/green` and `green`; on 6-pin CDIs, `white/green` and `black/white`. 2. Set the multimeter to AC voltage. With the connector unplugged, backprobe the two trigger pins and crank the engine. 3. A healthy pick-up coil produces **0.5–2.5 V AC** at cranking speed. 4. If voltage is 0 V, set the meter to resistance (Ω). A healthy pick-up coil measures approximately **80–120 Ω** across the two trigger wires. Open-circuit (OL) or a short to earth means a failed coil. 5. Also test the stator charging coil (the yellow/yellow wires): should produce **2–5 V AC** at cranking speed and read **1–3 Ω** resistance. ## Step 4 — Test the Ignition Coil The ignition coil takes the CDI's capacitor discharge and steps it up to ~15,000–25,000 V for the spark plug. Testing it in-circuit is straightforward: 1. Disconnect the primary coil wires (normally `orange` from the CDI and `black` earth). 2. Measure resistance across the primary winding (the two thin wires): should read **0.3–1.5 Ω**. Open-circuit = failed coil. 3. Measure across the secondary winding (between the HT cap and the earth wire, with the spark plug removed from the cap): should read **6–15 kΩ**. 4. If both windings are in spec but there is still no spark, the coil may have an internal insulation breakdown only visible under the load of a real discharge. Swap with a known-good coil as the final check. ## Step 5 — Test and Replace the CDI Unit CDI units are solid-state and cannot be repaired — they must be swapped. However, test the input signals first so you know whether a new CDI will cure the fault: 1. Plug the CDI back in. Backprobe the charging input pins (yellow wires) at the CDI connector with the multimeter on AC voltage. Crank the engine. You should see **at least 2 V AC**. If you see 0 V, the fault is upstream (stator/wiring), not the CDI. 2. Backprobe the trigger input pins. Crank. You should see a pulsing voltage (0.5–2.5 V AC). If no pulse, the pick-up coil or its wiring is the fault. 3. If both inputs are present but there is still no spark at the output (ignition coil primary), the CDI has failed internally. Replace it. ## Replacing the CDI Identify the correct replacement before ordering — count the pins on your CDI connector (5-pin or 6-pin) and note whether your engine uses AC-CDI (most carburetted and EFI scooters) or DC-CDI (battery-powered, found on some EFI conversions). The connector positions vary by manufacturer but the wiring function is standardised:
Wire Colour (typical)Function
Yellow / YellowStator AC charging input
White / GreenPick-up coil trigger input
GreenEarth / Ground
OrangeIgnition coil output
Black / White (6-pin)Kill switch / EFI trigger signal
Red (DC-CDI only)Battery +12 V input
1. Locate the CDI unit — usually mounted under the seat or behind the front fairing, secured with a rubber strap or bracket. 2. Unplug the harness connector (press the release tab, pull straight out). 3. Fit the new CDI, routing the harness away from hot engine parts and sharp edges. 4. Reconnect, crank, and confirm spark before reassembling bodywork. ## Diagnostic Quick-Reference

No spark; kill switch disconnection fixes itFaulty kill switch earthing CDI signal wire
No spark; 0 Ω across pick-up coilShorted pick-up coil — replace stator plate
No spark; OL (open) pick-up coil resistanceBroken pick-up coil wire — replace stator plate
No spark; coil primary resistance OLOpen-circuit ignition coil — replace coil

As engine RPM rises, centrifugal rollers inside the variator push the pulley faces together, forcing the belt to ride higher — effectively changing the gear ratio automatically without any driver input. ## When to Replace

Place the scooter on its centre stand on level ground. 2. Locate the CVT cover on the left side of the engine (the large plastic or alloy cover with ventilation slots). 3. Remove all cover bolts — typically 6–8 bolts of 8 mm or 10 mm. Keep them together; they are often different lengths. 4. Gently tap the cover with a soft mallet to break the gasket seal if it is stuck. Do not pry against the casting — it cracks easily. 5. Remove the cover. Inspect inside for belt dust, cracked rubber fragments, or oil contamination (indicates a crankshaft seal leak). **Step 2 — Remove the Drive Belt** 1. With the cover off, you will see the drive belt running between the two pulleys. 2. Compress (push together) the faces of the rear clutch pulley by hand while simultaneously lifting the belt off the front variator pulley. This creates slack in the belt loop. 3. Slide the belt off the rear clutch, then off the front variator. If the belt is stiff or cracked, it may snap during removal — wear eye protection. 4. Inspect the belt: cracks along the edge, fraying, glazing, or visible rubber chunks missing all indicate the belt needs replacement. **Step 3 — Install the New Belt & Reassemble** 1. Route the new belt over the rear clutch pulley first, ensuring it sits centrally in the groove. 2. While compressing the rear pulley faces together, loop the belt over the front variator. Release the rear pulley — the spring tension will pull the belt taut. 3. Rotate the rear wheel by hand to seat the belt evenly and check that it tracks centrally on both pulleys without twisting. 4. Clean the CVT cover interior and replace the gasket if torn or compressed flat. 5. Refit the CVT cover. Tighten bolts in a cross pattern to approximately **10–12 Nm**. Do not overtighten — the cover threads strip easily. **Break-in tip:** After fitting a new belt, avoid full-throttle acceleration for the first 100–200 km. New belts need time to seat and conform to the pulley surfaces. Premature hard acceleration can glaze or crack a new belt prematurely. --- ## Part 2 — Variator Pulley Disassembly & Roller Replacement This section covers full variator removal, inspection of the pulley ramps, and roller replacement. Required when rollers are worn, you're tuning for performance, or belt-only replacement hasn't resolved your CVT symptoms. **Additional tools required for this section:** - Variator holding tool (universal GY6 type) — do not attempt to jam the variator with a screwdriver - Impact wrench or breaker bar (the variator nut is torqued very tight) - Torque wrench **Video:** "GY6 Variator/Roller Replacement & Tips (Step by Step)" | YouTube   [↗ Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SQ5GmXbJKQs) ### Step-by-Step: Variator & Rollers **Step 1 — Remove the CVT Cover & Belt** Follow Part 1, Steps 1 and 2 above to remove the cover and belt first. **Step 2 — Remove the Variator** 1. Use the variator holding tool to lock the front pulley against rotation. 2. With an impact wrench or breaker bar, remove the variator nut. Note: threads vary by manufacturer — if the nut won't loosen counter-clockwise, try clockwise (some GY6 variants use a standard right-hand thread). This nut is typically torqued to **49 Nm (36 ft-lb)**. 3. Slide off the outer face of the variator. Note the orientation — there is often an arrow or chamfer indicating the correct fitting direction. 4. Lift off the outer pulley face and set it aside. **Step 3 — Inspect & Replace Rollers** 1. Remove the rollers from the guide cage. There are typically 6 rollers. Inspect each one: flat spots, grooves worn into the surface, or irregular wear all indicate replacement is needed. 2. **Roller specifications by engine:** - GY6 50cc (139QMB): **16×13 mm** @ 7.5–8.5 g (OEM stock; aftermarket range 5–11.5 g) - GY6 125cc (152QMI): **18×14 mm** @ 12–13 g (OEM ~12.8 g) - GY6 150cc (157QMJ): **18×14 mm** @ 12–14 g Always use the correct diameter for your engine — mixing sizes causes CVT failure. Heavier rollers delay engagement (better top speed); lighter rollers engage earlier (better acceleration). Do not deviate more than 2 g from stock unless tuning intentionally. 3. Inspect the variator ramp surfaces for grooving or cracks. Shallow grooves from flat-spotted rollers are normal; deep grooves mean the variator body needs replacement. **Step 4 — Inspect the Rear Clutch (while you're in there)** 1. Inspect the clutch bell interior for glazing (shiny hard surface) or scoring. Light glazing can be scuffed with coarse sandpaper; heavy scoring means replacement. 2. Check the clutch shoes for uneven wear. The shoes should contact the bell evenly around the circumference. **Step 5 — Reassemble** 1. Clean the variator ramp surfaces and roller guides with a dry rag. **Do not apply grease to the rollers** — they must run dry. Grease attracts belt dust and accelerates wear. 2. Install new rollers in the guide cage. 3. Reinstall the outer variator face in the correct orientation and torque the nut to **49 Nm**. 4. Refit the belt (Part 1, Step 3) and CVT cover. ## Torque Specifications Summary

## Introduction

The drive belt is the only link between the engine and the rear wheel on a GY6 CVT scooter. It sits inside the variator cover on the left side of the engine and transfers power from the driving pulley (connected to the crankshaft) through to the driven pulley (connected to the gearbox). A worn or broken belt causes loss of drive, reduced top speed, belt slip under load, or squealing on acceleration.

Replacing a GY6 drive belt is one of the most beginner-friendly maintenance tasks on these engines — the belt can be swapped in around 30 minutes without removing the variator assembly, provided the variator and clutch are in good working order.

<Callout type="warn">
  Always let the engine cool completely before opening the variator cover. The CVT components reach high temperatures during normal operation.
</Callout>

## Drive Belt Sizes

The correct belt depends on the engine variant. Using the wrong size causes slipping, premature wear, or inability to close the variator cover.

| Engine | Belt size (circumference × width × height) |
|--------|--------------------------------------------|
| GY6 50cc 139QMB | 743 × 20 × 30 mm |
| GY6 125cc 152QMI | 835 × 20 × 30 mm |
| GY6 150cc 157QMJ | 835 × 20 × 30 mm |

The size is stamped on the outside face of the original belt. Always verify before ordering. Quality replacement belts are available from Scooterworks USA, VMC Chinese Parts, and NCY Store.

## When to Replace the Belt

Replace the drive belt when any of the following are observed:

- Visible cracks, fraying, or missing teeth/chunks on the belt surface
- Belt width less than 18 mm (standard width is 20 mm — a worn belt narrows over time)
- Scooter revs freely but has sluggish or delayed acceleration
- Squealing or slipping sound from the variator cover under load
- Belt has exceeded 8,000 km (approximately 5,000 miles) since last replacement

<Callout type="tip">
  Belts are inexpensive — if you are already opening the variator cover for roller or clutch work, replace the belt at the same time regardless of wear, as you will have no additional labour cost.
</Callout>

## Tools & Parts Needed

- Replacement drive belt (correct size for your engine — see table above)
- Phillips screwdriver (variator cover screws)
- 10 mm socket and ratchet (if cover uses bolts)
- Flat-head screwdriver or small pry bar
- Vernier calipers or ruler (to measure old belt width before discarding)
- Clean cloth (wipe dust from pulleys)

## Step-by-Step Procedure

### Step 1 — Let the Engine Cool

The variator and driven pulley operate at high temperatures. Wait at least 20 minutes after the last ride before opening the cover. Touching a hot variator assembly can cause burns.

### Step 2 — Place the Scooter on its Centre Stand

The scooter must be stable and the rear wheel must be able to spin freely. The centre stand is the correct position — side stand leaves the variator cover inaccessible.

### Step 3 — Remove the Variator Cover

The variator cover (CVT cover) is the large plastic or pressed-steel panel on the left side of the engine. It is held by 4–6 Phillips or 10 mm hex screws arranged around its perimeter. Remove all screws and store them safely. Pull the cover straight off — it may be lightly stuck to a gasket; a gentle twist will free it.

<Callout type="tip">
  Take a photograph of the belt routing before removing it. The belt passes around the driving pulley (front/upper) and the driven pulley (rear/lower). The photo helps confirm correct routing when fitting the new belt.
</Callout>

### Step 4 — Remove the Old Belt

With the cover off, the drive belt is visible running between the two pulleys. The quick-change method (without removing the variator or clutch) works as follows:

1. Rotate the rear wheel slowly by hand until the belt is at its loosest position — the driving pulley will be at its smallest effective diameter (rollers pushed inward).
2. Grip the belt firmly and push it down toward the bottom of the driving pulley, compressing it inward to create slack.
3. Work the belt off the driving pulley first by rolling it over the pulley face — this takes a little force but no special tools.
4. Once off the driving pulley, the belt has enough slack to lift off the driven pulley easily.

If the belt has snapped, simply pull the pieces out.

### Step 5 — Inspect the Pulleys

With the belt removed, visually inspect both pulleys. The pulley faces should be smooth and free of deep grooves. Light surface marks are normal. Check for:

- Deep score marks or ridges (belt wear pattern — indicates misalignment or worn rollers)
- Grease or oil contamination (if present, identify and fix the leak source before fitting a new belt — oil will destroy a new belt quickly)
- Variator roller condition (visible through the front pulley face — if rollers look flat, replace them while the cover is open; see the CVT Variator & Roller Inspection Guide)

Clean both pulley faces with a dry cloth. Do not use grease or lubricant on the pulley contact surfaces.

### Step 6 — Fit the New Belt

Loop the new belt around the driven pulley (rear/lower) first — it sits in the groove easily at this stage. Then stretch the belt over the driving pulley by holding it at the top and bottom and rolling it onto the pulley face while rotating the rear wheel slowly. The belt will seat itself into the groove as the pulleys are turned.

<Callout type="warn">
  Do not force the belt into position with a screwdriver or pry bar — this can nick or crack the new belt. Use hand pressure and wheel rotation only.
</Callout>

### Step 7 — Verify Belt Seating

Rotate the rear wheel by hand several full turns and observe the belt tracking. It should run centrally on both pulleys with no twisting or bunching. Check that the belt is not rubbing against any edge of the variator housing.

### Step 8 — Refit the Cover

Check that the cover gasket (if present) is intact and correctly seated. Refit the cover and tighten all screws evenly in a cross pattern. Do not overtighten — the screws thread into plastic or soft alloy and strip easily. Finger-tight plus a quarter turn is sufficient.

### Step 9 — Break-in the New Belt

New belts require a brief break-in period. For the first 50–80 km, avoid full-throttle acceleration and high-speed sustained riding. Gentle to moderate throttle allows the belt to conform to the pulley profiles and reach its final operating dimensions.

Inspect the belt again after the first 100 km by removing the cover briefly and checking for any unusual wear marks.

## Specifications Summary

| Parameter | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| Belt replacement interval | Every 8,000 km (5,000 miles) |
| Minimum belt width (scrap threshold) | 18 mm |
| Cover screw torque | 6–8 Nm (finger-tight + ¼ turn) |
| Belt break-in distance | 50–80 km at moderate throttle |

import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; ## What Is Intake Flooding on an EFI Scooter? **This guide covers EFI (fuel-injected) GY6 engines only** — scooters with a throttle body, fuel injector, and ECU. There is no float bowl or needle valve. If your scooter has a carburetor with a float bowl, see the [GY6 Carburetor Intake Flooding guide](gy6-hard-start-intake-flooding.html) instead. Most hard-start guides tell you the engine is starved of fuel. This guide covers the opposite problem: **too much fuel in the intake**. When excess petrol pools in the intake port or cylinder, the spark plug drowns and cannot ignite the mixture. The engine cranks normally but refuses to fire — or fires once with a cough of black smoke and immediately dies. On EFI GY6 engines, intake flooding has two common causes: a **cracked rubber intake insulator** (the mounting block between the throttle body and the cylinder head) or a **leaking fuel injector** that drips raw fuel into the intake port when the engine is switched off. Both allow liquid fuel to pool in the port rather than being delivered as a precisely metered mist on demand. ### Video: EFI Intake Flooding — Real Example Video shows a real EFI scooter with fuel pooled in the intake — cracked insulator and injector leak identified and repaired. ## Symptoms
SymptomFlooding Likelihood
Engine cranks freely but will not fire at allHigh
Starts briefly, fires once or twice, then immediately diesVery high
Black smoke from the exhaust on the rare occasions it firesVery high
Strong petrol smell from the airbox or around the engineHigh
Spark plug electrode is wet and smells of petrol when removedDefinitive confirmation
Engine starts after leaving it overnight (fuel evaporates)High
Fuel visible or wet residue inside the intake portDefinitive confirmation
No fault codes on the ECU (flooding is a mechanical problem, not a sensor fault)Supports flooding diagnosis
**Do not confuse with a lean no-start.** A lean no-start (blocked injector, failed fuel pump, bad TPS) produces a dry, light-coloured spark plug. An intake flood produces a wet, fuel-soaked plug. Remove the plug first — it tells you immediately which problem you are dealing with. If you have ECU fault codes, check the [EFI Fuel Injection Troubleshooting guide](/diagnostics/gy6-efi-fuel-injection-troubleshooting.html) first. ## The Two Main Causes ### Cause 1 — Cracked Intake Insulator (Manifold Gasket Block) The intake insulator is the rubber block connecting the throttle body to the cylinder head inlet port. It absorbs vibration and provides a heat barrier. After several years, the rubber cracks — often across the top, along the inner bore, or at the mounting flange. On an EFI engine, a cracked insulator allows unmetered air in (confusing the ECU's fuelling calculations) and, critically, lets condensed or dripped fuel bypass the intake air path and pool directly in the port. ![Cracked GY6 rubber intake insulator held in hand, showing a visible crack across the top of the inner bore](/repair-guides/images/intake_gasket_broken.jpg) **Cracked intake insulator.** Crack visible across the top of the inner bore — this is the rubber block between the throttle body and the cylinder head. Once cracked, it must be replaced; silicone is not a permanent fix. ![GY6 EFI engine intake port with fuel pooled inside, visible as wet residue around the port opening](/repair-guides/images/intake_full_of_fuel.png) **Intake port flooded with fuel.** Fuel has pooled in the intake port — this is what the engine encounters when a cracked insulator or leaking injector allows raw fuel to collect rather than reaching the cylinder as a calibrated mist. ### Cause 2 — Leaking Fuel Injector The fuel injector on a GY6 EFI engine is held in the intake manifold by two rubber O-rings (top and bottom). When these O-rings harden and crack with age, fuel weeps past the seal and drips into the intake port while the engine is at rest — the fuel rail remains pressurised for some time after the engine is switched off. Even a slow drip accumulates quickly enough to flood the cylinder overnight. A leaking injector body itself (cracked solenoid housing, degraded pintle seal) is less common but produces the same symptom. **Quick check:** Switch off the engine and wait 5 minutes. Remove the air intake duct and shine a torch into the throttle body bore. If you can see a wet sheen or fuel droplets on the port walls — and the engine has been off for several minutes — the injector is leaking past its seals. ## Tools & Parts Needed

## Step-by-Step Procedure ### Step 1 — Confirm Flooding and Clear the Cylinder 1. Turn the ignition off. On EFI engines the fuel pump stays primed — if possible, locate the fuel pump fuse and remove it to depressurise the rail before opening anything. 2. Remove the spark plug using a 16 mm plug socket. Inspect it: if it is wet and smells strongly of petrol, flooding is confirmed. 3. With the plug still out, hold the throttle fully open and crank the engine for 5–8 seconds (electric starter). This expels excess fuel from the cylinder as vapour. 4. Leave the plug out for 5–10 minutes to allow the cylinder to air out further. 5. Reinstall the spark plug (or a new one if the old plug is fuel-fouled). Tighten finger-tight plus one-quarter turn. **Test start now:** Reinstall the fuel pump fuse, turn the ignition on, wait for the pump prime cycle (2–3 seconds), then start. If it starts and runs normally, the flooding was a one-off event. If it floods again within minutes of stopping — there is an underlying leak to fix. ### Step 2 — Inspect the Intake Insulator 1. Remove the side panel or access cover to expose the throttle body. 2. Loosen both clamps securing the throttle body — the air duct side and the head-side insulator clamp. 3. Twist and pull the throttle body slightly away from the insulator to expose it. You do not need to disconnect all wiring harness connectors at this stage — just rotate it enough to see the insulator. 4. Squeeze and flex the insulator in all directions. Cracks often hide on the inner bore surface, along the top edge, or at the head-facing flange. Look for crazing, splits, or any visible gap. 5. CRACKED: Replace immediately — see Step 4. 6. INTACT: Refit the throttle body clamp. Proceed to Step 3 to check the injector. ### Step 3 — Inspect the Fuel Injector O-Rings 1. With the fuel pump fuse removed, fully disconnect the throttle body (harness connectors, throttle cable, coolant hoses if fitted). Set it on a clean rag. 2. Locate the fuel injector — it sits in a bore in the intake manifold or throttle body, held by a retaining clip or bracket. Release the clip and pull the injector straight out. 3. Inspect both O-rings on the injector body. They should be soft, uniformly round, and black. If they are flat, cracked, or shiny-hardened, they are no longer sealing. 4. Also inspect the injector body for fuel staining or wetness at the O-ring grooves — this confirms the leak path. 5. O-RINGS DEGRADED: Replace with a new O-ring kit — see Step 5. 6. INJECTOR BODY DAMAGED: Replace the entire injector — match the part number stamped on the injector body. 7. O-RINGS INTACT: Reinstall and check float height (not applicable — EFI). Re-examine for other causes such as a leaking fuel pressure regulator or a failed fuel pump check valve holding rail pressure after shutdown. ### Step 4 — Replace the Intake Insulator 1. Fully disconnect the throttle body (wiring harness, throttle cable, breather hoses) and set it aside. 2. Remove the two M6 nuts or bolts holding the insulator to the cylinder head studs. Use a 10 mm spanner or socket. 3. Pull the insulator free. Clean the cylinder head mating face — remove any old gasket material or debris. 4. Fit the new insulator. Ensure the paper or rubber gasket on the head-facing side is in place. Tighten the mounting nuts evenly to approximately 10 Nm — do not overtighten in the aluminium head. 5. Refit the throttle body into the insulator bore. Tighten both clamps firmly but not so tight that the clamp cuts into the rubber. 6. Reconnect all harness connectors, throttle cable, and hoses. **Do not use RTV silicone** on the intake insulator as a repair or seal. Silicone pieces can detach and enter the engine. Always replace with a new insulator. ### Step 5 — Replace the Injector O-Rings 1. Source an O-ring kit for your injector. Most GY6 EFI injectors use standard 14 mm × 1.5 mm and 11 mm × 1.5 mm Viton O-rings — confirm by measuring the old ones or searching your injector part number. 2. Lubricate the new O-rings lightly with clean engine oil before fitting — this prevents tearing on installation and ensures a proper seat. 3. Slide both O-rings onto the injector body into their respective grooves. 4. Push the injector squarely back into its bore in the manifold. It should seat without force — if it resists, check the O-ring is not folded or misaligned. 5. Refit the retaining clip or bracket so the injector cannot be pushed out by fuel pressure. 6. Reconnect the fuel rail and injector electrical connector. ### Step 6 — Verify the Repair 1. Reinstall the fuel pump fuse. Turn the ignition to ON (do not start) — you should hear the pump prime for 2–3 seconds. Wait 60 seconds and check around the injector and manifold for any fuel drips. 2. If no drips: start the engine and allow it to reach operating temperature (approximately 4–5 minutes). 3. Switch the engine off and wait 10 minutes. Remove the spark plug and confirm it is dry. Reinstall and start normally. 4. A cold start should now require just the normal key-on pump prime and one or two cranks. ## Troubleshooting Table
Problem after repairLikely causeAction
Still floods immediately after stoppingInjector O-ring not seated correctly, or injector body itself is crackedRe-inspect O-rings. If body has visible cracks or fuel staining through the housing, replace the whole injector.
Floods after sitting overnight but not immediatelyFuel pump check valve failed — rail depressurises slowly, injector weeps under lower pressureReplace the fuel pump assembly (check valve is internal). Confirm by installing a fuel rail pressure gauge and watching if pressure bleeds off after shutdown.
Erratic idle after insulator replacementThrottle body-to-insulator clamp loose, or air duct not reseatedTighten both clamps. Re-run the spray test from the Air Leak Diagnosis guide. Check for new ECU fault codes (unmetered air will upset fuelling trim).
CEL / fault code after repairECU learned incorrect fuel trim during the flooding periodClear fault codes with a diagnostic tool or by disconnecting the battery for 30 seconds. Allow the ECU to re-learn idle trim over a short test ride.

import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; import SourceBox from '@components/SourceBox.astro'; Added: 2026-05-12 | Sources: [Buggy Depot](https://www.buggydepot.com/tech-center/gy6-150cc-ignition-troubleshooting-guide-no-spark/), [Moo Wiring](https://moowiring.com/), [ScootDawg Forum](https://scootdawg.proboards.com/) | GY6 Electrical Wiring Electrical faults are among the most common and misdiagnosed problems on GY6-engine scooters. Poor grounding, corroded connectors, and misunderstood wiring configurations account for the majority of intermittent starting failures, charging issues, and lighting faults. This guide explains the GY6 electrical system architecture and provides a systematic diagnostic process. ## GY6 Electrical System Overview The GY6 uses a **magneto-based AC/DC charging system**. All modern GY6 scooters use a DC electrical system (battery-powered), but the stator generates AC current which the regulator/rectifier converts to regulated DC. There are two common ignition system configurations: #### AC CDI System Older configuration. CDI fires directly from AC current produced by the stator's pickup coil. Does not rely on battery voltage for spark. Common on pre-2010 GY6 50cc models. #### DC CDI System Modern configuration. CDI draws energy from the battery (12V DC). Requires a charged battery to fire spark. Standard on 125cc/150cc models and all Euro 4 variants. ## Key Electrical Components
ComponentFunctionTypical Failure Symptoms
Stator (Magneto)Generates AC current for charging and (on AC systems) ignitionNo charge, no spark (AC CDI), weak spark
Regulator/Rectifier (RR)Converts AC to DC, regulates voltage to ~14VBattery overcharge or no charge, flickering lights
CDI UnitControls spark timing and ignition pulseNo spark, spark only at low RPM, intermittent starting
Ignition CoilSteps up low voltage CDI pulse to 20,000+ V for spark plugNo spark or weak spark, spark plug fouling rapidly
Pickup Coil (Trigger)Detects crankshaft position and signals CDINo spark at all RPMs, engine won't start
Battery (12V 5–7 Ah)Powers DC CDI, starter motor, lights, hornNo electric start, no spark (DC CDI), weak crank
Main Fuse (10–15 A)Protects main wiring harness from overcurrentComplete electrical shutdown
## Standard GY6 Wire Colour Codes Wire colour conventions are relatively consistent across GY6 manufacturers, though not 100% universal. Always verify against your specific wiring diagram:
Wire ColourTypical Function
RedBattery positive (+12V switched or permanent)
BlackGround (chassis / battery negative)
YellowAC output from stator (charging coil)
GreenGround (often for lighting circuits)
BlueDC power from regulator/rectifier
WhiteAC lighting coil or kill switch
OrangeCDI signal / ignition pulse
Pink / Light GreenPickup coil signal
Grey / BrownLighting circuits (varies by model)
� **Always obtain the wiring diagram for your specific model.** ScootDawg Forum and 49ccScoot host generic GY6 wiring diagrams. Many BTC Riva, La Souris Sourini, and Santini Capri models use a nearly identical loom to the generic GY6 150cc Chinese scooter diagram. ## Systematic Fault Diagnosis ### Before You Start — Ground First Poor grounding is the single most common electrical fault on Chinese scooters. Before testing any component, do the following: 1. Locate the main ground point — usually a black wire bolted to the engine case or frame near the battery. 2. Unbolt it, clean the contact surface with sandpaper until shiny, and re-bolt firmly. 3. Inspect all black wire connectors in the loom. Clean or replace corroded connectors. 4. Check that the battery negative cable makes a solid connection to the frame. ### No Spark Diagnosis 1. **Check for spark:** Remove the spark plug. Reconnect the plug lead. Hold the plug against the engine case (ground). Crank the engine. You should see a strong blue spark. A weak yellow spark or no spark means a fault in the ignition chain. 2. **Check the kill switch:** Disconnect the kill switch wire from the CDI (usually the white/black wire). Try cranking again. If spark returns, the kill switch is shorted — clean or replace it. 3. **Check the sidestand switch:** Many GY6s cut ignition when the sidestand is down. Disconnect the sidestand switch and jump its two terminals together. If spark returns, the switch is faulty. 4. **Check CDI input voltage (DC CDI only):** With a multimeter, probe the red/battery wire on the CDI connector to ground. You should read 12V when the ignition is on. No voltage → check fuse and ignition switch. 5. **Test the pickup coil:** Disconnect the pickup coil from the CDI. Measure resistance across the two pickup coil wires with a multimeter. Typical specification is 80–150 Ω. Open circuit (infinite resistance) or short to ground means replace the stator assembly. 6. **Test the ignition coil primary:** Measure resistance between the coil's two primary terminals (where the CDI wire connects). Typical: 0.3–0.8 Ω. Test secondary (plug cap to ground): 5,000–15,000 Ω. Out-of-specification → replace coil. 7. **Substitute the CDI:** If all components test within specification but there is still no spark, the CDI itself is likely faulty. CDI units are inexpensive (€10–30); swap with a known-good unit to confirm. ### Charging System Diagnosis 1. **Battery voltage:** Measure battery voltage at rest (engine off, 15 minutes after last use). Healthy 12V AGM battery: 12.6–12.8V. Below 12.0V indicates a discharged or failing battery. 2. **Charging voltage:** Start the engine. Measure battery voltage with the engine running at ~3,500 RPM. Should read 13.8–14.5V. Above 15V indicates a failed regulator/rectifier (RR). Below 13.5V at speed indicates a weak stator or failed RR. 3. **Stator AC output:** Disconnect the stator yellow wire from the RR. With the engine running at 3,500 RPM, measure AC voltage between the yellow wire and engine ground. Should read 30–60V AC. Low output suggests a weak stator winding. 4. **RR diode test:** With a multimeter in diode test mode, test each diode leg of the rectifier section of the RR. A shorted diode (reads 0 in both directions) means replace the RR. ### Lighting Fault Diagnosis 1. **Headlight not working:** First check the main fuse and the dedicated headlight fuse/relay if fitted. Check for 12V at the headlight connector with ignition on. If voltage is present, the bulb is blown — replace with correct rating (typically 12V 35/35W halogen, BA20d base). 2. **Indicators flashing too fast or too slow:** Caused by mismatched bulb wattage or a failing flasher relay. Replace with standard 10W indicator bulbs and/or the flasher relay. 3. **Brake light not working:** Check both front (lever) and rear (pedal) brake light switches. Measure resistance across the switch — should read closed circuit (0 Ω) when brake is applied. Clean or adjust switch if sticking open. ## Essential Multimeter Tests at a Glance

Ignition coil secondaryResistance (Ω)5,000–15,000 ΩOL or <1,000 Ω

� **GY6 wiring diagrams:** Generic DC CDI GY6 150cc wiring diagrams are available at [moowiring.com](https://moowiring.com/) and on the [ScootDawg forum](https://scootdawg.proboards.com/). The BTC Riva 50, La Souris Sourini, and Santini Capri all use a loom closely matching the standard Chinese 50cc GY6 DC CDI diagram. ## Common Wiring Connector Problems on GY6 Scooters GY6 scooters use generic Molex-style multi-pin connectors that are vulnerable to corrosion, especially in wet climates. The most problematic connectors to check are the main harness junction block (usually under the headset covers), the CDI connector, the RR connector (which handles high charging current and can melt if undersized), and the ignition switch connector. Apply dielectric grease to all connectors when reassembling to prevent future corrosion.

import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; import SourceBox from '@components/SourceBox.astro'; The fuel pump on a GY6-engine scooter is a small but critical component. A failing pump is responsible for a surprisingly wide range of symptoms: hard starting, stalling at speed, power loss on hills, and erratic idling. This guide covers both the **vacuum-operated diaphragm pump** found on carburetted GY6 scooters and the **electric fuel pump** used on EFI (fuel-injected) variants. **Applies to:** GY6 50 cc (139QMB), GY6 125/150 cc (157QMJ / QMI152), and GY6 180 cc — carburetor and fuel-injection variants. Typical scooter models include BTC Riva, La Souris Sourini/City, Santini Capri, and similar Chinese/Taiwanese GY6-platform scooters. ## Types of Fuel Pump Used on GY6 Engines ## Vacuum-Diaphragm Pump (Carburettor Models) Most carburetted GY6 scooters use a simple vacuum-operated diaphragm pump. Engine vacuum from the intake manifold flexes an internal rubber diaphragm back and forth, drawing fuel from the tank and pushing it to the carburettor float chamber. Operating pressure is low: typically **2–4 PSI (0.14–0.28 bar)**. The pump has three connections: a vacuum port (thin hose to intake manifold or carburettor), a fuel inlet (from the tank petcock), and a fuel outlet (to the carburettor). On many 50 cc models the pump is mounted to the carburettor body; on 125/150 cc models it is usually a separate unit on the frame. ## Electric Fuel Pump (EFI Models) Fuel-injected GY6 scooters use a 12 V electric pump, typically submerged inside or mounted directly on the fuel tank. Electric pumps operate at significantly higher pressure: **15–25 PSI (1.0–1.7 bar)**. They are controlled by the ECU and run for a 2–3 second prime cycle when the ignition is first switched on, then run continuously when the engine is cranking or running. ## Symptoms of a Failing Fuel Pump
SymptomCarb PumpEFI Pump
Hard to start, especially cold✓✓
Stalls when throttle is opened quickly✓✓
Power loss at sustained high speed✓✓
Engine starts OK but cuts out after 5–10 minutes✓ (diaphragm heat-cracking)✗
No start; no fuel at carburettor inlet when primer bulb pressed✓—
No start; no whirring sound at key-on—✓ (pump or fuse)
EFI fault codes P0087 / P0230—✓
## Diagnosing the Vacuum-Diaphragm Pump (Carburettor Models) ## External Fuel Source Test 1. Disconnect the fuel outlet hose from the carburettor. Place the open hose end in a clean container. 2. Crank the engine for 5 seconds. Fuel should pulse out of the hose rhythmically with each engine stroke. 3. If no fuel or only a weak dribble: the pump diaphragm has perforated, or the vacuum hose to the intake is blocked/split. 4. If fuel flow is good but the engine still runs poorly: the fault is in the carburettor, not the pump. ## Vacuum Line Check 1. Trace the thin vacuum hose from the pump to its port on the intake manifold or carburettor body. 2. Inspect for cracks, kinks, or disconnection. A split vacuum line delivers no operating signal to the diaphragm. 3. Blow through the line with your mouth — it should not leak at any joint. ## Pump Disassembly (Carb Models — Serviceable Pump) Some OEM vacuum pumps can be rebuilt by replacing the internal rubber diaphragm and check valves. However, replacement pumps cost so little (€5–15) that replacement is usually faster and more reliable than rebuilding. 1. Remove the four small Phillips screws holding the pump halves together. 2. Carefully separate the halves — a spring, diaphragm, and two small ball-valve check valves are inside. 3. Inspect the rubber diaphragm for holes, tears, or hardening. Any crack means replace the pump. 4. Clean all passages with carburettor cleaner. Reassemble with a new diaphragm if available. ## Diagnosing the Electric Pump (EFI Models) ## Listen at Key-On 1. Sit close to the rear of the scooter and switch on the ignition (do not crank). 2. Listen for a brief 2–3 second whirring or buzzing from the pump. If you can hear this, the pump is receiving power and running. 3. No sound at all: check the fuel pump fuse (usually a 10 A or 15 A inline fuse near the battery) and the ECU relay. A blown fuse that blows again immediately on replacement suggests a pump winding short — replace the pump. ## Fuel Pressure Test 1. Obtain an inline fuel pressure test gauge kit (available for under €20 at auto parts retailers). 2. Disconnect the fuel rail inlet hose. Fit the T-gauge adapter between the pump outlet and the fuel rail. 3. Switch on the ignition (pump prime cycle). Pressure should read **15–25 PSI**. Below 10 PSI confirms a weak pump. 4. Shut the ignition off. Pressure should hold (drop off slowly over 30–60 seconds). Rapid drop to zero with the ignition off indicates a leaking injector or leaking fuel rail check valve — not a pump fault. ⚠️ **Important for EFI pump installation:** The fuel pump draws, not pushes — it cannot suck fuel uphill against gravity. Always ensure the inlet fuel line from the tank runs downward to the pump. If the pump inlet is located above the bottom of the tank, it will not prime correctly and will suffer premature wear. ## Replacing the Vacuum-Diaphragm Pump 1. Close the fuel petcock or clamp the inlet hose to prevent spillage. 2. Remove the vacuum hose, inlet hose, and outlet hose — note which is which (mark with tape if needed). 3. Undo the 2 mounting bolts or hose clamp holding the pump to the frame or carburettor. 4. Fit the new pump. Reconnect the three hoses in the same positions. Tighten hose clamps securely. 5. Open the petcock and check for leaks before starting. ## Replacing the Electric Pump (EFI) 1. Disconnect the battery negative terminal. 2. Drain or remove the fuel tank to access the pump (varies by model — refer to the model-specific service manual). 3. Disconnect the pump electrical connector and the fuel outlet hose. 4. Unscrew the pump retaining ring (counter-clockwise, often requires a strap wrench) and lift the pump assembly out of the tank. 5. Transfer the fuel level sender to the new pump if the new pump does not include one. 6. Fit new pump, torque retaining ring to spec (usually 25–35 Nm), reconnect hose and electrical connector. 7. Reconnect battery, switch on ignition, and listen for prime. Check all connections for fuel leaks before first start. ## Maintenance Tips - Always use fresh, clean petrol — old or contaminated fuel deposits varnish residue inside pump check valves, causing premature failure. - On carburetor models, inspect the vacuum hose annually. The thin hose deteriorates with heat exposure and splits invisibly from the inside. - On EFI models, the in-tank filter sock (strainer) on the pump inlet should be replaced with every pump or every 30,000 km. A blocked strainer starves the pump and causes overheating. - Never run the fuel tank to empty repeatedly — on EFI scooters the pump relies on fuel for both lubrication and cooling. Running dry shortens pump life significantly.
GY6 Hard Start — Cracked Insulator & Carb Overflow
GY6 hard starting caused by intake flooding — cracked intake insulator gasket or leaking carburetor needle valve. Diagnosis and repair guide with real photos.

import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; ## What Is Intake Flooding? **This guide covers carbureted GY6 engines only** (PD18/PD22/PD24 and CVK-type carburetors). It does not apply to EFI/injected scooters — those have a fuel injector controlled by an ECU, which is a different system entirely. If your scooter has a throttle body and no float bowl, see the [EFI Fuel Injection Troubleshooting guide](/diagnostics/gy6-efi-fuel-injection-troubleshooting.html) instead. Most hard-start guides tell you the engine is starved of fuel. This guide covers the opposite problem: **too much fuel in the intake**. When excess petrol collects in the intake port or cylinder, the spark plug drowns and cannot ignite the mixture. The engine cranks normally but refuses to fire — or fires once with a cough of black smoke and immediately dies. On carbureted GY6 engines, this flooding usually has one of two causes: a **cracked rubber intake insulator** (the mounting block between the carburetor and the cylinder head) or a **leaking needle valve** inside the carburetor float chamber. Both allow raw fuel to pool in the intake port rather than being drawn through as a calibrated mist. ## Symptoms
SymptomFlooding Likelihood
Engine cranks freely but will not fire at allHigh
Starts briefly, fires once or twice, then immediately diesVery high
Black smoke from the exhaust on the rare occasions it firesVery high
Strong petrol smell from the airbox or around the engineHigh
Spark plug electrode is wet and smells of petrol when removedDefinitive confirmation
Engine starts after leaving it overnight (fuel evaporates)High
Fuel visible or wet residue inside the intake portDefinitive confirmation
Engine starts on the kick but not on the starter motor (starter cranks faster, worsening the flood)Medium
**Do not confuse with a lean no-start.** A lean no-start (caused by a blocked pilot jet or air leak) produces a dry, light-coloured spark plug. An intake flood produces a wet, fuel-soaked plug. Remove the plug first — it tells you immediately which problem you are dealing with. ## The Two Main Causes ### Cause 1 — Cracked Intake Insulator (Manifold Gasket Block) The intake insulator is the rubber or plastic-rubber block that connects the carburetor to the cylinder head inlet port. It absorbs vibration and provides a heat barrier. After several years, the rubber cracks — often across the top, along the inner bore, or at the mounting flange. A cracked insulator does two things: it introduces an air leak (lean symptoms at idle) and, critically, it allows liquid fuel that condenses on the carburetor inlet face to drip directly into the intake port rather than being vaporised into the airflow. ![Cracked GY6 rubber intake insulator held in hand, showing a visible crack across the top of the inner bore](/repair-guides/images/intake_gasket_broken.jpg) **Cracked intake insulator.** Crack visible across the top of the inner bore. This insulator is from a GY6 engine — the crack allows fuel to drip straight into the intake port rather than being drawn in as vapour. ### Cause 2 — Leaking Needle Valve (Float Chamber Overflow) The needle valve (also called the float valve or fuel shutoff needle) controls how much fuel enters the float bowl. It is a small brass or plastic needle with a rubber cone that seats against a brass seat when the float rises to the correct level. If the rubber cone is worn (it develops a visible groove after 3–5 years), the needle no longer seals — fuel continues entering the bowl, overfills it, and overflows through the pilot circuit and idle port directly into the intake bore. This is sometimes called a **rich flooding condition** and is distinct from a stuck or misadjusted float, though the result is the same. **Quick check:** Remove the fuel line from the carburetor with the fuel tap open (engine off). If fuel runs freely even after you manually lift the float to the closed position, the needle valve is not sealing and must be replaced. ## Tools & Parts Needed
ItemWhy neededApprox. cost
Flat-blade screwdriver (3 mm & 5 mm)Carburetor screws, clamp screws—
Phillips #2 screwdriverSide panel screws, air filter cover—
10 mm spannerIntake insulator mounting nuts (if present)—
Clean ragsAbsorbing spilled fuel—
GY6 intake insulator (rubber manifold gasket block)Replace if cracked€2–5
Carburetor needle valve kitReplace if leaking (usually sold with float bowl gasket)€3–8
Spark plug (NGK CR6HIX or equivalent)Replace if plug was severely fouled with fuel€4–8
## Step-by-Step Procedure ### Step 1 — Confirm Flooding and Clear the Cylinder 1. Turn the fuel tap to **OFF**. 2. Remove the spark plug using a 16 mm plug socket. Inspect it: if it is wet and smells strongly of petrol, flooding is confirmed. 3. With the plug still out, hold the throttle fully open and crank the engine for 5–8 seconds (electric starter or kick). This expels excess fuel from the cylinder as vapour. 4. Leave the plug out for 5–10 minutes to allow the cylinder to air out further. 5. Reinstall the spark plug (or a new one if the old plug is fuel-fouled). Tighten finger-tight plus one-quarter turn — do not overtighten in the aluminium head. **Test start now:** With fuel tap back to ON, try starting. If it starts and runs normally, the flooding was a one-off event (perhaps the scooter was left on its side, or the fuel tap was left on PRI overnight). If it floods again within minutes of stopping — there is an underlying leak to fix. ### Step 2 — Inspect the Intake Insulator 1. Remove the side panel or access cover to expose the carburetor. 2. Loosen (do not remove) both clamps — the airbox-side clamp and the head-side clamp — so the carburetor can twist free. 3. Twist and pull the carburetor away from the insulator. You do not need to disconnect throttle or fuel lines at this stage — just push the carb aside far enough to see the insulator. 4. Inspect the insulator carefully: squeeze and flex it in all directions. Cracks often hide on the inner bore surface, along the top edge, or at the head-facing flange. Look for crazing, splits, or any visible gap. 5. CRACKED: Replace immediately — see Step 4. Do not seal with RTV; a cracked insulator must be replaced with a new one. 6. INTACT: Reinstall the carburetor. Proceed to Step 3 to check the needle valve. ### Step 3 — Inspect the Carburetor Needle Valve 1. With the fuel tap off, remove the float bowl retaining screw and lower the bowl carefully. 2. Slide out the float hinge pin and lift out the float assembly. The needle valve will come away attached to the float arm or hanging from the float seat. 3. Inspect the needle valve tip (the rubber or brass cone). If you can see a groove worn into the rubber, the needle is no longer sealing properly. 4. **Bench test:** Blow through the carburetor fuel inlet nipple while holding the float in the raised (closed) position. You should feel complete resistance — zero air should pass. If air passes easily, the needle is not seating and must be replaced. 5. LEAKING: Replace the needle valve — see Step 5. 6. SEALING: Check float height: with the carb body held so the float bowl face is horizontal, the float arms should be parallel to or just slightly below that face. If the float is sitting too low (too much fuel allowed in), bend the tab that contacts the needle valve slightly upward to raise the float level. ### Step 4 — Replace the Intake Insulator 1. Fully disconnect the carburetor (throttle cable, fuel line, choke cable) and set it aside on a clean rag. 2. Remove the two M6 nuts or bolts holding the insulator to the cylinder head studs. These are often behind the insulator flange — use a 10 mm spanner or socket. 3. Pull the insulator free. Clean the cylinder head mating face with a rag — remove any old gasket material or debris. 4. Fit the new insulator. On most GY6 engines the insulator has a paper or thin rubber gasket on the head-facing side — do not omit it. Tighten the mounting nuts evenly to approximately 10 Nm (hand-tight plus about one-quarter turn with a spanner). Do not overtighten — the aluminium head threads strip easily. 5. Refit the carburetor into the insulator bore. Push it in squarely and tighten both clamps — firm, but not so tight that the clamp bites into the rubber. 6. Reconnect the fuel line, throttle cable, and choke cable. **Do not use RTV silicone or exhaust paste** on the intake insulator as a repair or seal. Silicone pieces can detach and enter the engine. Always replace with a new insulator — they cost €2–5 and are a consumable service item. ### Step 5 — Replace the Needle Valve 1. Source a replacement needle valve for your carburetor model. For GY6 PD18/PD22/PD24 carburetors, a standard GY6 carburetor rebuild kit (€3–8) includes the needle valve, float bowl O-ring, and main jet O-ring — replacing all of these at once while the carb is open is good practice. 2. Remove the old needle valve from the float arm clip or the float seat housing. 3. Seat the new needle valve. Press it gently into the seat housing — it should drop in squarely. Attach the float arm. 4. Set float height: hold the carb body with the bowl-mating face level. The float arms should be parallel to that face (±1 mm). Adjust by carefully bending the small brass tab on the float arm that contacts the needle valve tip. 5. Install a new float bowl O-ring if one is included in the kit. Refit the bowl and tighten the retaining screw — snug, not tight. ### Step 6 — Verify the Repair 1. Turn the fuel tap to ON. Wait 60 seconds — do not start yet. Check underneath the carburetor for any fuel drips (indicates the needle valve is still not seating or the float bowl O-ring is pinched). 2. If no drips: start the engine and allow it to reach operating temperature (approximately 4–5 minutes). 3. Observe idle quality. If it was previously erratic due to the cracked insulator admitting unmetered air, it should now be smoother. Adjust the idle speed screw as needed. 4. After the engine has cooled and sat for 30 minutes, remove the spark plug and confirm it is dry. Reinstall and start normally. A cold start should now require just choke + one or two cranks. ## Troubleshooting Table
Problem after repairLikely causeAction
Still floods immediately after stoppingNeedle valve not seating — wrong part, seated crooked, or seat itself is damagedRe-inspect needle and seat. If seat has a groove worn into it, the carb body needs replacement.
Floods after sitting for an hourFuel tap (petcock) not closing — diaphragm failedTest by turning tap to OFF after every ride. If flooding stops, replace the fuel tap diaphragm.
Erratic idle after insulator replacementCarb-to-insulator clamp loose, or air filter joint not reseatedTighten both clamps. Re-run the spray test from the Air Leak Diagnosis guide.
Starts fine but runs rich (black smoke, poor fuel economy)Float level set too low after needle valve replacementRe-open float bowl, re-check float height, bend the tab to raise the float slightly.

import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; The ignition coil (French: _bobine d'allumage_) transforms the low-voltage pulse from the CDI unit into the 15,000–20,000 V needed to fire the spark plug. A failed coil results in no spark and a no-start condition. However, the coil is only one of four components that must all work together — always diagnose systematically before replacing parts. ## How the GY6 Ignition System Works The GY6 uses a **CDI (Capacitor Discharge Ignition)** system with four main components in the spark circuit:
ComponentFunctionFailure symptom
Stator / Pickup coilGenerates trigger signal as flywheel rotatesNo spark, weak spark
CDI unitStores charge, fires on trigger signalNo spark — most common failure
Ignition coil (bobine)Steps CDI pulse up to ~20,000 VNo spark, cuts out when hot
Spark plug + capProduces arc in combustion chamberNo spark, misfires
� **On GY6 clones, the CDI unit fails far more often than the ignition coil.** Always swap or test the CDI before buying a new coil. A replacement CDI costs €5–15; a coil costs €8–20. ## Symptoms of a Faulty Ignition Coil - **Engine cranks but will not start** — no spark at the plug - **Starts cold, cuts out when warm** — classic thermal failure (coil breaks down under heat) - **Intermittent misfires** or sudden stalling while riding - **Visible physical damage** — cracked coil body, scorched or melted insulation, corroded HT lead connector - **Weak orange spark** instead of a sharp blue-white arc 🎬 Video Guide — GY6 No Spark Diagnosis (CDI, Coil & Stator) **Video:** "GY6 No Spark Diagnosis — CDI, Ignition Coil and Stator" | YouTube   [↗ Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kZY1XVcIzhA) ## Diagnostic Procedure — Step by Step ️ High-voltage ignition circuits can deliver a painful shock. Do not hold bare HT wires while cranking. Keep fingers away from the spark plug cap end of the HT lead during testing. ### Step 1 — Confirm No Spark 1. Remove the spark plug from the engine. 2. Reconnect the plug to the HT cap (spark plug cap). 3. Lay the threaded body of the plug against bare engine metal (earth/ground). 4. Crank the engine with the kickstart or electric start. 5. Observe: **bright blue arc = healthy spark**. Weak orange glow or nothing = ignition fault. ### Step 2 — Eliminate the Spark Plug Substitute a known-good spark plug and repeat the spark test. A fouled or dead plug can mimic a coil failure. ### Step 3 — Check the Kill Switch 1. Locate the black wire running from the kill switch to the CDI/coil. 2. Disconnect this wire completely. 3. Try to start. If spark is now present, the kill switch is faulty — it is permanently earthing the circuit. ### Step 4 — Check Earth Connections A loose or corroded earth (ground) connection is an extremely common cause of no-spark on GY6 clones. Check: - Ignition coil mounting bolts — they must contact bare metal, not paint. - Battery negative terminal and its connection to the frame. - Engine earth strap from engine to frame. ### Step 5 — Test the Coil with a Multimeter Set your multimeter to resistance (Ω) mode:
Test pointHealthy readingFailed coil
Primary winding (between the two low-voltage terminals)0.3 – 0.5 ΩOpen (∞) or short (0 Ω)
Secondary winding (HT lead to earth terminal)3,000 – 7,000 ΩOpen (∞) or far outside range
If either reading is outside the normal range, the coil is defective and should be replaced. ### Step 6 — Swap the CDI If the coil tests OK, the CDI is the next most likely culprit. Swap it with a known-good unit (or a new €10 replacement). If spark is restored, the CDI was faulty. ## Ignition Coil Replacement Procedure 1. **Disconnect the battery** — negative terminal first. 2. **Locate the ignition coil.** On GY6 engines it is mounted on the frame or engine bracket near the cylinder head — typically a black rectangular block with one HT lead going to the spark plug and two small wires (or a 2-pin connector) going to the CDI and kill switch. 3. **Remove the HT lead** from the spark plug cap — unscrew counter-clockwise if threaded, or pull straight off if clip-type. 4. **Disconnect the low-voltage wiring connector.** 5. **Unbolt the coil** (2 × M6 bolts) from its mounting bracket and remove it. 6. **Fit the new coil** — ensure the mounting bolts make clean metal-to-metal contact with the frame/engine for proper earthing. Tighten bolts firmly. 7. **Reconnect all wiring** and the HT lead to the plug cap. 8. **Reconnect the battery** (positive first, negative last). 9. **Test for spark** as described in Step 1 above before reassembling any bodywork. � **Pro tip:** Buy a spare CDI and ignition coil together (under €30 total for GY6 parts). Carry them when touring. Intermittent ignition failures that only appear when hot are impossible to diagnose by the roadside without a spare to swap in. ## Applicable Models This guide applies to all GY6 CDI ignition systems — `139QMB`, `152QMI`, `157QMJ` engines used in **BTC Riva**, **La Souris Sourini / City**, **Santini Capri**, and all Chinese 50–150cc clones. Vespa Primavera and Sprint with electronic injection use a different ignition architecture (integrated ECU) — coil testing values and replacement procedures differ; consult the Piaggio workshop manual. ## Related Videos #### How to Replace a Scooter Ignition Coil Physical coil removal and installation on a GY6 scooter — shows connector locations, HT lead removal, mounting bolt access and post-install spark test. import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; import SourceBox from '@components/SourceBox.astro'; Ignition timing determines exactly when the spark plug fires relative to piston position. On GY6 4-stroke engines (139QMB 50cc and 157QMJ 125cc/150cc, as found in scooters such as the BTC Riva 50, La Souris Sourini/City, and Santini Capri), the timing is controlled by the position of the stator plate inside the magneto cover. Correct timing is essential for starting, fuel economy, power delivery, and preventing engine damage from detonation (pinging). ## Symptoms of Incorrect Timing
SymptomLikely timing condition
Hard starting, especially when hotTiming too advanced or too retarded
Pinging or knocking under loadTiming too far advanced
Poor acceleration, low powerTiming too retarded
Overheating at normal speedsTiming too advanced
High fuel consumptionTiming too retarded
Engine runs but won't idle cleanlyPossible timing fault among other causes
## Tools and Parts Required - Timing light (stroboscopic) — or a multimeter in AC voltage mode as an alternative - 10 mm socket and ratchet - Screwdrivers (flat and Phillips) - Feeler gauges (optional, for air gap check) - Workshop manual or timing specification for your specific engine variant - Permanent marker � **Note on GY6 timing marks:** GY6 engines have timing marks on the flywheel/magneto rotor and a reference mark on the engine casing. Common marks are `T` (Top Dead Centre) and a further mark (often a line or triangle) indicating standard ignition timing advance — typically **15–20° BTDC** at idle. Consult your service manual for the precise figure. ## Step-by-Step Procedure ### Step 1 — Warm the Engine Run the engine for 5–10 minutes until it reaches normal operating temperature. Timing specifications are given for a warm engine. ### Step 2 — Access the Magneto Timing Window 1. Locate the small rubber inspection plug on the left-side engine casing (magneto side). Remove it to expose the timing marks on the flywheel. 2. On some GY6 variants there is no inspection window and you must remove the left-side engine cover to access the stator plate directly. Remove the three or four bolts and ease the cover off, taking care not to damage the gasket. ### Step 3 — Identify the Timing Marks 1. Slowly rotate the flywheel by hand (or bump the starter briefly) until you can see the marks through the inspection window. 2. The `T` mark indicates Top Dead Centre (TDC) — piston at the highest point of its travel. 3. The advance mark (a line, triangle, or `F` depending on the engine batch) indicates where the spark should fire at idle. This mark should align with the reference pointer on the casing. 4. Use a permanent marker to make the marks more visible if needed. ### Step 4 — Check Timing with a Timing Light 1. Connect the timing light's inductive clamp to the HT lead (spark plug lead). 2. Connect the light's power leads to the battery. 3. Start the engine and let it idle at approximately 1,400–1,600 rpm. 4. Point the timing light at the inspection window. The strobe will "freeze" the rotating marks. 5. The advance/timing mark on the flywheel should align with the reference pointer on the casing. If it does not, the stator plate position needs adjustment. ### Step 5 — Adjust the Stator Plate 1. Stop the engine. Remove the magneto cover if not already done. 2. Locate the two or three stator plate mounting bolts. They pass through slotted holes that allow the plate to be rotated slightly. 3. Loosen the bolts — do not fully remove them. 4. To **advance** timing (move the spark earlier): rotate the stator plate in the direction _opposite_ to flywheel rotation. 5. To **retard** timing (move the spark later): rotate the stator plate in the _same_ direction as flywheel rotation. 6. Make small adjustments (2–3 mm of plate movement at a time). 7. Re-tighten the bolts, refit the cover, and recheck with the timing light. Repeat until correct. ️ **Do not over-advance:** Too much advance causes detonation (pinging under load), overheating, and can burn a hole through the piston on a GY6. If in doubt, err on the side of slightly retarded timing. ### Step 6 — Verify and Road Test 1. Refit the inspection plug or magneto cover securely. 2. Start the engine and allow it to warm up. 3. Test ride with light and heavy throttle loads. The engine should accelerate cleanly without pinging, idle smoothly at 1,400–1,600 rpm, and start readily both cold and hot. 4. If pinging is present under load, retard timing slightly and retest. ## Typical GY6 Timing Specifications
Engine variantDisplacementTiming (idle)
139QMB (long-case)50cc (stock)~15° BTDC
152QMI125cc~15–18° BTDC
157QMJ150cc~15–18° BTDC
Always verify against the service manual for your specific engine batch, as values vary. After fitting a big-bore kit, the optimal timing may need re-optimisation.

import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; The GY6 is a high-revving, air-cooled single-cylinder engine. Because it has no separate gearbox oil (the clutch and transmission share the engine oil), using the correct oil type and changing it regularly is critical. Neglected oil turns black and acidic within 2,000–3,000 km, causing accelerated clutch wear and premature piston and camshaft wear. ## Oil Specification | Engine | Recommended Oil | Standard | Capacity | |---|---|---|---| | GY6 50cc (139QMB) | 10W-40 or 15W-40 | JASO MA or MA2 | 0.7–0.8 litres | | GY6 125/150cc (157QMJ) | 10W-40 or 15W-40 | JASO MA or MA2 | 0.9–1.0 litres | Do NOT use car engine oil (API SN/SM) or oil with friction modifiers on GY6 engines. Car oils are formulated to reduce clutch friction — on a wet-clutch GY6, this causes clutch slip. Always use motorcycle-spec oil rated JASO MA or JASO MA2. For European riding conditions (Belgium, Netherlands, UK): **10W-40 JASO MA2** is the best all-round choice for year-round use. Switch to **15W-40** in summer above 30°C if you notice increased oil consumption. ## Tools & Materials Required - 17 mm socket or spanner (drain bolt, on most GY6 engines) - Drain tray or container (at least 1 litre capacity) - New oil (see specification above) - Clean rag - Replacement drain bolt washer (copper or aluminium crush washer, 12 mm) — recommended each change - Dipstick or level markings (built into the oil filler cap on most GY6 engines) ## Step-by-Step Oil Change Procedure 1. **Warm the engine for 3–5 minutes.** Warm oil flows more freely and carries more suspended contaminants with it when drained. Do not run to full temperature — the oil will be dangerously hot. 2. **Place the scooter on its centre stand** on a level surface. Tilt the scooter slightly to the right to help all the oil drain toward the drain plug. 3. **Position the drain tray** beneath the engine oil drain bolt. The drain bolt is located at the lowest point of the engine crankcase — usually a 17 mm bolt on the underside. 4. **Remove the oil filler cap** (the dipstick/cap on top of the engine) first. This allows air to enter and improves drainage. 5. **Remove the drain bolt** counter-clockwise. Hold the drain tray underneath — oil will flow immediately. Allow 3–5 minutes for full drainage. 6. **Inspect the drain bolt:** Check for metal particles (silvery flakes = normal fine wear; large particles or chunks = investigate further). Clean the bolt threads with a rag. 7. **Replace the drain bolt crush washer** if reusing; always use a new washer if available. Reinstall the drain bolt and tighten to **18–20 Nm**. Do not overtighten — the aluminium crankcase threads strip at moderate torque. 8. **Refill with new oil** through the filler cap opening. Add oil slowly — GY6 engines have a small capacity. Use a small funnel to avoid spills. 9. **Check the oil level** using the dipstick or the marks on the filler cap. Insert the dipstick without threading it in (rest it on the threads), and read the level. Fill to the upper mark but not above it. 10. **Reinstall the filler cap** and tighten firmly by hand. 11. **Start the engine and run for 2 minutes.** Shut off and wait 2 minutes for oil to settle. Recheck the level and top up if needed. 12. **Check for leaks** around the drain bolt and filler cap. Tighten if necessary. Tip: The GY6 dipstick is notorious for giving misleading readings on a slanted surface. Always check oil level with the scooter perfectly vertical and on the centre stand. ## Oil Filter Screen (Clean Every 3,000 km) Most GY6 engines do not have a replaceable spin-on oil filter. Instead, they have a **strainer screen** inside the crankcase near the drain bolt. Every third or fourth oil change, remove the screen and clean it with fresh oil or carburetor cleaner. A clogged strainer restricts oil flow and causes oil starvation in the engine top end. On many GY6 50cc engines, the strainer screen is accessed by removing a small secondary plug beside the main drain bolt. Consult your engine's service manual for the exact location. ## Oil Change Intervals — Summary | Situation | Interval | |---|---| | New / freshly rebuilt engine (break-in) | First change at 300–500 km | | Normal use, temperate climate | Every 1,000–1,500 km | | Hot summer use, urban stop-start | Every 800–1,000 km | | Annual minimum (if low km ridden) | Once per year regardless of km | | Oil strainer screen cleaning | Every 3,000 km or 3 oil changes | ## Applicable Models This procedure applies to all GY6-engined scooters including the **BTC Riva** (50cc Euro 2 and Euro 4), **La Souris Sourini** and **La Souris City S** (carbureted 50cc variants), **Santini Capri** (50cc), **AGM VX50**, **Senzo Rivalux**, **GTS Toscana**, and all other Chinese/Taiwanese scooters using the `139QMB` or `157QMJ` engine family. Piaggio ZIP 50/100 4T oil specifications — from the official Piaggio MSS ZIP 100 4T Service Station Manual: **Engine oil capacity:** approx. 850 cm³ | **Recommended oil:** SELENIA HI SCOOTER 4Tech — SAE 5W-40, API SL, ACEA A3, JASO MA (synthetic) **Drain plug torque:** 25–28 Nm | **Change interval:** Every 6,000 km (check level every 3,000 km) **Rear hub oil:** approx. 80 cm³ | AGIP ROTRA 80W-90 (SAE 80W/90, API GL3) | Replace every 1,000 km / 4 months initially The drain and fill procedure on the ZIP is similar to GY6, but the dipstick must be screwed fully in and then removed again to get a valid reading — do not just rest it in the hole. ## Related Videos
