import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; import SourceBox from '@components/SourceBox.astro'; The GY6 engine platform has been in production since the 1980s, and decades of aftermarket development means there is now a well-established upgrade path from a stock 50cc or 150cc scooter to a genuinely quick machine. This guide covers the main performance categories in order of impact and accessibility, from basic tuning to full engine rebuilds. Performance upgrades work best when approached as a system — improving airflow without matching the fuel delivery, or adding displacement without upgrading brakes, produces mediocre and potentially unsafe results. Work through stages sequentially for the best outcome. ## Stage 1 — Bolt-On Upgrades (Low Cost, High Impact) STAGE 1 These upgrades require no engine disassembly and are reversible. Start here if the scooter is stock. ### Air Filter Upgrade The stock air filter box on most GY6 scooters is restrictive by design — manufacturers balance performance against noise, emissions compliance, and durability across variable maintenance habits. Fitting a high-flow foam filter or a pod filter (cone filter) can improve airflow significantly. However, a pod filter removes the heat shielding of the stock box; on hot days this can cause lean running. Always re-jet after fitting a pod filter. ### Exhaust Upgrade The stock exhaust is heavily muffled. An aftermarket performance exhaust improves scavenging — the process by which outgoing exhaust gases help pull fresh mixture into the cylinder. A well-matched performance exhaust on a 150cc GY6 typically adds 1–3 hp at the top of the rev range. Pair any exhaust upgrade with carburetor re-jetting (richer main jet) as the engine will run leaner with improved exhaust flow. ### Carburetor Upgrade (Carbureted Models) The stock CVK24 slide-diaphragm carburetor on most 125–150cc GY6 engines is reliable but conservative. Replacing it with a performance slide carburetor (such as a VM-style 26 mm or 30 mm unit) allows more fuel and air delivery and eliminates the diaphragm — a common wear item. Requires re-jetting and idle circuit tuning. The Rolling Wrench ProBld carburetor is one example designed as a plug-and-play upgrade for the 150cc GY6 platform. ### CDI (Ignition Timing) Upgrade The stock CDI on GY6 engines is often rev-limited and has a conservative ignition advance curve. A performance CDI removes the rev limiter and may advance timing earlier in the RPM range for better low-to-mid throttle response. This is one of the cheapest per-gain upgrades available (~€10–30). Note: aftermarket CDIs vary significantly in quality. Stick to known brands (NCY, Naraku, or similar) and match the pin count and AC/DC type to your system. ## Stage 2 — CVT Tuning STAGE 2 The Continuously Variable Transmission (CVT) determines how engine power reaches the rear wheel. Stock rollers and springs are set conservatively for smooth commuter behaviour. Tuning the CVT can dramatically improve acceleration. ### Variator Rollers Variator rollers control how quickly the CVT shifts to a higher ratio under acceleration. Heavier rollers shift up sooner (better top speed, slower acceleration). Lighter rollers keep the engine at higher RPM for longer (better acceleration, lower top speed). Stock 150cc GY6 rollers are typically 7–8 g. Performance setups often use 4–6 g rollers for more aggressive acceleration. Always replace all rollers as a matched set. ### Clutch Springs Stiffer clutch springs raise the RPM at which the centrifugal clutch engages. Combined with lighter rollers, stiffer springs keep the engine in its power band during acceleration. Standard spring rates are usually 1000–1500 RPM engagement; performance springs raise this to 3000–4000 RPM. ### Performance Variator Aftermarket variators (NCY, Polini, Malossi for GY6 applications) offer a more optimised ramp profile than the stock unit. The ramp profile controls the speed at which roller displacement translates into belt-ratio change. A performance variator makes CVT tuning more consistent and responsive. ## Stage 3 — Engine Upgrades STAGE 3 Internal engine modifications for serious performance gains. Requires engine disassembly and mechanical competence. ### Big Bore Kit (150cc → 171cc) Fitting a 61 mm cylinder and piston to a `157QMJ` crankcase increases displacement to approximately 171 cc without any crankcase machining. This is the single most impactful engine upgrade for the GY6 platform. See the [GY6 Big Bore Kit guide](gy6-big-bore-kit-guide.html) for full installation details. Requires carburetor re-jetting or EFI remapping. ### Performance Camshaft A performance camshaft increases valve lift and dwell (the duration valves remain open). This allows more mixture into the cylinder and better exhaust scavenging at high RPM. Performance cams are most effective at higher RPM and work best combined with a big bore kit and upgraded air/exhaust. Low-RPM torque may decrease slightly — not ideal for urban commuting but effective for higher-speed riding. ### Head Porting and Polishing Smoothing and enlarging the intake and exhaust ports in the cylinder head reduces turbulence and improves gas flow. This is typically done by a specialist with die-grinder tools. Combined with a big bore and performance cam, head work can produce significant peak power gains. Not a DIY job without experience. ## Stage 4 — Fuel System Upgrades ### EFI Conversion (Carbureted Models) Converting from carburetion to fuel injection — using kits from manufacturers like Ecotrons or Rolling Wrench's ProBld system — delivers precise, auto-tuning fuel delivery that adapts to altitude, temperature, and load. EFI eliminates cold-start enrichment problems and varnishing during storage. Requires a compatible stator (11, 12, or 18-pole — 8-pole stators will not work) and a fuel return line to the tank. See the [GY6 EFI Troubleshooting guide](/diagnostics/gy6-efi-fuel-injection-troubleshooting.html) for diagnostic reference. ### Fuel Pump Upgrade High-performance engines may require higher fuel delivery capacity than the stock vacuum-operated fuel pump provides. Electric fuel pumps deliver consistent pressure regardless of manifold vacuum. See the [GY6 Fuel Pump guide](gy6-fuel-pump-maintenance.html) for replacement and specification details. ## Stage 5 — Brakes and Safety **⚠️ Brake Upgrades Are Not Optional at Higher Performance Levels:** A scooter with a 171cc engine and performance exhaust will travel meaningfully faster than stock. Brakes must be upgraded to match. Riding faster on stock brakes is dangerous. ### Drum to Disc Brake Conversion Many Chinese 50cc and some 125cc GY6 scooters use drum brakes front and/or rear. Converting to disc brakes substantially improves stopping power, consistency in wet conditions, and fade resistance. Conversion kits exist for common GY6 scooter chassis. Requires a matching caliper, disc rotor, bracket, and hydraulic master cylinder. ### Brake Pad Upgrade On scooters already equipped with disc brakes, switching to sintered metal pads (over organic/resin pads) gives better performance when hot and in wet conditions. Note that sintered pads are harder on rotors and may squeal when cold. ## Recommended Upgrade Order
PriorityUpgradeApprox. CostGain
1stPerformance CDI (remove rev limiter)€10–30Higher rev ceiling, better top speed
2ndVariator rollers (lighter weight)€10–20Improved acceleration
3rdPerformance exhaust€40–150Better top-end power; re-jet required
4thAir filter upgrade + re-jet€15–40Better mid-range; works with exhaust upgrade
5thBig bore kit 171cc€80–200Most significant power gain; requires re-jet
6thPerformance carburetor€40–120Better fuel delivery at high power levels
7thBrake upgrade (disc conversion or better pads)€50–200Safety — mandatory before stage 3+ upgrades
**💡 Always Re-Jet After Air/Exhaust Changes:** Every change to the intake or exhaust affects the air/fuel mixture. Running lean (too little fuel for the air) overheats the engine and risks piston damage. Check spark plug colour after any air or fuel system modification: a correct mixture produces a light tan/brown plug colour. Black and sooty means rich; white or blistered means dangerously lean.

## Introduction

The rear wheel on a GY6 scooter is held on a single axle nut. With the right socket, removing it is straightforward and takes under an hour. This guide covers the full procedure: loosening the axle, removing the wheel, changing or patching the inner tube, fitting a replacement tyre if needed, and reassembling everything correctly. The process applies to all GY6 139QMB (50 cc), 152QMI (125 cc), and 157QMJ (150 cc) variants, including BTC Riva 50, La Souris Sourini/City, and Santini Capri models.

<Callout type="warn">
  Work on a flat, stable surface. Place the scooter on its centre stand before starting. Never work under a scooter supported only by its side stand.
</Callout>

## Tyre Specifications (common GY6 sizes)

| Engine | Front | Rear |
|--------|-------|------|
| GY6 50cc (139QMB) | 3.00-10 or 90/90-10 | 3.50-10 or 100/90-10 |
| GY6 125/150cc (QMI/QMJ) | 90/90-10 | 100/90-10 or 110/80-10 |

Always confirm the tyre size printed on the sidewall of the original tyre before purchasing a replacement.

## Tools & Parts Needed

- 17 mm or 19 mm socket with breaker bar (axle nut — check your specific model; most GY6 50 cc use 17 mm, 125/150 cc often 19 mm)
- 8 mm spanner for brake cable adjuster
- 2–3 plastic or metal tyre levers
- Valve core removal tool
- Bicycle or compressor pump
- Patch kit with rubber cement and patches (if repairing rather than replacing the tube)
- Replacement inner tube (if fitting new — match the size printed on the tyre)
- Replacement tyre (if worn or damaged)
- Torque wrench capable of 40–55 Nm

## Step-by-Step Procedure

### Step 1 — Deflate the Tyre

Remove the valve cap and use the valve core tool to fully deflate the tyre before attempting wheel removal. A deflated tyre makes it easier to break the bead and fit the wheel back through the chain/brake assembly.

### Step 2 — Loosen the Brake Adjuster

On drum-brake GY6 models (most 50 cc), the rear drum brake cable passes through an adjuster nut on the brake plate. Loosen this adjuster fully with an 8 mm spanner so the brake arm has maximum slack — this is essential for sliding the axle out.

On disc-brake models the caliper stays on the swingarm and the wheel simply slides off the rotor.

### Step 3 — Loosen the Axle Nut

With the scooter on its centre stand and the rear wheel still on the ground, place your 17 mm or 19 mm socket on the axle nut (right side of the wheel). Break the nut loose with the breaker bar — it is torqued tightly from the factory. Do not remove it fully yet.

<Callout type="tip">
  If the nut is very stiff, a brief spray of penetrating fluid (WD-40 or equivalent) and a 5-minute wait will help. Do not use heat near the tyre or fuel lines.
</Callout>

### Step 4 — Support the Rear of the Scooter

Once the axle nut is loose, place a hydraulic floor jack or a sturdy block under the rear frame rail to lift the rear wheel clear of the ground. Alternatively, have an assistant hold the scooter while you work — do not rely on the centre stand alone once the axle is removed.

### Step 5 — Remove the Axle Nut and Axle

Remove the axle nut completely and retain any washers or spacers in the order they came off — photograph them if helpful. Slide the axle bolt out from the left side of the swingarm. On some models the axle is threaded at one end only; on others it passes through freely.

### Step 6 — Remove the Rear Wheel

Slide the wheel rearward out of the swingarm. On drum-brake models, disconnect the brake arm rod or cable from the brake plate (pull the rod pin or unclip the cable end) to allow the wheel to come free. Keep track of any chain tensioner or spacer plates that sit between the wheel hub and swingarm.

### Step 7 — Remove the Tyre from the Rim

Lay the wheel flat. Insert a tyre lever between the tyre bead and the rim at the valve hole and push the bead over the rim edge. Work around the tyre with a second lever, keeping the first in place. Once one side of the bead is fully off, push the valve core inward and pull the inner tube out from between the tyre and rim.

<Callout type="warn">
  Metal tyre levers can damage the rim if used aggressively. Use smooth, controlled movements and keep levers away from the valve stem area.
</Callout>

### Step 8 — Locate the Puncture (if repairing the tube)

Inflate the tube slightly. Submerge it in a tub of water and look for a stream of bubbles, or simply listen and feel for escaping air. Mark the puncture location with a pen. Once found, deflate the tube fully before patching.

To patch: rough up the area around the hole with sandpaper (included in most kits), apply a thin, even coat of rubber cement and let it dry for 2–3 minutes until tacky, then press the patch firmly down and hold it for at least 60 seconds. Inflate the tube to check the repair holds before refitting.

### Step 9 — Fit the New or Repaired Tube

Inflate the replacement or repaired tube just enough to give it shape (not firm). Dust it lightly with talcum powder if available — this prevents pinching. Feed the valve stem through the valve hole in the rim first, then work the tube evenly inside the tyre cavity all the way around.

### Step 10 — Refit the Tyre Bead

Starting at the valve, push the tyre bead back over the rim edge by hand, working away from the valve in both directions. The last section near the valve is hardest — use a tyre lever carefully if needed, checking that the inner tube is not caught between the lever and rim. Once both beads are seated, check the valve stem is straight and not pulled to one side.

<Callout type="warn">
  Before inflating, run your fingers around both sides of the rim and confirm the tube is not pinched between the tyre bead and the rim edge. A pinched tube will puncture immediately on inflation.
</Callout>

### Step 11 — Inflate to Correct Pressure

Inflate the tyre to the recommended pressure. Most GY6 50 cc models specify **1.75–2.0 bar (25–29 psi)** at the rear; 125/150 cc models typically **2.0–2.25 bar (29–33 psi)** depending on load. Check your owner's manual or the label inside the frame for the specific value.

| Model size | Recommended rear tyre pressure |
|------------|-------------------------------|
| GY6 50cc | 1.75–2.0 bar (25–29 psi) |
| GY6 125cc | 2.0–2.25 bar (29–33 psi) |
| GY6 150cc | 2.0–2.25 bar (29–33 psi) |

### Step 12 — Refit the Wheel

Slide the wheel back into the swingarm, aligning the brake arm rod with the brake plate pin (drum brake) or the disc into the caliper (disc brake). Replace any spacers or chain tensioner plates in their original positions. Feed the axle back through from the left side.

### Step 13 — Reinstall and Torque the Axle Nut

Thread the axle nut on by hand first, then torque it to **40–55 Nm** (check your service manual for your specific model). Most GY6 50 cc axle nuts are torqued to 45 Nm; 150 cc variants to 50–55 Nm.

<Callout type="warn">
  An undertorqued axle nut can work loose while riding, causing catastrophic loss of the rear wheel. Always use a torque wrench.
</Callout>

### Step 14 — Readjust the Rear Brake

On drum-brake models, re-tighten the brake cable adjuster until there is approximately 10–15 mm of free play at the brake lever or pedal. Check that the wheel spins freely and the brake does not drag.

On disc-brake models, pump the brake lever a few times before riding to re-seat the caliper piston.

### Step 15 — Test Ride

Lower the scooter off the jack or stand. Check tyre pressure once more (pressure can change slightly after the tyre seats fully). Ride slowly and brake gently for the first few stops to confirm correct brake function before resuming normal riding.

import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; import SourceBox from '@components/SourceBox.astro'; A scooter left in storage for a year or more will not simply spring back to life. Petrol turns to varnish, rubber hardens and cracks, batteries sulfate, and drive belts go brittle. Working through the repairs in order — safety first, then fluids, fuel system, drivetrain, and finally a systematic first start — is the fastest route to a reliable daily rider. Skipping steps or doing them out of sequence is what turns a weekend job into a month-long frustration. ️ **Work safely:** Always work with the engine cold, the fuel tap closed, and in a well-ventilated space away from open flames or sparks. Wear nitrile gloves when handling fuel, oil, and brake fluid. 🎬 Full Revival Walkthrough — 50cc Scooter from Storage **Video:** "50cc Scooter Oil Change — GY6/QMB139" — [↗ Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=P0Rw-qDR58U) **📋 Revival Progress** 0 of 5 phases complete Phase 1 · Safety Phase 2 · Fluids Phase 3 · Fuel Phase 4 · Drivetrain Phase 5 · Test Ride 🔴 Phase 1 ## Safety & Visual Inspection Before touching anything mechanical, do this first. You are looking for show-stoppers: dangerous corrosion, major leaks, seized brakes, cracked frame. If you find any of these, fix them before proceeding. ### Frame, Welds & Bodywork Storage rust can be cosmetic or structural — you need to tell the difference before spending money on anything else. 1. **Frame rails:** Look for cracks at welds, especially near the headstock (steering tube) and engine mounts. Surface rust is fine; deep pitting or cracks mean stop — this is not a DIY fix. 2. **Forks:** Check for bent lower legs, pitting on the stanchions, and dried or leaking fork oil seals. Grab the front brake and rock the bike — excessive play indicates worn bearings. 3. **Swingarm:** Check the pivot bolt for rust/seize. Grab the rear wheel and wiggle side-to-side — any play means worn swingarm bearings. 4. **Bodywork:** Cracks are cosmetic, but check that panels are not hiding fuel leaks or damaged wiring underneath. � **Stop if:** The frame is cracked at a weld or near a load-bearing joint. This requires professional assessment — do not ride. ### Brakes — Visual & Function Check Brakes seize in two ways after storage: drum brake shoes can bond to the drum, or disc caliper pistons corrode and stick. Both are common after several years. **Drum brakes** (common on rear, sometimes front): 1. Spin the wheel by hand. If it barely turns, the shoe has bonded to the drum. Apply the brake lever fully then release — this sometimes breaks the bond. If not, remove the drum and clean with brake cleaner. 2. Inspect shoe thickness through the drum opening. Under 2 mm — replace. 3. Check the brake cable for fraying, kinks, or rust inside the outer sheath. Stiff or sticky cable — replace. **Disc brakes** (common on front): 1. Check brake fluid in the handlebar reservoir. Dark or brown fluid means moisture contamination — replace. Low level means worn pads or a leak. 2. Squeeze the lever slowly. It should feel firm and return fully. Spongy feel means air in the line. No return means a seized caliper piston. 3. Inspect the brake line along its full length — rubber hoses harden and crack over time. Any cracking — replace before riding. 4. Check the disc surface. Light rust is normal and wears off. Deep grooves or scoring — replace the disc. ️ **Brake fluid:** Use DOT 4 (check your manual). Never mix DOT types. Flush completely — do not top up old fluid. 🎬 Rear Brake Shoes — 50cc/150cc GY6 [↗ Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sLbDUwhhDg0) ### Tyres — Dry Rot & Age Check This step is non-negotiable. A tyre that looks fine can blow out at speed if the rubber has dried internally. Tyre age matters as much as tread depth. 1. **Find the DOT code** on the sidewall — the last 4 digits are the week and year of manufacture (e.g. 3219 = week 32, 2019). Over 5 years old — replace regardless of tread. 2. **Dry rot:** Look for fine cracks in the sidewall or between tread blocks. Any cracking — replace. This is not cosmetic. 3. **Flat spots:** Tyres sitting for years develop a flat patch at the contact point. Inflate to correct pressure and check if it rides out after a slow loop. If it persists after warming up — replace. 4. **Inflate to correct pressure** before riding. Typically 26–32 PSI front, 30–36 PSI rear for 50cc — check the frame sticker. � **Do not ride on cracked or dry-rotted tyres.** At speed they can delaminate suddenly. Budget €30–50 per tyre for a 50cc replacement. 🟡 Phase 2 ## Fluids, Rubber & Consumables Everything that degrades with age regardless of mileage. After 5+ years, all of the following gets replaced — no exceptions. ### Engine Oil — Drain & Fill Fresh Oil sitting for several years oxidises, collects moisture, and turns acidic. Running even a short revival session on old oil accelerates bearing and cam wear. Do this before the first start. 1. Warm the engine slightly (1 min if it starts) so oil flows more easily. If it will not start yet, drain cold — still better than running on old oil. 2. Drain bolt is typically 17 mm on the underside of the engine. Place a pan underneath and let it drain fully for at least 5 minutes. 3. Inspect the drained oil: black or tar-like means very degraded; milky means water contamination (investigate further for a blown head gasket); dark brown is normal degradation. 4. Replace the drain bolt (do not overtighten — aluminium thread). Fill with fresh 10W-40 semi-synthetic motorcycle oil.

GY6 50cc (139QMB)10W-40 semi or full synthetic, motorcycle-grade~0.8 L
GY6 125/150cc10W-40~0.9–1.0 L
Other 50cc CVTCheck frame sticker or owner's manual0.7–1.0 L
� **Rear gearbox oil:** The rear gearbox has a separate oil fill — a small bolt on the rear diff housing. Often overlooked. Use SAE 80W-90 or 85W-90 gear oil, approximately 120 ml. 🎬 Oil Change — 50cc QMB139 Clear walkthrough with tools shown — [↗ Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=k4tyxUhk21M) ### Spark Plug & Air Filter Both are cheap and both will be past their best after 5 years sitting. **Spark plug:** 1. Remove the plug with a spark plug socket (usually 18 mm or 21 mm). It sits under the side cover, accessed from the right-hand side. 2. Read the electrode: light tan/grey is healthy; black and sooty means a rich mixture or oil burning; white or blistered means running lean and hot; corroded or pitted after 5 years — replace regardless. 3. Check the gap: typically 0.6–0.7 mm for GY6/QMB139. Use a feeler gauge — worn plugs have wider gaps and misfire. 4. Replace with OEM spec: **NGK C7HSA** or equivalent. Install by hand first to avoid cross-threading, then snug — do not overtighten. **Air filter:** 1. After 5 years sitting, a paper or foam element will be brittle and possibly mouldy — replace it. A clogged air filter richens the mixture and kills performance. 2. Check the airbox for mouse nests, debris, or cracks in the inlet snorkel — a genuinely common storage problem. 3. Foam filters can be washed in dish soap, dried fully, then lightly re-oiled with filter oil or a few drops of engine oil before reuse. � GY6 50cc spark plug: **NGK C7HSA** (resistor type). Approximately €2–3 each. Buy two and keep one as a spare. ### Rubber Hoses, Seals & Gaskets Rubber has a lifespan regardless of use. UV exposure, heat cycling, and time harden and crack rubber compounds. After 5–6 years, most rubber components on a scooter are past their reliable life. **Replace these — no exceptions:** 1. **Fuel lines** — main line from tank to carb plus overflow hose. Replace with correct-bore fuel-rated hose (5–6 mm ID typically). Old lines collapse internally under suction and starve the engine under load. 2. **Vacuum lines** — the thin 3–4 mm lines connected to the carb, fuel tap, and airbox. Cracks cause air leaks that lean out the mixture and cause a hunting idle. 3. **Carburettor intake manifold seal/O-ring** — the rubber boot between carb and engine. A hairline crack lets unmetered air in. Replace as a matter of course. 4. **Throttle cable** — inspect the inner wire for fraying and check that it returns smoothly. Stiff or slow return after storage is a safety issue — replace. **Inspect and replace if needed:** - **Brake fluid reservoir cap diaphragm** — the rubber diaphragm under the cap can collapse or crack, letting air into the system. - **Fork seals** — look for oil staining on the fork legs. Oil on the stanchion means the seal has blown. - **Engine gaskets** — if you see oil seeping around the cylinder head or crankcase joints, the gaskets have dried out. ️ **Vacuum leaks are sneaky:** They cause the engine to rev fine at idle but lose power or hunt (fluctuate) once you are moving. Spray soapy water around carb joints while the engine runs — bubbles reveal where air is leaking in. #### Fuel & Vacuum Hose Replacement — GY6 All hose positions shown — same layout for 50cc and 150cc. [Watch on YouTube →](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0NwRbp6-vtY) #### Fuel Line Upgrade — Chinese Scooter Why old fuel lines fail and how to replace them correctly. [Watch on YouTube →](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RWOwoYogQ6Y) ### Battery — Replace or Revive A scooter battery left discharged for years almost always sulfates — the lead plates develop a hard crystal layer that a charger cannot penetrate. Test it, but budget for a new one. 1. Test voltage with a multimeter. A healthy 12 V battery reads 12.4–12.7 V at rest. Under 11.5 V after charging — replace. 2. Slow charge attempt: use a smart charger (not a fast charger) at 0.5–1 A for 12–24 hours. If voltage does not rise above 12 V, the battery is dead. 3. Check terminals for white corrosion. Clean with a wire brush and baking soda solution before condemning the battery. 4. Replace with a spec-matched battery — most 50cc scooters use a **YTX5L-BS** or **YTX7A-BS**. Check the old battery label. � A new sealed AGM battery for a 50cc scooter costs €20–35. If the old one is over 3 years old, replace it — a weak battery wastes more time to diagnose than it costs to replace. Also check: pop the fuse box cover and check all fuses visually. Replace any blown fuse with an identical-ampere fuse. Inspect all visible wiring for rodent damage — mice love insulation. Any bare wire must be repaired with heat-shrink before powering up. 🔵 Phase 3 ## Fuel System Old fuel leaves varnish throughout the entire fuel path — tank, tap, filter, and carburettor all need attention. This phase is the single most common reason a scooter will not run properly after storage. ### Fuel Tank — Drain, Inspect & Clean 1. **Drain completely.** Old fuel smells sour and looks dark. Even if it appears fine after 5 years it has lost combustibility — do not mix with fresh fuel, dispose of it properly. 2. **Torch inspection:** Shine a light inside. Light surface rust — clean and seal. Heavy flaking rust — treat with a rust remover or tank liner kit. 3. **Rust treatment:** Fill with white vinegar diluted 50/50 with water. Shake for 10–15 minutes. Drain, rinse with clean water, then flush with fresh petrol to displace water. Dry immediately with compressed air or leave in sun with cap off. 4. **Fuel tap (petcock):** Remove from the tank. Clean the internal strainer screen with carb cleaner. Flow-test by holding a container under the disconnected fuel line with the tap set to ON — it should flow freely and steadily. 5. **Inline fuel filter:** Replace. Costs €1–2. Non-negotiable after 5 years — it is your last line of defence before the carburettor. ️ **Use fresh 95+ RON petrol only.** Avoid E10 fuel where possible — 10% ethanol attacks rubber seals and fuel lines faster, especially on older scooters. ### Carburettor — Full Disassembly & Clean After 5 years, old fuel has left a sticky varnish coating on every internal surface. The pilot jet (idle circuit) is especially vulnerable — it is tiny and a partially blocked pilot jet produces exactly the symptoms of a scooter that will not pull properly even though the engine sounds otherwise fine. 1. **Remove the carb:** Close the fuel tap. Disconnect the throttle cable, choke cable, fuel line, and overflow hose. Two 8 mm bolts hold it to the intake manifold. 2. **Drain the float bowl:** Unscrew the drain screw or float bowl bolt. Note the colour — varnish-coloured residue confirms heavy deposits. 3. **Remove the float bowl:** 4 screws underneath. Inside you will see the float, needle valve, main jet (large brass), and pilot jet (tiny brass — often tucked away). Remove both jets. 4. **Soak in carb dip** for 20–30 minutes minimum. Use a zip-lock bag with carb cleaner or a dedicated carb dip bath. 5. **Blow out every passage** with compressed air. Every single hole — main jet, pilot jet, idle passages, emulsion tube holes. Never use wire to ream jets — it enlarges them permanently. 6. **Check the needle clip:** Middle groove is factory. If someone previously moved it to richen or lean the mixture, reset to middle. 7. **Air/fuel mixture screw:** Gently seat it (do not overtighten), then back out 1.5–2.5 turns. Fine-tune after the engine is fully warm. 8. **Reassemble with a fresh float bowl gasket** if available. Cracks or compression sets on old gaskets let air in and lean out the mixture. � **Quick leak test after reassembly:** Before starting, turn the fuel tap ON and wait 30 seconds. No drips from the carb body, float bowl, or joints means you are good. Any dripping indicates a gasket issue or float level problem. #### Clean GY6 Carburettor — 50cc/150cc Full disassembly and jet cleaning with close-up shots of every passage. [Watch on YouTube →](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=T4YPi-qLLUo) #### Troubleshoot & Fix GY6 Carb Issues Covers slow or no power after storage — systematic diagnosis. [Watch on YouTube →](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gWX34-_6qL0) 🟢 Phase 4 ## CVT Drivetrain The transmission that connects the engine to the rear wheel — belt, rollers, and clutch all degrade with age and inactivity. A scooter that revs freely but barely moves is almost always a CVT problem. ### Drive Belt & Variator Rollers After years in storage the drive belt goes hard, cracks, or glazes, losing its grip on the pulleys. The variator roller weights flatten on one side from sitting under their own weight. Either fault causes the engine to rev with little power reaching the rear wheel. 1. **Remove the CVT cover** — 7–9 × 8 mm bolts around the perimeter. Use a rubber mallet to break the seal; do not pry with screwdrivers or you will damage the mating face. 2. **Blow out with compressed air** before touching anything — belt and clutch dust is harmful to breathe. Wear a mask. 3. **Belt inspection:** Look for cracks (especially on the inner V-face), hardness, glazing (shiny surface), fraying edges, or missing chunks. Any of these — replace. 4. **Lock the variator** with a holder tool. Undo the centre nut and pull off the variator face — rollers will fall out. 5. **Inspect rollers:** They should be perfectly round. D-shaped flat spots — replace as a complete set. Also check for wear grooves on the ramp surfaces inside the variator. 6. **Contra spring (rear pulley):** Check it is not collapsed or visibly shorter on one side. A weak contra spring keeps the scooter stuck in high ratio and kills acceleration.

� Replace belt and rollers together as a set. Mixing old rollers with a new belt causes uneven wear and the problem returns quickly. A full CVT kit (belt + rollers + contra spring) costs approximately €15–25. #### Belt & Variator — 50cc GY6/QMB139 Full removal and replacement with torque specs. [Watch on YouTube →](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xh37xm0fWmY) #### GY6 Variator & Rollers — Step by Step With tips on spotting worn rollers and checking ramp surfaces. [Watch on YouTube →](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2EjW-iSP-Q8) ### Clutch Bell & Pads The centrifugal clutch engages when engine revs rise, pressing friction pads against the bell (drum). After storage, the bell can surface-rust, pads can glaze, and belt dust can compact inside. The result is clutch slip under load — the engine revs but the scooter barely accelerates. 1. **Clutch bell interior:** Should be dull grey. Mirror-shiny means glazed. Light surface rust is cleanable with emery cloth; deep pitting — replace the bell. 2. **Pad thickness:** Under 2 mm — replace. The pad surface should be slightly rough, not glassy smooth. 3. **Clutch springs:** Three small springs on the clutch arms. Equal length is correct. One shorter or softer causes asymmetric engagement and vibration. 4. **Clean the bell interior** with brake cleaner spray. Never lubricate — any oil on pads or bell causes instant glazing. � **Never use oil or WD-40 near clutch pads or the bell interior.** Even a light oil mist causes slipping that requires pad replacement to fix. 🎬 50cc Scooter Clutch & Variator Install Shows clutch assembly, pads, and springs — [↗ Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vfNJ9jL1T_I) ### Final Drive Most modern CVT scooters (GY6, QMB139, Honda, Yamaha, Kymco equivalents) use a sealed rear gearbox — power goes from the CVT into a sealed rear hub. There is no external chain to worry about. Keep the gear oil filled as covered in Phase 2. If your older or sport scooter has an external chain, check for rust and seized links, verify tension (20–30 mm of free play at mid-point), and lubricate generously with chain lube. ✅ Phase 5 ## First Start & Test Ride A systematic approach to the first start. Do this in order — not all at once. ### Pre-Ride Checklist Tick everything before attempting to start: - Engine oil filled — correct spec and level - Fresh fuel in tank — 95+ RON, fuel tap functional - New spark plug fitted — correct gap (0.6–0.7 mm) - Air filter clean or replaced - Fuel lines replaced — no drips with fuel tap open - Carburettor cleaned — jets clear, float bowl dry - Battery charged — voltage above 12.4 V - Both brakes checked — lever firm, wheel spins freely - Tyres inflated to correct pressure — no dry rot visible - CVT cover fitted — all bolts torqued - Throttle returns fully and smoothly when released - Lights and horn working ### First Start Procedure 1. **Choke on / enrichment on.** Let fuel flow to the carb for 30 seconds before cranking. 2. **Crank for maximum 5 seconds** at a time, then rest 10 seconds. Do not flood the engine with continuous cranking. 3. **Once started, do not rev.** Let it idle and warm up for 2–3 minutes with choke still on or being gradually reduced. 4. **Listen:** Ticking is normal (valves). Knocking means an internal problem — stop immediately. Rattling from the CVT area means the belt or variator is loose. 5. **Check for leaks** while running — fuel, oil, coolant (if applicable). Any dripping — stop and fix before riding. 6. **Warm ride:** First 10 minutes, keep speed under 20 km/h. No hard acceleration. Let the engine, seals, and CVT reach operating temperature gently. 7. **After 10 minutes:** Gradually increase speed. Apply the brakes firmly once to check feel. If all is good, push to normal riding speed. 8. **Change engine oil again** after the first 50–100 km of running. The revival run will have stirred up sediment and old deposits — flush them out. ️ **Won't start after the carb clean?** Check: (1) Fuel reaching float bowl — unscrew drain screw, it should drip. (2) Spark — remove plug, hold against engine block, crank — should spark. (3) Choke position. (4) Kill switch not accidentally engaged. ## Tools & Parts for the Full Revival 🔧 Socket set (8–22 mm) 🔧 Spark plug socket (18/21 mm) 🔨 Rubber mallet 💨 Compressed air 🧴 Carb cleaner + dip bath 🧽 Brake cleaner spray 📏 Feeler gauge set ⚡ Multimeter 🔋 Smart battery charger ⚙️ Variator holder tool 🛢️ 10W-40 engine oil (1 L) 🛢️ 80W-90 gear oil (200 ml) ⛽ Inline fuel filter ⚙️ Drive belt 669×18 mm ⚙️ Roller weight set (5.5–7 g) 🔌 NGK C7HSA spark plug 🔵 DOT 4 brake fluid 🔋 Battery YTX5L-BS or YTX7A-BS 🧱 Fuel line (5–6 mm ID) 🧱 Vacuum line (3–4 mm ID) ## Troubleshooting

import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; The spark plug is one of the cheapest and most impactful maintenance items on any petrol scooter. A worn or incorrectly gapped plug causes hard starting, rough idle, misfires, and increased fuel consumption. Replacing it takes 10–15 minutes and costs less than €5 for a standard NGK. ## Spark Plug Specifications | Engine | Standard Plug | Upgrade (Iridium) | Gap | |---|---|---|---| | GY6 50cc (139QMB) | NGK C7HSA | NGK CR7HIX | 0.6–0.7 mm | | GY6 125/150cc (157QMJ) | NGK CR7HSA | NGK CR7HIX | 0.6–0.7 mm | | Vespa Primavera 125 iGet | NGK ILZKBR7B8DG (OEM) | — | 0.7–0.8 mm | Tip: Keep a spare NGK CR7HSA under your seat. It weighs nothing, costs under €4, and can save a long walk home if the plug fails on the road. ## Tools & Materials Required - Spark plug socket — **16 mm** for most GY6 engines (check your cap diameter first) - Socket wrench extension (the plug is often deep in the head) - Feeler gauge (to verify the gap on the new plug) - Torque wrench (optional but recommended — 10–14 Nm) - Compressed air or a rag to clean the plug recess - New spark plug (see specifications above) ## Reading the Old Plug — What It Tells You Before discarding the old plug, inspect the electrode. The color and condition reveal a lot about engine health: | Electrode appearance | Diagnosis | Action | |---|---|---| | Light tan/grey, slight electrode wear | ✅ Normal — engine running correctly | Replace at service interval | | Dry black, sooty carbon deposits | Rich mixture or clogged air filter | Check/clean air filter; check carb jetting | | Wet/oily, black | Oil in combustion — worn piston rings or valve seals | Engine inspection needed | | White or pale grey, blistered | Lean mixture or overheating | Check fuel delivery, coolant/air flow | | Rounded/eroded electrode | Normal wear — replace now | Standard replacement | ## Step-by-Step Replacement Procedure 1. **Let the engine cool for at least 10 minutes.** Working on a hot engine risks burns and can cause the plug to seize in the aluminium head if torqued incorrectly when hot. 2. **Remove the spark plug cap** by pulling it straight off the plug. Pull the cap, not the wire — pulling the wire can damage the HT lead connection inside the cap. 3. **Clean around the plug recess** with compressed air or a dry rag. Any debris that falls into the cylinder when the plug is removed can score the bore. 4. **Unscrew the old plug** counter-clockwise using the spark plug socket. If it is tight, apply penetrating oil (WD-40 or equivalent) around the base and wait 5 minutes before trying again. Do not force it. 5. **Inspect and note the condition** of the old plug electrode as described in the reading guide above. 6. **Check the gap on the new plug** with a feeler gauge. For GY6 engines, the gap should be **0.6–0.7 mm**. Most NGK plugs are pre-gapped but verify. To adjust, carefully bend only the side (ground) electrode — never the centre electrode. 7. **Thread the new plug in by hand** for the first 3–4 turns. Cross-threading an aluminium cylinder head is an expensive mistake. If it does not thread smoothly by hand, stop and recheck alignment. 8. **Tighten with the socket.** With a new plug and a copper washer seat: hand-tight + **¼ turn**. With a torque wrench: **10–14 Nm**. Do not overtighten — aluminium threads strip easily. 9. **Reconnect the spark plug cap** firmly until it seats fully. A loose cap is a common cause of intermittent misfires. 10. **Start the engine** and confirm it runs cleanly at idle and through the rev range. Note on anti-seize compound: Do not apply anti-seize paste to spark plug threads in aluminium heads. The torque specification is designed for bare threads. Anti-seize changes the effective clamping force and can cause under- or over-tightening. ## Spark Plug Service Intervals | Plug type | Inspection | Replacement | |---|---|---| | Standard copper (NGK C7HSA / CR7HSA) | Every 3,000 km | Every 3,000–5,000 km | | Iridium (NGK CR7HIX) | Every 5,000 km | Every 10,000–15,000 km | | Vespa OEM iridium | Per Piaggio service schedule | Every 8,000–10,000 km | Upgrade tip: The NGK CR7HIX iridium plug is a genuine upgrade for GY6 engines. It produces a stronger, more consistent spark which improves cold starting and smooth idle. At roughly €8–12 it costs more than the standard plug but lasts 3× longer. ## Applicable Models This procedure applies to all GY6-engined scooters including the **BTC Riva**, **La Souris Sourini / City**, **Santini Capri**, and all other `139QMB` / `157QMJ` engine family scooters. For Vespa Primavera and Sprint models, the plug location and cap type differ but the procedure is identical — consult your model's service manual for the exact plug recess location. Piaggio ZIP 50/100 4T spark plug specs — from the official Piaggio MSS ZIP 100 4T Service Station Manual: **100 cc:** Champion RG4HC / Champion RG4PHP / NGK CR9EB  |  Gap: **0.7–0.8 mm**  |  Torque: **10–15 Nm** **50 cc:** NGK CR8EB / Denso U24ESR-NB3  |  Gap: **0.7–0.8 mm**  |  Torque: **10–15 Nm** The ZIP uses a hotter plug (CR9EB vs CR7HSA on GY6) due to its SOHC combustion chamber design and compression ratio (10.5–11.5:1).

import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; On GY6-platform 50cc scooters the speedometer is driven mechanically: a small plastic drive box on the front wheel hub spins the inner cable, which runs up through the fork to the speedometer head. When this cable breaks or seizes, the speedometer needle stops moving — or starts jumping erratically. The fix is almost always straightforward: a replacement cable costs around €5–10 and the job takes under an hour with basic tools. 📹 Quick Reference — Speedometer Cable Replacement **Video:** Speedometer cable replacement short tutorial — [↗ Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/V1ZQe-nvpbs) ## How the Mechanical Speedometer Drive Works A drive box is press-fit into the front wheel hub and contains a small pin that engages with slots in the wheel axle area. As the wheel turns, the drive box rotates the square-ended inner cable inside a flexible outer sheath. The cable routes up through the fork, through any cable guides on the fairing, and connects at the back of the speedometer head. Inside the speedometer, a magnet assembly converts this rotation into needle deflection. The inner cable is the most common failure point. It is a thin steel wire and will eventually fatigue and snap — especially if it was ever run dry (no grease), kinked sharply, or routed with too tight a bend radius. When the inner cable breaks, the outer sheath and drive box are usually still fine and do not need replacing. **ℹ️ Mechanical vs electronic speedometer:** GY6 50cc scooters sold under various brand names (La Souris, BTC, Santini, Jonway, etc.) almost all use a mechanical cable drive. If you see a plastic sensor on the fork/hub area with a wire going to the instrument cluster — not a cable housing — you have an electronic speedometer and this guide does not apply. ## Symptoms #### ⛔ Broken inner cable - Speedometer needle completely dead at all speeds - Odometer has stopped advancing - No resistance when you try to spin the cable end by hand - You may find a piece of cable rattling inside the sheath #### ⚠️ Dry / worn cable - Needle fluctuates or jumps erratically at low speeds - Squealing or grinding noise from the front wheel area, more pronounced under acceleration - Speedometer reads correctly at high speed but drops out at idle ## Diagnosis ### Step 1 — Visual inspection of both ends Trace the cable from the speedometer head (under the instrument panel or handlebar cover) down to the front wheel hub. Look for: - The upper ferrule nut at the speedometer — is it still screwed in, or has it worked loose? - Kinks, sharp bends, or crushed sections anywhere along the cable run - The lower end at the wheel drive box — is the cable housing still clipped in? ### Step 2 — Test the inner cable 1. Unscrew the knurled ferrule nut at the speedometer head by hand (anti-clockwise). On some models it is a push-and-twist bayonet fitting. 2. Pull the cable housing away from the speedometer by about 3–4 cm to expose the inner cable tip. 3. Try to spin the inner cable between your fingers. It should rotate freely with a slight resistance from the cable's own weight. **If it spins without resistance (no feel of the cable), the inner cable is broken inside the sheath.** 4. Ask a helper to slowly push the scooter forward whilst you watch the inner cable tip — it should rotate at the same pace as the wheel. If the wheel moves but the cable does not rotate, the drive box is the fault, not the cable. **💡 Tip:** Before ordering a cable, disconnect it completely from the drive box and try spinning the drive box stub by hand whilst turning the wheel. If the drive box stub does not turn when the wheel does, the drive box is cracked or stripped — order a drive box as well. ## Tools & Parts Required
ItemNotes
Phillips (cross-head) screwdriverFor instrument panel screws and cable guide clips
White lithium grease or thick gear oilTo lube the new inner cable before installation
Replacement speedometer cable — GY6 50ccGeneric "universal" cables for GY6 139QMB fit most Chinese clone scooters. Verify length against the old cable (~€5–10). Order the drive box too (~€3–5) if Step 2 showed the box is faulty.
## Replacement Procedure ### Step 1 — Disconnect the upper end (speedometer head) 1. If the instrument panel has a cover or surround, unclip it to gain access to the back of the speedometer. On most 50cc scooters this is a simple two-piece plastic housing held by two or three Phillips screws. 2. Unscrew the ferrule nut at the speedometer end by hand — it should be finger-tight only. If it is seized, grip the hexagonal section with pliers and turn gently. 3. Pull the cable housing away and set the speedometer end aside. ### Step 2 — Free the cable along the routing 1. Follow the cable down the fork leg and note any cable clamps, zip ties, or plastic clips holding it to the frame or fairing. Release them — do not cut zip ties you plan to reuse. 2. On scooters where the cable runs inside a fairing panel, you may need to remove one or two body panels. Take note of the exact routing as you go — a photo on your phone before disassembly saves time on reassembly. ### Step 3 — Disconnect the lower end (wheel drive box) 1. At the front wheel hub, locate the drive box — a small dome-shaped plastic fitting on the hub, with the cable housing plugging into it. 2. The cable housing usually has a simple push-in clip or a small retaining nut. Unclip or unscrew it, then pull the cable housing straight out of the drive box. 3. Withdraw the full cable and sheath from the routing path. ### Step 4 — Prepare and route the new cable 1. Before threading the new inner cable into its sheath, apply a thin, even coat of white lithium grease — or a few drops of thick gear oil — along the full length of the inner cable. This is the single most effective way to prevent premature failure and squealing. 2. Route the new cable through the same path as the old one. The key rule: **no bend tighter than 90°, and no bend with a radius smaller than ~5 cm.** A sharp kink will snap the cable within a few hundred kilometres. 3. Ensure the cable is not routed near the exhaust or any heat source. ### Step 5 — Connect the lower end first 1. Push the cable housing into the drive box and clip or screw it in. The square tip of the inner cable must seat into the square socket of the drive box stub. You will feel it click or seat positively — if it does not engage, rotate the inner cable slightly until it drops in. 2. Turn the front wheel by hand and confirm the inner cable rotates at the top end. ### Step 6 — Connect the upper end (speedometer head) 1. Feed the square tip of the inner cable into the back of the speedometer. Rotate it slightly until it seats into the drive slot inside the speedo body. 2. Push the cable housing ferrule into the speedometer port and screw the ferrule nut on finger-tight. Do not overtighten — the nut only needs to be snug. 3. Refit any panel covers or cable clips you removed during disassembly. ### Step 7 — Test 1. Push the scooter forward at walking pace and watch the speedometer needle. It should move smoothly with no jumping. 2. Listen for any grinding or squealing from the front wheel area — if present, the cable is binding somewhere or the inner cable is not fully seated in the drive box. 3. Take a short test ride and confirm the odometer is advancing and the speedometer reads plausibly at riding speed. **💡 Long-term tip:** Every 10,000 km, disconnect the cable at the speedometer head, pull the inner cable out fully, wipe it down, re-grease it, and reinstall. A greased cable will last the life of the scooter; a dry one will snap within a season. ## Troubleshooting
SymptomMost Likely CauseAction
Needle still dead after new cable fittedInner cable not seated in the drive box or speedometer slotDisconnect both ends, confirm the inner cable tip is square (not rounded), re-seat both ends
Needle jumps or is erraticSharp bend in the cable routing, or cable not greasedRe-route with gentler bends; grease the inner cable
Grinding noise from front wheel after new cableDrive box cracked or worn; inner cable tip rounded offReplace the drive box; inspect the inner cable tip
Cable broke again quickly after replacementSharp kink in the routing, or the drive box is worn and putting side-load on the cableCheck routing for tight bends; replace drive box
Wheel turns but drive box stub does not rotateDrive box cracked or stripped internallyReplace the drive box — ~€3–5 for a GY6 universal unit

import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; import SourceBox from '@components/SourceBox.astro'; The stator is the fixed generating coil assembly inside the magneto (flywheel magneto alternator) on the **right side** of the GY6 engine (the non-drive side — the left side houses the CVT/variator). As the flywheel's permanent magnets spin around it, the stator produces AC power which is then rectified to DC by the regulator/rectifier to charge the battery and power the electrical system. A failed stator typically causes a flat battery that will not hold charge, dim or dead lighting, or — if the CDI pickup coil is also on the stator — total ignition failure. ## Diagnosing a Faulty Stator Before Replacing Before pulling the flywheel, confirm the stator is the fault. Most stator failures show up as charging problems, not ignition failures — the pickup coil is a separate winding and can fail independently. **Charging test (battery voltage method):** 1. Start the engine and bring it to normal operating temperature. 2. Set a multimeter to DC voltage and probe the battery terminals. 3. At idle (~1,800 rpm): expect **12.5–13.5 V**. 4. At ~4,000 rpm: expect **13.5–14.5 V**. 5. If voltage barely rises above 12 V at any rpm, the stator, regulator/rectifier, or wiring harness is at fault. **Stator AC output test (with engine off, by resistance):** 1. Disconnect the stator connector (usually a 3-wire yellow AC output plus a separate 2-wire pickup coil connector). 2. Measure resistance between each yellow wire pair with the multimeter on Ω: - A healthy 8-coil GY6 stator typically reads **0.4–0.8 Ω** between each pair of yellow leads. - Open circuit (infinite/OL) = broken coil winding → replace stator. - Very low resistance near 0 Ω = shorted winding → replace stator. 3. Check pickup coil (trigger coil) resistance between its two leads: typically **100–400 Ω** on GY6 engines. **Do NOT use a 3-jaw puller to remove the GY6 flywheel.** The flywheel is tapered onto the crankshaft with no key — a 3-jaw puller will distort and destroy the stator coils before the flywheel breaks free. You must use a dedicated GY6 flywheel puller that threads into the flywheel centre boss. ## Tools & Parts The flywheel puller thread size varies between GY6 variants: - **Most 50cc (139QMB):** M27×1.0 left-hand thread or M28×1.0 right-hand thread — check your flywheel - **Most 125/150cc (157QMJ):** M28×1.0 right-hand thread Confirm before ordering a puller. Replacement stators are available in 5-coil (AC-only) and 8-coil (DC) configurations — match the winding count to your original. The 8-coil DC stator is standard on modern Euro 4/5 GY6 scooters. ## Step-by-Step Procedure ### 1 — Prepare and Disconnect Battery 1. Park the scooter on its centre stand on a level surface. 2. Remove the seat and access panels to reach the left side of the engine. 3. Disconnect the **negative (−) terminal** of the battery first. This prevents accidental shorts through the electrical system while working. ### 2 — Remove the Right-Side Cooling Shroud and Fan 1. Locate the black plastic cooling fan shroud on the **right side** of the engine. 2. Remove the shroud bolts (typically four 6 mm hex-head bolts, 8 mm spanner). 3. Lift the shroud away to expose the white plastic cooling fan and the flywheel behind it. 4. Remove the cooling fan: four 8 mm bolts secure it to the flywheel face. Note the fan orientation (it is directional). ### 2b — Remove the Magneto Cover 1. With the fan removed, the cast alloy magneto cover is now accessible. Remove its bolts (typically five or six 8 mm hex-head bolts around the perimeter). 2. Carefully pry the cover free — it may be sealed with a gasket or RTV sealant. Note the condition of the gasket; replace it if torn or compressed. 3. The flywheel is now fully exposed inside the engine casing. ### 3 — Remove the Flywheel 1. Prevent the flywheel from rotating: use a flywheel holding tool, or place the transmission in gear and apply the rear brake firmly. 2. Loosen and remove the large central flywheel nut (19 mm). Note the thread direction — on GY6 engines this is a **standard right-hand thread** (counter-clockwise to loosen). 3. Thread the flywheel puller into the central boss of the flywheel until fully engaged (at least 5–6 full turns). **Check your puller's thread direction** — most GY6 pullers are right-hand thread (turn clockwise to engage), but some 50cc variants use a left-hand thread boss; confirm before forcing. 4. Hold the puller body still and turn the central bolt clockwise. As the puller pushes against the crankshaft end, the flywheel will pop free with a sharp crack — this is normal. 5. Carefully slide the flywheel off the tapered crankshaft. **Check woodruff key:** As the flywheel comes off, a small semicircular woodruff key should be visible on the crankshaft taper. Do not lose it — it aligns the flywheel timing. If the key is damaged (sheared), replace it before reassembly. ### 4 — Remove the Old Stator 1. The stator is secured to the right engine casing (inside the magneto cover) by 2–3 bolts (Phillips or 8 mm hex). 2. Trace the stator wiring loom through the engine casing grommet. Disconnect the main stator connector and the pickup coil connector from the main wiring harness. 3. Unroute the wiring and remove the stator. ### 5 — Install the New Stator 1. Position the new stator in the casing, aligning the mounting holes. 2. Route the wiring loom back through the casing grommet. Ensure the grommet seals properly to prevent oil leaks. 3. Apply a small drop of medium-strength threadlock to the stator bolts and torque to approximately **8–10 Nm**. Do not overtighten — the casing is aluminium. 4. Reconnect the stator and pickup coil connectors to the main harness. **Wire routing matters:** Before refitting the flywheel, check that no wires are routed anywhere near the flywheel path. Any wire that contacts the spinning flywheel will be severed within minutes of riding. Tuck all wiring clear of the flywheel sweep area. ### 6 — Refit the Flywheel 1. Clean the crankshaft taper and the inside of the flywheel boss with a clean rag — no oil or grease on these surfaces. 2. Reinstall the woodruff key into its groove on the crankshaft. 3. Align the flywheel keyway with the woodruff key and slide the flywheel onto the taper. The flywheel magnets will pull it snugly into position. 4. Refit the flywheel nut and torque to **30–40 Nm** (or the specification in your service manual). Under-torquing allows the flywheel to work loose; over-torquing can damage the crankshaft thread. 5. Refit the magneto cover with a new gasket (or fresh RTV sealant if no gasket was used). Torque the cover bolts evenly in a cross pattern to approximately **8–10 Nm**. 6. Refit the cooling fan in the correct orientation, then reinstall the cooling shroud. ### 7 — Post-Install Test 1. Reconnect the battery negative terminal. 2. Start the engine and perform the charging voltage test described above. 3. At ~4,000 rpm the voltage should read 13.5–14.5 V DC at the battery. If it does not, suspect the regulator/rectifier before concluding the new stator is faulty. ## Stator Output Specifications (typical GY6)
ParameterValue
Charging coil resistance (yellow leads, each pair)0.4–0.8 Ω
Pickup coil resistance100–400 Ω
AC output at 5,000 rpm (before rectifier)40–80 V AC
DC charging voltage at battery (at 4,000 rpm)13.5–14.5 V
Flywheel nut torque30–40 Nm
Stator bolt torque8–10 Nm

## Introduction

The GY6 engine family — covering the 139QMB (50 cc), 152QMI (125 cc), and 157QMJ (150 cc) — uses a single-cylinder overhead-cam (SOHC) design driven by a timing chain. The timing chain must stay precisely tensioned to synchronise the crankshaft and camshaft. An automatic hydraulic tensioner, mounted on the right-hand side of the cylinder, applies constant pressure to a plastic chain guide to maintain correct tension.

When the tensioner wears out, the timing chain develops slack. Left unattended, a slack chain can skip a tooth on the sprocket, jump timing, and destroy the engine. Fortunately, diagnosis is straightforward and replacement is a straightforward intermediate-level job.

<Callout type="warn">
  Do not continue riding if you hear persistent timing chain rattling. Chain skip can cause valve-to-piston contact, bending valves and requiring an engine rebuild. Replace the tensioner at the first sign of failure.
</Callout>

## How the GY6 Tensioner Works

The GY6 uses a spring-loaded, oil-fed hydraulic tensioner. Engine oil pressure fills a small internal piston, which extends a plunger outward to push against the chain guide blade. As the chain stretches over time, the piston extends further to compensate. A ratchet mechanism locks the piston to prevent it retracting — if the ratchet wears or oil pressure drops, the piston can retract, causing the chain to rattle.

A second component — the timing chain guide — is a curved nylon or plastic blade that the chain runs against. This guide can crack or wear through, requiring separate replacement.

## Symptoms of a Failing Tensioner

**Cold-start rattle:** A metallic rattling or slapping sound from the top-right of the engine on first start-up, which reduces or disappears after 10–20 seconds once oil pressure builds. This is the clearest indicator of a weakening tensioner.

**Persistent rattle at idle:** If the rattle does not clear once the engine is warm, the tensioner is no longer compensating adequately — this is a more urgent failure requiring immediate attention.

**Rough running or misfires:** A chain that has jumped one or more teeth will cause ignition and valve timing errors, resulting in rough idle, backfiring, or a no-start condition.

**Metallic debris in oil:** Fine metal particles in the engine oil, visible when draining, can indicate that the chain guide has cracked and shed material.

**Visible chain slack:** With the engine off, remove the tensioner inspection plug (on the cylinder, above and behind the spark plug) and look for visible chain slack in the timing chain.

## Tools & Parts Needed

The OEM tensioner for the GY6 157QMJ / 152QMI / 139QMB is a standardised part widely available from GY6 parts suppliers. The part typically includes: tensioner body, internal spring and plunger, sealing washer or O-ring, and in some kits, the chain guide set.

Recommended replacement kit: NCY G-Cam Chain Tensioner Guide Kit (includes tensioner, upper guide, and lower guide) — suitable for 125 cc and 150 cc GY6 engines. For 50 cc 139QMB engines, a separate 50 cc-specific upper and lower guide set is required as the guide geometry differs slightly.

## Step-by-Step Replacement Procedure

### Step 1 — Prepare the Engine

Allow the engine to cool to ambient temperature. Place the scooter on its centre stand on a level surface. Remove the seat and right-side body panel to gain clear access to the right-hand side of the engine cylinder.

Do not drain the engine oil unless you suspect the chain guide has shed debris into the sump. If debris is suspected, drain and replace the oil after the repair.

### Step 2 — Locate the Tensioner

The timing chain tensioner is mounted on the right-hand face of the cylinder, approximately halfway up the cylinder between the crankcase and cylinder head. It is secured by either one or two bolts (depending on the GY6 variant) and protrudes outward. The tensioner body is typically 25–30 mm in diameter with a hexagonal or flat outer cap.

### Step 3 — Release the Tensioner Plunger

Before removing the tensioner, you must retract the plunger. Insert a small flathead screwdriver into the slot on the tensioner cap (on auto-tensioners) and rotate 90° clockwise to retract the ratchet, or push the plunger inward gently with a pencil while rotating it. This prevents the plunger from springing out under tension when the tensioner is unbolted.

<Callout type="warn">
  On some GY6 tensioners the spring load is strong. Keep a finger over the plunger as you loosen the tensioner body to prevent it from shooting out. The spring and plunger are small and easily lost.
</Callout>

### Step 4 — Remove the Old Tensioner

Using an 8 mm or 10 mm spanner (depending on your variant), unscrew the tensioner body in an anticlockwise direction. Remove it carefully, keeping the plunger retracted. Inspect the old tensioner: if the plunger is worn, the ratchet teeth stripped, or the spring compressed and weak, replacement is confirmed.

While you have access, look through the tensioner bore into the cylinder with a torch. You should see the chain guide blade and the timing chain. Check the guide blade for cracks, heavy wear marks, or missing sections. If the guide is cracked or worn through to the metal backing, replace it as part of this service.

### Step 5 — Install the New Tensioner

Thread the new tensioner into the cylinder with the plunger fully retracted. Tighten to 12–15 N·m — do not over-tighten as the cylinder threads can strip. Ensure the sealing washer seats correctly against the cylinder face to prevent oil weeping.

### Step 6 — Release the Plunger

Once the tensioner is installed and torqued, release the plunger:

- **Spring-only tensioners:** Simply pull the retaining pin or rotate the cap back 90° anticlockwise. The spring will push the plunger outward.
- **Hydraulic auto-tensioners:** Release the ratchet lock. Oil pressure will extend the plunger once the engine starts.

### Step 7 — Check the Timing Chain Guide (If Required)

If the guide blade requires replacement, you will need to remove the right-side engine cover (the magneto/flywheel side cover) to access and replace the upper and lower guide blades. This is a more involved procedure covered separately in the engine rebuild section. The guide blades slide over metal retaining pins inside the cylinder and crankcase.

### Step 8 — Start the Engine and Verify

Start the engine cold and listen carefully. A correctly tensioned chain should be silent within 3–5 seconds of start-up as oil pressure builds and extends the tensioner. Warm the engine to operating temperature and recheck. If rattling persists after replacement, suspect a worn timing chain itself or a damaged chain guide.

<Callout type="tip">
  After replacing the tensioner, change the engine oil if it hasn't been done recently. Fresh oil improves tensioner operation. GY6 engines take approximately 800 ml (139QMB 50 cc) or 1,100 ml (157QMJ 150 cc) of 10W-40 JASO MA2 oil.
</Callout>

## Specifications

| Component | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| Tensioner torque (standard GY6) | 12–15 N·m |
| Engine oil grade | 10W-40 JASO MA2 |
| Oil capacity — 139QMB (50 cc) | ~800 ml |
| Oil capacity — 152QMI (125 cc) | ~1,000 ml |
| Oil capacity — 157QMJ (150 cc) | ~1,100 ml |
| Chain replacement interval | Every 15,000 km or if stretched >3% |
| Guide replacement | When visibly cracked or thinned to ≤2 mm |

## Timing Chain vs. Tensioner vs. Guide — What to Replace?

If the engine is cold-start rattling only: replace the tensioner.
If rattling persists when warm: replace tensioner AND inspect/replace guides.
If the chain has jumped timing (rough running, backfire, no start after chain work): replace the chain, tensioner, and guides as a set.

Replacing all three components at once is good practice on high-mileage GY6 engines (above 15,000 km), as the chain, guide, and tensioner wear together.

This guide covers both a standard piston ring swap (rings only) and a full top end rebuild with new cylinder, applicable to the **GY6 139QMB** (50cc) and **GY6 157QMJ** (125cc/150cc) engine families. ️ **Safety note:** Always work on a cold engine. Allow at least two hours after last use before disassembling. Dispose of used engine oil responsibly at a recycling centre. ## When Is a Top End Rebuild Needed? - Persistent blue or white smoke from the exhaust, especially on acceleration - Compression below 100 psi (service limit) on a compression gauge test - Engine consuming more than 0.1 litre of oil per 1,000 km - Severe loss of power not resolved by carburetor or valve adjustment - Worn or scuffed cylinder bore visible on inspection (score marks) - Piston rings with end gap exceeding 0.5 mm (worn past service limit) ## Tools & Parts Required - Metric socket set (8 mm, 10 mm, 12 mm, 17 mm) - Torque wrench (0–30 Nm range) - Piston ring compressor (or a hose clamp as a substitute) - Piston pin circlip pliers (snap-ring pliers) - Feeler gauges (for valve clearance check after rebuild) - Cylinder bore gauge or vernier callipers - Assembly lubricant (clean engine oil or light grease) - Gasket set (head gasket + base gasket) - New piston + piston ring set (matched to your engine code) - New cylinder (if bore is worn beyond tolerance) - Piston pin (gudgeon pin) — replace if visibly worn or blued - New piston circlips (always replace — they are single-use) ### Identifying Your Engine Code The engine code is stamped on the left crankcase, above the kickstand mount. Common codes and their standard bore sizes are shown below:
Engine CodeDisplacementStandard BoreStandard Stroke
139QMB50 cc39 mm41.4 mm
152QMI125 cc54 mm54.5 mm
157QMJ150 cc57.4 mm57.8 mm
161QMK150 cc57.4 mm57.8 mm (A-block variant)
Before ordering parts, measure the existing bore diameter with callipers. Cylinders are often available in standard bore and +0.25 mm, +0.50 mm oversizes to accommodate light honing of a worn bore. ## Video Reference 🎬 GY6 Piston Ring Installation — Ring Order and Clocking Piston ring installation, ring order, and clocking for GY6 157QMJ/152QMI engines. ## Step-by-Step Procedure ### Step 1 — Prepare the Engine 1. Park the scooter on its centre stand on a flat surface. 2. Drain the engine oil completely via the drain bolt (allow 10 minutes to drain fully). 3. Turn the fuel tap to **OFF** and disconnect the fuel line from the carburettor. 4. Remove the seat and any body panels needed to access the engine. 5. Disconnect the spark plug lead and remove the spark plug. ### Step 2 — Remove the Cylinder Head 1. Remove the intake manifold and carburettor (or throttle body on EFI variants) from the head. 2. Remove the exhaust pipe at the cylinder head flange — two 12 mm nuts. 3. Remove the valve cover (two or four 8 mm bolts). Take note of the camshaft timing marks. 4. Rotate the crankshaft by hand (kick-starter) until the piston reaches **Top Dead Centre (TDC)** on the compression stroke — both valves closed, timing marks aligned. 5. Loosen the cam sprocket bolt. Slide the timing chain off the sprocket and secure the chain with a wire or zip-tie so it cannot fall into the crankcase. 6. Remove the camshaft and rocker arm assembly. Keep parts in order for reassembly. 7. Undo the four cylinder head nuts in a cross pattern, gradually and evenly. Lift the head straight up. 8. Remove the old head gasket. Note any coolant passages if your engine is liquid-cooled. ### Step 3 — Remove the Cylinder and Piston 1. Remove the two cylinder base nuts (or bolts, depending on variant). 2. Lift the cylinder straight up over the studs. Support the piston with your hand as it exits the bore. 3. Remove the old base gasket and clean the mating surface on the crankcase. 4. Using circlip pliers, remove both piston pin circlips (one on each side). **Do not reuse old circlips.** 5. Tap the piston pin (gudgeon pin) out with a smooth punch. The pin should slide out with light hand pressure — heat the piston crown gently with a heat gun if it is tight. 6. Slide the piston off the connecting rod and set aside. ### Step 4 — Inspect the Old Parts Before ordering replacements, inspect the old piston and cylinder: - **Bore taper:** Measure the cylinder bore at the top and bottom of the piston travel using callipers. A difference of more than 0.05 mm indicates taper — the cylinder should be replaced or honed by a machine shop. - **Piston ring end gap:** Insert each ring into the bore and square it with the piston. Measure the end gap with a feeler gauge. Standard gap is 0.10–0.30 mm; replace rings if gap exceeds 0.5 mm. - **Piston skirt clearance:** Measure the piston diameter 10 mm from the bottom of the skirt (perpendicular to pin). Standard clearance between piston and bore is 0.02–0.05 mm. - **Piston pin play:** Wiggle the pin in the piston boss. Perceptible rocking (more than 0.02 mm clearance) means replace the pin and possibly the connecting rod small-end bearing. � **Tip:** If the cylinder bore shows light scoring (scratches less than 0.1 mm deep), honing with a ball hone and light oil can restore a good surface for rings to seat. Heavy scoring or taper beyond 0.05 mm requires a new cylinder. ### Step 5 — Install the New Piston Rings GY6 pistons use three rings in two grooves: 1. **Top groove:** one compression ring (barrel-face profile, marked "T" or "TOP" — install this mark facing up). 2. **Second groove:** one compression ring (tapered-face, often chrome-edged — marked "2" or "TOP", install mark facing up). 3. **Third (oil) groove:** a three-piece oil ring set — two thin steel rails with a corrugated spacer/expander between them. Install the oil ring set first: fit the spacer/expander into the bottom groove (ends must not overlap — butt them together), then fit one rail above and one rail below the spacer. Install the second compression ring, then the top compression ring. **Clock the ring end gaps:** space the end gaps 120° apart from each other, and ensure no gap is aligned with the piston pin axis or the thrust side of the piston. ️ **Caution:** Piston rings are brittle cast iron. Expand them only just enough to slide over the piston. Over-expanding breaks them. Use a piston ring installer tool if available. ### Step 6 — Install the New Piston 1. Lubricate the small-end bearing, piston pin, and pin bores with clean engine oil. 2. Note the directional arrow or "IN" mark on the piston crown — this must face the intake side (towards the carburettor). 3. Slide the piston onto the connecting rod, align the pin bore, and push the piston pin in by hand. It should slide smoothly with light oil applied. 4. Install both new circlips. Seat them fully in their grooves — check that each circlip is flush and cannot be displaced by a fingernail push. ### Step 7 — Install the New Cylinder 1. Fit the new base gasket over the studs (no sealant required on paper gaskets). 2. Lubricate the cylinder bore lightly with clean engine oil. 3. Compress the piston rings with a ring compressor tool (or carefully squeeze rings by hand, one at a time). 4. Lower the cylinder over the piston, guiding the timing chain through the chain tunnel. 5. Gently tap the cylinder down with the palm of your hand — never force it. If it sticks, a ring has escaped — lift the cylinder and re-compress. 6. Fit the base nuts and tighten to 10 Nm in a cross pattern. ### Step 8 — Reinstall the Cylinder Head 1. Place the new head gasket over the studs. 2. Lower the cylinder head onto the studs. 3. Hand-tighten all four nuts, then torque in a cross pattern to **20–22 Nm** (GY6 139QMB) or **24–26 Nm** (GY6 157QMJ). Always use a torque wrench — over-tightening warps aluminium heads. 4. Reinstall the camshaft, aligning the timing marks. Fit the cam sprocket and timing chain. Tighten the cam sprocket bolt to **12–15 Nm**. 5. Reinstall rocker arms, valve cover, and all ancillaries. 6. Set valve clearances: intake 0.08–0.10 mm, exhaust 0.10–0.12 mm (cold, at TDC compression). ### Step 9 — Run-In Procedure 1. Refill the engine with fresh oil to the correct level (0.8 L for 139QMB, 1.0 L for 157QMJ). 2. Reconnect the spark plug, fuel line, and all electrical connectors. 3. Start the engine and let it idle for 5 minutes. Check for oil leaks at the head and base gasket joints. 4. For the first **500 km** after rebuild: avoid sustained full throttle. Vary engine speed frequently to allow rings to seat evenly against the bore. 5. Change the engine oil after the first 500 km — the oil will contain metallic particles from the ring bedding-in process. 6. After the run-in period, re-check valve clearances and re-torque cylinder head nuts (heads often settle slightly after first heat cycle). ## Torque Reference
FastenerGY6 139QMB (50cc)GY6 157QMJ (150cc)
Cylinder head nuts (M7)20–22 Nm24–26 Nm
Cylinder base nuts (M6)8–10 Nm10–12 Nm
Cam sprocket bolt (M6)12–15 Nm12–15 Nm
Valve cover bolts (M6)8–10 Nm8–10 Nm
Spark plug (M10×1.0)12–15 Nm12–15 Nm
## Compression Specification After rebuild, a healthy GY6 should produce 120–150 psi (8.3–10.3 bar) on a compression gauge. Values below 100 psi (6.9 bar) after a fresh rebuild indicate a ring seating problem or valve leak. Squirt a small amount of engine oil into the spark plug hole and retest — if compression rises significantly, the rings are the problem; if it stays the same, suspect valves.
