import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; Valve clearance (also called valve lash) is the small gap between the rocker arm and the top of the valve stem. Too little clearance causes valves to stay slightly open — leading to burnt valves, overheating, and compression loss. Too much clearance produces a characteristic ticking noise and reduced power. On GY6 engines, the valves are the single most commonly neglected maintenance item. ## Valve Clearance Specifications
EngineIntake ValveExhaust ValveCondition
GY6 50cc (139QMB)0.05 mm (0.00197 in)0.05 mm (0.00197 in)Cold engine
GY6 125cc (152QMI)0.05 mm (0.00197 in)0.05 mm (0.00197 in)Cold engine
GY6 150cc (157QMJ)0.05 mm (0.00197 in)0.05 mm (0.00197 in)Cold engine
Always measure and adjust valve clearance on a **cold engine** (not run for at least 2 hours). Hot metal expands — measuring hot gives an incorrect reading. ️ **Critical:** These are tight tolerances. A feeler gauge of exactly 0.05 mm should pass through with _slight drag_ when the engine is cold. These specifications come from the official Tank GY6 workshop manual and apply across all GY6 variants (139QMB, 152QMI, 157QMJ). ## Tools Required - Feeler gauge set (metric) — must include 0.05 mm blade (essential for GY6) - 10 mm spanner or socket (for valve cover bolts) - 8 mm spanner (for rocker arm lock nuts, on some variants) - Flat-head screwdriver - 17 mm socket (for crankshaft rotation via CVT or flywheel bolt) - Timing mark inspection torch ️ **Do not attempt valve adjustment on a warm engine.** Thermal expansion will cause you to set the clearance incorrectly, which can lead to immediate valve damage when the engine reaches operating temperature. 🎬 Video Guide — Highly Detailed GY6 Valve Adjustment Step By Step **Video:** "Highly Detailed GY6 Valve Adjustment Step By Step" | YouTube   [↗ Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5vl1mrTVCQ0) ## Step-by-Step Procedure 1 Access the Valve Cover 1. Remove the seat and any panels necessary to access the top of the engine cylinder head. On most GY6 scooters the head is under the floor panel or accessible from under the seat. 2. Disconnect the breather hose from the valve cover (small rubber hose, usually routing to the air box). 3. Remove the valve cover bolts — typically two bolts, 10 mm. Remove the cover and set the gasket aside carefully (reuse it if it is not torn or compressed flat). 4. You will see two rocker arms — the **intake rocker** (connected to the intake valve, facing toward the carburetor side) and the **exhaust rocker** (facing toward the exhaust pipe). 2 Find Top Dead Centre (TDC) Valve clearance must be measured when the piston is at Top Dead Centre (TDC) on the compression stroke — the moment when both valves are closed and the cam lobe is pointing away from both rocker arms. 1. Locate the inspection window on the left side of the engine casing (round rubber or metal plug). Remove it to see the flywheel timing marks. 2. Also remove the small plug on the top of the cylinder head — this is the manual decompressor or TDC inspection port on some models. 3. Rotate the engine slowly by hand using the rear wheel (in gear) or by turning the flywheel bolt clockwise (when viewed from the flywheel side). Do not use the electric starter for this. 4. Watch the timing mark through the inspection window. When the line marked **"T"** (or "上" on some Chinese engines) aligns with the pointer, the piston is at TDC. 5. Confirm you are on the **compression stroke** (not the exhaust stroke, which also puts the piston at TDC): at compression TDC, both rocker arms should be loose — you should be able to wiggle them slightly by hand. If one rocker is pressing down on a valve, rotate the engine one full turn and realign the T mark. 3 Measure Valve Clearance 1. Slide the 0.05 mm feeler gauge blade between the rocker arm and the top of the valve stem (or the cam follower surface, depending on configuration). 2. The gauge should slide through with light, uniform drag — not tight, not loose. If it slides freely with no resistance, the clearance is too large. If it does not fit at all, the clearance is too small. 3. Repeat for both intake and exhaust rockers. 4. Record the current clearance: too tight (gauge does not fit), correct (slight drag), or too loose (gauge falls through). 4 Adjust if Required 1. Locate the adjustment screw on the rocker arm — it is a slotted screw with a lock nut. 2. Hold the adjustment screw with a flat-head screwdriver to prevent it rotating, and loosen the lock nut with an 8 mm spanner (counter-clockwise). 3. With the feeler gauge in place, turn the adjustment screw: - Clockwise → decreases gap (tightens clearance) - Counter-clockwise → increases gap (widens clearance) 4. Adjust until the feeler gauge moves with a slight, consistent drag. 5. Hold the adjustment screw firmly in position and tighten the lock nut. The act of tightening the lock nut often rotates the adjustment screw slightly — recheck clearance after the nut is tight. 6. Repeat for the other valve. 7. Recheck both valves one final time after all lock nuts are tightened. � **Tip:** If your engine has been difficult to start, runs roughly at idle, or you hear a persistent ticking from the cylinder head area, check valves before replacing the spark plug or cleaning the carburetor. Tight valves are frequently misdiagnosed as carburetor problems. 5 Reassemble 1. Clean the valve cover mating surface on the cylinder head with a clean rag. 2. Refit the valve cover gasket. If the gasket is compressed or cracked, replace it — a leaking valve cover allows oil to contaminate the air filter via the breather. 3. Refit the valve cover and tighten the two bolts to approximately **10 Nm**. Do not overtighten — the cylinder head is aluminium and strips easily. 4. Reconnect the breather hose. 5. Reinstall the timing inspection plug and any engine covers removed. 6. Start the engine. A slight increase in idle smoothness and a reduction in valve noise confirm a successful adjustment. ## Symptoms of Incorrect Valve Clearance
SymptomLikely Cause
Ticking/clattering from engine top at idleValve clearance too large (excessive lash)
Hard starting, especially when coldValve clearance too small (insufficient lash — valves may not seat fully)
Loss of compression / low powerIntake or exhaust valve stuck open from zero clearance
Engine backfires on decelerationExhaust valve not seating fully — check exhaust valve clearance
Oil in air filter / blue smokeValve cover gasket leaking (secondary issue from valve access)
� **Piaggio ZIP 50/100 4T valve clearances** — from the official Piaggio MSS ZIP 100 4T Service Station Manual: **Intake:** 0.10 mm  |  **Exhaust:** 0.15 mm  |  Check cold engine only  |  Lock nut torque: **7–9 Nm** Note: the Piaggio ZIP 100 4T uses **different** valve clearances from GY6 engines — the ZIP intake is twice the GY6 spec, and the exhaust is three times wider. Do not cross-apply these figures. The procedure is the same (cold engine, piston at TDC on compression stroke), but always use the specification for your specific engine. Check at every 6,000 km service on the ZIP. See the [Piaggio ZIP 100 Technical Overview](/models/piaggio-zip-100-technical-overview.html) for full specification table. ## Related Videos #### QMB139 & GY6 Valve Adjustment — The Easy Way Clear demonstration of finding TDC and setting valve clearance on both 50cc (139QMB) and 125/150cc (157QMJ) engines with a feeler gauge. import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; Added: 2026-05-08  |  Updated: 2026-05-08  |  Sources: [wemoto.com](https://www.wemoto.com/info/guide-to-scooter-clutches-variators-and-rollers), [louis-moto.com](https://www.louis-moto.com/en-ww/magazin/rund-ums-bike/schraubertipps/variomatik-und-kupplung) GY6 Piaggio Vespa CVT The continuously variable transmission (CVT) is the automatic gearbox found on virtually all modern petrol scooters — both GY6-platform Chinese machines and Piaggio/Vespa models. It consists of two pulleys connected by a rubber drive belt, with the engine-side pulley (the variator) automatically adjusting its effective diameter based on engine speed. The result is a smooth, stepless gear ratio change without the rider needing to do anything. CVT components wear gradually and silently. Many riders only notice problems when performance has already significantly degraded. Routine inspection every 6,000–10,000 km will prevent most CVT-related failures. ## Video Guide **Video:** GY6 150cc CVT Variator Rollers Swap, Belt, and Clutch Inspection [↗ Watch on YouTube](https://youtube.com/watch?v=v22AaQeuiH8) **Difficulty:** Intermediate  |  **Time Required:** 1.5–2 hours  |  **Cost:** $40–$120 (parts only) ️ **Safety Warning:** The variator can spin freely when disassembled. Always wear eye protection when working with springs and roller weights, as they can fly out under tension. Do not lose the small roller weights—they're easily misplaced and difficult to source individually. ## Tools Required - Socket set (metric: 8mm, 10mm, 12mm, 14mm) - Combination wrench set (metric) - Torque wrench (0–60 Nm range) - Strap wrench or flywheel holder tool (to prevent variator spin) - Screwdriver set (Phillips and flathead) - Gasket scraper (plastic preferred to avoid gouging) - High-temperature grease (bearing or molybdenum disulfide grease) - Shop rags or clean cloth - Oil drain pan - Vernier caliper (for measuring clutch shoe lining thickness) ## Parts & Materials

� **Pro Tip:** Roller weights are often sold by weight (grams), not as a standard set. Stock weights suit most riders; lighter weights (5–8g) improve acceleration but increase engine wear; heavier weights (11–15g) improve fuel economy and reduce peak revs. Always replace all six rollers together—mixing weights causes vibration and reduces CVT lifespan. ## How the GY6 / Piaggio CVT Works At low engine speed (idle, pulling away), the variator ramps push the rollers inward — the front pulley is narrow, the belt runs low, giving a low gear ratio for easy acceleration. As engine speed rises, centrifugal force pushes the roller weights outward along the ramps, widening the front pulley and raising the gear ratio until the belt is running at the top of the pulley — effectively "top gear". The rear clutch pulley (torque server / driven pulley) has a spring that provides resistance, ensuring the belt shifts smoothly between ratios. ### Interactive Diagram — Drag the slider to see how ratio changes with RPM Engine RPM 1 500 rpm LOW GEAR Rollers inward · Belt rides low on drive pulley ## Key CVT Components - **Variator (front pulley assembly):** Two-piece aluminium pulley with internal roller weights and ramps - **Roller weights:** Small cylindrical or barrel-shaped weights (typically 6 per variator); they move the movable pulley face as engine speed changes - **Drive belt:** Reinforced rubber V-belt; transfers power between front and rear pulley - **Rear clutch / torque server / driven pulley:** Spring-loaded; also contains the centrifugal clutch shoes that engage the rear wheel above a set engine speed - **Clutch bell (driven housing):** The outer drum that the clutch shoes press against to drive the final-reduction gears ## Symptoms of CVT Wear
SymptomLikely ComponentSeverity
Jerky, notchy acceleration (no longer smooth)Flat-spotted roller weightsMedium — replace soon
Reduced top speed; engine over-revving at speedWorn belt (too narrow) or worn rollersHigh — replace belt promptly
Scooter creeps forward at idle / won't disengageClutch spring weakened; sticky clutch shoesMedium — inspect clutch
Scooter does not pull away until high revsClutch shoes worn below minimum thicknessHigh — replace clutch shoes
Rattling or knocking from transmission cover at low speedWorn rollers or loose variator nutHigh — inspect immediately
Belt squealingBelt contaminated with oil (chain case seal leak) or glazed belt surfaceHigh — replace belt; find oil leak source
Vibration through floorboards at all speedsBelt worn unevenly; variator face damagedMedium
## Roller Weight Specifications Roller weights are sold by diameter, length, and mass in grams. Using the correct weight is important: heavier rollers shift up earlier (better fuel economy, lower peak revs at speed); lighter rollers shift up later (more low-down acceleration, higher revving). Stock weights should be used for commuting; lighter weights suit performance builds.

️ **Critical correction:** GY6 50cc (139QMB) uses **16×13mm** rollers, NOT 15×12mm. GY6 125cc (152QMI) uses **18×14mm**, NOT 16×13mm. Incorrect roller sizes will cause CVT failure and reduced performance. Always verify against your engine's workshop manual. ️ **Replace rollers as a complete set of six.** If even one roller has a flat spot, the whole set is unbalanced. Mixing old and new rollers will not restore smooth operation. ## Roller Replacement Procedure (GY6 Platform) 1. Remove the transmission cover (variator cover) — usually 4–6 bolts on the left side of the engine. Note the gasket or O-ring seal. 2. To prevent the variator from spinning when loosening the centre nut, insert a strap wrench around the variator face, or use a flywheel holder tool. _Do not jam the belt — this can damage it._ 3. Remove the variator centre nut (typically M14 × 1.25, right-hand thread). On most GY6 engines this is torqued to 40–50 Nm. 4. Slide the outer variator face off the shaft, then lift the belt off the front pulley (it will remain on the rear clutch). 5. Remove the inner variator face (it may slide or require gentle persuasion). The six roller weights will be visible in the ramp housing. Tip them out. 6. Inspect ramps for grooves. Light polishing marks are acceptable; deep ridges require variator replacement. 7. Install six new rollers of the correct weight. Grease the ramp surfaces lightly with high-temperature grease. 8. Reassemble in reverse order. Torque the variator nut to spec (40–50 Nm GY6; consult your service manual for Piaggio). 9. Refit the cover with a new gasket if the old one is damaged. ## Clutch Shoe Inspection Clutch shoes are the friction material pads on the rear clutch spider that press against the clutch bell drum. They wear thin over time and must be replaced when the lining thickness falls below approximately 2 mm (check your service manual for the exact limit). Worn shoes cause late clutch engagement (needing higher revs to pull away) and eventually slipping under load. To inspect: with the rear clutch assembly removed, measure lining thickness with a vernier calliper. Also check the inside of the clutch bell for scoring. Lightly scored bells can be polished with fine emery cloth; deeply grooved bells must be replaced. ## Related Videos & Resources ![GY6 Variator and Roller Replacement](https://img.youtube.com/vi/SQ5GmXbJKQs/mqdefault.jpg) #### GY6 Variator/Roller Replacement & Tips Step-by-step walkthrough of variator disassembly, roller swap, and reassembly on GY6 models [Watch →](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SQ5GmXbJKQs) ![Vespa Primavera Roller Change and Variator Cleaning](https://img.youtube.com/vi/v1KLE1uY7YQ/mqdefault.jpg) #### Vespa Primavera Roller Change & Variator Cleaning Roller replacement and variator cleaning procedure specific to the Vespa Primavera [Watch →](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=v1KLE1uY7YQ) ![Centrifugal Clutch Explained](https://img.youtube.com/vi/D9d4qXreb8Q/mqdefault.jpg) #### Centrifugal Clutch — Explained How centrifugal clutches work — the mechanical principles behind scooter CVT engagement [Watch →](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D9d4qXreb8Q) � **Related ISMR Guides:** [GY6 CVT Variator and Drive Belt Replacement](gy6-cvt-variator-belt-replacement.html) | [GY6 Spark Plug Replacement](gy6-spark-plug-guide.html) | [GY6 Oil Change Guide](gy6-oil-change-guide.html)

import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; import SourceBox from '@components/SourceBox.astro'; Piaggio Vespas — including the Primavera 50/125/150, the Sprint, the Zip 50/100 4T, and the GTS range — are well-engineered machines with a reputation for long service lives when properly maintained. While some tasks genuinely require a dealer's diagnostic tools (particularly on fuel-injected models with EOBD systems), a substantial portion of routine maintenance is well within reach of a careful owner with basic tools. This guide focuses on tasks that can be performed at home to extend service intervals, reduce dealer bills, and keep the scooter running reliably. ## Tools You Will Need Before starting any work, assemble a basic toolkit for Vespa maintenance: - Socket set (metric): 8, 10, 12, 14, 17, 19 mm - Combination spanners (matching the above) - Torque wrench (5–50 Nm range) - Screwdrivers: JIS/Phillips No. 2 and No. 3, flat-blade assortment - Feeler gauges (for valve clearance on carbureted models) - Oil drain pan (2 litre capacity minimum) - Funnel and measuring jug - Brake bleeder kit (for hydraulic brake maintenance) - Tyre pressure gauge - Multimeter (for electrical diagnostics) **💡 JIS vs Phillips:** Japanese-standard JIS screws are common on Piaggio fasteners. They look similar to Phillips but have a different tip angle — using a Phillips driver risks rounding the head. JIS screwdrivers are inexpensive and well worth buying before starting any disassembly. ## Task 1: Oil Change Engine oil is the single most important consumable for Vespa longevity. Piaggio specifies oil changes every 3 000 km or annually — many owners do it more frequently (every 1 500–2 000 km) for peace of mind. The procedure is identical across most modern Vespas. ### Procedure 1. Run the engine for 5 minutes to warm the oil — warm oil drains more completely and carries more suspended particles with it. 2. Place a drain pan under the engine. 3. Remove the oil drain bolt (usually 17 mm on the underside of the engine). Allow the oil to drain fully — typically 5–10 minutes. 4. Replace the drain bolt with a new sealing washer. Torque to 18–22 Nm. 5. Remove the oil filler cap/dipstick. Fill with the specified quantity of approved oil. 6. Refit the cap. Start the engine and allow it to idle for 60 seconds. Shut off and wait 2 minutes. Check the level on the dipstick — it should sit between the MIN and MAX marks.

Vespa GTS 125 / 150 / 300Piaggio recommends Agip/Eni Scooter 4T Ultra Tech (5W-40 full synthetic)~1.0–1.2 litres
Piaggio Zip 50 4T / Zip 100 4TSAE 5W-40 or 10W-40 (JASO MB)~0.75 litres
## Task 2: Air Filter Inspection and Cleaning The air filter on Vespa Primavera, Sprint, and Zip models is housed in a plastic box under the right-side body panel or under the seat. It should be inspected every 3 000 km and replaced at 6 000 km intervals, or more frequently in dusty conditions. ### Procedure 1. Remove the right-side body panel (Primavera: two or three screws/clips beneath the panel) or the underseat access panel (Zip models). 2. Locate the air filter housing. Undo the clips or screws securing the lid. 3. Remove the filter element. 4. On foam elements: wash in warm soapy water, rinse thoroughly, allow to dry completely (never ride with a wet filter), then apply a thin coat of filter oil before refitting. 5. On paper elements: hold up to a light source. If it is grey or black, replace it. Tapping out loose dust is acceptable as a temporary measure, but a dirty paper element should be replaced at the earliest opportunity. 6. Wipe out the inside of the filter housing with a clean cloth. 7. Reassemble in reverse order. ## Task 3: Spark Plug Check and Replacement Inspecting the spark plug takes less than 15 minutes and reveals a great deal about engine health. Replace the plug every 5 000–8 000 km or whenever the electrode shows wear. ### Reading the Plug - **Light tan or grey:** Correct mixture — engine is running well - **Black and sooty:** Rich mixture (too much fuel) or oil burning - **White or blistered:** Lean mixture (too little fuel) — investigate immediately; risks piston damage - **Oily black:** Oil entering combustion chamber — worn rings or valve seals ### Common Vespa Plug References
ModelStandard PlugGap
Vespa Zip 50 4T / Primavera 50NGK CR7HSA0.7–0.8 mm
Vespa Primavera 125 / Sprint 125 (carb)NGK CR7EB or NGK CR7HSA0.7–0.9 mm
Vespa Primavera 125 i-get (injection)NGK CR7EIB-10 (iridium)Factory set — do not adjust
## Task 4: Tyre Pressure and Condition Tyres are the most safety-critical component on any scooter. Check pressures at least weekly — Vespa tubeless tyres lose pressure gradually even without punctures. Always check when cold (the scooter has not been ridden for at least 2 hours).
ModelFront (bar)Rear (bar)Two-Up Rear (bar)
Vespa Primavera 50 / 1251.5 bar (22 psi)2.0 bar (29 psi)2.25 bar (33 psi)
Vespa Zip 50 / 100 4T1.75 bar (25 psi)2.25 bar (33 psi)2.5 bar (36 psi)
Piaggio Zip 50 / 1001.75 bar (25 psi)2.25 bar (33 psi)2.5 bar (36 psi)
Inspect tyre sidewalls for cracks, bulges, or embedded debris. Replace any tyre showing sidewall cracking — this indicates age degradation of the rubber compound, regardless of remaining tread depth. ## Task 5: Brake Inspection Modern Vespas use hydraulic disc brakes front and rear on most models, with drum rear brakes on the Zip 50. Check brake operation and pad condition every 5 000 km. ### Disc Brake Pads 1. Locate the caliper (front: behind the front wheel; rear: on the swing arm). 2. Look through the caliper inspection slot or remove the wheel for a clear view of pad thickness. 3. If the friction material is at or below 2 mm, replace the pads as a complete axle set (both front pads together; both rear if dual-disc). 4. Check the disc rotor for deep grooves or scoring. A lipped rotor edge indicates significant wear. ### Brake Fluid Check the front brake reservoir (on the handlebars) and rear reservoir (under the floorboard on most models) monthly. The fluid level should be between the MIN and MAX marks. If the level is low without obvious cause, suspect pad wear (pads wear down and fluid fills the caliper gap) or a leak. Flush and replace brake fluid with fresh DOT 4 every two years. **⚠️ Never Mix DOT 4 and DOT 5:** DOT 5 is silicone-based and incompatible with DOT 4 systems. Most Piaggio/Vespa hydraulic systems use DOT 4. Using the wrong fluid will cause seal degradation and brake failure. ## Task 6: Drive Belt Inspection The CVT drive belt is a wear item with significant safety implications — a snapped belt at speed can cause sudden loss of drive and instability. Inspect the belt every 3 000 km; replace at 6 000–8 000 km or immediately if any cracking, fraying, or missing teeth are visible. ### Procedure (Primavera / Zip) 1. Remove the left-side CVT cover (on the Zip: three or four bolts; on the Primavera: requires removing additional body panels first). 2. Inspect the belt visually: run your fingers along the full length of both edges and the inner surface. 3. Replace if any cracking, exposed cords, or glazing (hard shiny surface) is present. 4. Note the belt specification printed on the old belt — match it exactly when ordering a replacement. ## Task 7: Carburettor Idle & Mixture (Carbureted Models Only) Applies to **carbureted Vespa Primavera 125/150 3V** (pre-2018, before the i-get injection engine). If your dashboard has a fuel injection warning light, skip this section. These models use a **Dell'Orto PHBN or VHST carburettor**. Two adjustments are accessible without removing the carburettor: - **Idle speed screw** (large, spring-loaded, on the carburettor body) — turning clockwise raises idle; target **1,700–1,900 rpm** when fully warm. - **Pilot/mixture screw** (small, recessed, near the float bowl) — baseline is **1.5–2.5 turns out** from gently seated. Turn out in ¼-turn steps until idle peaks, then back in ¼ turn. Always set with engine fully warm. ### Dell'Orto Jet Specifications
ModelCarburettorMain JetPilot JetNeedle Clip
Primavera 125 3V (carb)Dell'Orto PHBN#92#35Position 3 of 5
Primavera 150 3V (carb)Dell'Orto VHST#96#38Position 3 of 5
Always confirm jet size against the number stamped on the existing jet — sizes vary by batch. Never probe a jet with wire; use carburettor cleaner and compressed air only. ## When to See a Dealer Some tasks are beyond practical DIY scope on modern Vespas with fuel injection: - **Fault code reading and clearing (FI models):** Requires a compatible OBD diagnostic tool (Piaggio-specific or generic OBD2 with the correct protocol) - **Valve clearance adjustment (Primavera 125/150 i-get):** Requires camshaft access and precise tools; the i-get engine is compact and tight to work in - **Throttle body synchronisation (multi-throttle body models):** Requires vacuum gauges and specialised knowledge - **Warranty-relevant work:** If the scooter is under warranty, have authorised service centres perform work to avoid invalidating coverage

## Introduction

All modern Vespa and Piaggio scooters — the GTS 250/300, Primavera 125/150, Sprint 125/150, and Zip 4T — use liquid-cooled engines. The cooling system circulates a water–antifreeze mixture through the engine block, radiator, water pump, and hoses to keep temperatures stable under all load conditions. Unlike air-cooled classics, liquid-cooled Vespas require periodic coolant changes to maintain corrosion protection and heat-transfer efficiency.

This guide covers the complete coolant maintenance routine: level checks, visual hose inspection, coolant flush and refill, and bleeding the system.

<Callout type="warn">
  Always work on a cold engine. Opening the radiator cap on a hot engine releases scalding pressurised steam and fluid. Allow the engine to cool for at least 30 minutes before starting any coolant work.
</Callout>

## Which Models Use Liquid Cooling?

All Vespa models from the GTS/GT generation onward (2005–present) are water-cooled. The Primavera and Sprint families (2013–present) are also fully liquid-cooled. The older LX/S 50 and 125 two-valve models vary — the 50 4T versions are air-cooled, while larger-displacement 125–150 cc 3V (three-valve) units are liquid-cooled. The Piaggio Zip 50 4T is air-cooled; the Zip 100 4T is water-cooled.

## Tools & Parts Needed

- T25 Torx screwdriver (radiator cap cover screw on most models)
- Phillips screwdriver (body panel screws)
- Drain container of at least 1 litre capacity
- Funnel for refilling
- 30 cm of clear hose (for bleed procedure)
- Distilled water — never use tap water
- Approved coolant/antifreeze: Piaggio recommends a 50:50 pre-mixed OAT (Organic Acid Technology) coolant, equivalent to ASTM D3306. Motul Mocool or SIP Scootershop own-brand coolant are widely used by Vespa owners.

## Maintenance Schedule

| Service | Interval |
|---------|----------|
| Coolant level check | Every 1,000 km or monthly |
| Visual hose inspection | Every service or 3,000 km |
| Full coolant flush & replacement | Every 2 years or 10,000 km |
| Thermostat check | Every 4 years or 20,000 km |

## Step 1 — Check the Coolant Level (Quick Check)

On Vespa GTS, Primavera, and Sprint models, the coolant expansion tank is accessible without removing any body panels. Open the front storage compartment and locate the translucent expansion tank on the right side of the engine bay. The fluid level should sit between the MIN and MAX marks on the tank.

If the level is below MIN, top up carefully with a 50:50 distilled-water/antifreeze mixture. Do not overfill above MAX — excess fluid will be expelled when hot and can damage surrounding components.

<Callout type="tip">
  If you need to top up frequently (more than once per season), the system has a slow leak. Inspect hoses and the water pump seal. Low coolant combined with an overheating warning indicates a more serious issue — stop the engine and allow it to cool before continuing.
</Callout>

## Step 2 — Visual Hose Inspection

Each time you wash or service your scooter, take 60 seconds to inspect the coolant hoses. Run your fingers along each hose, feeling for:

- **Softness or sponginess** — indicates internal corrosion of the rubber
- **Surface cracking** — a sign of age and impending failure
- **Swelling at clamp points** — the clamp may be over-tightened or the hose already failing
- **Staining or dried residue** — coolant leaves a white or green chalky residue at the site of a small leak

Replace any hose that shows cracking or softness. Use only OEM or high-quality silicone replacement hoses suitable for 50:50 antifreeze mixtures.

## Step 3 — Full Coolant Flush and Refill

This procedure applies to the Vespa GTS 300, Primavera 125/150, Sprint 125/150, and Piaggio Zip 100 4T. Steps for other models are similar; consult your owner's manual for panel removal specifics.

### Step 3.1 — Prepare the Scooter

Place the scooter on the centre stand on a level surface. Allow the engine to cool completely — at least 30 minutes after the last ride.

### Step 3.2 — Access the Radiator Cap

On the Vespa GTS 300, remove the small plastic cover on the radiator cap using a T25 Torx screw. On Primavera and Sprint, open the front storage compartment — the expansion tank cap is accessible directly.

### Step 3.3 — Drain the Old Coolant

Locate the water pump casing on the right side of the engine (left side from the rider's perspective, near the exhaust). Unscrew the two or three Phillips screws securing the pump casing drain plug/cover. Position your drain container below the pump and allow the fluid to drain fully — this typically takes 5–10 minutes.

Once drained, retighten the pump casing screws. Torque to approximately 4–5 N·m (do not over-tighten plastic or aluminium pump casings).

<Callout type="warn">
  Coolant is toxic to animals and has a sweet smell that can attract pets. Dispose of old coolant at a recycling centre or automotive waste collection point — never pour it down a drain.
</Callout>

### Step 3.4 — Refill with Fresh Coolant

Using a funnel, pour the fresh 50:50 coolant mixture into the radiator/expansion tank slowly. Fill until the fluid reaches the MAX mark. Do not cap it yet — you need to bleed the system in the next step.

### Step 3.5 — Bleed the Air from the System

Air pockets trapped in the cooling system cause localised overheating and prevent accurate temperature readings. To bleed the system:

1. Locate the bleed valve on the thermostat housing (on the GTS 300, this is near the top of the radiator on the left side).
2. Connect a 30 cm length of clear hose to the bleed nipple and place the other end into the expansion tank opening.
3. Start the engine and let it idle. Watch the clear hose — bubbles will rise into the expansion tank as air purges.
4. Continue idling until no more bubbles appear — typically 3–5 minutes.
5. Top up the expansion tank to MAX if the level has dropped during bleeding.
6. Stop the engine, cap the expansion tank firmly, and replace any covers.

## Step 4 — Post-Service Check

Start the engine and allow it to reach operating temperature (the fan should cycle at least once on liquid-cooled models). Watch the temperature gauge — it should stabilise in the normal range. Check around the water pump area for drips or weeping coolant. Recheck the expansion tank level once the engine is cold again.

## Coolant Specification Summary

| Parameter | Specification |
|-----------|---------------|
| Type | OAT (Organic Acid Technology) antifreeze |
| Mix ratio | 50% antifreeze / 50% distilled water |
| System capacity (GTS 300) | ~1.0 litre |
| System capacity (Primavera/Sprint) | ~0.7 litre |
| Freeze protection | −35 °C at 50:50 ratio |
| Replacement interval | Every 2 years or 10,000 km |
| Water pump screw torque | 4–5 N·m |
| Thermostat cover torque | 3–4 N·m |

## Common Coolant System Issues

**Overheating despite correct coolant level** — usually indicates a failing water pump impeller, blocked radiator fins (inspect and clean with compressed air), or a faulty thermostat stuck in the closed position.

**Coolant in the oil (milky oil)** — indicates a blown head gasket or cracked cylinder head. This requires engine disassembly and professional repair. Stop riding immediately if milky oil is detected.

**Low coolant with no visible external leak** — the system may be consuming coolant internally through the combustion chamber. A cylinder compression test and combustion gas analysis can confirm this.

**Fan running constantly** — normal on hot days at low speed or in traffic, but if the fan runs even when ambient temperatures are cool, suspect a faulty coolant temperature sensor or thermostat.

import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; import SourceBox from '@components/SourceBox.astro'; 📹 Dent Repair and Paint on a Vespa Primavera The Vespa Primavera's steel monocoque body is one of its defining characteristics — unlike plastic-bodied scooters, the steel shell can be repaired with conventional metalworking and automotive paint techniques. This guide covers dent removal, body filler application, and colour-matched repainting for minor to moderate body damage on the Vespa Primavera 125 and 150. ## Why Steel Body Repair is Viable on the Primavera Modern Piaggio Vespa models — including the Primavera, Sprint, and GTS — use a pressed steel body shell that is primed and painted at the factory. Small dents (up to approximately 50 mm across) can often be repaired without panel replacement. Larger dents may require professional panel beating but can still be filled and repainted by a competent DIY operator. Unlike plastic bodywork, steel does not require flexible filler and responds well to heat and mechanical persuasion during dent removal. ## Assessing the Damage Before starting, assess the dent carefully to choose the correct approach:
Damage TypeRecommended Approach
Small shallow dent, no crease, paint intactPDR (paintless dent repair) or gentle panel pushing from inside
Dent with creased metal or paint crackingBody filler, primer, colour coat, clear coat
Dent through to bare metal, rust startingRust treatment first, then body filler and repaint
Panel deformed beyond ~100 mm or structurally affectedPanel replacement (workshop or specialist)
## Materials Required - Automotive body filler (polyester-based, e.g. Bondo or equivalent) - Hardener (included with most body filler kits) - Spreader / applicator blades - Sandpaper: 80, 120, 180, 240, 400, 800, 1200 grit - Sanding block - Automotive primer (aerosol or spraygun) - Colour-matched aerosol paint (matched to your Vespa's paint code) - Clear coat aerosol - Masking tape and masking paper/plastic sheet - Tack cloth (for dust removal before painting) - Rust converter or phosphoric acid primer (if bare metal is exposed) ## Finding Your Vespa's Paint Code The Vespa Primavera's paint code is found on a sticker on the frame, typically under the seat in the storage compartment or on the frame rail near the front fork. Common Primavera colour codes include: - `A67` — Bianco Innocenza (White) - `A68` — Rosso Dragon (Red) - `A51` — Azzurro Boreale (Blue) - `A55` — Verde Relax (Green) - `A56` — Nero (Black) - `A53` — Grigio Titanio (Grey) With the paint code, colour-matched aerosol paint can be ordered from Vespa dealers, automotive paint suppliers, or online paint-matching services. Providing the full frame number (VIN) ensures accuracy, as colour shades can vary between production years. ## Dent Repair and Repainting Procedure 1. **Clean the damaged area:** Wash thoroughly with panel wipe or isopropyl alcohol to remove wax, grease, and road contamination. 2. **Access from the inside (if possible):** Many Vespa body panels can be accessed from the inside by removing interior trim. Use a body hammer or spoon tool to gently push the dent outward. Work from the outside edges of the dent inward. 3. **Prepare the surface:** Sand the damaged area with 80-grit sandpaper to remove paint and provide a key for filler. Feather the sanding 50–75 mm beyond the dent perimeter. 4. **Treat bare metal:** If the paint has been sanded to bare steel, apply rust converter or a phosphoric acid etching primer before filler application. 5. **Mix and apply body filler:** Mix body filler with hardener per manufacturer ratio (typically a small amount of hardener per golf-ball sized portion of filler). Apply with a spreader in smooth, slightly overlapping strokes. Overfill slightly — the filler will be sanded back. 6. **Rough sand:** Once the filler has cured (typically 20–30 minutes at 20°C), sand with 80-grit to remove high spots. Work toward a flat, contoured surface matching the surrounding panel shape. 7. **Progressive sanding:** Work through 120, 180, then 240-grit. At 240-grit the surface should feel smooth to the touch with no scratches visible under raking light. 8. **Apply primer:** Mask surrounding areas. Apply two or three thin coats of automotive primer, allowing each coat to flash off. Sand lightly with 400-grit between coats. 9. **Final primer sand:** Wet-sand the primed surface with 800-grit, then 1200-grit. The surface should appear uniformly matt-grey. 10. **Apply colour coat:** Remove masking, re-clean with tack cloth. Apply colour coat in light passes — 3–4 coats for full coverage, allowing each to flash off (typically 5–10 minutes). 11. **Apply clear coat:** After the colour coat has dried for at least 30 minutes, apply 2–3 coats of clear coat. The clear coat provides UV protection and gloss depth. 12. **Polish (optional):** After full cure (24–48 hours), wet-sand any orange peel with 2000-grit and machine or hand polish to blend the new paint into the surrounding original finish. � **Tip — Temperature matters:** Do not apply body filler or paint below 15°C or above 30°C. Cold temperatures slow curing; excessive heat causes the filler or paint to bubble or cure unevenly. Ideal working conditions are 18–24°C with low humidity. ## Panel Replacement Alternative If the damage is too extensive for repair, front body panels, legshields, and tail sections for the Vespa Primavera are available as genuine Piaggio parts or from independent suppliers such as SIP Scootershop or Scooter Center. Replacement panels arrive primed but unpainted — they require the same painting procedure described above, minus the body filler steps. Colour-matched panels can also be ordered from some Vespa dealers at higher cost.

## Introduction

The battery on a Vespa Primavera and Sprint sits under the seat, directly accessible without tools once the seat is released. Replacement takes around 15 minutes and requires no specialist equipment. This guide applies to all petrol Primavera and Sprint variants produced from 2013 onwards — both 50 cc (carburetor) and 125/150 cc (i-get fuel-injected) engines share the same battery compartment layout and battery type.

A healthy battery is critical on modern Vespas. The fuel injection system, electric starter, instrument panel, and immobiliser all depend on stable 12 V supply. A weak or failing battery commonly presents as intermittent no-start, an instrument panel that resets, or an engine that cranks sluggishly in cold weather.

<Callout type="warn">
  Always disconnect the **negative (–) terminal first** when removing the battery, and reconnect it **last** when fitting the new one. Reversing this order while the key is off risks short-circuiting the electrical system.
</Callout>

## Battery Specification

| Parameter | Value |
|-----------|-------|
| Type | 12V Sealed AGM lead-acid |
| Part number | YTX7L-BS |
| Voltage | 12 V |
| Capacity | 6 Ah |
| Cold Cranking Amps | 100 A |
| Terminal polarity | Positive (+) on left side (viewed from front of battery) |
| Compatible OEM ref | Piaggio 584662 / 1D001965 |

Acceptable replacement brands include Yuasa, Piaggio branded PTX7L-BS (OEM), Prima (Scooterworks), and equivalent sealed AGM units. Lithium LiFePO4 drop-in replacements (e.g., PowerTex YTX7L-BS LiFePO4) are also compatible if the charging system is healthy.

<Callout type="tip">
  Buy a sealed, **pre-activated** (maintenance-free) AGM battery whenever possible. These arrive ready to install and do not require acid activation. If you purchase a dry-charged unit, follow the acid-filling instructions before installation.
</Callout>

## Tools & Parts Needed

- Replacement battery: YTX7L-BS (12 V / 6 Ah sealed AGM)
- Phillips screwdriver (for seat release if applicable to your year)
- 8 mm spanner or socket and ratchet
- Clean cloth or latex gloves (battery acid protection, even on sealed units)

## Step-by-Step Procedure

### Step 1 — Open the Seat

Insert the Vespa key and turn it to the seat-release position (or press the remote release button on models so equipped). Lift the seat fully open. The battery is located on the left side of the under-seat compartment, forward of the fuel filler cap.

### Step 2 — Remove the Battery Cover

On most Primavera and Sprint models a small plastic cover or foam pad sits over the battery. Pull it straight up or unclip it — no screws are required on the majority of variants from 2013 onwards.

### Step 3 — Disconnect the Negative Terminal First

Using an 8 mm spanner, loosen the nut on the **black (–) negative lead** and slide the terminal off the battery post. Tuck the lead to one side so it cannot accidentally touch the positive post during the next step.

### Step 4 — Disconnect the Positive Terminal

Loosen the nut on the **red (+) positive lead** and remove it from the battery post. On some models a rubber boot covers the positive terminal — pull this back before loosening the nut.

### Step 5 — Remove the Battery

Lift the battery straight up and out of its tray. Vespa batteries on Primavera/Sprint models are not strapped down — they sit in a moulded plastic tray and are held in place by the cover. The battery weighs approximately 2 kg.

<Callout type="warn">
  Even sealed AGM batteries contain sulphuric acid. Do not tip the battery on its side. Dispose of the old battery at an approved recycling point — most auto parts shops accept used batteries free of charge.
</Callout>

### Step 6 — Inspect the Battery Tray

Before fitting the new battery, wipe out any dust or moisture from the tray. Check the terminal leads for corrosion (white or blue-green powder). If corrosion is present, clean the terminals with a small wire brush and a solution of bicarbonate of soda and water, then rinse and dry thoroughly.

### Step 7 — Install the New Battery

Lower the new battery into the tray with the **positive (+) terminal facing the same direction as the original**. On the Primavera/Sprint, the positive post faces toward the front of the scooter.

### Step 8 — Reconnect Positive Terminal First

Slide the red (+) lead onto the positive post and tighten the 8 mm nut firmly — snug but not over-torqued (do not strip the lead nut). Replace the rubber boot if present.

### Step 9 — Reconnect the Negative Terminal

Slide the black (–) lead onto the negative post and tighten the nut.

### Step 10 — Replace the Cover and Close the Seat

Refit the plastic battery cover or foam pad. Close the seat and confirm it latches correctly.

### Step 11 — Start the Scooter and Verify

Turn the key to the ON position. The instrument panel should illuminate normally. Start the engine and confirm normal idle. On i-get (injected) models the panel may perform a self-check sequence — this is normal after a battery disconnection.

## Post-Replacement Notes

After fitting a new battery on an injected Primavera or Sprint, the throttle body idle may need a short adaptation run. Ride the scooter for 10–15 minutes with a mix of idle, low-speed, and highway speeds to allow the ECU to re-learn the idle baseline.

If the scooter is stored for more than 3–4 weeks at a time, connect a 12 V smart trickle charger (0.8–1.5 A) to maintain battery charge. Allowing an AGM battery to fully discharge more than a few times will permanently reduce its capacity and lifespan.

Expected battery service life under normal conditions is 3–5 years.

## Introduction

The Vespa Primavera and Sprint (2013–present, all displacements) use a single-piston sliding caliper on the front wheel. Brake pads typically last 8,000–15,000 km depending on riding style and terrain. Squealing brakes and a spongy lever are the most common signs that pads need replacing. This guide covers front disc pads; the rear drum brake shoes on these models require a separate procedure.

<Callout type="warn">
  Never ride with worn pads past the minimum thickness (1 mm). Metal-on-rotor contact destroys the disc and leads to brake failure.
</Callout>

## Tools & Parts Needed

- 8 mm and 10 mm socket wrench set
- Flat-head screwdriver (for pad retaining pin extraction)
- Brake piston retraction tool or C-clamp with flat plate
- Brake cleaner spray
- Clean lint-free rags
- Replacement brake pads (OEM Piaggio or equivalent sintered pads for street use)
- Latex gloves

**Recommended OEM replacement pads**: Piaggio part number 647059 (front, single-disc models, 2013–present Primavera/Sprint). Confirm fitment with your VIN before ordering.

## Step-by-Step Procedure

### Step 1 — Safety Preparation

1. Place the scooter on its centre stand on level ground.
2. Allow the brake system to cool if the scooter was recently ridden.
3. Put on latex gloves — brake dust and old pad material are harmful if inhaled or absorbed through skin.

### Step 2 — Inspect Current Pad Thickness

1. Look through the inspection window on the caliper body (the gap between caliper and disc).
2. Each pad should have at least 1 mm of friction material remaining above the backing plate.
3. If either pad is at or below 1 mm, proceed with replacement.

<Callout type="tip">
  Even if one pad appears fine, always replace both pads as a matched pair to ensure even braking force.
</Callout>

### Step 3 — Remove the Caliper

1. Locate the two caliper slide-pin bolts on the rear face of the caliper (8 mm or 10 mm, depending on year).
2. Support the caliper with one hand and unscrew both bolts.
3. Slide the caliper off the disc — do not let it hang from the brake line. Secure it to the fork leg with a cable tie or rest it on a rag on the tyre.

<Callout type="warn">
  Never press the brake lever with the caliper removed. This will push the piston fully out and require bleeding the system to reset.
</Callout>

### Step 4 — Extract the Old Pads

1. The pads are held by a retaining pin or clip through the caliper body. Use a flat-head screwdriver to push out the retaining pin.
2. Slide both pads out of the caliper bracket.
3. Inspect the rotor surface — light grooves are normal; deep scoring (grooves you can feel with a fingernail) means the rotor needs replacing alongside the pads.

### Step 5 — Retract the Caliper Piston

New pads are thicker than worn pads. The caliper piston must be pushed back to make room.

1. Place the old pad (or a flat piece of metal) against the piston face to protect it.
2. Use a C-clamp or piston retraction tool to slowly compress the piston flush into the caliper body.
3. As the piston retracts, brake fluid is pushed back into the reservoir. Check the reservoir level — remove excess fluid with a syringe if it overflows.

<Callout type="tip">
  If the piston won't retract, the caliper slide pins may be corroded and binding. Clean and lubricate them with silicone grease before reinstallation.
</Callout>

### Step 6 — Clean the Caliper

1. Spray brake cleaner on the caliper bracket, pad channels, and slide pins.
2. Wipe clean with lint-free rags.
3. Apply a thin film of silicone-based brake caliper grease to the slide pin bores and the backs of the pad backing plates (not the friction material).
4. Never apply grease to the rotor or pad faces.

### Step 7 — Install New Pads

1. Insert the new pads into the caliper bracket. The inner pad (piston side) and outer pad are typically identical on single-piston designs.
2. Reinsert the retaining pin and ensure it is fully seated.
3. Slide the caliper back over the rotor, ensuring the pads are correctly seated on both sides of the disc.

### Step 8 — Reinstall Caliper Bolts

1. Thread both caliper slide-pin bolts in by hand first to avoid cross-threading.
2. Torque to specification:

| Fastener | Torque |
|----------|--------|
| Caliper slide-pin bolts | 25–28 Nm |

### Step 9 — Bed In the New Pads

New brake pads require a bedding-in process to transfer a thin, even layer of friction material onto the rotor.

1. Start with 5–6 moderate stops from 30 km/h, allowing the brakes to cool between each.
2. Progress to 5–6 firmer stops from 50 km/h.
3. Avoid aggressive stops for the first 100 km.

Squealing during the first 50 km is normal as the pad surface conditions. If squealing persists beyond 100 km, check pad-to-rotor contact and ensure the slide pins are moving freely.

---

## Specifications

| Parameter | Specification |
|-----------|--------------|
| Minimum pad thickness | 1 mm |
| Minimum rotor thickness (OEM disc) | 3.5 mm |
| Caliper slide-pin bolt torque | 25–28 Nm |
| Brake fluid type | DOT 4 (Primavera/Sprint) |
| Rotor diameter (Primavera 125/150) | 220 mm |

---

## Eliminating Brake Squeal

If brakes squeal after new pads are fitted and bedded in:

- Verify the caliper slide pins are clean and lubricated — seized pins prevent the pad from releasing cleanly.
- Apply anti-squeal compound (copper grease or specific brake shim compound) to the **back** of the pad backing plate only.
- Check that the rotor is clean and free of glazing — lightly scuff with 120-grit sandpaper if glazed.
- Ensure the caliper mounting bracket is torqued correctly and not loose.

import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; import SourceBox from '@components/SourceBox.astro'; Regular engine oil changes are the single most important maintenance task for any petrol scooter. The Vespa Primavera (2013–present) and Sprint (2014–present) share the same Piaggio 3-valve iGet engine family in 125 cc and 150 cc displacements. Both models use fuel injection and require an oil change every **3,000 km (approximately 1,900 miles)** or at least once a year — whichever comes first. This guide covers all current iGet-engine Primavera and Sprint variants: Primavera 125, Primavera 150, Sprint 125, Sprint 150, and their S, Sport, and Racing Sixties trim levels. The procedure is identical for all. ## What You Need
ItemSpecificationQuantity
Engine oilSAE 5W-40 full synthetic, JASO MA2 (or JASO MA), API SN or SL800 ml (125 cc) / 900 ml (150 cc)
Oil drain plug washer / copper gasketM12 × 1.25 sealing washer (Piaggio part: AP8121369)1 per service
Oil filler cap O-ringOptional — replace if hardened1
Drain panMinimum 1 litre capacity1
Socket or ring spanner17 mm (drain plug)1
Torque wrench0–25 Nm range1
Oil funnelSmall bore, approx. 10 mm spout1
Rags / absorbent matAnyAs needed
� **Oil choice:** Piaggio specifies **Agip/Eni Sint 2000 5W-40** as the factory fill. Any quality full-synthetic 5W-40 with JASO MA or MA2 approval is a suitable equivalent — the JASO motorcycle rating is important because it ensures the oil is compatible with wet-clutch transmissions found in automatic scooters. ## Difficulty & Time **Difficulty:** Beginner-friendly. No specialist tools required beyond a 17 mm spanner and a torque wrench. **Time:** 20–30 minutes including warm-up and clean-up. ## Step-by-Step Procedure ## Step 1 — Warm the Engine 1. Start the scooter and let it idle for 3–5 minutes. Warm oil flows freely and carries more contaminants out of the engine than cold oil does. 2. Shut the engine off and wait 2–3 minutes so the oil settles and cools slightly — you want warm, not scalding. ## Step 2 — Position and Prepare 1. Place the scooter on its centre stand on a level surface. 2. Place the drain pan below and slightly forward of the engine — the oil drain plug is on the underside-front of the engine casing, facing toward the front wheel. 3. Remove the front under-panel if fitted (two or three Phillips screws) to give clear access to the drain plug area. Some models allow access without removing any panels. ## Step 3 — Remove the Filler Cap 1. Open the seat and locate the oil filler cap on the top of the engine. It has a dipstick attached and is marked with an oil-can symbol. 2. Twist anti-clockwise and pull straight up to remove. Set aside on a clean surface. 3. Opening the filler cap first creates a small air vent that helps oil drain faster. ## Step 4 — Drain the Old Oil 1. Apply the 17 mm socket to the drain plug. Turn anti-clockwise (viewed from below) to loosen. Once loose, use your fingers to remove — support the plug so it does not drop into the drain pan. 2. Allow the engine to drain fully — typically 3–5 minutes. Tilt the scooter slightly toward the drain side if oil flow slows. 3. Inspect the old oil on a white cloth: black, gritty oil indicates normal combustion by-products; metallic flakes require further engine investigation before refilling. 4. Clean the drain plug threads with a rag. Discard the old copper sealing washer. ## Step 5 — Refit the Drain Plug 1. Fit a new copper sealing washer to the drain plug. 2. Thread the plug in by hand first to avoid cross-threading, then tighten with the torque wrench to **22 Nm (16 ft-lb)**. Do not overtighten — the crankcase is aluminium and strips easily. ## Step 6 — Fill with Fresh Oil 1. Insert the small funnel into the oil filler neck (accessible from under the open seat). 2. Pour in **800 ml for the 125 cc engine** or **900 ml for the 150 cc engine**. Do not use the full workshop capacity of 1,000 ml unless the engine has been fully stripped and the oil filter replaced — overfilling causes foaming and oil consumption through the breather. 3. Wait 1 minute for oil to settle, then check the level on the dipstick: oil should sit between the MIN and MAX marks, ideally just below MAX. 4. Refit the filler cap and tighten clockwise until snug. Do not use tools. ## Step 7 — Run and Check for Leaks 1. Start the engine and let it idle for 2–3 minutes. 2. The oil pressure warning light (if present) should extinguish within 3–5 seconds of starting. 3. Shut off and inspect the drain plug area for seepage. A correctly torqued plug with a new washer will be dry. 4. Recheck the dipstick level after shutdown — top up by 50–100 ml if below MIN. ## Disposal Used engine oil must not be poured down drains or disposed of in household waste. Decant it into the empty oil bottle and take it to a local recycling centre, garage, or auto parts shop — most accept used oil free of charge. ## Service Interval Summary
ModelEngine CodeOil Capacity (drain + refill)Interval
Primavera 125 (2013–)iGet 3V 125800 ml3,000 km / 1 year
Primavera 150 (2013–)iGet 3V 150900 ml3,000 km / 1 year
Sprint 125 (2014–)iGet 3V 125800 ml3,000 km / 1 year
Sprint 150 (2014–)iGet 3V 150900 ml3,000 km / 1 year
⚠️ **Reset the service counter:** After completing the oil change, use the Vespa MES (Maintenance & Efficiency System) light reset procedure: with the ignition on and the engine off, hold the SET button on the dash for 5 seconds until the spanner light extinguishes. Refer to the owner's manual for your specific dashboard variant.

import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; import SourceBox from '@components/SourceBox.astro'; Regular servicing is the single most effective way to keep a Vespa running reliably. Whether you ride a Vespa Primavera 125, a Vespa Sprint 150, a Piaggio Zip (50cc or 100cc 4-stroke), or an older geared model, the core service items remain consistent. This checklist covers everything a routine service should address, with notes on frequency and what to look for. � **Applies to:** Vespa Primavera 50/125/150, Vespa Sprint 125/150, Piaggio Zip 50 4T / 100 4T, Piaggio Fly, Liberty, and similar Piaggio-platform scooters. For GY6-engine models (BTC Riva, La Souris, Santini Capri), see the separate [GY6 maintenance schedule](gy6-4stroke-maintenance-schedule.html). ## Service Intervals
ItemInterval
Engine oil changeEvery 3,000 km or annually, whichever comes first
Transmission/gearbox oil changeEvery 6,000 km or every 2 years
Air filter service (clean or replace)Every 3,000 km; earlier in dusty conditions
Spark plug inspectionEvery 6,000 km; replace if worn
Drive belt inspectionEvery 6,000 km; replace by 12,000–15,000 km or if cracked
Variator rollers inspectionEvery 6,000 km; replace if worn flat
Brake pad inspectionEvery 3,000 km or when indicator reaches wear limit
Tyre pressure checkMonthly
Coolant change (liquid-cooled models)Every 2 years
Valve clearance check (4-stroke)Every 6,000 km
Full throttle body / carburettor cleanEvery 10,000–15,000 km or if idle/throttle response degrades
## Full Service Checklist ### Engine Lubrication - Drain and refill engine oil with the correct grade (see owner's manual — typically 5W-40 or 10W-40 semi/fully synthetic) - Check gearbox/transmission oil level; drain and refill at interval - Inspect oil filler cap and drain plug washers; replace if crushed or deformed - Check for oil leaks at gasket surfaces and drain plugs ### Air and Fuel System - Remove and inspect air filter element; clean or replace - Check fuel filter (inline type); replace if discoloured or blocked - On carburettor models: inspect float chamber for varnish deposits; clean pilot/idle jet with compressed air - On fuel-injected models: check for fault codes with a diagnostic tool; inspect fuel injector connector for corrosion - Inspect fuel hose and clips for cracks or leaks; replace rubber hose older than 5 years - On carburettor models: verify idle mixture screw is set correctly (typically 1.5–2.5 turns out from lightly seated) ### Ignition - Remove and inspect spark plug — check electrode condition, gap, and colour (light tan = correct mixture; black/sooty = rich; white = lean) - Reset spark plug gap to specification (typically 0.6–0.8 mm for Piaggio 4-stroke engines) - Replace spark plug at 6,000 km or if electrode is worn or damaged - Inspect HT lead and spark plug cap — no cracks, corrosion, or arcing marks ### Drive System (CVT) - Remove CVT cover and inspect drive belt for cracks, fraying, or glazing; measure width against wear limit - Inspect variator rollers for flat spots or uneven wear; replace as a set if worn - Check centrifugal clutch shoes for wear; measure thickness against service limit - Inspect clutch bell for scoring; light scoring is normal, deep grooves indicate clutch shoe failure - Clean CVT housing of rubber belt dust with compressed air - Lubricate variator slider guide faces with a small amount of grease (do not get grease on belt or clutch) ### Brakes - Inspect front and rear brake pad thickness; replace if below 2 mm - On disc brakes: check disc for warping and minimum thickness (typically 3.5 mm for Vespa Primavera/Sprint front disc) - On drum brakes: check cable adjustment and shoe wear - Inspect brake fluid level and colour (disc brake models); replace fluid every 2 years regardless of mileage - Test front and rear brake lever feel — firm with no sponginess ### Tyres and Wheels - Check tyre tread depth — legal minimum is 1 mm but replace before reaching this - Inspect tyre sidewalls for cracks, bulges, or cuts - Set tyre pressure (Vespa Primavera 125/150: typically 1.8 bar front, 2.0 bar rear — verify with your model's sticker or manual) - Check wheel rim for cracks or significant dents - Check wheel bearing play by rocking each wheel side-to-side ### Electrical System - Test battery voltage (should be 12.4–12.7 V static, 13.5–14.5 V with engine running at 3,000 rpm) - Check all lights: headlight (high and low beam), tail light, brake light, indicators, instrument backlight - Inspect wiring loom for chafe marks or loose connectors, particularly around the steering head and under the seat - Clean and grease battery terminals ### Controls and Cables - Check throttle cable for fraying or kinking; lubricate cable inner with cable oil - Verify throttle returns freely and snaps shut immediately on release (critical safety check) - Lubricate brake cables if non-hydraulic - Check choke cable / enrichment circuit operation (carburettor models) - Inspect handlebar grips — secure, no rotation ### Chassis, Suspension, and Bodywork - Check front fork for smooth travel and absence of oil leaks from stanchion seals - Check rear shock absorber for oil leaks and bounce test for damping (should settle after one cycle) - Inspect all visible nuts and bolts for security, especially engine mounts and wheel axle nuts - Lubricate centre stand and side stand pivots with light oil - Inspect bodywork fasteners — missing or broken plastic clips allow panels to vibrate and crack ## After the Service After completing all items, start the engine cold and allow it to warm up. Check idle speed (typically 1,500–1,800 rpm for Piaggio 4-stroke engines). Test ride and verify braking, acceleration, and throttle response. Record the service in your maintenance log with the date and odometer reading. � **Keep old parts:** When replacing components such as spark plugs, brake pads, or variator rollers, retain the old parts for inspection. The condition of worn parts is a useful diagnostic indicator — e.g., uneven brake pad wear suggests a sticking caliper piston.

import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; import SourceBox from '@components/SourceBox.astro'; A properly maintained CVT (Continuously Variable Transmission) is essential for smooth power delivery and consistent performance on all GY6 and Piaggio 4-stroke scooters. The CVT converts engine speed to wheel speed through a pair of pulleys connected by a drive belt — the front (drive) variator opens and closes based on centrifugal force from roller weights, while the rear clutch/driven pulley responds to belt tension. This video guides you through a complete CVT service inspection. ## Main Video: CVT Full Service Inspection **What this video covers:** - Removing the CVT cover and identifying all components - Inspecting and removing the front variator and roller weights - Checking drive belt width, cracking, and wear limit - Inspecting the rear driven pulley and clutch assembly - Measuring roller weight dimensions and selecting correct replacements - Full reassembly with correct torque sequence ## When to Service the CVT
ComponentInspection IntervalReplace When
Roller weightsEvery 5,000 kmFlat spots, weight loss, or more than 0.5 mm worn from original diameter
Drive beltEvery 10,000–12,000 kmWidth below wear limit, visible cracks, fraying, or glazing
Clutch pads/liningsEvery 10,000 kmLining thickness below 2 mm, uneven wear, or glazing
Clutch springsWith clutch lining replacementRattling clutch engagement, engagement at very low rpm, sagging springs
Driven pulley springEvery 20,000 kmWeak or sluggish top-speed recovery, premature downshift
## Key Service Points ### Roller Weights Roller weights are the small cylindrical or barrel-shaped weights (typically 6 per variator on GY6 engines, 6 per variator on Piaggio) that determine how and when the variator opens. As the engine speeds up, centrifugal force pushes the rollers outward against the variator ramp, pushing the front pulley halves apart and forcing the belt to ride higher (increasing the effective ratio for more speed). **Common signs of worn rollers:** - Jerky or stuttering acceleration, particularly from a standstill - Engine revs high but speed does not increase proportionally - Vibration through the floorboard at a specific speed - Flat spots on rollers visible on inspection **Roller weights for common GY6 engines:**
EngineStandard Roller WeightStandard Diameter
GY6 139QMB (50cc)6 g (some variants 7 g)15×12 mm
GY6 157QMJ (125/150cc)11 g (some variants 10 g or 12 g)18×14 mm or 20×12 mm
Piaggio Zip 50 4T / Zip 1005.5 g–7 g depending on variant15×12 mm
Always replace all rollers as a set — mixing old and new rollers causes uneven loading and accelerated wear of the variator ramp faces. ### Drive Belt The GY6 drive belt is a reinforced rubber V-belt that runs between the front variator and the rear driven pulley. It wears by getting narrower — as the belt wears, it rides lower in the pulleys, effectively changing the transmission ratio and reducing top speed. **Belt width is the critical measurement.** A worn belt that still looks intact externally may already be below the minimum width specification. Always measure belt width with a calliper, not just by eye. Standard GY6 157QMJ belt width is typically 17.0 mm new; replace when below 15.5 mm. For 139QMB (50cc): 17.0 mm new, replace below 15.5 mm. Check your service manual for the exact figures. **Cheap belts fail fast.** Use OEM-specification or well-known aftermarket brands (NCY, Malossi, Gates, Polini). A low-quality belt can snap without warning within a few hundred kilometres on a stock engine — leaving you stranded with a locked-up transmission. ### Clutch Assembly (Rear Pulley) The rear driven pulley assembly combines the driven pulley halves, the torque spring, and the centrifugal clutch bell. At idle, the clutch pads are retracted inside the bell — the engine can rev without moving the scooter. As engine rpm rises, centrifugal force expands the pads against the clutch bell, engaging drive to the rear wheel. Replace clutch pads when: - Lining material is thinner than **2 mm** - Lining is glazed (shiny, hard surface) — caused by slipping at low rpm; light sanding may temporarily restore grip, but replacement is recommended - Pads show uneven wear (one side more worn than the other) — indicates a bent or worn clutch spider Replace clutch springs at the same time as pads to ensure consistent engagement behaviour. ## Related Video: Clutch and Variator Change This second video demonstrates the complete replacement procedure for both the front variator and rear clutch assembly — useful if the service inspection above reveals components that need full replacement rather than just cleaning. ## Related Guides - [GY6 CVT Variator & Drive Belt Replacement Guide](/repair-guides/gy6-cvt-variator-belt-replacement.html) - [CVT Variator and Roller Inspection Guide](/repair-guides/scooter-cvt-clutch-variator-guide.html) - [Metallic Noise from Engine — CVT Roller Diagnosis](/diagnostics/gy6-cvt-roller-noise-diagnosis.html)

import VideoEmbed from '@components/VideoEmbed.astro'; import Callout from '@components/Callout.astro'; import SourceBox from '@components/SourceBox.astro'; Added: 2026-05-12 | Source: [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xoPVQCs919w) | Vespa Piaggio Carburettor Maintenance 🎬 Basic Carb Adjustments for Carbureted Vespa Scooters [↗ Watch on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xoPVQCs919w) ## Video Summary This tutorial covers the essential carburettor adjustments that every owner of a carbureted modern Vespa (and by extension, Piaggio-platform scooters) should be able to perform themselves. The video is particularly relevant to Vespa models with the Dell'Orto PHBN or Dellorto SI carburettor, including the **Vespa ET2 50**, **Vespa LX 50**, **Vespa S 50**, **Piaggio Zip 50**, **Piaggio Liberty 50**, and similar 50–125cc 4-stroke Piaggio-group scooters using the Piaggio Leader or Zip engine family. The techniques shown also apply broadly to any GY6-type or small 4-stroke scooter carburetor with the same idle speed screw and mixture screw configuration. ## Key Points Covered ### 1\. Prerequisites Before Adjusting Carburetor adjustment should only be attempted when the following are confirmed to be correct: - Ignition timing is correct (spark plug gap in spec) - Air filter is clean and properly seated - No air leaks at the intake manifold or carb-to-airbox junction - Throttle cable has correct free play (1–2 mm at the twist grip) - Engine is at full operating temperature before any idle adjustment ### 2\. Idle Speed Screw (Throttle Stop) The idle speed screw contacts the throttle slide and sets the minimum throttle opening. It is usually located on the right or bottom of the carburettor body with a slotted flat head. Turning it clockwise raises idle RPM; anti-clockwise lowers it. Target idle speed for most 50cc 4T Vespa/Piaggio models is **1,800–2,000 RPM** measured with a tachometer or judged by sound on a warm engine. ### 3\. Air/Fuel Mixture Screw The mixture (or pilot/fuel) screw regulates the air-fuel ratio at idle and light throttle openings. It is typically located on the engine-side of the carburettor float chamber, pointing down or at an angle. Many carburetors have this screw covered by a tamper-proof cap. Factory baseline setting is 1.5–2 turns out from lightly seated (clockwise to seat — do not overtighten). - **Too lean (too far in):** Engine surges, stalls when decelerating, runs rough at idle. - **Too rich (too far out):** Black sooty exhaust at idle, fuel smell, poor fuel economy. - To find the optimum: with the engine warm and idling, slowly turn the mixture screw out in ¼-turn increments. Stop at the position where idle RPM is highest. Then reduce idle speed back to target with the idle speed screw. ### 4\. Throttle Cable Play Before adjusting any mixture settings, ensure the throttle cable has the correct free play. With the handlebars turned to full lock in each direction, the idle RPM must not rise — if it does, there is insufficient cable slack and the carb slide is being lifted by the cable under steering input. Adjust the cable adjuster at the carburettor or handlebar grip. � **When to clean vs adjust:** If your Vespa idles poorly and adjusting the mixture screw makes no perceptible difference, the idle jet (pilot jet) is likely blocked with fuel varnish. Remove and soak the jet in carburettor cleaner before attempting further adjustment. See the separate [Carburetor Deep-Cleaning Guide](/repair-guides/gy6-carburetor-cleaning-guide.html) for the full procedure. ## Related Videos A companion video on cleaning or replacing the idle jet specifically on Vespa carbureted models: 🎬 Cleaning or Replacing the Idle Jet on a Carbureted Vespa Scooter Essential when carburettor adjustment alone cannot cure rough idle. ## Applicable Models

Vespa S 50 4T (2007–2014)Dell'Orto PHBN 12 HSSame engine as LX 50 4T
Piaggio Zip 50 4T (2001–2017)Dell'Orto PHBN 12 HSSee Zip 50 4T Overview page

Unlike basic belt replacement videos, this covers full disassembly of the driven pulley unit — including contra spring removal and replacement — along with clutch shoe inspection, measurement, and replacement. The video emphasises the use of the correct special tools and explains the consequences of improper assembly. ️ **Advanced procedure:** The contra spring in the driven pulley assembly is under significant preload. Compressing and releasing it without the correct spring compressor tool is dangerous. Do not attempt this procedure without the appropriate Piaggio special tool or an aftermarket equivalent. ## Models This Procedure Applies To The driven pulley and clutch configuration described in this video is common across a broad range of Piaggio/Vespa models. Exact part numbers and spring specifications vary by model, but the procedure is structurally the same for all models listed above. ## Key Topics Covered in the Video - Identifying wear symptoms that require driven pulley disassembly (vs simple belt replacement) - Required special tools: driven pulley nut socket, spring compressor, and holding tool - Step-by-step driven pulley disassembly sequence - Inspecting and measuring clutch shoes — minimum thickness measurements and wear pattern analysis - Contra spring inspection — correct free length, coil damage identification - Reassembly with correct spring preload orientation - Torque sequence and final checks ## Diagnosing Driven Pulley and Clutch Problems
SymptomLikely Cause
High clutch engagement RPM (engine revs high before moving)Worn clutch springs — insufficient centrifugal force at normal RPM
Harsh engagement / jerk from standstillStiff clutch springs or glazed clutch shoes
Scooter creeps forward at idle with brake offClutch shoes dragging — contaminated shoes or springs too soft
Poor acceleration, belt slippingWorn or glazed clutch shoes, insufficient clamping force
Vibration during accelerationUneven clutch shoe wear or contra spring preload imbalance
## Contra Spring Identification Piaggio contra springs are usually colour-coded or have identifying marks. The contra spring rate directly affects how aggressively the driven pulley closes (which governs how quickly the belt shifts to the high-ratio position). A stiffer spring improves low-end pull; a softer spring allows quicker upshifts. Stock springs are appropriate for standard riding — only consider alternatives if you have modified the engine output. ## Clutch Shoe Replacement Notes Clutch shoes on Vespa and Piaggio scooters are measured as a set — replace all shoes together, never individually. When fitting new shoes, avoid touching the friction surface with bare hands (skin oils cause glazing). Bed in new clutch shoes gently over the first 50–100 km by avoiding aggressive acceleration from standstill until the shoes have seated. ## Special Tools Required - Piaggio driven pulley nut socket (model-specific — check the official workshop manual for your model's socket size) - Contra spring compressor (Piaggio tool reference varies; universal scooter spring compressors are widely available) - Torque wrench (40–60 Nm range) - Clutch holding tool - Vernier caliper (for shoe thickness measurement)

This video covers the complete belt and transmission reassembly procedure for the Vespa Primavera 125/150 and Vespa Sprint 125/150 — the modern i-Get 3-valve engine family produced by Piaggio from 2013 onwards. The procedure applies to both carburettor variants (early market models) and the standard fuel-injected production models.

## Key Topics Covered in the Video

-   Removing the transmission side cover (right side engine cover)
-   Drive belt removal and inspection — what wear patterns indicate imminent failure
-   Driven pulley (rear variator) disassembly and contra spring inspection
-   Belt routing sequence during reassembly — correct wrap direction and tension check
-   Drive pulley (front variator) roller inspection — how to check for flat spots
-   Torque specifications for the driven pulley nut and cover bolts
-   Final alignment check before closing the cover

## When to Replace the Drive Belt

Piaggio recommends replacing the drive belt on the Primavera and Sprint every 20,000 km or 2 years, whichever comes first. Replace earlier if any of the following are present:

-   Visible cracking along the belt's inner face or across the top ribs
-   Belt width worn below the minimum (check current width against the specification in the service manual)
-   Glazed or shiny surface on the sides of the belt (indicates slippage history)
-   Any fraying at the belt edges
-   Vibration or jerking during acceleration — often the first symptom of a worn belt

## Key Torque Specifications

-   Driven pulley centre nut: **50–55 Nm** (Loctite threadlock recommended on reassembly)
-   Drive pulley (variator) nut: **45–50 Nm**
-   Transmission cover bolts: **10 Nm**

## Tools Required

-   Piaggio variator holding tool (or universal equivalent)
-   Torque wrench (0–100 Nm range)
-   Socket set (metric)
-   Rubber mallet
-   Contra spring compressor (for driven pulley disassembly)
-   Soft-jawed vice (for contra spring work)

## Genuine vs Aftermarket Belts

Piaggio OEM belts (part reference varies by market, check the parts catalogue for your VIN) are recommended for the Primavera and Sprint. Budget aftermarket belts vary widely in quality — if using an aftermarket part, choose brands such as Dayco, Gates, or Bando, which supply to OEM motorcycle manufacturers. Avoid no-brand belts for these Piaggio models as belt failure at speed can cause sudden loss of drive.
